News.title: Outrage as historic footie tradition where whole town come out to fight faces being wiped out for 250-home ‘mega-estate’
News.content:
A HISTORIC football tradition faces being wiped out to make way for a huge mega-estate, sparking outrage across the region.

For 350 years, residents of Ashbourne have played a massive annual football match spanning streets, rivers and fields – but plans to take over a huge chunk of farmland may spell the end of the derby.



Furious footy fans and locals are fighting to stop 35 acres – equivalent to 20 football pitches – from being developed into 250 new homes.

Steve Jones, secretary of the Ashbourne Royal Shrovetide Football Committee, has written to the council to oppose the build, saying it could cause “significant harm to Ashbourne’s most important culture and economic assets”.



The Up’Ards – born north of Henmore Brook – have traditionally played the Down’Ards – born south of the river – every Shrove Tuesday and Ash Wednesday since 1667 – though the game reportedly has its roots even earlier in the 12th century.

Known as “Royal Shrovetide Football”, the two-day game starts each day at 2pm and continues on until 10pm.

There is no fixed boundary and the goalposts are three miles apart at opposite ends of the town in Sturston Mill and Clifton Mill.

The plans for a housing development are close to the Sturston Mill goal – which Steve points out would “obstruct a large proportion of the gameplay area”.

He described the plumbing plans for the site as involving “a deep, steep-sided and muddy pit” which would cause injury and “impede the game”.

In his view the planned mega-estate would “fundamentally undermine the continued operation of the game in its historic form” and will plummet the game’s success and attraction to tourists.



“Consequently, the proposed development would not only provide significant harm to this unique cultural asset within Ashbourne, but it would also cause direct economic damage to the town through knock-on effects to the local economy and local tourism”, he said.

The famed match uses a specialty ball stuffed with corks to make it float in rivers, according to Ashbourne town council.

“Stout shoes are recommended if one decides to kick it in play”, they advised.



More than 670 people have signed a petition against the housing plans, warning that the scheme poses an “irreversible threat” to Ashbourne’s culture.

Petition organiser Brett O’Connell claimed the proposed mega-estate “cuts straight across where the Royal Shrovetide game goes”.

He told the BBC: “We feel it would become an issue and the developers are aware of this by keeping a portion as open space. But the game doesn’t stick to planned routes so I think there’ll be quite a few people if they move in, they’ll be quite shocked about what happens on the day.”

The developer, Hallam Land Management, has defended the plans and said that the development would “deliver a sensitively designed residential addition to Ashbourne”.

They added: “The various constraints and opportunities of the site have been carefully considered.”



Derbyshire Dales district council is currently considering the proposals.

The event draws thousands of players and spectators each year – King Charles has even starred as the “turner up” – the revered local chosen to start the match by throwing the ball in the air.

Wild photos show players dangling down into rivers in a match which notoriously has very few rules.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

Churchyards, cemetaries and places of worship are out of bounds however and more recently a ban on motorised vehicles was put in place to stop players from zooming the ball to the goal posts.

In this year’s match, the Up’ards won 3-0.

News.title: Trump says he’s ‘happy’ that Sussexes returned to UK and blasts Meghan for being ‘disrespectful’ to late Queen
News.content:
'NOT A FAN' Trump says he’s ‘happy’ that Sussexes returned to UK and blasts Meghan for being ‘disrespectful’ to late Queen

DONALD TRUMP has revealed he is “happy” Prince Harry and Meghan have left the US for the UK.

The President said he was “not a fan” of the pair and accused Meghan of being “terribly disrespectful” to the Queen.

He said: “I’m happy about it. I was not a fan. I didn’t like the way she acted.”

Trump added: “I thought she was terribly disrespectful to the queen. I would not have taken them back.”





It comes weeks after The Sun revealed in a World Exclusive the couple will make a shock return to the UK for “an extended period”, with kids Archie, 7, and Lilibet, 5, enrolling at school here.

Prince Harry and Meghan Markle landed at Birmingham Airport last week after six years living in California.

They are thought to have settled in the Cotswolds.

The Sussexes, who had a reunion with King Charles last month, have already found a new home in the UK.



Their relocation raises questions over the future of the 2020 Sandringham Agreement — dubbed “Megxit”.

News.title: Four arrested 32 years after gran, 64, ‘stabbed to death with a fork in burglary gone wrong’ before bungalow set on fire
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

COLD CASE RIDDLE Four arrested 32 years after gran, 64, ‘stabbed to death with a fork in burglary gone wrong’ before bungalow set on fire

COPS have arrested four people 32 years after a gran was allegedly stabbed to death with a fork before her bungalow was set on fire.

Doreen Morris, 64, was found dead inside her burned-out bungalow on the outskirts of Holyhead, Anglesey, back in March 1994.



Now, North Wales Police has confirmed four people have been arrested following a review of the 32-year-old murder investigation.

The suspects, a man and three women, are all from North Wales.



The force said that Doreen’s family have been informed of the latest developments.

Mark Pierce, Senior Review Officer, said: “Forensic results, combined with a detailed review of witness evidence, have provided grounds to interview four people on suspicion of perverting the course of justice as part of the ongoing review of the case.



“Throughout the review our thoughts have been with Mrs. Morris’ family, and I hope that this case shows that it doesn’t matter how much time has passed we will always seek out new opportunities to get justice for victims and their families.”

In the 32 years since the discovery of Dorren’s body, her killer has never been found.



Dorren’s death was initially linked to a suspected burglary at her home.

Joseph Carl Westbury was found not guilty of her murder in 1995.

He also denied breaking into the 64-year-old’s property on Mill Lane.

Westbury took his own life in May 2016.

A coroner later concluded that Doreen had been unlawfully killed.



In 2023, an inquest heard she had died from a stab wound to the neck.

The object believed to have been used was a fork.

North West Wales Senior Coroner Katie Sutherland said: “The evidence is indicative of murder.

“I am satisfied that the appropriate conclusion of the inquest into the death of Doreen Morris is unlawful killing.”

Cops have urged anyone with any information about the case to come forward.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

Information can be passed to North Wales Police on 101 or anonymously through Crimestoppers.

Anyone contacting police should quote Operation Epose.

News.title: Shocking moment mountain guide attacks climber on tiny ledge at 10,000ft after confronting him for barging past wife
News.content:
THIS is the shocking moment a mountain guide attacks a climber on a 10,000ft high tiny ledge.

The man had confronted the guide for barging past his wife as she navigated a precarious position up an Austrian mountain.



The two Polish climbers can be seen making their way down the mountain, with the man letting his wife down the mountain first.

She lowers herself down a rope when an Austrian guide forces himself between the couple and barges past.



The Polish climber said he had deliberately left extra space for his wife when the guide suddenly moved into the gap.

He can be heard telling the Austrian guide: “I should go first, shouldn’t I?”

But the guide replies: “No, no, no,”

He squeezes past the man’s wife on a narrow ledge, and encourages his group to do the same.



The climber confronts the guide, shouting: “Hey, are you out of your mind or what?”

He responds: “I’m a mountain guide, shut up!”

The argument escalates, with the Polish climber putting his middle finger up at the guide and calling him a “f***ing idiot”.



The Austrian guide then threatens: “Shut up, or I’ll come up and punch you.”

He can be seen charging back up the mountain, barging past the man’s wife again as he does so.

The guide grabs the climbers hands and gets in his face, yelling “Behave yourself”.

The confrontation took place on August 22 as both groups descended an exposed section of the Mürztalersteig route on Grossglockner.

The Polish climber shared the footage online, calling the guide “aggressive and confrontational”.



He said overtaking on the mountain was routine, but said this guide had endangered everyone around him.

He wrote that a professional guide should show “basic courtesy, good judgement and, above all, responsibility”, adding: “The mountains are for everyone, regardless of their experience, skills or pace.

“Mutual respect and consideration should always come first.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Police launched an investigation into allegations of endangering public safety, local papers reported.

The Kals Mountain Guides Association cut ties with the guide, describing his behaviour as “unacceptable.”

News.title: Travellers bulldozed our beauty spot FOUR months ago and the council has done nothing… now we’re fighting back
News.content:
FUMING residents are fighting back after travellers bulldozed their beauty spot four months ago and the idle council has still failed to take decisive action.

Locals will stage a protest tomorrow, demanding “enough is enough” over what they say is a continuing breach of planning rules at Willows Green, near Felsted, Essex.



The row began on the Early May Bank Holiday when around 30 lorries descended on the four-acre field just hours after the council offices closed.

Bulldozers ripped through the land and workers laid hardstanding as the site was rapidly transformed.



The field is home to protected great-crested newts and rare albino fallow deer.

Residents say the work continued through the Bank Holiday weekend, with caravans and mobile homes arriving on the site.



They claim the development has continued despite a High Court injunction obtained in May and made permanent in June.

Now the Willows Green Action Group says locals have been left watching the unauthorised development become increasingly established for four months.



A spokesperson said: “For four months, residents have watched an unauthorised development become increasingly established while the council has failed to take the decisive action its own legal orders appeared to make possible.

“The lack of action, lack of accountability and lack of effective enforcement is embarrassing for Uttlesford District Council.

“Residents have gathered evidence, reported suspected breaches and repeatedly asked for intervention, but the community is still waiting for a meaningful resolution.

“This protest is about saying that enough is enough. Planning rules must apply equally to everyone, and court orders must mean something.

“We are asking the council to explain publicly what it has done, what it has failed to do and exactly when effective enforcement action will now take place.”



Uttlesford District Council served a Temporary Stop Notice on May 5, which came into effect the following morning.

It then obtained an interim High Court injunction on May 7 prohibiting further development and residential occupation of the land.

The order was subsequently made permanent in June.



But residents claim work and residential use have continued despite the legal action.

Their anger has now grown further after a retrospective planning application was lodged seeking permission for 12 Gypsy and Traveller pitches.

The application was validated by Uttlesford District Council on August 26.

It covers mobile homes, touring caravans, day rooms, access roads, utility infrastructure and landscaping.

The group will protest outside Uttlesford District Council’s offices on September 3, ahead of a meeting of its Scrutiny Committee.



Residents say their frustration has been heightened by what they describe as a faster response to an unauthorised development at Sheering Mill Lane in Sawbridgeworth, Herts.

The group said: “Nobody is suggesting that every enforcement case is identical, but residents cannot ignore the stark difference in urgency.

“East Herts acted over a Bank Holiday weekend, returned to court when its first order was not respected and worked with the police to secure a swift outcome.

“At Willows Green, residents have been living with an apparently continuing unauthorised development since the first May Bank Holiday.

“Uttlesford residents deserve the same determination, urgency and visible leadership. We need action, not more explanations for delay.”



It comes as Hertfordshire’s Police and Crime Commissioner called for emergency powers to tackle serious unauthorised developments.

Local resident Tracy Williams previously said: “We feel we’ve been let down by the people who should be helping and supporting us.

“We pay our council taxes and we submit our planning in the right way. Doing nothing is not helpful – we should be proactive not reactive.”

Jonathan Ash-Edwards said: “If someone knowingly waits for a Bank Holiday, arrives with heavy machinery and carries out rapid, substantial works specifically to get ahead of enforcement, I believe that should become a criminal offence.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“The principle is straightforward, nobody should be able to game the planning system by ripping up our countryside first and asking for permission later.”



Uttlesford District Council was contacted for comment.

News.title: Reform UK MP Lee Anderson backs referendum on death penalty – despite pushback from Nigel Farage
News.content:
BRITAIN should have a referendum on reinstating the death penalty, Reform’s Lee Anderson has said.

The party chairman told The Sun that voters would overwhelmingly support bringing back capital punishment – but admits he has not convinced his leader Nigel Farage on the idea.



He said: “Referendums are very divisive. We learnt that with the Brexit referendum, it divides the country and gets families falling out with each other. So yes I would, but it would be divisive, very divisive.”

Mr Farage has consistently argued against the death penalty, warning that innocent people could slip through the net and pay the ultimate price.



Mr Anderson said: “We differ. People say, ‘Oh, Nigel doesn’t agree with the death penalty and you’re divided,’ what a load of b****s that is!

He adds: “This is how out of touch I think Parliament is. I think the public would vote for the death penalty. Parliament would never vote for the death penalty.”



Capital punishment was suspended in 1965 and officially abolished four years later.

More Britons support reintroducing capital punishment than oppose it, according to YouGov polling.

Data published last year found that 50 per cent of the public support it while 45 per cent are against it.

Mr Anderson aired his support for the death penalty in 2015 after claiming nobody had “ever committed a crime after being executed.”



The MP for Ashfield has suggested it should be used for murders where the case is clear cut.

He has regularly cited the murder of Fusilier Lee Rigby by an Islamist extremists Michael Adebolajo and Michael Adebowale.

Adebolajo was given a whole life term meaning he will die in prison.

The last people executed in Britain were Peter Allen and Gwynne Evans on 13 August 1964.

Britain would be prevented from re-introducing the death penalty as it is a signatory of the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR).

News.title: Reform MP rages at BBC, Royals and benefits… and reveals plans for his future
News.content:
HE is the so-called hardman of British politics who rails against snowflakes and all things woke.

But Lee Anderson is suddenly deeply pensive – and dare I suggest slightly emotional – as he looks to a life after politics.



“Life’s ebbing away, young man,” he tells me. “It’s slipping away so I’m going to try something else.”

He tells me the next election will be his last. Travelling the world, and perhaps returning to be a local councillor, are his future calling.



“I want to do one more term after this, which will take me up to my late 60s,” he says. “And then I want to do something else.”

Yet there is much to do before Anderson can sail off into the sunset.

Top of his intray is helping his pal Nigel Farage achieve his “destiny” of becoming Prime Minister.

After a bumpy few months, Reform will seek to dust itself down this week at their annual conference in Birmingham.

It has not been easy of late as questions over Farage’s own future swirl amid his financial affairs.

But Anderson is adamant it is his “destiny” to take the party to glory and defeat Labour at the ballot box.



“He’s the one who excites the public, whether you love him or loathe him,” the 59-year-old tells me.

He adds: “I think it’s his destiny. I’ve told him this, it’s his destiny. He’s our next Churchill, it has to be him.”

He points to Farage’s knack of working a room packed with donors, veterans, business owners, pensioners and ordinary punters.

“No other politician could do that,” he says.



As we sit on a park bench in his Ashfield constituency – what he dubs the “capital of common sense” – he tells me one of his proudest achievements was becoming the first MP born and bred here.

So proud, in fact, that if he were stranded on a desert island the one thing he would take is his parliamentary pass.

A reminder of how far he has come.

Anderson, a former coal miner, points to a memorial celebrating the area’s rich heritage of the coal industry before we start the interview.



But could the thousands of youngsters today facing a life on the dole really benefit from following him down the pits.

“Yes, 100 per cent.

“Because it’s not just about going to work and earning a wage and contributing. Going to work is good for you.

He adds: “The biggest talking point for us when I worked down the pit [on] a Monday morning was football. How did your team do?



“Sometimes men would actually, literally, just not come to work on a Monday morning if their team had lost… because of the bragging rights.

“It’s all that sort of stuff. Again, might seem like little things in life, but they’re huge.”

The Reform party conference will begin this Thursday.

Despite a few setbacks in the polls, Reform’s party chair remains bullish and promises it to be the most well-attended party conference yet.

He says the three-day jamboree will be about firing up the party faithful and plotting Reform’s path to power.



“We’re on a mission to get our country back, and everybody can play an important part in that,” he says.

Security will be tight, with the party ramping up protection at events and for its top brass.

The tragic death of their beloved colleague Ann Widdecombe will cast an inevitable shadow over the event both in tributes paid but also more precautions.

But it is not just Reform figures facing questions over their safety.

The row over who should get taxpayer-funded protection has also put Harry and Meghan’s security back in the spotlight.



Does he believe taxpayers should be forking out millions to protect the couple now they are back in Blighty?

“Is he at risk? Yes, he is at risk.

“Probably at more risk from her than he is from anybody else. I think she’s been a bad influence on him personally.

“That’s not the party line. That’s my line. I’m suspicious.

“I’m suspicious of why they’ve written these books, made these Netflix series slagging off the Royal Family, and then want to come back.



“I’m really suspicious.”

Next in the firing line is the BBC which he tells me he “begrudgingly” puts himself up for interview on.

He confirms that one thing the internal policy team are looking and speaking about is potentially making the Beeb a subscription service.

“I think the BBC have got a bit of a cheek. They’re not the cuddly Auntie Beeb anymore. They’re the anti-Britain channel.

He adds: “I think [the licence fee] needs to be scrapped.”



The death penalty is another controversial issue Anderson has supported since becoming an MP.

But he has disagreed with Mr Farage over the issue, after the Reform leader said the number of miscarriages of justice meant he could “never support it”.

Has Mr Anderson managed to change his leader’s mind on this issue?

“No, he doesn’t believe in it.

“We differ. People say, ‘Oh, Nigel doesn’t agree with the death penalty and you’re divided,’ what a load of b****s that is!



He adds: “This is how out of touch I think Parliament is. I think the public would vote for the death penalty. Parliament would never vote for the death penalty.”

Would he back a referendum on it?

“Referendums are very divisive.

“We learnt that with the Brexit referendum, it divides the country and gets families falling out with each other.

“So yes I would, but it would be divisive, very divisive.”



One issue which puts off Reform floating voters is its alleged lukewarm support for Ukraine.

The party came under the firing line after Nigel Farage claimed the West had “provoked”

Vladimir Putin’s invasion by expanding NATO and the European Union eastwards.

His comments triggered a furious backlash from the Tories and Labour, who accused the Reform leader of echoing the Kremlin’s justification for the war.

Anderson, whose partner is Ukrainian, says the party backs the war-torn country but funding should come with more strings attached.



“I think we should support Ukraine.

“But I’m very dubious where the money goes, it’s a corrupt country”

He adds: “I’m just very, very mindful of where the money goes.

“Zelensky, he’s always coming cap in hand. Don’t blame him. He’s the leader of a country. He’s got to do that.

“It’s awful what the Ukrainian people have been through. Dreadful.”



Much like Reform, Anderson is never without a bit of controversy. But his final admission almost floors me.

I ask if he’s ever done anything woke, and he confesses to once having had “vegetarian thoughts”, before his love of bacon sarnies made him see sense.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Many voters find Reform less than appealing, but it is Anderson’s firm belief the party is needed to save the country’s bacon.

News.title: Tragedy as toddler, 1, drowns days before his birthday after ‘falling headfirst into a bucket of water’ at family home
News.content:
TODDLER HEARTBREAK Tragedy as toddler, 1, drowns days before his birthday after ‘falling headfirst into a bucket of water’ at family home

A TODDLER has drowned just days before his second birthday after falling headfirst into a bucket of water.

Thalison Israel Figueredo Lopes, aged one year and 11 months, was found lifeless at his family home in the historic town of Acari in northeastern Brazil.



He was discovered by his mother – who took his body to a basic health centre in Petrópolis at around 9am on Monday.

She told medics that she had found her son submerged inside a bucket of water.



The bucket was able to carry around 20 litres, according to police, though this has not been verified by forensics.

Health workers frantically tried to resuscitate the tiny boy – and called in the town’s emergency department to help.



Tragically, one-year-old Thalison could not be saved.

The youngster would have celebrated his second birthday on Friday, September 4.

Police have launched a probe into his death and sealed off the family home for forensic investigations.

The child’s body has also been sent for post-mortem examinations to establish the official cause of death.



It follows the heartbreaking tragedy of a British toddler found floating in a hotel pool while the family were on holiday.

The one-year-old was pulled from the pool in the Canary Islands at around 10am before being airlifted to hospital.

For several days the youngster was fighting for her life – before tragically passing away surrounded by family.



Spain was forced to issue an urgent warning to tourists after six children drowned within 72hrs over a weekend in June at the popular holiday destination.

One expert blamed a “tragic lack of supervision” and warned holidaymakers to keep an eye on their kids at beaches and in pools.

Several heatwaves across Europe have also seen a surge in hot-car deaths.

One toddler died after being “forgotten” inside a nursery minibus for multiple hours.

The 18-moth-girl was discovered in “critical condition” in the Peugeot in Portugal – as temperatures outside soared to 30C.

In France, two young children were found dead in their family car amid a 40C heatwave.

The children – aged two and four – climbed into the car without their mother knowing, according to prosecutors.

News.title: Burnham pressed on economy at first PMQs as UK borrowing costs rise
News.content:
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has pressed Andy Burnham over UK borrowing and spending at his first Prime Minister's Questions.

Badenoch called on the PM to say where spending would be cut and how he would deal with the UK's increasing debt, after the cost of borrowing for the UK rose, reaching a new 18-year high on Wednesday.

The PM blamed the previous Conservative government saying that the "turbulence on global markets are because of that exposure that they left behind".

Burnham became prime minister in July, having taken over from Sir Keir Starmer just before Parliament's summer recess, and it was the first time he had faced the Tory leader at the Commons session.

The prime minister used the summer recess to tour the UK, and had announced a series of eye-catching policies, mainly aimed at tackling the cost of living.

MPs returned to Parliament on Tuesday and Burnham spent more than three hours in the Commons, making a statement and answering questions from MPs.

At PMQs, Badenoch said the prime minister had set out plenty of spending plans but no detail of how he would be paying the bill.

"The markets are clearly worried that we now have a spendthrift prime minister who wants to say yes to everyone but cannot tell us where the money is coming from," she said.

"He needs to pay for all his new promises and he has a choice - higher taxes, more borrowing, or spending cuts.

"Yesterday he said change begins with honesty, so will he be honest and tell us: is he preparing to raise taxes again, yes or no?"

Burnham had earlier said he had already cut taxes, including VAT on energy bills and a cut in business rates for hospitality.

"I've already indicated my first moves were to cut tax, but I'm not going to do what any prime minister has done and write the budget here," he said, adding he and Chancellor John Healey had agreed on an early date for the Budget in October to reduce speculation.

At PMQs, Badenoch also raised comments from economist and cross-bench peer Lord Jim O'Neill, who had been tipped to become Burnham's chief economic adviser, but who ruled out joining Burnham's government.

Speaking to the BBC, Lord O'Neill had praised the PM for "a great first five weeks" which he said had helped lift consumer and business confidence; adding the current spike in market interest rates for government debt would force Labour to start "dealing with the triple lock" on the state pension, and "excessive" welfare spending.

Badenoch pointed to a warning from Lord O'Neill that the prime minister's tone during his Tuesday Commons debut would have unsettled investors, although the peer had also said that spike was mostly mirroring US market upheaval concerning the Iran conflict.

The PM also sought to stress his administration's fiscal responsibility and said ministers were taking steps to reduce debt.

He said: "This will be a government grounded in fiscal responsibility. It will stick to the fiscal rules, but at the same time, we will help reduce cost-of-living pressure on our constituents, and that's the approach that we will take."

Interest rates on government bonds have been going up, with the yield on a 10-year bond at its highest level since 2008, while the yield on a 30-year bond is at its highest since 1998, meaning it costs the government more to borrow over the long term.

It could mean that the government's choices on what it wants to spend are constrained as the Budget approaches.

News.title: PMQs shows the challenge Burnham has in delivering new style of politics
News.content:
The backdrop to his first few days as prime minister with Westminster in full swing has been the increased cost of borrowing â a global trend but one to which the UK is exposed and which looks likely to limit the chancellor's room for manoeuvre at the budget come the end of October.

Burnham has promised a transformational government but he's facing many of the same challenges as Sir Keir Starmer, with difficult decisions on defence spending, welfare and social care - to name just a few - hurtling towards him.

These are the pressure points his political opponents will seek to exploit, as evidenced by Badenoch's approach at Prime Minister's Questions when she quizzed him over plans for taxes, spending and borrowing.

Burnham pointed to his early actions in office, cutting VAT on domestic electricity bills and business rates for pubs and music venues as a sign of his priorities, but he gave little more away â leaning back on another familiar refrain that prime ministers don't write budgets from the despatch box.

In reality, it would be unfair to expect much more in the way of detail about Burnham's plans for the economy during his very first session of PMQs, but these are questions his government will eventually have to answer.

And what is clear is that despite the promise of a more consensual style of politics, when it comes to the substance there are sharp ideological differences across the Commons.

Burnham's diagnosis for the country's problems centres on privatisation and deindustrialisation over recent decades, as well as Brexit.

Badenoch disagrees, pointing instead to high taxes and spending as constraints on economic growth.

While Burnham's early weeks in office have seen a shift in style with a summer tour around the country and heavy social media presence, the economic arguments between him and his political opponents remain, and now Westminster is back in session there will likely be a clamour for more detail about his planned direction.

Today's Prime Minister's Questions is a taste of what's to come.

As well as smart communications, the choices the prime minister makes against a tricky economic background will take careful navigation if he's to deliver the optimistic future he's promised.

News.title: King hails 'unprecedented' Bayeux Tapestry exhibition in London
News.content:
The King, speaking inside the Great Court of the British Museum, said the opponents depicted in the tapestry - the Normans and Anglo-Saxons - would have been glad to see this togetherness between France and the UK - "two great nations, which share such fundamental values".

"The tapestry's story is one of ambition and uncertainty, of oaths and journeys, of ships, councils, kings, comets and consequences," said the King.

"Yet it is not merely an English story, nor only a Norman one. Indeed, from the moment of its creation, it may have brought together our two peoples."

George Osborne, director of the museum, described the displaying of the Bayeux Tapestry as the "most ambitious exhibition we've ever mounted".

President Macron said a loan of this "masterpiece" had first been proposed in the 1930s, but he was delighted that the idea had come to fruition.

He spoke of the loan of the tapestry as an example of how "we are united" and a "reminder of what our countries can do if they join forces".

Along with the King and Queen he had a chance to see the historic embroidery in the atmospheric darkness of the British Museum.

The 70m (230ft) tapestry, originally embroidered in England but kept for centuries in France, tells the story of the Norman Conquest and the Battle of Hastings in 1066.

King Charles and Queen Camilla, Burnham and his wife Marie-France van Heel, and Macron and wife Brigitte were shown key scenes in the tapestry, including the Coronation of King Harold and his death in battle.

Sending the tapestry to the British Museum had been announced by Macron during the French state visit to the UK in July 2025, as an emblem of the strong partnership between the countries.

There had been some worries that moving the fragile tapestry could risk causing damage, but French government sources said ahead of the royal preview: "The display conditions at the British Museum are ideal."

The French authorities welcomed the way that visitors in London would see the tapestry lying flat, rather than upright, with this believed to be better for the conservation of the fibres, sewn more than 900 years ago.

It is believed the final scenes of the tapestry have been lost or destroyed, as it has not always had such careful owners. In the 18th Century, during the French Revolution, it was rescued from being cut up to make covers for soldiers' carts.

At a state banquet hosted by King Charles in Windsor, Macron had said the missing end of the tapestry was a symbol that "in the great mural of Franco-British history, the end is yet to be written - it is up to us to do it".

News.title: 'Nothing but mud and silt' - the village swept away by deadly floods in Nepal
News.content:
After the catastrophic flash floods along the Nepal-Tibet border a week ago, more than 1,000 people have died and nearly 4,000 more are missing, according to Nepal's disaster agency.

The BBC has travelled to the district of Betrawati in Nepal, as some people return to their homes to see the devastation caused by the floods.

South Asia correspondent Azadeh Moshiri spoke to a local, who is still waiting for his his wife's body to be retrieved as rescue efforts continue.

News.title: Lucy Letby 'boyfriend' doctor named as court order lifted
News.content:
Letby - who has always maintained her innocence - is serving 15 whole life prison terms. The Criminal Cases Review Commission (CCRC) is conducting a review of Letby's convictions.

At her criminal trial - the longest murder trial in UK history - Deakin gave evidence in relation to several babies. He was granted special measures as well as anonymity. These allowed him to give evidence from behind a screen so that Letby, the public gallery, and the media were prevented from seeing him.

Deakin's evidence provided detail of some of the emergency calls and resuscitations which he and Letby were jointly involved in. Their long nights of text messaging were laid bare and many of the messages shown to the jury.

When he was sworn in, on the first occasion he testified, Letby burst into tears, in what was the first display of emotion from her during the trial.

During her cross-examination, Letby was forced to deny that Deakin was her boyfriend, though she did accept that they had gone on a trip to London together.

The prosecuting barrister, Nick Johnson KC, said Letby "tried to get out the back of the dock" when the doctor first came to the witness box.

Letby said: "Yes, because I felt unwell."

Johnson said: "No, it's because you didn't like hearing your boyfriend giving evidence, did you?"

Letby said: "That's unfair."

Prosecutors also went through a WhatsApp message exchange between Letby and a friend who had teased her for being "flirty" with Deakin.

Johnson said: "She knew you were sweet on Mark, didn't she?"

Letby said: "What do you mean, sweet?"

Johnson said: "That you had a crush on him."

"No," said Letby.

"There was nothing between me and that Mark."

Johnson told the court that Letby told her friend she had received a "strange message" from the doctor.

Her colleague responded: "Did you? Saying what? Go Commando [laughing face emoji]."

The court also heard that, in Facebook messages exchanged between the two, Deakin had described Letby as "one of the few nurses across the region... that I would trust with my own children."

While some media reports have described him as "a key witness", Deakin was one of many former colleagues of Letby's whose joint testimony helped to build the prosecution case against her, and none of the convictions rested solely on his evidence.

Correction: The original version of this story was published with an incorrect picture which has since been amended

News.title: Watch: What we know about reported strike on Iran wedding celebrations
News.content:
Iran has launched missile and drone attacks at US targets across the Middle East, after American forces resumed strikes against Iran.

The Iranian Red Crescent said four people - including a child - were killed at wedding celebrations when a US missile hit a building in southern Iran.

BBC Verify has analysed footage released of the aftermath of the strike and spoken to a weapons expert to identify munition remnants.

The US military says it is aware of the reports but that it never targets civilians, and was striking Iranian targets in response to "recent attempted attacks" on American forces and commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.

Merlyn Thomas reports.

Produced by Kevin Nguyen. Graphics by Sally Nicholls. Verification by Paul Brown and Shayan Sardarizadeh.

News.title: Farage tells BBC 'we live in a complainants' society' after questions over Reform funding
News.content:
Asked if he knew whether or not money donated by Fiona Cottrell had come from her son George, Farage said he was not "involved in the transactions".

However, he added that he "had been told it's her money". Reform has insisted it has always complied with donations rules.

He added: "The point is, we live in a complainants' society. If you complain about me, automatically that triggers an investigation."

He said that political parties were "constantly writing to all the authorities", meaning Reform was "under investigation every day for virtually everything we do".

"There's a big picture here. The old two-party system that has dominated since the end of the First World War feels for the first time it faces an existential threat.

"There is a whole ecosystem with a century of development around this. And we come along from virtually nowhere and threaten the whole thing.

"So I think what you're seeing is the establishment, in a very co-ordinated way, fighting back."

Pressed on what he meant, he added: "I'm talking about normal human behaviour.

"People who hold positions of power, influence and money don't want new kids on the block succeeding. It's the whole ecosystem, it's everything."

Farage said he expected it "won't be too long" before he is interviewed by Parliament's standards commissioner Daniel Greenberg as part of his probe into whether he should have publicly declared the Â£5m he received from Harborne.

He continued to insist the sum, which he says was a personal gift, did not require registration under Commons rules.

He added he had "no questions" about Greenberg's impartiality, but hit out at the "political composition" of the standards committee that will recommend what action should be taken on his findings.

The 14-member panel includes seven MPs from Labour, the Conservatives and Liberal Democrats, but none from Reform UK.

He added: "Have you seen who's on the committee? I think we know the outcome already. I'm not going to say anything more than that."

"To be judged by members of Parliament by other political parties who you're fighting against in by-elections or general elections, I think that raises a question, I really do," he added.

News.title: Four in court over murder of baby stabbed to death
News.content:
Two men and two women have appeared in court charged with murdering a baby girl who had been repeatedly stabbed at a house in Sheffield.

The newborn - referred to as Baby S in court - was found at a property in Holywell Heights, in the Wincobank area, on Sunday, having suffered 33 wounds from 15 separate stabbings.

Andrea Skopova, 20, formerly of Robey Street, Sheffield, and Peter Horvath, 19, Nina Horvathova, 37, and Peter Horvath, 38, all of Holywell Heights, appeared at Sheffield Magistrates' Court.

The four Slovakian nationals have been charged with murder, causing or allowing the death of a child and perverting the course of justice by taking steps to conceal the killing of an infant.

A fifth person, a 15-year-old girl, who cannot be named for legal reasons, also appeared in the same court charged with perverting the course of justice.

All five defendants were remanded into custody to appear at Sheffield Crown Court on Thursday.

News.title: London mayor's untaxed car conviction withdrawn
News.content:
The DVLA has said a criminal prosecution against mayor of London Sir Sadiq Khan will be withdrawn after he was convicted of not taxing a 24-year-old Nissan Micra.

The Labour politician, 55, was found guilty of keeping an unlicensed vehicle by a magistrate last month in a criminal prosecution brought by the DVLA.

Court documents show letters addressed to the mayor about the unpaid tax bill were sent to Gordon Ramsay's east London restaurant and the car did not belong to the mayor.

A spokesperson for the mayor said: "This is a scam, which is a crime. It's not the first time the mayor has been victim of a scam involving people falsely stating that Sadiq is the owner of a vehicle."

The mayor's adviser told BBC London earlier that the DVLA was "urgently" looking into reopening the case and withdrawing the prosecution.

The DLVA said the withdrawal had been accepted but it needed to be formally reopened and withdrawn, which will be done at a hearing at Hereford Magistrates' Court on Thursday.

The DVLA will also investigate the false registration, the adviser said.

The magistrate, sitting in a private hearing of the Single Justice Procedure in Herefordshire, previously convicted Khan in his absence and ordered that he pay a Â£220 fine, Â£85 in costs, and settle the Â£35.84 bill for unpaid tax on the Micra.

After the mayor expanded the Ultra Low Emission Zone (Ulez) to cover the whole of London he faced a wave of protests, including from motorists who said they planned to register their car in his name - supposedly to make him liable for the Â£12.50 daily charge.

News.title: Inquest opens into death of family in Shoreham
News.content:
An inquest has opened into the death of four family members who died after getting into difficulty in the sea off the coast of Shoreham.

Hussam El-Khawas, 55, Zeina Alayan, 37, and their daughter Sara El-Khawas, 13, were pronounced dead after being brought to shore by lifeboat crews on 18 August. The couple's younger daughter, Saja El-Khawas, died at the Evelina Children's Hospital in London three days later.

Senior coroner Penelope Scholfield opened and adjourned the inquest to March 2027 and offered her "sincere condolences" to the wider family.

Six-year-old Saja was resuscitated but showed signs of a brain injury throughout treatment. No provisional cause of death was given for the other family members.

The family lived in north west London, where El-Khawas worked as a construction worker, while Alayan was a homemaker, the inquest in Horsham was told.

Both parents were Lebanese nationals with British passports, while the children were born in Kensington.

El-Khawas was a Palestinian refugee from the Rashidieh Camp in Lebanon, the Palestinian embassy previously said.

It is believed that the family travelled from their home in London to visit Shoreham and entered the water from the beach near Shoreham Fort at about 14:00 BST before getting into difficulty.

News.title: Four arrested over woman's murder 32 years ago
News.content:
Four people have been arrested on suspicion of perverting the course of justice in the case of a woman who was murdered 32 years ago.

Doreen Morris, 64, was stabbed to death with a fork after disturbing a burglary at her home, Penrhyn Uchaf, on Anglesey, in 1994, according to a 2023 inquest.

Joseph Carl Westbury denied breaking into Doreen's bungalow and was found not guilty of her murder in 1995. He took his life in May 2016.

North Wales Police said a man and three women, all from north Wales, were arrested on Wednesday morning.

The force said advances in forensic science and a review of evidence had led to the development and the Morris family had been told.

Mark Pierce, senior review officer, said: "Forensic results, combined with a detailed review of witness evidence, have provided grounds to interview four people on suspicion of perverting the course of justice."

He appealed for anyone with information about the case to get in touch.

News.title: About 700 prisoners to be freed on 1 October under revised early release plans
News.content:
About 700 eligible offenders will leave jails in England and Wales on the morning of 1 October and some 2,550 will have been released by the end of the year, the government's revised early prison release plan shows.

The new plan, signed into law and published online, shows Andy Burnham's government kept the promised original schedule of how and when offenders will leave jail, aside from delaying the start date by a month and excluding specific offences from the programme.

Under the original plan, offenders serving sentences of up to 19 months would have been eligible from 2 September to walk out of jail after serving a third of that time.

In the Commons on Wednesday, Burnham said he understood the "anguish" of victims and "listened to what they were saying".

"I came in and asked for changes to the early release scheme, and we excluded rape, grooming, and child sex offences," the prime minister added.

Prisoners will now qualify for their earlier release from 1 October and officials estimate that around 700 will walk out of the prison gates that day.

From 13 October, governors will release a second tranche of 650 prisoners who have been serving sentences of between 19 months and two years and five months.

Prisons in England and Wales are running at 97% capacity, with the latest Ministry of Justice figures showing the number of available spaces across the male prison estate at its lowest this year, with about 1,500 free spaces.

Under the original plan, prisons and probation services had almost six weeks to prepare this second group following the first releases, but they now have less than a fortnight.

The rest of the estimated 4,500 releases will then be phased in following the dates below. Some 1,400 more offenders were due to be released under the original plans before revisions made after certain offences were excluded.

The estimated numbers are Ministry of Justice calculations:

From 10 November, 650 offenders serving up to three years and two months

From 8 December, 550 offenders serving up to four years and three months

From 12 January 2027, 600 offenders serving up to five years and nine months

From 9 February, 500 offenders serving up to seven years and six months

From 9 March, 200 offenders serving up to nine years

From 13 April, 200 offenders serving up to 10 years

From 11 May, 250 offenders serving up to 12 years

From 9 June, 250 offenders serving more than 12 years.

The offenders serving the longer sentences, which do not become part of the scheme until next year, include more dangerous criminals who would have previously expected to spend two-thirds of their sentence behind bars.

News.title: Woman died of heatstroke climbing Yr Wyddfa, inquest hears
News.content:
A 35-year-old woman died of heatstroke on Wales' highest mountain, an inquest has heard.

Sophie Goodyer-Bird, from Birmingham, was climbing Yr Wyddfa - also known as Snowdon - on 10 July, a few days after her birthday.

On Wednesday, an inquest opening at Caernarfon Coroners' Court heard Goodyer-Bird became increasingly tired while coming down the mountain.

Near the end of the walk, she became unresponsive, and was confirmed to have died shortly afterwards.

Coroner Kate Robertson said emergency services were called and attempted CPR, but were unable to revive her.

A provisional cause of death was given as exertional heat stroke.

The inquest was adjourned to a full hearing, which will take place at a later date.

Following her death, an online fundraiser was set up to raise money for her 12-year-old son.

News.title: Family of murdered Stacy Hunter say new misogyny bill would not have protected her
News.content:
The family of Stacy Hunter has called for immediate action to protect victims of domestic abuse, after plans for a misogyny bill were announced by the Scottish government.

First Minister John Swinney announced plans to recognise misogyny as a "distinct form of prejudice and abuse" during his programme for government, external on Tuesday, alongside a public health campaign to target toxic male behaviour.

Stacy was murdered by her estranged husband, Jim Mair, at her home near Houston in Refrewshire in July. He was on bail for attacking her. His body was found nearby.

Her family is calling for tougher action on offenders.

Speaking on BBC Radio Scotland's Mornings programme, Stacy's brother said some aspects of the proposals were important but they are not "anywhere near good enough".

News.title: Nottingham attacks families not told 'stalker' had violent past
News.content:
Families of the Nottingham attacks victims said police did not tell them a man who had taken an interest in them had a history of violence when he attempted to visit them.

Barnaby Webber, Grace O'Malley-Kumar and Ian Coates were fatally stabbed by Valdo Calocane, who had been diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia in 2020, on 13 June 2023. He tried to kill three others.

Grace's father, Dr Sanjoy Kumar, said he was told in 2025 that a man had visited his GP surgery in London. Emma Webber, Barnaby's mother, said he had also travelled to Somerset, but neither were informed of the man's history of mental ill health.

Nottinghamshire Police said it had received a complaint and referred the matter to the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC).

The IOPC confirmed it had received a referral of a complaint from Nottinghamshire Police in relation to information the force allegedly withheld from the families of Calocane's victims about a potential witness who had tried to contact them.

News.title: UK long-term borrowing costs highest since 1998 ahead of October Budget
News.content:
All of those factors will make the Budget process trickier for Burnham, who on Tuesday addressed MPs for the first time as prime minister, and his Chancellor, John Healey.

Burnham told the House of Commons the economy and the cost of living were "the biggest issues facing the country".

Higher borrowing costs will reduce the amount of headroom the government has against its self-imposed fiscal rules, limiting the amount Healey can spend on consumer-friendly measures to ease the cost of living.

Despite the squeezed public finances, Burnham said he would bring about "more substantial change" to ease living costs.

"Britain is not where any of us would wish it to be," he added.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch accused Burnham of "living in the past".

"His diagnosis is completely wrong," she told the House of Commons. "His theory of growth is completely wrong. He thinks that if Government spends more money, we will all get richer.

"That is not how this works."

The chancellor has previously said he will stick to a set of fiscal rules imposed by his predecessor, Rachel Reeves, that restrict borrowing. These rules are designed to help markets have clarity about the path of borrowing.

The more that is forecast to be spent on interest payments, the more likely that there will be a squeeze on spending or some form of tax rise to meet these rules.

On top of that, higher government rates can feed through to higher business and household borrowing costs, and so weigh on the economy.

The prime minister was already facing a tough balancing act with taxing and spending, due to pressures on defence and the cost of living.

Burnham's ex-economic adviser Lord Jim O'Neill told BBC News that high government borrowing costs would force Labour to "get real" about "dealing with the triple lock" on the state pension, and "excessive" welfare spending.

Lord O'Neill, who recently turned down the offer of a formal position in the prime minister's team, said that current market pressure would force changes over "some of the things that no political figures ever seem to want to deal with".

As well as the rise to 30-year gilt yields, the yield on the benchmark 10-year gilt rose to 5.22% on Tuesday. This is its highest rate since June 2008, at the height of the global financial crisis.

Gilt yields move counter to the value of the bonds, meaning their prices fall when yields rise.

Parts of Texas have experienced around 30 inches of rain in the past 24 hours as the remnants of Tropical Storm Edouard led to flash-flood emergencies, water rescues and widespread power outages.

Rainfall was falling at a rate of five inches an hour Wednesday in areas northeast of Houston, ABC News reported.

The rapid, catastrophic downpours flooded streets and trapped people in their homes. A woman and her four children were rescued from their Livingston mobile home after a creek overflowed, according to Click 2 Houston.

People in the area also had to be pulled from their cars after becoming stranded on flooded roads, KTRE said.

A flash flood emergency was declared in Hardin and Tyler Counties with rain expected to continue through Tuesday into Wednesday. By Wednesday evening, Edouard is expected to dissipate.

open image in gallery Tropical Storm Edouard nears landfall along the Texas and Louisiana coast in this Tuesday image from a federal satellite. The storm has weakened - but forecasters say impacts will linger into Wednesday ( NOAA )

open image in gallery Flooded roads around Hickman Creek are seen in this image from Polk County, Texas ( Polk County Fire Marshal’s Office )

Village Creek in the area of Kountze, Texas, about an hour from Livingston, was forecast to reach major flood stage of 23.3 feet by midnight, according to storm chaser Reed Timmer.

“Widespread damaging and potentially catastrophic flooding is possible with a HIGH risk of flooding in effect,” the National Weather Service warned residents of southeastern Texas.

More than 1,100 state responders and 20 state agencies were working to protect Texans, the office of Republican Gov. Greg Abbott said on Facebook.

Social media videos showed cows moving their way through flooding and cars and trucks navigating water-covered highways.

open image in gallery Rescuers help residents of southeastern Texas cross muddy floodwaters on Wednesday in this photo from the Office of the Governor Greg Abbott ( Office of the Governor Greg Abbott/Facebook )

open image in gallery Flooding is seen in southeastern Texas on Wednesday. Rain has been falling at a rate of five inches an hour ( Office of the Governor Greg Abbott/Facebook )

The strengthening super El Niño climate pattern is tied to the “huge amounts” of rain in eastern Texas, meteorologist Ben Noll wrote on X. An El Niño typically brings warmer and wetter conditions to the Southeast.

But rain isn’t the only threat from Edouard. Trees fell into roadways and winds gusting up to 30 miles an hour in Livington’s Polk County have led to widespread power outages. The county’s emergency managers told residents to avoid travel Tuesday.

The storm had knocked out power for more than 72,000 customers by late Wednesday morning, according to tracker PowerOutage.US.

open image in gallery Rescue rafts are seen in this image from Polk County, Texas ( Polk County Fire Marshal’s Office )

open image in gallery A man watches flooding rain from Edouard fall in High Island, Texas, on Tuesday. Water rescues are underway in the area as the depression continues to dump inches of rain ( AP )

Some schools and government offices around Houston and the hardest-hit areas were closed, with plans to reopen on Wednesday, 12 News reported.

Edouard made landfall near the Texas-Louisiana border Tuesday afternoon with maximum sustained winds of 60mph, according to the National Hurricane Center.

One weather station in Port Arthur, Texas, recorded a 90mph wind gust from the storm.

Edouard is the fifth named storm of the Atlantic hurricane season, which has been less active than normal due to the El Niño.

open image in gallery A man tries to hold onto an umbrella as he walks out of a grocery storm on Tuesday in Port Arthur, Texas. Edouard made landfall along the Texas-Louisiana border on Tuesday afternoon ( Getty )

open image in gallery A damaged G.I. Surplus store is seen during Tropical Storm Edouard on Tuesday in Beaumont, Texas. Edouard is the fifth named storm of the Atlantic hurricane season ( Getty )

Its path was similar to Hurricane Harvey, which brought devastating flooding to the Houston metro area and claimed the lives of 107 people in August 2017.

Record-warm water in the Gulf has been supercharging storms due to human-caused climate change.

It’s also been fueling more rain-heavy storms, including July 2025 flooding that took the lives of 28 people at the Camp Mystic Christian girls’ summer camp.

With reporting from The Associated Press

A college graduate from Georgia is being denied his diploma until he pays back a medical debt he incurred while he was enrolled at the university.

Dylan Merrell played football for two years at Long Island University in New York. After he graduated, he learned that both his transcripts and his diploma were being held due to a $6,824 medical hold that was placed on his account.

"I found out that I had a medical hold on my record for insurance reasons, which completely blindsided me and caught me off guard," Merrell told CBS Atlanta. "I was told that my diploma was being withheld from me if those fees weren't cleared."

LIU, like many college athletics programs, requires student-athletes to have primary health insurance before they can participate in practices or other physical activities tied to their sports.

The university's student-athlete handbook requires players to upload their health insurance details, including front and back copies of their insurance cards, into the school's athletics portal for clearance before they play.

Dylan Merrell, a graduate of Long Island University in New York, says the school is withholding his transcripts and diploma due to a more than $6,000 medical hold he claims is being charged to him in error ( CBS News Atlanta )

Merrell says he followed the instructions by submitting his information for his Blue Cross Blue Shield policy. He waived the school's health insurance offering.

However, school administrators are claiming that he did not, and that he now owes the school more than $6,000.

"The school is telling me that even though I uploaded my own insurance, I didn't waive the school's insurance off," he said. "So that insurance was automatically applied anyway, which means I would have to pay that fee."

The situation has left Merrell in a difficult position when it comes to job hunting; prospective employers typically ask for his university credentials, but he cannot provide them due to the medical hold.

"It's extremely frustrating. I've been in multiple job interviews where they asked for my official transcript, or they asked for my diploma, and I haven't been able to provide it," he said.

Merrell said he believes at least 15 job applications have been stalled because he cannot produce his records.

His mother, Carla Merrell, said it's frustrating seeing her son have to face another hurdle just for the chance to work and make a life for himself.

"He finished, he graduated, and so this is your reward?" she told CBS Atlanta. "With AI being in place and young graduates looking for a job in this economy, competing with people with years of experience, to know that this is yet another hurdle that he has to get over is quite frustrating and disappointing."

According to Reginald Shareef with The EDGE Foundation — which helps students navigate campus issues — colleges have recently been bundling school insurance with students' tuitions. The only way for students to avoid the charges is to file a waiver rejecting the insurance each term.

"It's one of the top reasons why people owe balances to universities because of unexpected charges that people don't foresee, or a lack of communication," he told CBS Atlanta.

LIU said that it has sent reminder emails concerning the waiver policy since last August.

The university also told CBS Atlanta that it will provide transcripts and confirm degrees to graduate schools or employers who inquire about them, regardless of outstanding balances or holds on student accounts.

The Independent has requested comment from the university.

The King, the Queen, the prime minister and the French president have visited the Bayeux Tapestry together to mark the historic return of the centuries-old artwork to the UK.

The Tapestry – the woven record of the Norman Conquest – has returned to Britain for the first time in almost 1,000 years, on loan until September 2027 as part of a special trilateral agreement between the UK, France and the museum.

In a public display of warm Anglo-French relations, Charles and Camilla joined Andy Burnham, Emmanuel Macron and their wives as they walked the length of the 70-metre masterpiece at the British Museum in London on Wednesday afternoon.

The party stopped at key moments along the 11th-century artwork to hear from curators about historic events such as the coronation of Harold Godwinson and the much-disputed depiction of his death by an arrow to the eye at the Battle of Hastings in 1066.

open image in gallery Britain’s King Charles III, Emmanuel Macron, president of France, and Queen Camilla arrive to view the Bayeux Tapestry ( AP )

The King and Mr Macron delivered speeches in celebration of the loan at a reception in the museum’s Great Court for representatives from Britain and France involved in the process and schoolchildren from both countries.

Among those who greeted the royals and the Macrons was the museum’s director, Nicholas Cullinan, and its chair, former chancellor George Osborne.

The monarch and the president enjoy a friendly rapport, with the King hosting the Macrons for a state visit in July last year.

Charles rebranded the famous entente cordiale between the two nations as the entente “amicale” in his banquet speech in Windsor Castle.

Mr Macron is the first European leader to visit the UK since Mr Burnham took office, and it is the first time the pair will meet.

open image in gallery King Charles III and Queen Camilla alongside Emmanuel Macron view a section of the Bayeux Tapestry ( AFP/Getty )

The prime minister is then set to welcome Mr Macron to Downing Street on Thursday for their first bilateral meeting, which is expected to focus on tackling small boat crossings, the wars in Ukraine and Iran, and trade and energy.

The visit is seen as another sign the former mayor of Greater Manchester looks set to continue his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer’s policy of a “reset” of relations between the UK and the EU.

Mr Burnham said: “The return of the Bayeux Tapestry to England is a landmark moment in the history of our two nations, and I want people everywhere in the country to be able to enjoy it.”

He added: “As we celebrate our shared heritage, President Macron and I will continue to strengthen the relationship between our two nations.”

open image in gallery Andy Burnham (L) and his wife Marie-France van Heel (centre) are greeted by British Museum chair George Osborne (R) ( AFP/Getty )

The loan of the tapestry to the British Museum has been sponsored by billionaire Igor Tulchinsky, the founder, chairman, and chief executive of the quantitative investment firm WorldQuant.

At his first Prime Minister’s Questions, Mr Burnham also said: “The loaning of the tapestry is a great example of French-British co-operation, the same co-operation that has helped us reduce summer small boat crossings to a seven-year low.”

The Labour leader also said the Bayeux Around Britain programme, which will see the digital exhibition displayed in museums, galleries and castles in all four nations, would “give communities across the UK the opportunity to learn about one of the defining stories of our past”.

open image in gallery The Bayeux Tapestry is on exhibit at the British Museum ( AFP/Getty )

A live national history lesson on 14 October will teach thousands of schoolchildren about the significance of the tapestry.

Culture secretary Lisa Nandy said: “This will be the first generation in 1,000 years who will be able to see this unique part of our heritage and we are determined that children from all backgrounds across every part of Britain have the chance to see it.

“The British Museum has pulled out all the stops to ensure that a generation of British children will remember it for the rest of their lives.”

British Museum director Mr Cullinan said the initiative to ensure the exhibition was not confined to London marked “the most ambitious and inclusive programme we or any museum in the UK has ever done”.

News.title: Shooting reported at Virginia elementary school
News.content:

A shooting has been reported at Westwood Hills Elementary School in Waynesboro, Virginia, prompting an evacuation of the building.

The August County Sheriff's Office said that the incident is "contained and secured at this time."

One adult was injured in the shooting, according to Robin Lawson, a spokeswoman for the Virginia State Police, who spoke to ABC News.

A social media post from Waynesboro Public Schools said that police are maintaining a large presence around the school. The incident occurred just weeks after the school’s first day back following summer break.

Students have been taken to Westminster Presbyterian Church for reunification.

First responders outside Westwood Hills Elementary School in Waynesboro, Virginia, where a shooting was reported on Wednesday, September 2, 2026 ( WHSV-TV )

The sheriff's office said that the "children are safe" and asked for the public to avoid traveling to the school to ensure emergency vehicles and buses aren't blocked.

“For the safety of students, families, school personnel, and first responders, the public is asked to continue avoiding the immediate area until further notice,” the sheriff’s office said.

Governor Abigail Spanberger said she was aware of the shooting and is monitoring the incident.

"I am monitoring the emergency at Westwood Hills Elementary School this morning. My heart is with these young students, their parents and families, and the teachers and staff at the school," she wrote in a post on X. "Thank you to the first responders who are assisting at the scene."

Jim Wood, a Waynesboro city council member whose district includes Westwood Hills Elementary School, told ABC News that the shooting was an isolated incident and that the shooter is no longer a threat to the public.

He reportedly declined to comment on the status of the shooter. Wood called it a “one-on-one incident,” and added that the victim has been taken to a hospital with non life-threatening injuries, according to the outlet.

Tyson Fury has accused Anthony Joshua of being a coward as the wait for confirmation of their all-British blockbuster bout goes on.

Fury taunted his would-be opponent in a video on his Instagram story on Wednesday, having posted a mock-up of a poster a day earlier showing himself and Joshua facing off above the words ‘New York City’.

New York’s Madison Square Garden is widely expected to be announced as the venue despite Joshua’s camp preferring Wembley Stadium as Sela, the Saudi state-owned promotional company financing the fight, wants a bigger American audience on Netflix.

“Joshua, where are you? Still no deal done. It’s getting quite tiring,” Fury said.

open image in gallery Tyson Fury has called Anthony Joshua a coward (Bradley Collyer/PA) ( PA Archive )

“I’ve been down to fight every location that’s been mentioned – England, Ireland, Vegas, New York, back to England, back to Ireland, back to New York. Listen, I’ve said yep, yep, yep, yep, yep, every single time. Zero stipulations.

“The facts are I feel like you’re being a coward. I feel like you don’t want the fight and you’re just conning everybody. I feel like you’ve been doing that for years.

“You’ve had many opportunities to fight me, but deep down you’ve never really wanted it, so let’s see if you’re going to man up for a final time.

“We’re both f****** 37, 38 years old – let’s f****** fight. It’s a boxing match and you’ve been banjoed before plenty of times. You’ve been knocked spark out a few times. So what?

“What’s the worst that can happen? I’m going to f****** chin you, 100 per cent, but it’s nothing that hasn’t been done before!”

open image in gallery Frank Warren and Tyson Fury (Adam Davy/PA) ( PA Wire )

Joshua’s promotor, Eddie Hearn of Matchroom, has said an agreement hinges on his client’s net purse but Fury’s representative Frank Warren was unequivocal his man is already committed.

“It is signed by Tyson. Tyson is signed up for the fight and agreed for the fight,” he told Sky Sports News.

“He’s signed for it. One hundred per cent. We’re just waiting for AJ. I can’t speak for him, he’s with Matchroom.”

Warren said the location is not important, adding: “That’s up to the people putting up the money. Tyson just wants to get on.”

He also turned on those who have criticised his fighter Moses Itauma, who lost his IBF world heavyweight title challenge after a ninth-round stoppage by Filip Hrgovic at the O2.

open image in gallery Moses Itauma was defeated by Filip Hrgovic at the O2 (Steven Paston/PA) ( PA Wire )

Defending his 21-year-old prospect, he said: “They all come with their knives out afterwards. Before the fight there wasn’t anyone who tipped Hrgovic to win, other than Hrgovic’s team.

“No-one said this is too soon. Everyone saying this stuff, they’re all after-timers. He’s very, very disappointed but you can expect that, he really felt it was going to be his fight but it wasn’t to be.

“We can’t change it, all we can do is learn from it. There are lot of things we need to tweak, to put right, and I genuinely believe he will go on to become a world champion and hold the title.”

News.title: It is still in Britain’s interest to maintain good relations with an unpredictable America
News.content:

Whether it's investigating the financials of Elon Musk's pro-Trump PAC or producing our latest documentary, 'The A Word', which shines a light on the American women fighting for reproductive rights, we know how important it is to parse out the facts from the messaging. The Independent has never been under any illusion about this American president. As our world affairs editor Sam Kiley writes, Donald Trump’s “infantile” folly in the Middle East has strengthened outlaw nations Russia and Iran, while “locking America into another forever war”.

The United States, and the world, survived Mr Trump’s first term in the White House in reasonable shape. Although he revels in his unpredictability, it was hard to imagine quite how perverse he would be in his second.

In recent weeks, he has laid about America’s longstanding allies with the irresponsible abandon of, as Kiley puts it, “a toddler with a chainsaw”.

Mr Trump has insulted South Korea, cutting joint military exercises, while doubling down on his admiration for the North Korean dictatorship. He has pulled out of trade talks with Canada after making impossible demands to limit Canada’s ability to make deals with other countries, and to protect the French language.

In a fit of megalomaniac pique, he decreed that Lake Ontario be renamed “Lake America” – and lobbied Apple into changing its maps accordingly.

Closer to home, Mr Trump has said US support for British sovereignty over the Falkland Islands is “one of many” issues under review, which he appeared to believe was a way of putting pressure on the UK government to increase military spending further.

It was an outrageous and unprincipled comment, contrary to decades of American respect for the principle of self-determination. Yet it is the sort of nonsense that Mr Trump spouts so casually, simply because he can.

The Ukraine war, and Mr Trump’s habit of making excuses for Vladimir Putin, is a more serious case of undermining the rights of people to decide their own future – although, thankfully, the humiliation for America of a total sellout of the Ukrainian people seems to have acted, for once, as a brake on the president’s worst instincts.

It is in his conduct of the war with Iran, however, that Mr Trump has departed most dramatically not just from past American policy, but from present American interests and even his own previous opposition to “forever wars”.

Having launched, with Israeli forces, what was supposed to be a surgical strike on the Iranian leadership at the end of February, Mr Trump is now, six months later, intensifying the war against a regime that was supposed to have been toppled.

There is no end in sight – and no end in sight to the economic damage to the world, including America, caused by the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, which the US president has casually suggested be renamed as the “Strait of Trump”.

Mr Trump was told that Benjamin Netanyahu, the Israeli prime minister, was hoping to engage him in this doomed enterprise in order to save his political skin in Israel. All his advisers said that the Iranian people would be unable to rise up against their oppressive theocracy just because some of its leading personnel had been killed. All of them except Pete Hegseth, the secretary of war, whose credibility with anyone who understands the issues is minimal.

Andy Burnham, the new British prime minister, is expected to meet Mr Trump for the first time later this month, around the time of the United Nations general assembly starting on 22 September. The temptation might be for Mr Burnham to be more like Mark Carney, the Canadian prime minister, who has rallied Canadian opinion by taking a robustly oppositional stance, than like Sir Keir Starmer, who tried to manage the monstrous ego.

But Sir Keir’s approach was in the British national interest – and, for a while, it succeeded in protecting us from the worst of Mr Trump’s capricious tariffs.

Mr Burnham must recognise that, while the president may be unpredictable and many of his actions ruinous for America and the world, it remains in the British national interest to maintain good relations with America for the long term.
