Sports.title: Fury launches fresh swipe at Joshua as talks continue
Sports.content:
Tyson Fury has branded Anthony Joshua a "coward" and suggested the two-time world heavyweight champion is "conning everybody" as talks over a long-awaited all-British showdown continue.

Fury and Joshua had appeared closer than ever to agreeing a super-fight long-in-the-making, only for Saudi organisers Sela's wish to hold the event in the USA to emerge as a major stumbling block.

Joshua's side have maintained their desire for the fight to take place in the UK.

Fury took to Instagram once again on Wednesday to question the hold up.

"Joshua, where are you? Still no deal done. It's getting quite tiring," said Fury. "I've been down to fight in every location that's been mentioned - England, Ireland, Vegas, New York, back to England, back to Ireland, back to New York. I've said yep, yep, yep every single time with zero stipulations.

"The facts are that I feel like you're being a coward. I feel like you don't want the fight and you're just conning everybody. I feel like you've been doing that for years."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Eddie Hearn claimed that Anthony Joshua feels a responsibility to UK fight fans that AJ vs Fury should happen in the UK.

Joshua is coming off a second-round knockout victory over Kristian Prenga in July, during which he was notably floored twice in the first round.

Fury also last fought in July when he took on Mariusz Wach, with the 46-year-old retiring in the seventh round.

"You've had many opportunities to fight me, but deep down you've never really wanted it, so let's see if you're going to man out for a final time," Fury continued.

"We're both f***ing 37, 38 years old - let's f***ing fight. It's a boxing match and you've been banjoed before plenty of times.

"You've been knocked sparked out a few times. So what, what's the worst that can happen? I'm going to f***ing chin you, 100 per cent, but it's nothing that hasn't been done before!"

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Frank Warren insists Tyson Fury has done everything he can to make the showdown with Anthony Joshua happen but the fight is being held up by AJ.

Promoter Frank Warren insisted Wednesday that the ball was "100 per cent" in Joshua's court.

"Tyson has signed up for the fight and agreed to the fight," said Warren. "He's all good to go, just waiting for AJ. I can't speak for him, because he's with Matchroom. He [Fury] has signed."

He did, meanwhile, admit he was uncertain as to the fight's location, with Fury having this week teased Madison Square Garden on social media.

"That I don't know," he continued. "That's going to be up to the people who are putting up the money and the promoters and the TV company putting up the money.

"Tyson just wants to get on. He said 'I don't care where I'll fight, whether it's Wembley, New York, Isle of Wight, Isle of Man - I'll fight him anywhere'. He doesn't care."

Sports.title: Hadjar to miss Italian GP with ongoing wrist injury
Sports.content:
Isack Hadjar will miss this weekend's Italian Grand Prix due to his ongoing wrist injury, with Liam Lawson replacing him for a second consecutive event at Red Bull.

Hadjar suffered the injury while boxing in training during the summer break last month which forced him to miss the Dutch Grand Prix and he has not recovered in time for Monza.

With Lawson stepping up to be Max Verstappen's team-mate at Red Bull, Yuki Tsunoda will have another chance to impress at Racing Bulls.

Red Bull only made the decision on Wednesday afternoon to give Hadjar every chance to drive but medical staff have decided he should miss another event and hope to return for the following race in Madrid next weekend.

"Liam will drive alongside Max at the Italian Grand Prix in Monza, while Isack continues to make encouraging progress following the wrist injury sustained during the summer break," said Red Bull.

"The team is closely monitoring his rehabilitation and will take no unnecessary risks with his return to competition and wishes him a speedy recovery."

Sports.title: Cameron says talks are 'advanced' to fight Shields
Sports.content:
Chantelle Cameron says that talks for her to fight Claressa Shields are advanced and moving quickly following her victory over Mikaela Mayer.

Cameron defeated Mayer by unanimous decision in a thriller to become WBA, WBC and WBO super-welterweight world champion at MPW-06 in Birmingham on Saturday.

She emerged victorious, edging a tight contest 97-93, 97-93, 96-94 on the judges' scorecards, further glossing a stellar resume that already honours her as the only woman to ever defeat the great Katie Taylor in her professional career.

With the victory strengthening Cameron's claim to a place among the greats of the women's game, she now has eyes on taking on the self-proclaimed 'GWOAT' [Greatest woman of all time] in Shields.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Cameron says there's a 'very high possibility' of fighting Claressa Shields

Many thought a rematch with Mayer would be next on her list, but Cameron told Sky Sports that things are moving rapidly with the WBC and WBA middleweight champion, who has a record of 19-0 across multiple weight divisions.

"I fancy [fighting] Clarissa Shields. I think I really do want to dare to be great and Clarissa Shields, she's the GWOAT, she's No 1 and that's going to be a fight that will just be unbelievable.

"The teams are actually in talks for that now so there is actually movement on that fight and for me that makes me giddy because I think that really is me challenging the very, very best and what an opportunity if this fight comes off.

"They [talks] are very advanced; it is moving pretty quick is what my managers told me, and it is a very high possibility the fight will happen."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Cameron reflects on the flashpoints with Mikaela Mayer during their super-welterweight epic in Birmingham

Dmitriy Salita, Shields' promoter, confirmed that Cameron was firmly in contention for the fight.

Speaking exclusively to Sky Sports, Salita said: "Yes, Chantelle is under serious consideration as Claressa's next opponent. Claressa wants to fight the best, and Chantelle is unquestionably one of the elite pound-for-pound fighters in women's boxing. We are exploring the opportunity now, but it is too early to confirm a date.

Image: Promoter Dmitriy Salita guides the career of Claressa Shields [Pic courtesy of Stephanie Trapp/Salita Promotions]

"Absolutely [we are open to talks with MVP]. Our responsibility to the fighters we represent - and to the fans - is to do everything possible to make the best fights and create the biggest events. That is what being fighter-first means.

"Our track record demonstrates that we have worked with virtually every major promoter to make important fights, so working with MVP is certainly not an issue from our side. We also promote several of the best female fighters in the world, in addition to Claressa, and many of those fighters are involved in co-promotions with Claressa Shields' promotion.

"Definitely [Shields would welcome the challenge]. She has made that very clear on social media, and we have also had several conversations about it. Claressa wants to fight the best, and Chantelle represents exactly that kind of challenge."

What about Shields vs Price?

Back when Shields beat Kaye Scott in the sixth round to reclaim those belts in August, it was discussed that her next preferred opponent would be Lauren Price.

Indeed, Shields said she would like this fight to take place between December and January.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Claressa Shields reclaimed her place at the top of the middleweight division with a dominant sixth-round stoppage of Kaye Scott, regaining the WBC and WBA titles in Atlanta. Credit: DAZN

It is a fight that Price has also welcomed, but Salita, believes the "mega" event "belongs in the United States.

Sports.title: Premier League transfer talking points: three things we learned from the data
Sports.content:
Premier League clubs have invested more than £3.4bn in players this summer, an increase of 11.9% on last year. There are three aspects of this enormous spending worthy of closer scrutiny.

Priorities on player age have changed

Premier League clubs are spending less on players in the peak 24-27 age band even though those players are increasingly the core of their selections.

As recently as 2021-22, 40% of minutes were taken by players at least 28 years old at the start of the season. That proportion has dropped each year, reaching 26.6% in 2025-26. The reliance on veterans has declined. The bulk of their lost minutes went to players aged between 24 and 27, which is now the dominant age band.

The spend on that key demographic has fallen by 23% since last summer, though. Without Manchester City signing the 25-year-old Enzo Fernández for a British transfer record-equalling £125m shortly before the window closed, the drop would have been even greater.

Younger players account for some of the shortfall but a surprisingly high slice of it has gone towards older footballers. The Premier League has invested £323.3m in players aged at least 28, only around £50m shy of the outlay on this age range in the previous three summers combined (£370.5m). Their proportion of the total has not been as high for four years.

How much this increased spending on veterans affects the playing time figures depends in part on the selection decisions of Mikel Arteta. Arsenal signed two 28-year-olds for a combined £126m: Bruno Guimarães (£75m) and Ezri Konsa (£51m). Transfermarkt considers them to be the most expensive central midfielder and centre-back respectively aged over 27 in history.

The three most expensive Premier League signings of the summer before Fernández, Morgan Rogers, Elliot Anderson and Bradley Barcola, were 23 when their deals were completed. With only slightly less spent collectively on footballers who are 22, clubs have gone hard for players on the verge of entering their peak years rather than those in them.

The Premier League is becoming a closed shop

Perhaps the most notable aspect of transfer spending this summer is how much of it has remained within English football. Fourteen of the 19 signings that cost Premier League clubs at least £50m were made from within the division or from relegated West Ham. Where 30.2% of spending remained in the Premier League in summer 2022, the figure hit 39.3% this year.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

With the combined outlay growing by almost £1.5bn in that period, what appears a relatively small percentage shift becomes a significant figure in the accounts. The squad cost ratio rules are unlikely to stem this flow either, because clubs will be happy to sell for inflated fees which can almost only come from within the division.

Barcola was the oldest of the five costliest signings from overseas, with Matias Fernandez-Pardo and Jérémy Jacquet (aged 21), Johan Manzambi (aged 20) and Ayyoub Bouaddi (aged 18) completing the set. The Premier League is able to retain its top stars, its clubs exchanging them among themselves, while having the funds to hoover up the most exciting young talent from elsewhere.

Squad-building trends may be evolving in the Premier League, but the money is here and a significant portion of it is not going anywhere else. English football is starting to become an enclosed ecosystem.

The rest of Europe cannot keep up

Very few clubs across Europe come close to competing financially. The Premier League features a match this weekend between the top two teams in Europe for net spend and it isn’t Arsenal v Chelsea. Liverpool’s trip to Ipswich takes the honour.

The promoted sides have invested enormous sums to try to be competitive. They have all played League One football within the previous eight seasons, yet Real Madrid are the only club from another country with a higher net spend than Hull or Coventry.

The cream of the Premier League crop can probably only move within England. The transfer fee for Rogers (£117m) or Anderson (£116m) was above the net spend of 75 of the 76 top-flight clubs in France, Germany, Italy and Spain. Milan narrowly spent over the cost of Sandro Tonali (£92.5m) net, but no other side beyond Madrid from mainland Europe did. Most non-English sides would have to have a clearout of talent to raise funds for a single elite player from the Premier League, which isn’t practical.

This financial dominance can be seen in continental competitions. Five English clubs have featured in the past eight Champions League finals, as many teams as the rest of Europe has provided in that time. The Premier League has supplied three of the past four Europa League finalists and three of the past four Conference League winners. This is unlikely to change when relegation favourites in England can outspend all but the very richest clubs overseas.

Sports.title: Football Daily | War chests, deal sheets and online meltdowns: anatomy of a deadline day
Sports.content:
SHUT IT

Release clauses. War chests. Amortisation. Transfer requests. Surplus to requirements. Online meltdowns. Agents. Gazumping. Buy-back clauses. Options. Add-ons. Personal terms. Soft approaches. Grifters. Clickbait. Lowball bids. In The Knows. Serious bids. Super agents. Hijacked bids. Agreements in principle. Medicals. Undisclosed fees. Part exchanges. Deal sheets. Here we gos! Done deals. Some busker strumming a guitar in the Sky Sports News studio while reminiscing about Deadline Days passim through the medium of song. No really, some busker strumming a guitar in the Sky Sports News studio while etc, and so on. After a near relentless onslaught of media buzzwords, hype and assorted reputable (and thoroughly disreputable) transfer insiders announcing they “understand” things, the summer transfer window is finally shut. But what’s that Football Daily can see pressed up against the glass? The out-of-joint nose of an apoplectic David Moyes.

While the likes of Liverpool, Aston Villa, Coventry, Crystal Palace, Fulham and Manchester United were all flagged up as clubs who endured the worst summer transfer window by assorted experts in one of many deadline day post-mortems perused by Football Daily, we’re going to respectfully suggest their opinions were solicited and prepared for publication before news broke on Tuesday night that Folarin Balogun had decided Everton would not be such A Grand Old Team To Play For and absconded from Finch Farm leaving a trail of dust. The USA USA USA striker’s late change of heart when a deal for his transfer from Monaco to Merseyside had been all but signed, sealed and delivered is reported to have left Everton insiders “shocked”, “disappointed” and with just one out-and-out striker in the form of the endearingly hapless Thierno Barry to see them through until the new year. Indeed, such was the club recruitment department’s determination to get the Balogun deal over the line, nobody appears to have noticed they only have 18 outfield players, not one of whom looks particularly at home at full-back. While the obvious gag involves a late intervention from the White House, whether or not a certain free agent named Séamus Coleman can be tempted out of his recent retirement remains to be seen.

While Manchester City’s deadline day acquisitions of Iliman Ndiaye and Enzo Fernández sent Premier League spending during the summer window up towards a record £3.5bn mark, no last-gasp deal illustrated the sheer obscenity of this unseemly meat-market more than the tug-of-war between Sunderland and Crystal Palace to secure the services of Malick Fofana from Lyon. A young Belgium winger most fans of both clubs probably couldn’t have picked out of a police lineup before Tuesday, Fofana was ferried to a French airport where different private jets from both clubs had been dispatched to fly him to London or Wearside, depending on his mood. Cue: the arrival of a third plane containing Sunderland’s billionaire owner, who eventually persuaded him to board the one festooned with red and white stripes. “The club plays an integral role in economic and environmental change, helping to protect our great city from the effects of climate change,” brags a message that can currently be found on the Sunderland website, albeit in a position of far less prominence than the announcement of their newest recruit. And so until January, when the all the planes refuel and the madness inevitably restarts.

RECOMMENDED FOLLOWING

Now on BlueSpace, TikBook, Instachat, all the lesser disgraces.

QUOTE OF THE DAY

“It’s going to be difficult for me to stay with the national team. Because of the suspension as well, because of Leo’s decision … It’s ‌going to be difficult for everything to carry on as before” – Leandro Paredes says he may retire from international duty with Argentina after Lionel Messi’s decision to do likewise and his 10-match ban for going berserk after the Geopolitics World Cup final.

View image in fullscreen Leandro Paredes starts to ponder his international future. Photograph: Charly Triballeau/AFP/Getty Images

double quotation mark If you’d told me back in the golden era of Serie A in the 1990s that it would eventually become a dumping ground for underperforming (or past their best in the case of John Stones) Premier League players, judging by Tuesday’s front page of La Gazzetta dello Sport, then I wouldn’t have believed you. And if you’d told me in January that Donyell Malen, who scored seven goals in 35 Premier League games for Aston Villa before going on loan to Roma, would already be on 19 goals in 20 Serie A games, I definitely wouldn’t have believed you” – Noble Francis.

double quotation mark Looks like Argentina have lined up James Maddison to replace Lionel Messi. That is if a street artist in Mumbai (yesterday’s Quote of the Day) can be believed” – Vaughan Wilkinson.

View image in fullscreen Not a bad shout. Photograph: Ashish Vaishnav/SOPA Images/Shutterstock

double quotation mark So Folarin Balogun’s transfer to Everton collapsed at the last moment. Surely a call to Donald Trump would have solved the issue” – Nigel Sanders (and a few others).

double quotation mark I’m a bit disappointed in reader Justin Kavanagh announcing his international football retirement too (yesterday’s Football Daily letters). Why give up so abruptly? With the expansion of the Nations League World Cup Conmebol-CAF thingees, it’s easier than ever to get called up. Surely Mr Kavanagh has a relative from Mauritius, one who lives in the Galapagos, or at least a strong liking of Laotian food. Yeah, there are ways to make this work” – Mike Wilner.

If you have any, please send letters to the.boss@theguardian.com. Today’s prizeless letter o’ the day goes to … Vaughan Wilkinson. Terms and conditions for our competitions, when we run them, are here.

Sports.title: Richarlison could still leave Tottenham as Trabzonspor weigh up bid for striker
Sports.content:
Richarlison is the subject of firm interest from Trabzonspor and could move there from Tottenham before the closure of the transfer window in Turkey on Friday night.

The striker has asked to leave, according to the Spurs manager, Roberto De Zerbi, who did not stand in the way of two of his other players who did so before the deadline in England on Tuesday night: Kevin Danso and Pape Sarr. They were allowed to join Sunderland and Juventus respectively on loans with purchase clauses.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

De Zerbi said on Saturday after his team’s home loss to Newcastle that Richarlison had requested to leave “too many times” this summer. It looked as if the Brazilian might return to his former club Everton, as Spurs tried to sign Iliman Ndiaye, only for that not to happen. Ndiaye ended up going to Manchester City for £60m plus £5m in add-ons.

Richarlison was emotional when he used social media on Monday evening to say, in essence, that he would not be forced into a move he did not want. He appears to want Trabzonspor and is understood to have agreed personal terms. The 29-year-old, Spurs’ top scorer in the Premier League last season with 11 goals, has one year on his contract with the option of an extra year.

Trabzonspor signed Mohamed Salah on a free from Liverpool over the summer but have endured a bad start, taking four points from three league matches and losing 5-0 on aggregate to Ferencvaros in the Europa League playoff round.

Spurs currently have 18 senior non-homegrown players on their books including Richarlison – which is one more than the number permitted in a Premier League squad. Xavi Simons, however, is out until March or April, according to De Zerbi, with an anterior cruciate ligament injury. Clubs are permitted to make changes to their squads after the mid-season transfer window.

Sports.title: Women’s Super League 2026-27 preview No 12: Manchester United
Sports.content:
Guardian writers’ predicted position: 7th (NB: this is not necessarily Tom Garry’s prediction but the average of our writers’ tips)

Last season’s position: 4th

Prospects

It was all-change at Manchester United during pre-season, with the departure of their head coach Marc Skinner after five years followed swiftly by the appointment of Eva Olid as a new era begins. There have been significant outgoings from the playing group, including the senior squad members Melvine Malard, Gabby George, Millie Turner and Lisa Naalsund, as well as the end-of-contract exits of Leah Galton and Hannah Blundell, but the signings of the Spain youth international defender Andrea Medina, the former Germany youth international goalkeeper Janina Leitzig and the Sweden forward Monica Jusu Bah will give the squad a fresh feel.

Missing out on the Women’s Champions League places by nine points last season was disappointing and after a summer in which other clubs have spent big, it feels more likely United will be looking over their shoulder at challengers coming up from fifth and sixth than mounting a title challenge.

Tottenham’s and London City’s ambitious recruitment mean they could threaten United’s position but United have not turned into a bad team overnight. European quarter-finalists last season, their squad retains a strong level of quality international players, despite the sale of Malard to Chelsea in particular. The England internationals Maya Le Tissier and Ella Toone are the senior leaders in a squad that also retains a world-class goalkeeper in Phallon Tullis-Joyce, the dynamic England midfielder Jess Park and the talented Sweden wing-back Anna Sandberg. A top-half finish feels realistic and the club will hope for strong runs in the domestic cups. There is also understood to be a desire at the club to make the playing style more entertaining for supporters.

Off-field picture

As with the men’s club, the Glazer family own a majority stake and Ineos – led by Sir Jim Ratcliffe – has a minority stake but has control of football operations. The financial history of the women’s team divides opinion in the sport; some argue United are an example of how to run a professional women’s team sustainably, having recorded a profit of £397,000 in their most recent accounts and a profit of £1.34m since reforming their senior women’s team in 2018, while others lament a lack of investment from the ownership compared with the budgets of their rivals such as Arsenal, Chelsea and Manchester City.

The manager

Olid was appointed on 5 August on a two-year deal with the option of a further year. The Spanish coach, who turned 41 in late August, arrives after an impressive spell at Hearts, where she led the club to their first Scottish Women’s Premier League title in May. That made her the SWPL’s manager of the season. It is understood she was chosen by United’s hierarchy because they feel her CV demonstrates a strong track record of developing and improving young players.

Star signing

Bah, who has 11 caps, looks to be an important signing for United from BK Häcken for a fee reportedly of about £400,000. The 23-year-old helped the Swedish club to win the inaugural Women’s Europa Cup – European club-level women’s second competition – last season and she said the opportunity to work with Olid was “perfect” because she wants to improve. She provided seven assists and scored 16 goals for her club last season and United will hope she can settle into the WSL quickly.

View image in fullscreen Monica Jusu Bah arrives in Manchester from the Swedish club BK Häcken. Photograph: Poppy Townson/Manchester United/Getty Images

Stat attack

United made a mockery of underlying data last season. Only Arsenal overachieved against their attacking expected goals by more and only City conceded fewer compared with their xG at the back. They were ranked fourth for expected goal metrics at both ends but the combined variance of +9.86 against those numbers makes them hard to predict this season.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Set for a breakthrough

Layla Drury, an academy graduate, became United’s youngest player and goalscorer when given her debut in the Women’s FA Cup in January at 16, and this summer the 17-year-old became the youngest player to sign a professional contract with the club. She has been added to England’s Under-20 squad for the World Cup in Poland in September and last Saturday scored for the Young Lionesses in their 11-0 warm-up victory against New Caledonia. The forward had previously played for Wales’s youth teams.

What they say

“I always say: ‘My life is football.’ I don’t have other things. I spend probably 24 hours every day on football. It’s my life, my lifestyle and I give everything for the team and for the players. They always have me. Doubts, questions, [it] doesn’t matter the time of the day, I’m going to be there for them. I want to make them better, and that is how I’m going to feel good as a coach, seeing the improvement, seeing that they are better, and of course, winning matches” – Olid to MUTV.

Where are they playing their home games?

United play at Leigh Sports Village, a 12,000-capacity venue which is also the home of the rugby league club Leigh Leopards and the United’s men’s under-21s. It has been their home ground since 2018. The stadium hosted a quarter-final at Euro 2022. United’s final home WSL fixture, against Arsenal in May, has been scheduled for Old Trafford, although that match may have to be rearranged if Arsenal reach the semi-finals of the Women’s Champions League because the second legs are that weekend.

Sports.title: Which footballer has had the most glittering club career? | The Knowledge
Sports.content:
“Marquinhos won his 40th trophy in club football when Paris Saint-Germain beat Aston Villa in the Super Cup,” notes Paul Gage. “Has any player won more?”

The short answer is no: here’s Pete Tomlin with the breakdown. “I calculate that Marquinhos has actually won 41 trophies – one Copa Libertadores, 11 Ligue 1 titles, eight Coupes de France, six Coupes de la Ligue, 10 Trophées des Champions, two Champions Leagues, two Super Cups and one Intercontinental Cup.” Not a bad haul. “This puts him at No 1 in the list of club trophies won by a player. Just behind is Lionel Messi with 40 (10 La Ligas, 7 Copas Del Rey, 7 Supercopas de España, four Champions Leagues, three Super Cups, three Club World Cups, two Ligue 1 titles, one Trophées des Champions, one MLS Cup, one Supporters Shield and one Leagues Cup).

“Third on the list is the Egyptian midfielder Hossam Ashour with 39 (13 Egyptian League titles, four Egypt Cups, 10 Super Cups, six CAF Champions Leagues, one CAF Confederations Cup and five CAF Super Cups). Clear in fourth place is Dani Alves (one Copa do Nordeste, five Copas del Rey, five Supercopas de España, two Uefa Cups, four Super Cups, six La Liga titles, three Champions Leagues, three Club World Cups, one Serie A title, one Coppa Italia, two Ligue 1 titles, one Coupe de France, one Coupe de la Ligue, one Trophées des Champions and one Campeonato Paulista).”

Barcelona, Fifa and the Royal Spanish Football Federation credit Messi with winning the 2005 Supercopa de España, which would place him equal with Marquinhos, but he did not feature in the squad for either game so we’re not having that. If you have a player who can surpass that, drop us a line.

Oh brother(s)

“Three of Kevin Lisbie’s sons are playing professionally; in the Championship (Kyrell, Millwall), in League One (Kyreece, Reading) and League Two (Kaion, Colchester United),” wrote Stuart Willsher last week. “Have we ever had four brothers playing in all four top English divisions?”

Our thoughts immediately turned to the five Shankly brothers, Bill, Bob, Jimmy, Alec and John. All played professionally across Scotland and England but only including tiers one, three and four in England. Thankfully, Mike O’Dea and Michael Haughey were on hand with a better example. “As many will email in about, the five Clarke brothers of Willenhall – Frank, Allan, Derek, Kelvin and Wayne – all played league football but they were never spread across all four divisions,” Michael writes.

“Between 1975 and 1978 there were four Clarke brothers at league clubs. Kelvin in the third with Walsall, Derek in the second with Oxford and Orient, Frank in the second with Carlisle and Allan in the top flight with Leeds. Wayne made his First Division debut with Wolves in the final game of the 1977-78 season, so briefly there were five Clarke brothers playing in the league. That summer Frank and Kelvin retired, also Derek would play only one more game, while on loan at Carlisle. Allan joined Fourth Division Barnsley as player-manager. This was the only time one of the Clarke brothers played fourth-tier football. He promptly got Barnsley promoted at the first attempt.”

So the Clarke brothers played across the top four tiers in England if you allow for Allan covering tiers one and four, but they definitely didn’t cover all four in one season, missing out narrowly in 1978.

Caught in no-man’s land (part two)

It seems we have a new winner in regards to the question last month about the furthest up the field a keeper had been sent off, so kudos to Luke Levy, who got back in touch. “You mentioned Adrián’s incident in 2015 that got him red-carded outside the opponent’s box,” he writes, “but I can’t believe you’ve forgotten Oliver Kahn’s insane exploits in March 2001. With Bayern Munich trailing Hansa Rostock 3-2, Kahn went up for the corner and, using all his tenacity, explosiveness and wit, leapt above the rest to double-fist punch the ball into the opponent’s net. That was within the opponents’ six-yard box, with Kahn given a second yellow. I would like to see any other exploit in taking an early bath that beats that.”

“Midnite are the 26-27 shirt sponsors for three Championship sides; Middlesbrough, Sheffield United and Wolves,” Peter Skilton notes. “This means they will be the sponsors of at least one of the teams in 24% of Championship fixtures this season. Is this a record, and which brand has sponsored the most different teams in a single league?”

Dirk Maas comes in clutch with the answer here. “In 1987, Coca-Cola made a sponsorship deal with multiple Campeonato Brasileiro Série A teams. In 1990, 16 out of 20 teams were sponsored by Coca-Cola. Only Corinthians (Kalunga), Flamengo (Lubrax), Náutico (Banorte) and Portuguesa (Hudson) did not have Coca-Cola as shirt sponsor. Caixa almost matched Coca Cola’s feat in 2017: 14 out of 20 Campeonato Brasileiro Série A teams were sponsored by them.”

Knowledge archive

On 31 March 2012, towards the end of Stockport’s heroic 3-1 win at Kettering, a substitution took place with Daniel Lucas Rowe being replaced by Daniel Martin Rowe,” Alex Dixon wrote in 2012. “Both are known as Danny Rowe – is the first substitution involving two players with the same name?”

No, but luckily Henrik Hansen is on hand to elaborate and help us to flesh out this answer. “In the 1995-96 Danish Superliga season, FC Copenhagen had two players in their squad named Morten Nielsen,” he reveals. “One of them was usually referred to as Morten B Nielsen (short for Morten Bøhme Nielsen) to avoid confusion. On one occasion, an away game on 31 March at Vejle, the two players were substituted with Morten Nielsen replacing Morten B Nielsen after 73 minutes of play.”

Can you help?

“Slavia Prague and Fenerbahçe have played each other in the Conference League, Europa League and have been drawn to play each other in this season’s UCL league stage,” Önder Susam begins. “Has this happened before? Can it be bettered by teams who have also played each other in Intertoto Cup or Cup Winners’ Cup?”

“I read a few days ago that the Dutch outfit NEC Nijmegen have played six times in the Netherlands cup final and that they have lost all those (1972-73, 1982-83, 1993-94, 1999-2000, 2023-24, 2025-26),” Bogdan Kotarlic notes. “I have an impression that there must be an even worse team for losing cup finals, either in domestic or international cups. Am I right?”

“On Saturday, Clyde were winning 3-0 at The Spartans after an hour when Logan Dunachie was sent off. Twenty-eight minutes later, the score was 3-3. What is the biggest turnaround in a game following a red card/most quantitative blame that can be thrown at a player for getting sent off?” asks Jamie Wills.

“Chesterfield’s goalkeepers have saved the last five penalties they’ve faced (Zach Hemming with two and Ryan Boot with three.) Are they remotely close to a record?” wonders Stuart Basson.

Sports.title: Fernández completes record-equalling £125m move from Chelsea to Manchester City
Sports.content:
Manchester City have equalled the British transfer record with a £125m deal to sign Enzo Fernández from Chelsea, who were left raging after their attempts to replace the Argentina midfielder were dashed by Monaco reneging on an agreement to sell Lamine Camara on Tuesday night.

On a day of twists and turns, City emerged in a strong position after they bolstered their attack by signing Iliman Ndiaye from Everton for up to £65m and secured one of Enzo Maresca’s biggest targets on a five-year deal. Chelsea held out for a huge fee for Fernández and it seemed they were going to find a replacement for him as the transfer window drew to a close.

The club moved to agree a £47m fee with Monaco for Camara, who was poised to sign a six-year contract with the option of an extra year. Chelsea swooped when Everton’s attempts to sign the USA striker Folarin Balogun ran into difficulties. It left Monaco needing to raise funds from elsewhere, prompting Chelsea to revive their move for Camara after having a £38.1m offer for the 22-year-old Senegal midfielder rejected earlier in the day.

Chelsea had a written agreement with Monaco but were stunned by the Ligue 1 club pulling out of the deal as the deadline approached. Sources called Monaco’s conduct “deeply unprofessional”. As an extraordinary situation developed it emerged that Everton, who have also loaned Jack Grealish from City, had refused to give up on Balogun, renegotiating the fee for the former Arsenal forward only for that deal to also fall down just after midnight.

The collapse of Camara’s move did not lead to Chelsea cancelling the sale of Fernández to City. The deal means City have spent £327m on midfielders this summer following the arrivals of Elliot Anderson from Nottingham Forest for £116m and Ayyoub Bouaddi from Lille for £86m.

“I could not be happier to be here, and I am ready for the challenge of helping City continue winning trophies. This is a club built for success,” said Fernández, who becomes this country’s most expensive player alongside Alexander Isak, who joined Liverpool from Newcastle for £125m a year ago.

“I pride myself on continually improving my game. Anyone who’s worked with me will know how hard I train every single day and how much I put into matches. I give absolutely everything and I can promise Manchester City that will continue now I’m here.”

View image in fullscreen Iliman Ndiaye also completed his move to Manchester City on a busy deadline day for the club’s sporting director, Hugo Viana. Photograph: Manchester City FC

Maresca has a good relationship with Fernández after coaching him at Chelsea and a reunion has been on the cards for a while. City opened talks with Chelsea on Monday night and will feel they have successfully rebuilt their midfield after selling Rodri to Barcelona and losing Bernardo Silva to Real Madrid, while also selling Nico González to Newcastle. They were also not put off even after Chelsea’s unofficial deadline for clubs to lodge bids of £120m for Fernández passed last month.

Fernández has been angling for a way out of Chelsea since March and his departure was announced in a short statement on the club’s website. The 25-year-old, who scored 31 goals after joining from Benfica for £106.7m in January 2023, initially had his sights set on joining Real Madrid. He grew disillusioned following Maresca’s acrimonious split with Chelsea this year. Fernández, the unofficial vice-captain, spoke out after Chelsea were knocked out of the Champions League by Paris Saint-Germain in March. Chelsea responded by banning him for two games.

Fernández reported back to training after the World Cup and was booed by Chelsea fans during a pre-season friendly against Real Sociedad at Stamford Bridge. He featured in the club’s opening first game of the season, coming off the bench to help Xabi Alonso’s side to beat Fulham, but was left out of Chelsea’s next two fixtures.

Chelsea came round to the view that a sale was in their interests. There is a feeling within the club that Fernández, who won the Conference League and Club World Cup during his time in west London, had not shown himself to be vice-captain material.

Chelsea have made in the region of £500m in loans and sales this summer. They finished the window by selling Marc Guiu to RB Leipzig for £16m and loaning Dário Essugo to Strasbourg, Robert Sánchez to Como and Mykhailo Mudryk to Tottenham. Tosin Adarabioyo joined Spurs on a permanent deal.

Sports.title: Football connects communities but can pull them apart if governed carelessly | Cath Bishop
Sports.content:
The fight for the soul of football isn’t just happening in the offices of Uefa and Fifa, it’s taking place on pitches much closer to home. At the weekend games of football for 750 children aged five to six in Scotland were cancelled because of severe behavioural issues within the ironically named “Fun 4s” programme. Seventy-two red cards were handed out in the first week of the season. Accounts describe adults displaying aggression, intimidation and head-butting as if it’s the “wild west”.

This isn’t just a Scottish problem. Contacts I speak to in different roles around football confirm and almost accept that “youth football is atrocious”. This should be sounding major alarm bells, for the consequences go way beyond the pitch. The existing disciplinary systems and PR campaigns are not nearly enough to address and change the situation.

It’s incredibly selfish and socially corrosive for an adult to intervene and spoil the experience of kids playing football. There are no good outcomes. For the children, they learn to associate football, and potentially life more broadly, with violence and aggression. They are robbed of a space to be free, to play and develop and have fun alongside their friends. They see adults role-modelling a dog-eat-dog, win-at-all-costs mentality that is not laying the foundations for them to become good team players, school pupils or later civic-minded citizens. It also prevents young people from developing a love of being active and working positively in a team, perhaps one of the most powerful elements for a healthy life. It’s not a great way to develop parenting skills, either.

There is no shortage of evidence about how important it is – whether you are trying to develop skilful football players or healthy young people – that children need space to play, try stuff out and thrive. We also know that it’s what children want from sport. Research by Amanda Visek at the Milken Institute of Public Health at George Washington University, confirms that when it comes to organised sport, kids just want to have fun. What counts for girls and boys are things such as trying your best, working hard, playing well together as a team. When mapping 81 determinants of fun, “winning” ranked 40th in importance.

The Campaign for Children’s Rights in Football is an independent and impartial organisation. It’s preparing to launch and trying to create a greater platform for its work in the sport internationally. It’s needed more than ever.

The Centre for Young Lives set up the Raising the Nation Play Commission that published its report last year as part of a campaign for a national strategy to put play back into children’s lives. Last year the Scottish government published Scotland’s Play Vision Statement and Action Plan 2025-2030 to ensure that “every child is able to play across all stages and aspects of their life to support their social development, resilience, language and communication development, health, physical and mental wellbeing”. The Scottish FA had a “Let Them Play” campaign. But events playing out in Scotland show just how gaping the void is between government strategies, research and reality. This is going to take more than a communications campaign and a swathe of disciplinary proceedings. But investing in what is required for a deeper cultural change could create many positive ripples across our communities if the governing bodies get serious about making this their priority.

Creating thriving environments, ethics and focusing on the experience of those around you must become the first lesson in coaching training courses whether beginner or advanced. This needs to be the first part of training to be an official, or the conversation when your offer to volunteer is accepted by a local club. For any parents bringing their children to a club, clear standards, expectations and clarity on behaviours on and off the pitch should be integrated from the very first moment.

There is a bigger issue here. Sport is cited rightly as a great space to develop character, resilience, confidence. But that only happens in sports environments set up to develop those things. That wasn’t what was on offer on these Scottish youth football pitches. More sport may not help young people. Better experiences and environments will. That’s a crucial difference that has been missed when metrics have simply focused on growing participation and levels of activity.

Leadership is needed at the highest level. There’s a gap for our prime minister to call for sport to change itself in order to offer more to children and adults across the UK. When Andy Burnham called for “care to be at the heart of everything we do” that should include youth football and other sports experiences.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Elite football clubs have a responsibility, too, as key role models for how to play football. If there are things that happen in the Premier League that we wouldn’t want our children to emulate, we have to stop and ask why these things are happening at all. This question opens up a greater space for football to be a force for good. From their own talent-scouting interests, it’s also vital that future players are able to build on strong foundations of creativity, connection and strong intrinsic motivation – ie the love of the game, not just a love of winning.

Football and sport more widely have the power to unite a nation, to connect communities, to build positive solidarity. But we must also acknowledge, admit and understand that done poorly, without care, without strong leadership and clear cultural principles based on the experiences of all involved, it can pull apart the civic fabric we so desperately need to strengthen.

Sports.title: Women’s Super League 2 predictions: can Newcastle reach promotion and will Watford stay up?
Sports.content:
The Women’s Super League 2 season, which gets under way on Friday when Watford host Burnley, comes with a tweaked format and the introduction of a new fixture. After the expansion of the WSL this summer, only the WSL2 champions are guaranteed promotion and the teams finishing second and third will contest a new, pre-qualifying match to determine who will face the WSL’s second-bottom side in the end-of-season promotion/relegation playoff decider. But which of the 12 sides have the best chances of going up. and who may occupy the relegation places?

Bristol City

Head coach Charlotte Healy. Last season 4th. Predicted finish 2nd.

The division’s top scorers last season, Bristol City’s inconsistency and a tendency to concede too often meant they finished five points off the top three. After a productive-looking transfer window, achieving at least a playoff place feels realistic. The club, owned by the Mercury13 group that also controls FC Como Women and FC Badalona Women in Spain, do not lack ambition. The re-signing of the defender Brooke Aspin from Chelsea is a boost to their backline and they will hope Lotta Lindström can help to replace the goals scored by Lexi Lloyd-Smith, who has left to join the top-flight side Crystal Palace.

Burnley

Manager Jackie Bachteler. Last season Promoted from FAWNL. Predicted finish 8th.

Champions of tier three’s northern section after training full-time last term and completing an “invincible” season without a league defeat, Burnley have strengthened with an array of players with first- and second-tier experience, including the former England, Manchester United and Tottenham striker Rachel Williams, the former Chelsea, Reading and Newcastle defender Deanna Cooper and the former Birmingham captain Christie Harrison-Murray. Another, the Northern Ireland goalkeeper Jackie Burns, said: “We all know that it is very challenging [in WSL2] but we know we are capable of competing and actually putting our name out there as Burnley in this league.”

Durham

Head coach Willie Kirk. Last season 10th. Predicted finish 11th.

For a couple of anxious weeks in June, there was uncertainty as to whether Durham would reach the start line for this campaign. They issued a plea for investment, warned they would have to fold without an urgent cash injection and were saved by the local businessman Geoff Thompson. That was followed by the appointment of a new coach, Willie Kirk. Durham have been a continuous presence in WSL2 since its formation in 2014 and have frequently exceeded expectations, so underestimating them is dangerous, but for how long can this doggedly determined club defy the odds while the wealthier clubs around them spend significantly by comparison?

View image in fullscreen The Durham captain, Sarah Wilson, holds off Liverpool’s Alejandra Bernabé during a pre-season friendly in August. Photograph: Alan Edwards/Alamy

Ipswich Town

Manager David Wright. Last season 9th. Predicted finish 5th.

Ipswich did well in their debut WSL2 campaign last season to steer comfortably clear of relegation by winning their final three league games, and they have carried that momentum into the summer. They have raided the Scottish champions Hearts’ squad for three signings among more than a dozen in total, including Hearts’ top scorer from last season, Georgia Timms. No doubt their technical director, Sean Burt, previously Hearts’ head of recruitment, found his contacts book useful. With the former Spurs midfielder Kit Graham’s loan move made permanent too, the Suffolk club could be dark horses for a top-half push.

Leicester City

Manager Rick Passmoor. Last season Relegated from the WSL. Predicted finish 4th.

Winless since 14 December, Leicester endured a torrid campaign last term and were relegated in agonising fashion when they lost a penalty shootout against Charlton in the inaugural playoff. Inevitably, that prompted a vast number of senior players to depart, including good internationals such as Chantelle Swaby, Jutta Rantala and Hannah Cain. The relegation of the men’s team to League One cannot have helped the side’s resources. Nonetheless, any doom and gloom talk would feel hyperbolic: there remains a decent core of WSL-level players and they have done well to sign Sarah Mayling and Poppy Pritchard, as well as Tottenham’s Araya Dennis on loan.

Newcastle United

Manager Tanya Oxtoby. Last season 6th. Predicted finish 1st.

After drawing nearly half their games last season and not scoring enough, Newcastle have attempted to add quality to their forward line in a search for the goalscorers who can fire them to promotion. The arrivals of the former Manchester United forward Martha Thomas from Tottenham, the Republic of Ireland forward Leanne Kiernan from Liverpool and the Scotland striker Kathleen McGovern – who scored 51 times in 65 games for Hibs and has 10 goals in 14 matches for her country – should propel them to the promised land.

View image in fullscreen Martha Thomas brings a wealth of WSL experience to the Magpies. Photograph: Michelle Mercer/NUFC/Getty Images

Nottingham Forest

Head coach Tom Mallinson. Last season 7th. Predicted finish 6th.

Forest are one of three clubs – with Burnley and Durham – who have hired new coaches, with the appointment of their former men’s under-18s coach Tom Mallinson. The club have said they aim to “push towards the WSL”. They finished mid-table last season and are likely to continue building. The Forest goalkeeper Emily Batty said: “We want to get promoted, that’s the aim of the club. We know that isn’t a given, so it requires a lot of hard work. [It’s about] making sure we’re strong as a collective to get the best out of each other and hopefully help us get to that end-goal, come May.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Sheffield United

Head coach Stephen Healy. Last season 11th. Predicted finish 9th.

Having struggled in the past two years – finishing bottom but getting a reprieve from relegation in 2025, then finishing four points above the drop zone – Sheffield United look likely to face another tricky campaign. Survival depends largely on whether the division’s third-top scorer from last season, Amy Andrews, is still at the club when the transfer window closes on Thursday. She scored nearly half of United’s measly total of 21 goals last season. But they have had a relatively stable, settled summer and have kept the core of their team, and one of their additions – Lucy Quinn – helped Birmingham to win this division last season.

Southampton

Head coach Simon Parker. Last season 5th. Predicted finish 7th.

With their budget understood to have been cut significantly, Southampton have endured a testing summer, and Sunderland signing Atlanta Primus, Tara Bourne and Fran Stenson will have been a blow after such an encouraging campaign last season and their run of five games without defeat at the end. Only Birmingham and Bristol City scored more WSL2 goals last season than Southampton. They have a good coach in Simon Parker, who has overcome adversity in this division before and defied a small budget at Blackburn, so his side should not be completely discounted.

Sunderland

Head coach Melanie Reay. Last season 8th. Predicted finish 3rd.

Sunderland have been taken over by the Bay Collective and have hired the former Tottenham and West Ham manager Rehanne Skinner as their technical director, so hopes are high that they can mount a challenge and become a force in the women’s game again. Melanie Reay is by far the division’s longest-serving head coach, having been in charge for more than nine years, and her team are finally getting true backing behind the scenes. Elise Hughes feels like a good signing from Palace and there is a feelgood mood that may make the difference.

Watford

Head coach Renée Hector. Last season Promoted from FAWNL. Predicted finish 12th.

Promoted as southern section champions, Watford averaged nearly four goals a game. Their signings include the promising England youth international Vera Jones on loan from Chelsea. They look stronger than when last in the second tier in 2023-24 but staying up will be hugely challenging. Watford’s captain, Megan Chandler, who has been at the club since 2019, said: “The last time we were in this league, we were still part-time. Now we’ve transitioned to full time, that’s a huge step in the right direction. We’ve come on leaps and bounds. [We’d like to] establish ourselves in this league. People may think we’re a ‘yo-yo’ team because we have been previously, so I think this year is important for us to show people we’re not just here to survive, we’re here to compete as well.”

View image in fullscreen Flo Fyfe is one of 12 players to have signed a professional contract with the Hornets over the summer. Photograph: Tom Sandberg/PPAUK/Shutterstock

Wolves

Manager Dan McNamara. Last season Promoted from FAWNL. Predicted finish 10th.

Another team who have transitioned to full time, professional status this summer are Wolves, who triumphed in the FAWNL promotion playoff against Plymouth Argyle in May after finishing second in the northern section, a point behind Burnley. Their revamped squad is a blend of new faces who have played at this level or higher and long-serving club stalwarts who will experience WSL2 for the first time. The step up will feel vast but they recruited well, aided by the arrival of their head of women’s and girls’ football, Russ Fraser, who has overseen recruitment at WSL clubs including Liverpool, Leicester, Reading and West Ham. The additions of Melissa Lawley, Yana Daniëls and Mel Filis, for example, should help them to stay up.

Sports.title: Richarlison to get move away from Tottenham and could triple his wages
Sports.content:
Richarlison to get move away from Tottenham and could triple his wages

Richarlison has agreed terms on a lucrative deal to join Trabzonspor ahead of the Turkish transfer window closing, talkSPORT understands.

The Turkish club want to sign the Brazilian and unite him with former Liverpool star Mohamed Salah.

3 Richarlison has asked to leave Tottenham Hotspur Credit: Getty

They have had two offers turned down so far by Tottenham Hotspur.

The first bid was £15million and the second was £20m. However, they are expected to come in with another offer as they look to get the deal tied up.

Fabrizio Romano is reporting that Richarlison will triple his salary if he makes the move.

Roberto De Zerbi told reporters after the 2-0 defeat to Newcastle United at the weekend that the forward had asked to leave the club.

He was one of three, with Kevin Danso and Pape Matar Sarr the other two. Danso joined Sunderland and Sarr is with Juventus, both on loan.

However, Richarlison stayed put. He had looked to be returning to Everton in a deal that was meant to see Iliman Ndiaye go the other way.

They were billed as separate deals, but a series of events unfolded that ensured neither transfer happened.

What happened with Richarlison?

Spurs agreed a fee with Everton to take Ndiaye from them. In return, Richarlison was set to head back to Merseyside, but he failed to agree terms with Everton.

In the time Tottenham were waiting, Manchester City saw a deal for Cody Gakpo collapse. Gakpo chose a switch to the Etihad Stadium over Spurs, but the two clubs couldn't agree a deal.

The reason they couldn't agree a deal is because Liverpool didn't have time to find a replacement. That saw City switch attention to Ndiaye, and he picked Man City over Tottenham.

3 Ndiaye has left Everton for Man City in a £65million deal

And at the same time, Richarlison took to Instagram and emotionally revealed that he felt disrespected by Tottenham.

He made it clear he would only move on his terms as well.

It was in Portuguese, but translated as follows: "After everything I've been through in recent years, I decided that they would never again decide my future for me.

"I've been through a lot of bad things these days and almost all of them happened because of decisions made by other people.

"Pressure, threats, retaliations, none of this scares me. I've been through worse things… believe me!

"I have always made it clear, at every opportunity, that an exit of mine to another place would also have to be good for the club.

3 Richarlison might get the move he carves Credit: Getty

"If it wasn't, I would never accept… as I didn't accept when everything here was falling apart and they needed me.

"I stayed and gave my life. So, I hope you treat my situation with the same respect that I always had for Spurs and for all the people who worked with me during this period. Just don't want to decide for me.

"If they enter into an agreement between Spurs and Everton, I go back to my favourite team.

"My intention was to return to the place where I was very happy. But the negotiations were the way people wanted and it won't be like this anymore.

"Despite this riot, I have a contract with Spurs and I will be at the club's disposal."

Turkish transfer window

The Turkish transfer window is still open, and it is when the main European one closes that these sides usually spring into life.

Teams in Turkey have until Friday, September 4 to sign players.

So, they still have plenty of time to get Richarlison wrapped up as long as they agree a fee with Spurs.

Sports.title: Enzo Fernandez lands Premier League icon’s shirt number in Man City move
Sports.content:
Enzo Fernandez will wear the No.17 shirt at Manchester City - previously worn by Premier League icon Kevin De Bruyne.

The midfielder finally joined the Citizens from Chelsea for £125million on transfer deadline day in record-equalling deal.



3 Fernandez left Chelsea for Man City in a record-equalling Premier League deal on transfer deadline day Credit: PA

It spelled the end of a long-running transfer saga involving Fernandez, who flirted with an exit from Stamford Bridge all summer.

Having first had his heart set on a move to Real Madrid, the Argentina star sealed a Premier League switch at the 11th hour after Man City emerged as suitors in recent weeks.

Chelsea previously set a deadline of 5pm on Friday, August 14 for interested clubs to meet their £120m asking price, only for the cut-off point to pass without City making an offer.



Despite the Blues' stance, the deal accelerated in the final hours of the transfer window and was announced just after the 11pm deadline.

Fernandez's departure came in a chaotic end to Deadline Day, which saw Chelsea miss out on signing Monaco's Lamine Camara as a replacement, with the Ligue 1 side turning their back on the £47m deal previously agreed between the two clubs.



Fernandez inherits De Bruyne's shirt

Having sealed a move to the Etihad, Fernandez is now looking to inspire City to glory, and has been handed an iconic shirt number.

Less than 24 hours after his arrival, the Citizens confirmed the 25-year-old will wear the No.17 jersey.



He inherits the number from club legend De Bruyne, who vacated it last summer after a trophy-laden ten years at the club.

During that time, De Bruyne scored 108 goals and provided 177 assists in 422 appearances, as well as winning 17 trophies.

Before the Belgian great, winger Martin Petrov took ownership for three years until 2010, while Jerome Boateng, Michael Johnson and Jack Rodwell have all previously donned the shirt too.

3 De Bruyne established himself as one of the Premier League's all-time greats whilst wearing the No.17 shirt for Man City Credit: Getty



But with De Bruyne becoming synonymous with the jersey during his time at City, Fernandez has some way to go to live up to his legacy in Manchester.

The Argentine revealed the number carries personal significance when explaining his picking of the No.17 shirt.

He told Man City's official website: “It’s a number I like.

“It embodies me. It was my first number in the national team, so I’m very happy to choose this number.”

While Fernandez cannot yet touch any of De Bruyne's achievements in a City shirt, he heads to the Etihad as a proven winner.



The ex-Benfica star boasts 2022 World Cup glory with Argentina on his CV, while lifted the Conference League and Club World Cup trophies at Chelsea - winning both under new City boss Enzo Maresca.

3 Fernandez has now reunited with his former boss at Chelsea, Enzo Maresca Credit: Getty

And Fernandez shared his delight at joining the Citizens and sealing a reunion with Maresca.

He said upon arrival: “Every player wants to be part of a club like this because everyone knows how well-run City are.



“I could not be happier to be here, and I am ready for the challenge of helping City continue winning trophies. This is a club built for success.

“If you look across the squad, City have quality in every area. I want to learn from my new teammates and become a better player.

“I pride myself on continually improving my game. Anyone who’s worked with me will know how hard I train every single day and how much I put into matches. I give absolutely everything and I can promise Manchester City that will continue now I’m here.”

Sports.title: Morgan Whittaker secures Middlesbrough exit in record-breaking move
Sports.content:
Morgan Whittaker is set to join MLS side Colorado Rapids from Middlesbrough in a $10.7million (£7.9m) deal, talkSPORT understands.

With the MLS summer transfer window closing on Wednesday night, Whittaker is primed to complete a club-record move to the US outfit before the deadline.

3 Whittaker is set to leave Middlesbrough after 18 months at the Riverside

According to reports, the Middlesbrough winger is flying to the US to finalise the move after completing a medical in London on Tuesday.

Whittaker joined Boro for a fee of around £7m in January 2025 from Plymouth Argyle.

The 25-year-old went on to play an instrumental role for the club last season as the Championship side secured a play-off finish.

He registered 14 goals and seven assists in 40 appearances, as Boro's promotion push initially ended at the semi-final stage after they crashed to a final-four loss to Southampton.

However, as a result of the 'Spygate' scandal, they were reinstated at Saints' expense, only to fall to a late 1-0 defeat to Hull in the Championship showpiece at Wembley back in May.

Whittaker's impressive displays have made him a hot property this summer, with West Ham previously showing an interest.

talkSPORT previously revealed in July that the Hammers were looking to complete a deal for the forward before the start of the Championship season, having seen star winger Crysencio Summerville depart to join Al Hilal.

But Whittaker now looks set to follow in Summerville's footsteps by securing a move away from English football.

Rapids' big business

Whittaker is now on the brink of joining the Colorado Rapids in a new record transfer for the club.

The Rapids' previous record is $7m (£5.2 m) to sign current star Paxten Aaronson from Eintracht Frankfurt in 2025.

3 Whittaker will no longer be plying his trade under Boro boss Kim Hellberg Credit: Getty

Once he completes a move, Whittaker will join up with English coach Matt Wells in Colorado.

Wells has overseen an attacking overhaul this summer and is now placing an emphasis on wide play, with Whittaker viewed as the main man to spearhead this.

With the Rapids set to shell out a landmark fee for the Boro star, they are also doing business in the opposite direction.

According to the Athletic, forward Rafa Navarro is set to join St. Louis City in a deal worth $12m (£8.8m).

The MLS Western Conference side also sold centre-back Lucas Herrington to Hull this summer for an initial fee of $17m (£13m) plus add-ons that could take the deal past £20m, in a record fee for an Australian player.

As well as Whittaker, Israel international forward Sayed Abu Farchi has also completed a move to Colorado for a $6m (£4.4m) fee.

3 Herrington was a high-profile departure from the Colorado Rapids this summer, and has since made his Premier League debut for Hull Credit: Getty

MLS sides are allowed to sign a maximum three designated players - a rule that allows franchises to sign up to three players considered outside their salary cap.

And Whittaker's anticipated arrival will see to become the Rapids' club second DPs, alongside Aaronson.

Colorado have enjoyed a solid season so far, and currently sit seventh in the Western Conference with 31 points after 22 matches.

Sports.title: Burnley staged outrageous deadline day hijack with player already travelling to join rivals
Sports.content:
Burnley staged outrageous deadline day hijack with player already travelling to join rivals

New Burnley signing Reo Hatate was travelling to join Blackburn Rovers when the Clarets hijacked the deadline day deal.

talkSPORT has learned an agreement between Celtic and Blackburn was in place to loan the 28-year-old midfielder before Burnley swooped in under the noses of their fiercest rivals.



1 Celtic's Hatate joined Burnley after agreeing to sign for rivals Blackburn Credit: Kenny Ramsay

Hatate was given permission to travel and looked set to link up with compatriots Yuki Ohashi and Ryoya Morishita at Ewood Park.

Blackburn were under the impression that, even by late afternoon, the deal would go through for the Japan international.

Yet while en route to undergo a Rovers medical, and with only hours left on deadline day, Burnley moved in to agree a fee with Celtic, with the Scottish champions favouring a permanent exit.



The Clarets have paid around £6.5million plus add-ons for Hatate and he has signed a three-year contract at the club.

In a fortunate coincidence, Hatate was already heading in the right direction, so the change of destination was easy.



Burnley’s Turf Moor and Blackburn’s Ewood Park are only 15 miles apart.

And he won’t have to wait too long to come up against the club he could have joined, as Burnley host Blackburn on November 22 in the East Lancashire derby.



Hatate made 191 appearances and scored 33 for Celtic since joining from Kawasaki Frontale in 2022.

He won five league titles, two Scottish Cups and two Scottish League Cups during his time at Celtic Park.

Hatate now heads to Turf Moor to bolster the midfield as Burnley seek an immediate return to the Premier League.

Hatate: 'A great move for me'

Hatate was delighted to join Burnley after the hijack, joining up with Nicky Hayen's side ahead of their clash against Middlesbrough.



"This is a great move for me," he told the club's website. "It's my first time playing in England and it's a fantastic club to be joining.

"I'm hoping to bring my experience and knowledge to the dressing room and help the team on the pitch as much as possible to achieve our aim."

Burnley take on Boro on Wednesday evening at 8pm, with talkSPORT 2 providing exclusive coverage of the action.

Commentary will come from Ian Danter and Cameron Jerome.
