World.title: Thousands of U.S. service members arrive in Thailand after record stint at sea
World.content:
LAEM CHABANG, Thailand — The USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier arrived Wednesday at a port in eastern Thailand, where thousands of U.S. sailors and Marines are disembarking for the first time in more than 280 days after a record-setting deployment in the Middle East.

The toll of the more than nine-month deployment, most of it spent supporting military operations in the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran, was visible on the carrier as it pulled into Laem Chabang Port in Chonburi province. Paint has worn off and the metal underneath is rusted on the 1,092-foot warship, which is one of the largest in the world.

Service members ofrom the USS Abraham Lincoln arrive at a hotel in Pattaya, Thailand, on Wednesday. Sakchai Lalit / AP

The Lincoln is in Thailand for a four-day “rest and relaxation” stop on its way home to San Diego after having spent weeks in the headlines as the lengthy deployment raised concerns about supply shortages and the effect on sailors’ mental health.

The USS Abraham Lincoln approaching Laem Chabang Port near Pattaya on Wednesday. Mithil Aggarwal / NBC News

The U.S. Navy confirmed the ship’s arrival in a statement, saying the Lincoln strike group arrived in Laem Chabang while the destroyer USS Frank E. Petersen Jr. docked in nearby Sriracha and the guided-missile cruiser USS Robert Smalls went to Map Ta Phut in neighboring Rayong province.

The Navy said it was the Lincoln’s first full port stop after 286 days at sea since the deployment began in November.

This will be the first time on dry land for the sailors after a record-setting stint at sea. Anthony Wallace / AFP via Getty Images

“Our arrival in Laem Chabang provides a well-deserved opportunity for our sailors and Marines to rest and recharge,” said Rear Adm. Robert E. Loughran, commander of Carrier Strike Group 3. “It also underscores the strong and enduring partnership and alliance between the United States and Thailand.”

About 5,000 sailors and Marines are expected to hit the streets of Pattaya, a nearby coastal resort city that is one of the most popular tourist destinations in Thailand. Each service member will get three “liberty days” and one day of duty aboard the ship, a U.S. military official said.

Local businesses in Pattaya have welcomed the sailors with large banners outside restaurants and bars. Sakchai Lalit / AP

Upon the Lincoln’s arrival in the morning, service members could be seen working aboard the deck as loudspeakers played announcements about the process for disembarkation. A whistle could be heard ringing across the deck, a Navy tradition that signals coming ashore.

00:16 Thai police crackdown on sex workers 00:00 00:00

Around 1 p.m. local time (2 a.m. ET), service members began disembarking from the ship in civilian clothes, some carrying backpacks. One service member was carrying his golf clubs. Waiting for them across the way were dozens of Ford pickup trucks and buses lined up in columns to take them into town.

“Please be on your best behavior,” a commanding officer could be heard saying over loudspeaker.

Locals in tourism-dependent Pattaya have eagerly awaited the arrival of the Lincoln, which pulled into sight from the shore after sunrise before it made a wide turn and harbored itself at a major cargo terminal.

Officials in Pattaya, where international tourist arrivals have dropped because of travel disruptions and soaring fuel prices stemming from the conflict in the Middle East, say the visit is expected to inject about $3 million into the local economy.

Authorities in Pattaya have stepped up security, with heightened police patrols and checks along the roads. Businesses here are also trying to woo the sailors, with some putting up banners to welcome them.

About 5,000 sailors and Marines are expected to hit the streets of Pattaya. Anthony Wallace / AFP via Getty Images

Wichai Yuankham, 35, a factory worker who came to watch the ships arrive, said the naval visit was a welcome boost to the local economy.

“I am just excited to see the destroyer docking,” he said. “This is my first time seeing the destroyer, and I feel good seeing it, and we can boast to our neighboring countries about this.”

World.title: Colin Kaepernick believes Jay-Z has a ‘guilty conscience’ over deals with NFL and Target
World.content:
Colin Kaepernick said he believes that Jay-Z’s recent comments about him speak to a “guilty conscience,” as the fallout between the former quarterback and the rapper deepens. Kaepernick responded as part of an extensive interview with NBC News after Jay-Z dissed the athlete during a recent concert.

In July, Jay-Z took aim at Kaepernick, the former San Francisco 49ers star, mentioning him and his settlement with the NFL in an impromptu rap during a series of concerts at Yankee Stadium.

“They run out of characters, had to bring back up [Kaepernick] again,” Jay-Z said, referring to people who have criticized him for a recent partnership with Target. “Buddy took a check, I ain’t even mad at him, but along with that check you have to sign a non-disparagement. I’m the one [the NFL] can’t control.”

Earlier this year, Jay-Z drew ire when it was announced that he would sell an exclusive version of his “Reasonable Doubt” album at the retailer, which has been subjected to boycotts by Black shoppers after it rolled back its diversity, equity and inclusion practices.

Kaepernick, on the other hand, is honoring the boycott despite the potential financial cost. A spokesperson for the former quarterback confirmed he would not be selling his upcoming memoir, “The Perilous Fight,” in Target stores. Target did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

For his book tour, Kaepernick is partnering with the National Association of Black Bookstores.

More Colin Kaepernick coverage on NBC News Kaepernick will be the first guest on “Before & After with Lester Holt,” available as soon as Sept. 7.

Kaepernick is set to appear on “TODAY” on Sept. 16.

Jay-Z was freestyling about the hypocrisy of his critics in July when he mentioned Kaepernick. The lyrics were a far cry from 2017, when Jay-Z dedicated a performance of his song “The Story of O.J.” to Kaepernick after he had taken a knee to protest police brutality in America.

At the time, Kaepernick was a free agent. He never found employment in the NFL again after he protested during the national anthem in the 2016 season. Jay-Z, who wore Kaepernick’s jersey during a performance on “Saturday Night Live” in 2017, was one of Kaepernick’s highest-profile supporters.

Jay-Z was critical of the NFL, rapping on the 2018 song “Apes---” with his wife, Beyoncé, “I said no to the Super Bowl. You need me; I don’t need you.”

In his book, Kaepernick wrote that Jay-Z asked him in 2017 to kneel onstage during a performance of “The Story of O.J.” but that he declined, in part because he objected to the use of racial slurs in the lyrics. Kaepernick also wrote that before he was asked to join Jay-Z onstage, he had difficulties connecting with him on the phone as they exchanged emails in an effort to join forces on social justice issues.

Their relationship flipped in August 2019, when Jay-Z announced that Roc Nation, the entertainment company he co-founded, would partner with the NFL. Roc Nation has since produced every Super Bowl halftime show, and it partners with the league on social justice work.

Roc Nation declined to comment to NBC News for this article.

In his book, Kaepernick wrote that Jay-Z told him about the partnership only after it had been agreed to, and Kaepernick expressed his displeasure.

“I just want you to know, one, you’re serving the culture up to a bunch of racists and, two, they don’t care about you,” Kaepernick wrote about what he told Jay-Z when they spoke. “You’re the music guy to them. They quite literally need a Black face—and have said as much.”

In 2019, Jay-Z faced blowback for the NFL deal, as many viewed it as his turning his back on Kaepernick, who remained unemployed by the league.

At a news conference announcing the partnership, Jay-Z defended the decision.

“I think we have moved past kneeling. I think it’s time for action,” he said. “We forget that Colin’s whole thing was to bring attention to social injustice. In that case, this is a success. This is the next phase.”

The NFL declined to comment.

Kaepernick, who told NBC News’ Lester Holt that he did not sign a non-disparagement agreement with the NFL after having settled in 2019 with the league over his collusion lawsuit, said several people sent him the video of the freestyle.

“First and foremost, what it speaks to is power of people,” Kaepernick said about his reaction. “The backlash that [Jay-Z] received for partnering with the NFL and going counter to people’s interests in 2019 was a major problem for him, so much so that he’s still bringing it up in 2026.”

He added: “People are now realizing, ‘Why are you so comfortable stepping into these positions that are counter to the positions that people on the ground actually want?’ And to me, I view that as speaking to a guilty conscience and trying to reposition or reframe the conversation.”

Kaepernick said people who supported him have been consistent in not agreeing with Jay-Z’s actions.

“I haven’t publicly spoken about him in any matter, but it speaks to the level of impact that people are having and being able to continue to move not only individuals but corporations,” he said.

As for why he didn’t respond to Jay-Z immediately after the freestyle, particularly in regard to the misinformation about a non-disparagement agreement, Kaepernick said that there have always been efforts to discredit him and that Jay-Z is “another player” in that effort since he partnered with the NFL.

“He has built the alignment with the NFL, the NFL that has blackballed me, the same NFL that, in a players-owners meeting in 2017, said we need a Black face to help us get rid of the protests,” Kaepernick told NBC News. (The NFL has long denied Kaepernick’s blackballing claims.)

Kaepernick added: “I understand why he’s trying to do reputational recovery. I get it. I don’t agree with the actions, but I’m also not gonna respond to everything that’s said about me, because I also believe the actions and the work that I do will speak for themselves.”

World.title: Arizona congressman heard ‘freight train crash’ sound during Grand Canyon flash flood
World.content:
Rep. David Schweikert, R-Ariz., said he heard what sounded like “a freight train smashing into a boulder” as a Grand Canyon flash flood consumed the landscape near his rafting group Saturday.

Schweikert told NBC News from his office in Washington on Tuesday that the loud crash was followed by a powerful stream of mud and debris-filled water.

Two visitors died and another is still missing after flash flooding from a sudden deluge of rain briefly transformed Bright Angel Creek into a full-fledged river. About 80 people were evacuated from campsites around the historic Phantom Ranch area of the park.

The retiring member of Congress and the rest of his group were about 100 yards away from the danger zone without cellphone service. His guide led the group to an area off the Colorado River near Bright Angel Creek.

They later left the area on foot — traveling on higher ground — and camped for the night nearby.

It is “monsoon season” in Arizona, but Schweikert said there was not more than a drizzle of precipitation where he was when the dangerous flood ripped through, underscoring the potential randomness of such events.

“At some point, you realized this is a big deal; something’s really gone haywire. ... It was a ginormous flash flood,” he said.

“It’s remarkable beauty, but you always take it seriously because the canyon will sneak up on you if you’re not prepared,” Schweikert said. Al Drago / Bloomberg via Getty Images file

The intricate terrain of the Grand Canyon can invite the type of deadly flood conditions that hit the southern part of the national park over the weekend.

“The deluge downpour could have been miles away and was channeled into the canyon, and what used to be a creek now is a river,” said Schweikert, who is a regular Grand Canyon hiker.

The water supply system for the park was also severely damaged, along with part of a new $208 million water pipeline project that was underway near the ranch.

Schweikert said he would likely be involved in working to get the damage addressed once proper assessments are made. “Right now, the heartbreak is a couple of people lost their lives,” he added.

He also cautioned visitors to the park to carefully monitor the weather and to use extreme caution if storms are expected in the vicinity at all. If storms are nearby, hikes through narrow passages known as slot canyons should be strictly avoided because of the risk of getting trapped, the seasoned adventurer said.

“It’s remarkable beauty, but you always take it seriously because the canyon will sneak up on you if you’re not prepared,” Schweikert said.

World.title: Ariana Grande tearfully ends 41-show tour and steps back from public life
World.content:
LONDON — A teary and visibly emotional Ariana Grande bid a temporary farewell to her fans as her 41-show “Eternal Sunshine Tour” concluded in London on Tuesday night, kickstarting her planned withdrawal from public life.

Addressing the audience in London’s famed O2 arena, the pop singer said she was “grateful” to her fans for making her show “so special.”

“This has been one of the most beautiful, extraordinary experiences of my life,” Grande said, dressed in black and perched on a stool on stage. “I just wanted to express my gratitude without sobbing completely.”

“I’ll cherish this experience always,” she added.

Grande, known for hits including “thank you, next” and “hate that i made you love me,” made global headlines in August when she said she would be taking a “step back from visibility” following “public scrutiny.”

The announcement came after the release of her latest music video, “petal,” which reignited a public debate about her health.

Representatives for Grande said last month that she was looking forward to finishing her tour “on a high note, both healthily and happily, and then taking a much-deserved break from public-facing work and appearances, which has led to endless, ongoing public scrutiny.”

Grande concluded her tour in knee-high boots rather than her signature heels after stating she was “bandaged up underneath” following a “deep cut” on her foot, which she called a “minor injury.”

Grande’s “Eternal Sunshine Tour,” which promoted the 2024 album of the same name, began in Oakland, California, in June. She previously labeled the shows “one last hurrah” and has expressed her desire to take on more acting roles.

Grande was nominated for an Oscar for her performance as Glinda in the hit musical movie “Wicked.”

She had been set to reunite with “Wicked” co-star Jonathan Bailey in a revival of Stephen Sondheim’s “Sunday in the Park With George,” in London next summer, before she pulled out last month.

In a statement Tuesday on Instagram, Bailey said he has also decided to “step back” from the Sondheim show. He added that “Ari is one of my dearest friends, and my support for her is unwavering.”

World.title: Customers are losing their appetites over disturbing AI-generated menus
World.content:
AI “slop” is now increasingly on offer at brick-and-mortar establishments.

As AI image-making technology has grown more advanced — and cheaper to use, in some cases being free — images with a distinct “slop” flavor, namely ones with surreal or even disturbing attributes, have begun appearing on bodega, café and restaurant menus.

There’s the shrimp scampi whose shrimp look more like miniature life preservers.

A breakfast burrito with filling that looks more like something out of a horror movie.

And “protein” options that look like they’re covered in bugs.

One X user said she attempted to order an item advertised on a café’s outdoor menu only to learn it didn’t exist and was instead the product of ChatGPT.

The trend comes as the use of AI has grown from a tech-employee specialty to a nearly ubiquitous pursuit among white-collar workers — and as overall inflation in the economy has remained stubborn. The confluence of lingering cost pressures and advancing technology appears to be translating into a boom in smaller businesses deploying AI-designed graphics and logos.

There have been real-world consequences to the trend of AI slop making the jump from online into the real world. A coffee shop in San Francisco paid hundreds of dollars to have graffiti removed that appeared to be in response to its use of AI-generated food images on its facade, SFGate reported.

“I want people to come to our restaurant, but, like, why is this such a big deal that it influences people on such intense level?” co-owner Lyndsey Lozano told the outlet. “Like, is it really that horrific that you have to act on such a feeling?”

Lozano could not be reached for additional comment.

Many of the establishments displaying the food images likely created by AI are smaller, likely family-owned establishments, said Paul Shovlin, an assistant professor of English at Ohio University who studies AI. He said that it may simply be the case that many of the places displaying the AI food are running on shoestring budgets.

For some longtime designers, the advent of AI-related image making has been maddening — not to mention bad for their bottom lines.

World.title: Forget crude oil. The real energy crisis right now is in diesel.
World.content:
The average price of diesel gas on Wednesday hit its highest level since the Iran war started, as a global supply bottleneck tightens and seasonal demand is poised to rise.

The fuel that powers everything from boats and trains to farm equipment and 18-wheelers hit $5.69 a gallon nationwide, according to AAA data. That’s up 33 cents from just a month ago, and 54% from September 2025, when the average price was $3.69 a gallon.

The pace of price increases for diesel have been much higher than for unleaded gasoline, which is up about 29% percent from the same period last year.

“There are more alarms going off for diesel than for other crude oil products,” said Gregory Brew, an analyst with the Eurasia Group consultancy.

Following a diesel-price surge this summer that was largely due to airstrikes targeting refineries in the Middle East, experts say that now the Ukraine war, and specifically Ukrainian drone strikes on oil refineries inside Russia, is having an equal or even greater effect on diesel prices.

The increased cost of producing food this Fall will likely be reflected in prices next Spring. Brandon Bell / Getty Images

Russia is the world’s second largest exporter of diesel fuel after the U.S., Brew noted. With key Russian oil refineries forced offline, the result has been a massive reduction in Eastern European diesel exports, he said.

Meanwhile, U.S. diesel stockpiles in late August had fallen to seasonal levels not seen since the 1980s, according to the federal Energy Information Administration.

As global demand for diesel remains steady, the current supply shock means that refiners in the U.S. and Canada can charge a premium for their diesel products.

Profit margins for major diesel refiners recently hit record highs, according to the EIA. In response to the market forces, U.S. refiners have increased their exports of diesel and related fuels by approximately 28% over the past 12 months.

For major refiners like Valero and Marathon, this has meant a windfall in profits. Since mid-June, both companies have seen their share prices climb by more than 45%.

The growing role that refining capacity is playing in gas prices has also caught the eye of the White House, which is looking for ways to cut consumer prices and slow inflation.

On Tuesday, President Donald Trump summoned about a dozen major U.S. oil refiners to Washington to discuss how to increase capacity.

“This was not a ‘drill, baby, drill’ meeting. This was a ‘refine, baby, refine’ meeting,” said White House Deputy Press Secretary Taylor Rogers, following the meeting.

Rogers told NewsNation the president and the oil executives had discussed potential ways to expand their refining capacity — including possible regulatory changes — but she did not provide specifics.

Across the broader economy, surging prices for a wholesale product like diesel fuel also leaves retailers in a quandary. Do they lower their own profit margins to absorb the higher costs, or pass them on to inflation-weary consumers and risk a drop in sales?

Experts say it’s more likely to be the former, which means that grocery prices could resume their march higher this Fall.

Driving demand for diesel even higher will be farmers around the world, who need it to power agricultural equipment. The annual harvest season in the northern hemisphere corresponds with the planting season below the equator.

The increased cost of producing food this Fall will likely be reflected in prices next Spring, too.

J.P. Morgan analysts recently warned that the global food inflation is expected to hit 5% in the first half of 2027, nearly double the rate in the first half of this year.

More immediately, however, the key month for diesel demand will be October, when home heating, seasonal agriculture and global shipping ahead of the holidays all overlap.

World.title: New immigration court tactic leads to huge lines and chaos in Miami
World.content:
New immigration court tactic leads to huge lines and chaos in Miami

toggle caption Eva Marie Uzcategui for NPR

MIAMI — Yerandy Gonzalez looks at the line of hundreds of people in front of him and shakes his head.

He takes a step aside and lights up a cigarette.

"This is crazy, man," Gonzalez says in Spanish.

The line — which stretches across a few blocks on this humid Tuesday morning — is of people waiting to go inside Miami's immigration court. All of the people in line have a scheduled hearing – for many it's their first court appearance.

Avene Jeanite, a 52-year-old Haitian man, is among those waiting. He was here last month accompanying a friend facing deportation. But today is his appointment.

Sponsor Message

"It was not like this — you would go to the door and they'd let you in," Jeanite said. "Today is completely different."

toggle caption Sergio Martínez-Beltrán/NPR

The long lines are not a glitch. They are the result of a new Trump administration tactic, known as "mega master" calendar hearings ," designed to quickly deport people.

Under the old system, each judge would handle about three dozen cases per day.

But now, judges more regularly have a docket of over 100 people, and they are seeing dozens of immigrant cases at once.

Trump administration officials say the accelerated calendar is needed to clear a massive backlog; critics call it a tactic to unfairly speed up deportations.

"It's a very unfair, but a very effective tactic," said David Wilson, the vice chair of the American Immigration Lawyers Association's immigration court committee.

He said "mega masters" create chaos because the court is cramming a lot of immigrants in one docket, making it hard for the court itself to send notices in a timely manner and for the immigrant to find legal representation.

"When that happens, it generates a significant no-show rate," Wilson said.

toggle caption Eva Marie Uzcategui for NPR

A spokesperson for the Justice Department said in a statement to NPR that "reducing the immigration court backlog remains one of the highest priorities for this administration."

Sponsor Message

Meanwhile, a spokesperson for the Executive Office for Immigration Review, the agency that oversees immigration courts, said that as the agency continues to add immigration judges, it "will continue to make scheduling adjustments to ensure all cases are handled in a timely and lawful manner."

Since mega master calendar hearings started, in-absentia deportation orders have spiked to a record high, according to the legal tech platform bklg . In July, more than 54,000 immigrants nationwide were ordered deported for missing their court hearing. That number was similar to the 56,000 in June. Both reflect a 60% increase over the last few months.

In the Miami immigration court, the increase of in-absentia orders in July spiked from 1,383 in May to 2,886 in July — a 108% increase.

Crammed courtrooms, confusion and frustration

On this day, it's standing room only in courtroom 24. Recording is not allowed. But NPR saw Judge Xavier Racine call a group of some 30 people at once. He reads them their rights, and assigns them a new court hearing — a month from today. Other judges assign court hearings as quickly as in two weeks.

The Miami immigration court docket has exploded for three key reasons: The Trump administration is arresting a record monthly number of immigrants , it is moving up people's court dates that had been scheduled for 2027, and making people show up for cases that previous administrations deemed low priority because they have a high chance of being dismissed.

Yeriné, a 30-year-old Venezuelan mother who asked NPR to use her first name because she fears jeopardizing her immigration case, says she's concerned about being on these massive dockets. She had an appointment for May 2027 and it got rescheduled for Tuesday.

toggle caption Eva Marie Uzcategui for NPR

Standing in line outside the Miami immigration court, she says she's concerned about everything.

"I see this long line of people and they might not make it on time to their hearings," she said. "That scares me."

Sponsor Message

Billie Botch, a court observer with the American Friends Service Committee, a social justice group founded by the Quakers, told NPR this is causing a lot of operational issues. People are also showing up late to their court appointments because they are waiting in line for hours.

"You can't deny the correlation," Botch said. "You put more people into proceedings on shorter notice with less resources to go around to argue their case, You're going to end up with more removal orders."

World.title: Iran fires on its Gulf neighbors, retaliating for U.S. strikes after a monthlong lull
World.content:
Iran fires on its Gulf neighbors, retaliating for U.S. strikes after a monthlong lull

toggle caption Masoud Mohammadi/Tasnim News Agency via AP

DUBAI, United Arab Emirates — Iran fired on U.S. allies in the Gulf early Wednesday following a night of American bombardment that Iranian officials say included a deadly strike on a wedding party.

The latest violence came after a monthlong lull in fighting. The six-month war has led to a spike in oil prices, roiled the global economy and posed increasing political problems for U.S. President Donald Trump's Republican Party ahead of November midterm elections.

Sponsor Message

Fighting has escalated since the American military hit Iranian rocket launchers on an island in the Strait of Hormuz over the weekend, saying Iran was planning to use them to shoot mines into the waterway. Iran retaliated by firing missiles at American bases in Jordan that were intercepted.

American military resources are stretched and political pressure in Washington is mounting, while Iran's economy falters. Iran's currency hit another record low on Wednesday, with traders in Tehran exchanging 2.20 million rials for one U.S. dollar, a 10% hike from last week's record.

Neither side can continue indefinitely between full-scale war and a truce, said Hamidreza Azizi, senior Iran analyst at the Crisis Group, an international think tank.

"At some point, one of the sides may see a need to escalate in order to break this cycle," he cautioned. "So that could bring the two sides to a point that they have been trying to avoid until now, which is a full-scale war."

The struggle is focused on the Strait of Hormuz and oil prices

The latest flare-up in violence came as the standoff seemed to be shifting slightly more in the U.S.' favor, with the price of oil around $80 a barrel and Iranian leaders talking about growing economic hardships, said Sascha Bruchmann, an analyst with the International Institute for Strategic Studies' Middle East office in Bahrain.

toggle caption Razieh Poudat/ISNA via AP

Last week, U.S. Central Command's Adm. Brad Cooper said the strait had been secretly cleared of mines and that the U.S. Navy had helped nearly 1,500 commercial vessels carrying some 750 million barrels of oil pass through in recent months — still far below prewar levels.

Sponsor Message

"He basically told the world oil is flowing out and Iran is not capable of restricting the U.S.'s approach," Bruchmann said. "The U.S. is trying to reinstall some kind of confidence into the global oil markets … and the Iranians had to respond to that by reinserting insecurity and doubt."

Since the fighting resumed, the price of Brent crude oil, the international standard, has climbed to around $95, up more than 30% from the start of the war.

U.S. allies in the region fend off Iranian attacks

Following the strikes at Jordan, Kuwait and Bahrain said they had also come under attack, without reporting any casualties.

"You will soon see that Iran's new strategy on the battlefield, in diplomacy, and in confronting the economic blockade will shatter your foundations," the recently appointed head of Iran's powerful Supreme National Security Council, Mohsen Rezaei, said on X.

In Iraq, where Iranian-backed forces are active, Kurdish authorities said they had intercepted 10 drones laden with explosives in the Irbil area. Iranian television reported that American bases in Irbil had been targeted.

Israel's military also said that Iran-backed Hezbollah fired two explosive drones at its soldiers in southern Lebanon, without causing casualties.

The U.S. Central Command said Tuesday's strikes focused on Iranian military targets, including air defense sites, radar systems and maritime assets.

Casualties in Iran include people at a wedding party

One U.S. strike hit a home hosting a wedding in Kuhestak, a small coastal town overlooking the Strait of Hormuz, according to Iranian media.

Four people were killed — two women and two children, aged 4 and 16 — and at least 68 were wounded, the state news agency IRNA and state TV said Wednesday. Just after the strike, Ahmad Nafisi, the province's deputy governor, had told Iranian state television that five people were killed. There was no explanation for the change.

toggle caption Vahid Salemi/AP

Several heavy explosions shook Kuhestak, with fireballs that lit up the night sky, according to security camera footage carried by the semiofficial Fars news agency.

Sponsor Message

Images from Iran's semiofficial Tasnim news agency showed several hospitalized children being treated for injuries at a hospital in the nearby town of Minab, where a U.S. missile strike on the opening day of the war hit a primary school, killing more than 100 children.

Footage from the Iranian Red Crescent showed rescue workers entering a damaged home in the wake of the strike. It showed a hole in the roof of one house in a neighborhood of densely packed homes.

Experts say a "very precise" weapon appears to have been used

Two weapons experts told The Associated Press that images of fragments of a missile, which Iranian media said was used in the strike, were from a U.S.-made SLAM-ER cruise missile.

Trevor Ball, conflict researcher at the investigative group Bellingcat, said the SLAM-ER was "developed as a very precise weapon" that can be retargeted in flight by a human operator watching by infrared camera.

N.R. Jenzen-Jones, director of Armament Research Services, said the air-launched missile is also used by the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia. Neither has reported carrying out any recent strikes on Iran.

"Make no mistake: these crimes will not go unpunished," Ebrahim Azizi, chairperson of the Iranian parliament's National Security and Foreign Policy Committee, said on X.

U.S. Central Command spokesman Capt. Tim Hawkins said the U.S. military was "aware of the reports, which originated from Iranian state media, and we are looking into them." He would not say if CENTCOM had launched a formal investigation.

Separately, Iran has said four members of its paramilitary Revolutionary Guard and 10 members of the Guard's volunteer Basij forces died in the U.S. attacks.

The Strait of Hormuz remains largely shut down

During last month's lull in fighting, the U.S. ramped up economic pressure on Iran as Washington sought to fully open the Strait of Hormuz.

Sponsor Message

About a fifth of the world's traded oil was shipped through the key waterway before Israel and the U.S. attacked Iran on Feb. 28 and Iran largely shut it down in response. Despite many pronouncements from Washington that the strait is open, only a handful of ships are making the passage each day and Iran has regularly attacked vessels.

On Wednesday, Saudi shipping company Bahri said two Filipino sailors were killed in an attack late Monday as their vessel transited the strait.

A ceasefire deal reached in June quickly fell apart amid exchanges of strikes that same month. Mediator Pakistan has been working to restart talks.

Late Tuesday, Trump said he would not force Iran to the bargaining table.

"I couldn't care less if they sign a worthless, to them, agreement. I like our position now much better, with almost total control of the Hormuz Strait, and their economy totally collapsing. They are just playing out the inevitable. When are the Iranian people going to rise up and fight?" Trump wrote on social media.

World.title: Greetings from the Royal Pavilion, a stunning reminder of India in southern England
World.content:
Greetings from the Royal Pavilion, a stunning reminder of India in southern England

Lauren Frayer/NPR

Mughal arches, onion domes, chhatri-topped towers. Living in India for five years, I'd Instagram my way through a maharaja's palace, Sikh temple or sultan's fort every weekend. I got used to strolling through scalloped arches. How I miss them!

Which is why I froze in my tracks last winter when I spotted this building in Brighton, on England's south coast. The day was drizzly gray, I'd gone for a bracing swim in the English Channel, and was walking back to the train station, shivering, when I was flooded with warm memories from India.

It's the Royal Pavilion, built in the late 18th century by British royals fascinated by South Asian architecture, as they commandeered the subcontinent. It's funny: In Mumbai, I'd marvel at how many buildings look Victorian, in the same stone and style of my husband's hometown in northern England. Looking up at this pavilion, I realized the British didn't just impose their style on India. They also took India's style home.

Sponsor Message

Queen Victoria herself — who also went by "Empress of India" — lodged in the Royal Pavilion in the 1830s and '40s, before the construction of railways brought the working-class masses to Brighton — spoiling, she complained, her private seaside oasis. She decamped to Buckingham Palace and took the pavilion's lotus-flower chandeliers with her.

During World War I, the building became a military hospital, treating thousands of Indian soldiers fighting for the British. Separate kitchens catered to different castes. Muslim soldiers prayed to Mecca from the east lawn.

Nowadays, the gardens designed for King George IV are being restored, a green lung for the city. They hosted some of the first weddings after the United Kingdom legalized same-sex marriage in 2014. And having survived centuries of royal caprice, and at least one arson attack, the pavilion is now a museum, open to the masses.

I wonder what Queen Victoria would think of that.
