John Vargas, head of the Forensic Biology Section at the Judicial Investigation Organization’s Department of Forensic Sciences, said the rising number of seizures points to an ongoing problem that requires both scientific research and greater public awareness. Vargas also pushed back on a common misconception about what wildlife trafficking actually looks like.

The problem, he said, extends well beyond the smuggling of live animals. Items commonly confiscated include reptiles such as boas, amphibians, feline claws and bones, insects, mollusks and corals, plants including orchids, and the eggs of parrots and other birds.

Andrea Borel, executive director of Humane World for Animals, framed the campaign’s central message simply. Protecting wildlife, she said, is not solely the responsibility of authorities. Everyday choices by travelers and residents play a role in conservation and in ensuring wildlife can continue to be enjoyed responsibly for years to come.

The campaign’s core appeal asks visitors to take home experiences, photographs and memories instead of physical pieces of the biodiversity. Officials emphasize that even seemingly minor souvenirs, a piece of coral, a dried starfish, an orchid pulled from the forest, carry real ecological cost. Vargas noted that what a traveler carries away also leaves a void behind, a gap in the ecosystem that the removed specimen once filled.

The campaign lands at a moment when Costa Rica’s reputation as a global biodiversity destination continues to be one of its strongest tourism pluses, and also one of its most exploited. Wildlife trafficking remains a persistent challenge across the international airports, land borders and coastal areas, feeding both international demand for exotic pets and plants and a domestic market for animal parts and curiosities sold to unsuspecting visitors.

By reframing the issue as a shared responsibility rather than strictly a law enforcement matter, organizers hope to shift traveler behavior before it happens, discouraging the buying or collection of wildlife specimens in the first place rather than relying solely on detection at ports of exit. Whether the campaign meaningfully reduces the confiscation numbers will likely become clearer as authorities track seizures in the coming year, but for now, the message to visitors is Costa Rica’s wildlife is not a souvenir.

World.title: Court Frees Wife of Pecho de Rata as Prosecutors Appeal
World.content:
A court in Limón ordered the release of the wife of extradited trafficking suspect Edwin López Vega today, rejecting a prosecution request to hold her for a year in preventive detention and imposing lesser restrictions instead. Prosecutors have appealed the ruling and the woman, identified by the surnames Smith de la O, is under investigation on suspicion of money laundering and unlawful association.

She has not been tried, and the accusations against her remain allegations to be established in court. The Deputy Prosecutor’s Office against Money Laundering and Asset Forfeiture had asked the Limón penal court for a year of preventive detention. The court declined and set lesser conditions.

Under the terms imposed, she must sign in every 15 days, surrender her passport and is not allowed to leave the country. Her defense lawyer, Andy Jack Sánchez, confirmed the conditions after being notified of the resolution this morning. The Public Prosecutor’s Office said it had appealed the decision and would renew its request for preventive detention at a new hearing.

Accounts of how she came into custody differ. Authorities said she was detained on Sunday, August 30, by professional migration police at Juan Santamaría International Airport as she entered the country on a flight from Switzerland, acting on an outstanding international arrest alert. Her lawyer said she returned that afternoon and presented herself to authorities.

An Interpol alert had been active against her since June 23, the day investigators executed the raids in the case known to police as Riverside. Migration records incorporated into the file show she left Costa Rica on June 17, six days before those raids, travelling with another defendant surnamed Mulins, a Swiss national who remains at large. She was absent from the country for 74 days.

The Riverside operation involved roughly 1,500 officers and about 146 searches of homes, restaurants, farms, hotels, guesthouses, a quarry, a gym and a bullring, among other assets attributed to López Vega and his alleged associates. It has been described as the largest single action against drug trafficking carried out in Costa Rica. Investigators say the organization operated from Limón and maintained international connections for moving cocaine and marijuana. The file names more than 50 other defendants, among them four of López Vega’s children.

In the investigative file compiled by the Judicial Investigation Organization, the OIJ, Smith de la O appears under the contact name Tóxica J in López Vega’s phone. Investigators allege she handled bank deposits and transfers and moved and administered funds connected to him, and that she appears in several companies that hold his assets.

The OIJ describes the pattern as consistent with arrangements in which leaders of criminal structures share control of resources with their partners. Those are investigative conclusions, and the case file states they must still be determined within the judicial process.

The couple married on February 17 at the La Reforma prison in San Rafael de Alajuela, where López Vega was held in maximum security, according to records of the Supreme Elections Tribunal. He was extradited to the United States on March 20 to face charges related to international drug trafficking, roughly a month after the wedding.

Smith de la O is a resident of Cahuita, the Caribbean coastal town that was among the areas most heavily affected by the June raids. Her detention on Sunday closed one of the gaps left when several suspects left the country shortly before the operation began. No date has been set for the appeal hearing. Until it is heard, the restrictions imposed on Tuesday stand.

World.title: Two Pococí Judges and a Judicial Agent Detained in Diablo Probe
World.content:
Agents of the Judicial Investigation Organization (OIJ), acting under the functional direction of the Public Prosecutor’s Office, detained two judges and a judicial agent from the Pococí courts, in the Caribbean province of Limón this morning. The Deputy Prosecutor’s Office for Probity, Transparency and Anti-Corruption identified the three as suspects in the alleged offenses of procuring impunity, bribery, corruptor liability and misuse of public property. None has been charged, and all are presumed innocent while the investigation proceeds.

In a written statement, the Public Prosecutor’s Office said the conduct under investigation took place between 2023 and 2026, when the accused apparently used their positions to collaborate with a group dedicated to drug trafficking. Investigators are examining whether they accepted gifts and neglected their duties in order to use their offices for personal ends.

The three were identified by the surnames Rojas, a woman, Valverde and Ramírez. Each is to give a sworn statement before authorities decide what precautionary measures to request. Investigators say the alleged favoring benefited defendants in a case known to police as Colorado, tied to the criminal structure attributed to Alejandro Arias Monge, known by the alias Diablo.

In that file, prosecutors are examining Arias Monge’s partner, his sister and former brothers-in-law on suspicion of money laundering. When the case became public, authorities said the relatives were not directly connected to the violence attributed to the network itself. The Pococí penal court closed for the day as a result.

A sign posted at the entrance advised that no service would be provided today and the closure was attributed to searches being carried out in the offices of the detained officials. Separately, Nils Rojas, acting deputy director general of the OIJ, confirmed that one of the day’s operations was carried out at the offices of the Judicial Branch’s solidarity association in Barrio Luján, San José.

The preliminary hearing in the Colorado case was scheduled to open on September 1 before the court specializing in organized crime, with 33 people named in the file and proceedings expected to run about a month. Prosecutors allege the organization operated principally in Limón and Pococí, where they say it managed drug distribution and sales.

Arias Monge was captured on July 24 in San Bernardino de Sarapiquí at the close of an operation authorities named Némesis. He remains in custody at La Reforma prison in Alajuela. The U.S. State Department had offered a reward of $500,000 for information leading to his capture. Michael Soto, director of the OIJ, said in July that the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration had not formally requested his extradition, and no extradition order was in force at that time.

Today’s detentions extend a pattern of alleged institutional infiltration around the same network. In August, wiretap material surfaced alleging that police officers had tipped off the group ahead of operations. A separate police intelligence report linked 116 officers to criminal groups across several provinces. Until Tuesday, however, the accusations had centered on police rather than on the courts.

The judiciary’s capacity to pursue these cases has itself become politically contested. The Judicial Branch has spent much of the year arguing against reductions to its budget, and thousands of people filled a plaza in San José in August in a demonstration organized in defense of judicial independence.

The Judicial Branch had not issued a statement on the three officials’ employment status as of Tuesday afternoon. Detention in Costa Rica does not by itself constitute a charge; prosecutors must present detainees before a judge, who then decides whether to impose precautionary measures.

Pococí and the surrounding Caribbean lowlands have absorbed a disproportionate share of the country’s organized crime prosecutions over the past two years. The allegation that officials inside the courthouse hearing those cases were working the other side, if it is borne out, would mark a shift in what investigators have so far described as a problem of policing.

World.title: Costa Rica’s Medical Tourists Are Trading Dental Chairs for Operating Room
World.content:
The foreign patient arriving in Costa Rica for a dental implant or a cosmetic procedure is no longer the whole picture. Hospitals here are reporting a rising share of international patients who come for surgery that requires admission, anesthesia and a supervised recovery — cancer treatment, orthopedic work, procedures that cannot be finished in an afternoon and slept off at a hotel.

Hospital Internacional La Católica treated roughly 300 international patients in inpatient and surgical care during 2025, up from about 180 the year before, according to figures released by the hospital. Melissa Sánchez Villalobos, who heads customer success at the facility, said the international patient now arrives looking for more than a discount — specialized care, technology, credentialed physicians and coordination that lets them travel with confidence and go home knowing the treatment met a standard.

The economics behind that shift are large and well documented. Central Bank of Costa Rica data compiled by the Costa Rican Chamber of Health puts medical tourism at 13.4% of international arrivals, roughly 70,000 patients a year, generating approximately $465 million — around 10.4% of the country’s tourism economy. The average medical traveler spends about $6,600 against roughly $1,200 for a conventional visitor, and most arrive with two or three companions who spend on hotels, transport and food without setting foot in a clinic.

What is changing is what those patients are buying. Costa Rica built the category on dentistry, which still accounts for 42% of demand for international medical services, and on plastic surgery, a trade that dates back more than fifty years. Hospital-grade care sits at a different price point and carries a different risk profile, and the country’s private sector has spent the past several years positioning for it.

Oncology is the clearest example. Radioterapia Siglo XXI has drawn international referrals on the strength of radiosurgery capacity — high-dose radiation delivered with millimeter precision to tumors in the brain, spine, liver, lung or pancreas — and has developed agreements with Canadian organizations that refer patients abroad. The Caja Costarricense de Seguro Social has also referred insured Costa Rican patients requiring radiosurgery to the center, which is a useful signal about capacity: the public system does not outsource lightly.

Massimo Manzi, executive director of the Costa Rican Chamber of Health, has argued that international accreditation is what makes any of this legible to a patient sitting in Ohio or Ontario. Accreditations demonstrate that services delivered in Costa Rica meet global quality and safety standards, he said, and that is the factor that attracts international patients and strengthens the country’s position as a specialized destination.

The pressure pushing patients out of their home systems has not eased. Rising premiums, high deductibles and waiting lists in the United States and Canada continue to send people looking elsewhere, and Costa Rica’s proximity to North America — direct flights, same or near-same time zone, no visa requirement for stays up to 90 days — makes it an easier decision than Turkey or Thailand. Roughly 83% of medical travelers here come from the United States and 11% from Canada.

But a bigger procedure changes the calculation in ways that a cleaning and a set of veneers does not. Complications after abdominal or orthopedic surgery are more likely and more serious than after dental work. Recovery timelines are longer, which means the return flight cannot be booked tight. And follow-up care, once the patient is home, is harder to arrange when the operating surgeon is 3,000 kilometers (about 1,900 miles) away and the domestic physician was not consulted.

Anyone weighing a hospital procedure here can check credentials independently before committing. Physicians and surgeons practicing in Costa Rica must be registered with the Colegio de Médicos y Cirujanos, which maintains a public register — a separate body from the dental college that governs the dentists covered in our earlier report on Costa Rica’s dental clinic certification. Facilities, hospitals included, must hold a Certificado de Habilitación from the Health Ministry covering premises and equipment.

Insurance is where most people get caught. Medicare does not cover care received outside the United States, with narrow exceptions that rarely apply to planned surgery. Standard travel insurance policies typically exclude elective procedures undertaken abroad — the trip is the reason for the treatment, not an accident during it — and may also exclude complications arising from them. Medical evacuation coverage is a separate purchase and worth pricing before departure rather than after a problem.

The oversight question is not academic. The death of a tourist at a psychedelic retreat this month drew renewed scrutiny to a wellness sector operating with thinner regulation than hospitals, and the contrast is instructive: accreditation, licensing and habilitación are precisely the mechanisms that separate the regulated end of health tourism from the unregulated one. Patients rarely know which side of that line a provider sits on until they check.

There is also a competitiveness problem forming that has nothing to do with medicine. The colón’s run to historic highs against the dollar has made everything in Costa Rica more expensive for visitors paying in dollars, and a savings pitch built on a 40% to 70% discount against US prices narrows when the exchange rate moves against it. Mexico competes on proximity, Colombia on cosmetic and surgical volume, and both are cheaper.

World.title: PM Briceño on Gilroy Usher fence incident: ‘You have to admire him taking his role seriously’
World.content:
PM Briceño on Gilroy Usher fence incident: ‘You have to admire him taking his role seriously’

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Prime Minister John Briceño says that while Minister of State Gilroy Usher should have handled a controversial land dispute differently, “you have to admire him taking his role seriously” as an elected representative trying to resolve a problem in his constituency.

Briceño made the remarks on Wednesday when questioned about Usher’s actions over the weekend, when the Port Loyola Area Representative was captured on live video personally cutting down a portion of a fence at the centre of a land dispute.

The Prime Minister said Usher had become “over-anxious” and was likely frustrated while trying to address a land issue, noting that disputes over property have previously resulted in violence and even deaths.

“Would I do it differently? Of course, I’ll do it differently,” Briceño said.

He explained that Usher should instead have allowed the legal process to take its course, including allowing police to address any complaint and having the Ministry of Natural Resources conduct a survey to establish the lawful property boundaries.

Briceño noted that Usher has since acknowledged that his approach was wrong and publicly apologized.

“I think I would not have done it that way, but at the same time, you have to admire him taking his role seriously as a representative,” the Prime Minister said.

Asked whether an ordinary citizen could face legal consequences for doing the same thing, Briceño responded, “I believe so.”

He added that if a person feels aggrieved by Usher’s actions and does not accept his apology, that person retains the right to seek redress through the courts.

Usher has maintained that he intervened in an ongoing dispute over the boundary between neighbouring properties. The incident generated public criticism after video circulated showing the minister personally removing sections of the fence.

World.title: International News: El Niño strengthens across Pacific, raising concerns for Agriculture across Americas
World.content:
International News: El Niño strengthens across Pacific, raising concerns for Agriculture across Americas

By Zoila Palma: El Niño is strengthening across the equatorial Pacific, putting farmers, agribusinesses and commodity markets across the United States and Latin America on alert as the 2026/27 agricultural season approaches.

The climate phenomenon could bring significant changes in rainfall and temperatures, affecting crops, livestock, water supplies, transportation and agricultural trade.

The U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) reported on August 13 that there is more than a 90 percent chance El Niño will become a very strong event during the Northern Hemisphere fall and winter of 2026-27.

Sea surface temperatures have already risen substantially across the Pacific, with July anomalies reaching 1.4°C in Niño 3.4, 1.7°C in Niño 3 and 2.9°C in Niño 1+2. NOAA estimates a 69 percent chance that the event could reach historic strength between October and December.

In the United States, farmers will closely monitor how El Niño influences weather across major agricultural regions.

NOAA’s seasonal outlook favors above-normal temperatures across much of the western and central United States during September through November, while precipitation patterns are expected to vary by region. Conditions could affect corn, soybeans, wheat, cotton and livestock, as well as soil moisture and preparations for the next planting season, Agro Latam reports.

Latin America faces a more varied outlook. Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay and Uruguay will be watching rainfall and soil moisture closely during the 2026/27 crop season, particularly in major soybean, corn, wheat, rice and livestock-producing areas.

Peru and Ecuador have greater exposure to conditions in the eastern Pacific, while parts of northern South America have historically experienced reduced rainfall during El Niño.

Central America and the Caribbean are also considered vulnerable, with FAO identifying areas where strong El Niño events have historically been associated with a greater than 50 percent probability of drought.

The potential impacts extend beyond farms to agricultural trade and commodity markets. Weather-related disruptions could affect supplies and prices for corn, soybeans, wheat, coffee, sugar and animal products while increasing transportation, feed and infrastructure costs.

However, a stronger El Niño does not automatically mean higher prices, as market reactions will depend on where production is affected, global inventories, competing harvests and international demand.

With El Niño developing alongside a warmer global climate, farmers and agribusinesses are being urged to prepare early.

Soil-moisture monitoring, seasonal forecasts, crop and livestock planning, water reserves, insurance and other climate-smart tools could help reduce risks.

FAO has emphasized that El Niño can often be anticipated months in advance, giving agricultural communities time to protect crops, livestock and infrastructure as the Americas prepare for potentially significant weather impacts through 2026 and into 2027.

World.title: Ministry of Education says More Tomorrow Primary School will remain open
World.content:
Ministry of Education says More Tomorrow Primary School will remain open

By Breaking Belize News Staff: The Ministry of Education, Culture, Science and Technology has officially clarified that More Tomorrow Primary School in the Cayo District is not being closed.

In a statement issued on September 2, 2026, the Ministry said it is currently engaging with parents and members of the school community to address challenges affecting the school, including staffing issues.

“These discussions are intended to identify appropriate solutions that will ensure the continued provision of education to students in More Tomorrow,” the Ministry said.

The statement follows an earlier media report claiming that the Ministry planned to close the school as early as Friday and transport students to another nearby institution. That report also said residents were preparing to hold a community meeting and launch a petition opposing the alleged closure, citing concerns about the additional distance children would have to travel.

Concerns reportedly arose amid longstanding difficulties in securing teachers for the school, which serves an area considered challenging for staffing. The school’s current situation has been further complicated by a staffing matter involving its only teacher.

The Ministry has now firmly rejected reports of an impending closure, saying it remains committed to working with parents, teachers and the wider community to find a solution in the best interest of students.

World.title: Ministry of Education engages parents to address challenges at More Tomorrow Primary
World.content:
Ministry of Education engages parents to address challenges at More Tomorrow Primary

By Zoila Palma: Today, the Ministry of Education, Culture, Science and Technology issued a statement clarifying that More Tomorrow Primary School located in the Cayo District, is not being closed.

The Ministry says that it is currently engaging with parents and members of the school community to address the challenges facing the school, including matters related to staffing.

“These discussions are intended to identify appropriate solutions that will ensure the continued provision of education to students in More Tomorrow,” the Ministry said.

The Ministry says that it remains committed to working collaboratively with parents, teachers, and the wider community in the best interest of the students

World.title: Viral video allegedly shows Forest Department vehicle, employee in attempted sale of confiscated lumber
World.content:
Viral video allegedly shows Forest Department vehicle, employee in attempted sale of confiscated lumber

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A viral video posted by Guardian Newspaper reportedly shows an employee of the Forest department using the Belize Forest Department’s vehicle allegedly attempting to illegally sell confiscated lumber.

The video begins showing the man accompanied by police breaking a lock and entering a property to reportedly confiscate lumber.

Another part of the video shows the same man in the night using a Government assigned vehicle loaded with Mahogany and purportedly attempting to illegally sell it to a lumber yard.

The person filming is heard accusing the employee of illegally attempting to sell the confiscated lumber.

World.title: Belize @ 45 Magical history tour with Assad Shoman coming to Belize City
World.content:
Belize @ 45 Magical history tour with Assad Shoman coming to Belize City

By Zoila Palma: Residents of Belize City will have an opportunity to explore lesser-known chapters of Belize’s history when historian Assad Shoman brings the Belize @ 45 Magical History Tour to the city next week.

The event is scheduled for Tuesday, September 8, 2026, at 7:00 p.m. at the Belize City House of Culture. The tour will invite participants to delve into historical accounts and perspectives that may not always be included in traditional textbooks.

NICH is encouraging residents to take part in the discussion and engage with Belize’s history by asking questions and exploring the events and experiences that have shaped the nation.

The initiative carries the message: “Belize @ 45 — time to ask the hard questions.”

The event is being made possible through the support of the National Celebrations Commission and the National Institute of Culture and History (NICH).

Residents interested in attending are encouraged to RSVP in advance.

For additional information, they can contact [email protected] or WhatsApp 671-9456.

World.title: From High School to high-tech: Belize moves to build next generation of Engineers
World.content:
From High School to high-tech: Belize moves to build next generation of Engineers

By Zoila Palma: The University of Belize (UB), Ministry of E-Governance, Belize Robotics Federation (BRF) and VEX Robotics are advancing plans to establish a national robotics education pathway connecting high school students to university studies, engineering and technology careers, competitive robotics and emerging industries.

Representatives of the four organizations met on September 1 to discuss how existing programs, training resources and national initiatives can be aligned to strengthen robotics education and workforce development.

A key proposal is the creation of a structured high school-to-UB pathway that would allow students developing skills in robotics, coding and engineering to clearly transition into university programs and careers in technology, engineering, education, research and industry.

Belize Robotics Federation President Jamie Lee Usher said the goal is to ensure robotics extends beyond school clubs and competitions and becomes part of a broader education and career pipeline.

The initiative would build on UB’s existing robotics activities, including the integration of robotics into programming and algorithms courses, use of the VEX curriculum and investment in competition infrastructure as the university works toward developing its own robotics team.

The partners also discussed teacher training, curriculum development, student recruitment and the creation of potential future electives, specialized courses and academic credentials at UB, subject to the university’s established approval processes.

BRF said it will support participating schools and UB through educator training and capacity building, while VEX representative Eli Osornio reaffirmed the company’s willingness to provide educational resources, technical guidance and professional development.

The initiative is also expected to focus on practical applications of robotics and emerging technologies in areas such as agriculture, environmental monitoring, automation, sensors, drones, logistics and electronics. Ministry of E-Governance CEO Jose Urbina emphasized the importance of connecting education and technology to Belize’s national needs, while the Ministry has provided VEX V5 Classroom Super Kits to BRF and UB’s Jaguar Tech Studio and plans to support BRF with a VEX Air Drone system.

The partners said a proposed high school pilot would initially involve schools already introducing foundational robotics, coding and engineering activities, while also expanding opportunities for girls and young women, mentorship by UB students and the development of future STEM educators.

The long-term objective is to create a coordinated national robotics ecosystem that allows students to progress from early exposure and competition to tertiary education, applied research, employment and innovation, helping prepare more Belizeans to become the engineers, programmers, teachers and technology innovators the country needs.

World.title: Ministry of Health and Wellness extends condolences on passing of Milagro Garel
World.content:
Ministry of Health and Wellness extends condolences on passing of Milagro Garel

By Zoila Palma: The Ministry of Health and Wellness has joined in extending its deepest condolences to the family, friends, and colleagues of Milagro Garel, as well as the World Pediatrics community.

“Garel dedicated many years to supporting Belizean children and families through her work with World Pediatrics, helping to expand access to specialized medical care and strengthening collaboration with Belize’s health system,” the Ministry said.

“Her compassion, dedication, and commitment to improving children’s lives have left a lasting legacy that will be remembered with gratitude and admiration,” the Ministry added.

The Ministry extends its heartfelt sympathies to her loved ones during this difficult time.

World.title: Leon Bailey to move to Olympiacos — reports
World.content:
In this file photo Reggae Boyz winger Leon Bailey attempts a cross in his AS Roma debut against Inter Milan in the Serie A on Saturday October 18, 2025 at the Stadio Olimpico. .

Reggae Boy Leon Bailey is expected to leave Aston Villa for Greek Club Olympiacos, according to international reports.

The move from the English Premier League club is said to be permanent, with a contract until June 2029. It follows Bailey’s loans from Villa to various clubs, including Roma.

Bailey had several rough, injury-plagued seasons with Villa and did not feature at all for the club this season.

An £8 million Hull City move had been in the works but fell through before the close of the EPL transfer window. Several other clubs had shown interest in the 29-year-old, including Saudi-based Al Ittihad and Diriyah Club.

With over 100 titles across national, regional and youth competitions, Olympiacos is the most successful Greek Club on record and consistently dominates its league.

The club’s home ground is the 33,000-capacity Karaiskakis Stadium, in Piraeus near Athens.

Reports are that Bailey is travelling to Athens for medical testing.

World.title: Harbour View FC salutes academic stars’ exceptional CSEC results
World.content:
Harbour View FC's 2026 Academic stars from left Dominic Thompson, Jelani Harvey Jaden Smith Tristan Riley and Emmanuel Donalds

KINGSTON, Jamaica — Harbour View Football Club is celebrating an academic feat after five of its young players excelled in the classroom, with General Manager Clyde Jureidini challenging them to become role models for the next generation of footballers.

Dominic Thompson, Jaden Smith, Jelani Harvey, Tristan Riley and Emmanuel Donalds were singled out by Jureidini for their outstanding academic achievements, which he said demonstrated that success in football and education can go hand in hand.

Thompson of St George’s College achieved 10 CSEC subjects with nine distinctions; Smith of Wolmer’s Boys has nine subjects with seven distinctions; Campion College’s Harvey has nine subjects and six distinctions; Donalds of Jamaica College has eight subjects and six distinctions; and Riley of St George’s College has nine subjects and five distinctions.

Jureidini heaped praise on the youngsters for their “focus, hard work, diligence and discipline”, while making it clear that their accomplishments were largely the result of the support provided by their parents, teachers and school communities.

“We really want to credit them for their focus, for their hard work, for their diligence, for their discipline and even more so for their achievement,” Jureidini said.

“We know they didn’t do it without the strong guidance, assistance and support of their peer group at school, of course their parents and at home. The club did a little bit but could not in any way take credit for what they and, by extension, their parents and their teachers have put in.”

Jureidini believes the achievement could be a significant moment for the Harbour View programme, noting that it is a rare feat.

“We think it’s one of the few times, if not the first, that so many Harbour View youngsters have excelled at the same time,” he said.

The achievement is also a reflection of Harbour View’s long-term youth development programme, with most of the five players progressing through the club’s ranks from the Under-11 level.

“Many have done it over the years, and these have done it because the majority of them have been in Harbour View from Under-11 through Under-13, Under-15, Under-17, Under-18,” Jureidini said.

Harvey’s progression has been particularly notable. After advancing through the Harbour View youth system, he moved into the Under-20 programme and senior Premier League squad before earning an overseas scholarship.

Jureidini wants the five high achievers to set an even higher bar for those following behind them.

“Set the highest standard for yourselves, for your teammates, for the football fraternity and the many youngsters from our Under-11, Under-13, Under-15 and Under-17 who are behind them,” he said.

For Jureidini, the message is bigger than football.

He believes combining academic excellence with sporting ambition gives young athletes a stronger foundation for life beyond the pitch.

“Go after the academic excellence as well as the football dominance because it’s a good mix that gives you a good opportunity in life, not just in the game of football or in sports,” he said.

And with five Harbour View youngsters leading the way, Jureidini is hoping their success will become contagious.

“So big up and congratulations, and we hope many more will exceed, follow their example and achieve greater heights,” he said.

— Howard Walker

World.title: $500m more for drought fight
World.content:
Minister of Water, Environment and Climate Change Matthew Samuda looks on at pipe-laying works being carried out by the National Water Commission on Old Hope Road in St Andrew on Tuesday. (Photo: Joseph Wellington)

AHEAD of next week’s reopening of schools, an additional $500 million has been allocated to ease Jamaicans’ torment caused by drought and severe heat brought on by Super El Niño weather conditions. Cabinet approved the measure Monday and Minister of Water, Environment and Climate Change Matthew Samuda provided an update to the media yesterday.

“We’ll see $150 million being sent to the National Water Commission (NWC) for them to dedicate trucks to schools, [for] back-to-school; to health centres and hospitals; and indeed to critical infrastructure, including police stations, with a priority on those that are places of detention. From the approved $500 million we will see $200 million being channelled through the offices of the Members of Parliament to provide support in their constituencies, and it will see $150 million of support going to all municipalities to ensure that they’re able to respond in areas where the utility footprint is not,” Samuda announced.

He was speaking during a tour of a multi-billion-dollar pipe-laying and rehabilitation project on Old Hope Road in St Andrew.

The minister stressed that if weather conditions improve, the funds will not be spent. However, he acknowledged that meteorological forecasts indicate that the situation is not likely to improve any time soon.

Brutal heat, reduced rainfall, and drought are some of the conditions that accompany what is on track to be the strongest El Niño on record. The weather pattern has been unleashing extreme weather across the globe, and Jamaicans have been reeling from the impact.

“Because the forecast has said we’re unlikely to see a major change in our current rainfall levels until early next year, we’ve made this provision to ensure that we’re able to respond to those most in need, and to critical infrastructure needs and, of course, support back-to-school as best as possible,” Samuda shared.

He said it is clear the drought is having a terrible impact on social stability and economic activity as well as the general comfort of citizens, and sought to assure that the Government is doing everything within its power to shore up its emergency response to the situation.

Samuda said he is aware that nothing makes people feel better than when they have water running through their pipes at home.

“The Government is spending over $15 billion this year alone on infrastructure work to upgrade the pipes. For those who find themselves in dire straits, we’re clear that we have to provide a particular level of support in a number of ways. It’s important to note that the Government already, since the start of this drought, has expended $86 million in trucking of water to those critically affected and to critical infrastructure,” the minister said.

Turning his attention to adherence to water restrictions imposed by Government, Samuda said generally there is a great consciousness within the society that the country is experiencing a weather crisis, and there is support for the push to get citizens to conserve.

“We are seeing that [conservation] in stabilisation and reduced rate of decline at major storage facilities. We always have errant ones, but generally we are getting compliance. We deal with weather crises annually, sometimes rainy seasons and sometimes dry spells. I think the consciousness related to this particular drought is there,” he added.

World.title: Learning the game
World.content:
Casino Gaming Commission Director of Human Resources Shainee Myles speaking at this week’s Jamaica Observer Monday Exchange. (Photo: Joseph Wellington)

THE Casino Gaming Commission (CGC) says it has been preparing its regulators to face a new challenge, not only learning how casinos operate, but knowing enough about roulette, blackjack, and other games to spot when something is going wrong.

With much of the specialised expertise not readily available locally, the commission has partnered with overseas bodies and international regulators to train its staff and expose them to established casino operations.

Director of human resource and administration at the CGC, Shainee Myles said the training push was driven by the need to establish the level of expertise required to regulate the new sector to international standards.

“One of the first things that we needed to do was to establish what the requirement is for that First World standard, and we had to work closely with the operational team to also understand what the training gaps are and the type of people that we need,” Myles said at this week’s Jamaica Observer Monday Exchange.

She said the commission recognised early that simply transferring knowledge from Jamaica’s existing gaming environment would not be enough, given the specialised nature of casino regulation.

“A lot of the expertise does not reside locally in Jamaica so we had to create these persons. We partnered with overseas bodies and also looked keenly on what other international regulators are doing so that they can effectively manage the sector, and we identified several training opportunities that are needed. Our persons had to be very keen on upskilling as well so they can bring in that information and be fully prepared for the regulatory rules that they will fill,” she explained.

The preparation comes as Jamaica moves towards the launch of its first licensed casino under the Casino Gaming Act, 2010.

The CGC granted Jamaica’s first casino operator’s licence to Adamas Grand Casino Limited on July 29. The casino is proposed for Princess Grand Jamaica Resort in Green Island, Hanover, where it will operate under a management agreement with Spanish gaming and hospitality entity Grupo Orenes.

Myles said the commission has already completed training in table games and slot machines, while investigations training is ongoing and further practical exposure is planned.

That practical component is particularly important because casino regulation requires officials to understand the mechanics of the games they will be responsible for overseeing.

Asked specifically about table-game training, Myles said regulators must be able to distinguish ordinary play from manipulation or cheating.

“They need to understand how a roulette is played, how a blackjack is played, and also identifying when cheating is happening. You’ll have people coming in who know what they’re doing so we cannot sit and say we don’t know as yet — we have to know as well. So, we need to know how to play those games and to detect when cheating is taking place,” she explained.

According to Myles, the commission has also launched an online academy offering staff and partner agencies access to specialised regulatory courses, with areas including surveillance, risk management and anti-money laundering.

She noted that the aim is to ensure that knowledge does not become concentrated in a handful of employees who could leave the organisation and take that expertise with them.

“The Casino Gaming Commission is ready to regulate that difficult sector. It’s [going to be done] through continuous development as well of our people and upskilling them, and also continuous learning and institutionalising that knowledge, because it cannot reside in a single individual,” she expressed.

She said the academy currently offers 29 courses and is also designed to strengthen the capabilities of agencies that will work alongside the CGC.

“We also have to train our partner agencies. You have Customs, you have BGLC [Betting, Gaming and Lotteries Commission], MOCA [Major Organised Crime and Anti-Corruption Agency] — all those other areas that will be a part of the process. If there’s an investigation, if there are machines coming in, they need to know what to look for and how they can be a part of what is happening,” she explained.

The emphasis on training is part of a broader effort by the CGC to establish a regulatory system for a sector that is new to Jamaica in its full casino form.

Th country has long had gaming lounges regulated by the BGLC but those establishments are not casinos in the legal sense. Gaming lounges generally offer gaming machines while a CGC-licensed casino can offer full casino gaming including live table games such as blackjack, roulette, baccarat, craps and poker, as well as gaming machines.

Casino gaming is also restricted to approved integrated resort developments (IRDs), rather than standalone premises. The model ties casino gaming to larger tourism developments anchored by hotels and other amenities.

The CGC’s regulatory framework was completed with the Casino Gaming (General) Regulations, 2025, which set out detailed requirements covering licensing, management qualifications, record keeping, inspection, enforcement, and responsible gaming. The House of Representatives approved the regulations in February 2026 and the Senate affirmed them on April 17, completing the legal framework for licensing.

World.title: The Building Returns: Kartel leads dancehall back to the club
World.content:
The National Arena was jam-packed for The Return of the Building on Saturday night.(Photo: Ashb Media)

HUNDREDS poured into the National Arena on Saturday for the highly anticipated Return of The Building. Promising patrons a trip down memory lane, organisers transported eager partygoers back to an era when Kingston’s nightlife was ruled by its hottest clubs.

Headlined by Vybz Kartel, the event leaned heavily into the unpredictability and movement that once defined places such as The Building, Fiction and Quad. Instead of unfolding as a traditional concert, with one performance neatly following another, the evening was a mix of music, artistes, selectors, dancers and familiar faces, all operating inside a space transformed by disco lighting, liquor and a heavy dose of nostalgia.

Ahead of the event, organisers outlined that today’s party scene is increasingly being driven by patrons following brands, promoters, and concepts from venue to venue. They argued that Jamaica’s entertainment landscape has shifted away from the era when the nightclub itself was the destination. Still, Saturday’s event proved that though much has changed, Jamaica’s love for music remains unshakeable, and with that love comes unwavering support for an active nightlife, no matter the venue.

For much of the night, music remained at the centre of the experience. Selectors moved patrons through a slew of dancehall hits, including a host of tracks from Kartel’s early days.

“When Building did deh bout, a lot of unnu inna fifth grade, sixth grade and seventh grade. You were in school when Gully/Gaza war did active,” DJ Escobar said as he riled up the crowd during his brief juggling session.

“All who know say a Gully/Gaza make you know fi defend yuhself a school, buss a blank,” he continued, with the crowd willingly following his instructions.

ZJ Chrome, Ricky Platinum and a host of others also enjoyed brief juggling stints as they got the crowd ready for the man of the moment.

Before long, Vybz Kartel had full command of the National Arena.

“Long time me nuh deejay fi me people dem from dem levels yah,” he said.

Perched atop a raised platform overlooking the jam-packed crowd, Kartel served up songs such as Touch A Button, Send A Hell, Dumpa Truck, One Man, Was Dat Jah and others, catering to both his female fanbase and his ‘thugs’.

Leaning into the kind of unpredictability that once governed the club scene, Kartel treated patrons to several guest appearances throughout the night. Shawn Storm, Harry Toddler, Future Fambo, Jamal, Ishawna, Pamputtae and Laden were among those who joined the festivities, serving up energetic performances of their own.

Of course, it would hardly be a Vybz Kartel showcase without a moment that underscored his own legacy. Encouraging the men in attendance to commit to their responsibilities as fathers, the entertainer handed over the microphone to his son, Likkle Vybz.

“Mi father never rich, but him was a good father. Always remember, ghetto youths: From you man enough to get a girl pregnant, be man enough fi take care a di yute. Memba yuh babymadda know seh you is a trying yute so just be there for her and the child…in a few years, you might get a son like mine,” he said before turning things over to his son.

“The entire experience was phenomenal. We saw how patrons were in complete awe that the arena could indeed be transformed into a club for one night. They enjoyed themselves as Kartel interacted with them in such a genuine way, which was what The Building experience was,” said Kennika Johnson, one of the organisers of The Return of The Building.

“I’m happy he was able to bring that energy back to the people and just revive the club culture for one night. It was exactly what we wanted it to be.”

Whether Jamaica’s nightclub culture is poised for a full-scale comeback remains to be seen but for the hundreds who packed the National Arena on Saturday, that question could wait.

For a few hours the selectors juggled, the dancehall faithful answered every call, familiar faces appeared without warning, and Kartel once again held court over a crowd gathered to experience the music up close.

The Building may no longer stand at its old New Kingston address but on Saturday night its energy found a new home.

World.title: China trade surge
World.content:
CHINA is closing in on a milestone in its trade with Jamaica.

After selling a record US$878.6 million worth of goods to the island last year, the Asian manufacturing giant is now within striking distance of becoming a US$1-billion-a-year supplier to Jamaica. And it has got there quickly.

In 2021, Jamaica imported US$463.8 million worth of goods from China, according to official data compass, the Statistical Institute of Jamaica (Statin). Four years later, that bill had climbed by almost US$415 million, with China’s share of the island’s imports moving from 7.8 per cent to 11.7 per cent.

The increase last year alone was steep. Imports from China jumped by US$181.8 million, or just over 26 per cent, from US$696.8 million in 2024.

But look beyond the clothes, shoes, furniture, and other finished goods for which China is well-known and a large part of the business is in machinery, equipment, industrial supplies, and building materials.

Detailed trade tables supplied to the Jamaica Observer by Statin show imports of machinery and transport equipment from China rising from US$321.3 million in 2024 to US$416.2 million last year, accounting for almost half of everything Jamaica bought from the Asian country.

Manufactured goods classified mainly by material, a category that includes industrial supplies and building materials, climbed even faster, from US$196 million to US$271.3 million. Together those two categories accounted for more than three-quarters of Jamaica’s imports from China last year.

Chemicals and related products increased from US$39.8 million to US$44.2 million, while miscellaneous manufactured articles moved from US$125.9 million to US$132.8 million.

Statin said some of the leading individual products imported from China over the five-year period included new pneumatic rubber tyres for motor cars, parts for air-conditioning machines, and lithium-ion and other electric accumulators. Its broader machinery and transport category also covers vehicles, industrial machinery, telecommunications equipment, and other technical components.

The data have renewed a much older debate about what Jamaica should be importing and what it should be trying to make, assemble or otherwise add value to itself.

Businessman and manufacturer Metry Seaga does not believe the answer is to attempt to replace imports wholesale.

“Truth is, we’re an island and we don’t have a great supply chain here in the island. So because of that, we are going to import product. There’s no doubt about that. And we have to import various things,” Seaga, a former Jamaica Manufacturers and Exporters Association president said in a recent interview with the Business Observer.

“However, what we need to do is, we need to start realising that our policies need to have the ability to force people to buy with a local component,” he continued.

He wants Government to start with industries that already benefit from tax concessions, arguing that the support should come with a greater effort to keep some of the spending and production in Jamaica.

“If you’re giving an industry — the hotel industry, the BPO industry — if you are giving them benefits, tax benefits, then what you need to ask Government to say to them is, ‘listen, you need to have some value-added production for the import of your products’,” Seaga said.

“If you buy furniture, if there’s no capacity here, which there is, then buy from a local furniture manufacturer or one that’s in and does semi-production here. We need to add more value to the industries that are getting benefits from the Government,” he argued.

Seaga has long pushed local production, but his thinking on what that should look like has changed over the years. Full-scale manufacturing of a finished product is not always necessary, he reasoned. Jamaica could import inputs and undertake part of the production process here, particularly where the finished goods can then be sold into much larger markets.

“The opportunities are endless, and I’ll tell you why; because Jamaica is located in the best place in the Caribbean, in the Americas actually. Where Jamaica is located in the Americas is like where Singapore is located in Asia,” added Seaga, who also sits as chairman of JFP Limited, a manufacturer of custom-built commercial contract furniture.

“We have the ability to use our location as an asset… and we have to develop our economy as a logistics-centred economy where people can come in, add value to products here, and then distribute them throughout the Americas. We have never taken advantage of that,” he added.

China was not always so far ahead of Jamaica’s other suppliers.

In 2021 Jamaica imported US$463.8 million worth of goods from China, according to official data compass, the Statistical Institute of Jamaica (Statin). Four years later, that bill had climbed by almost US$415 million, with China’s share of the island’s imports moving from 7.8 per cent to 11.7 per cent.

Statin’s tables show that in 2021 Brazil sold US$514.3 million worth of goods to Jamaica, more than China’s US$463.8 million. China moved ahead the following year and has continued to pull away.

By 2025 it was Jamaica’s second-largest source of imports, behind only the United States. US goods entering Jamaica were valued at US$2.83 billion last year, compared with China’s US$878.6 million, Brazil’s US$396.8 million, Japan’s US$299.7 million and Trinidad and Tobago’s US$279.1 million.

Responding to queries from the Business Observer about China’s growing share of Jamaica’s import market, the Planning Institute of Jamaica (PIOJ) said the pace of the increase mirrors a wider global trend, particularly in Chinese exports of manufactured goods and capital equipment.

PIOJ also pointed to evidence in Statin data that China’s share of machinery and electrical goods has been increasing while the US share has declined.

“Statin trade data show declining US share in machinery and electrical goods, while China’s share has risen,” the PIOJ said.

It listed lower costs and China’s economies of scale, financing linked to Chinese investment projects and the country’s place in global supply chains for intermediate goods among the factors behind the change.

Importantly, PIOJ noted that products featured heavily among China’s imports line up with demand from construction, tourism, renewable energy, and infrastructure projects locally. While electronics and appliances bought by households remain part of the trade, the institute said “investment-driven demand is the primary driver of the import surge.”

PIOJ, however, sees some risk in Jamaica becoming increasingly reliant on a handful of countries for important imports.

“China’s growing role in Jamaica’s trade is both an opportunity and a risk. It supports investment and growth but raises concerns about over-reliance and trade imbalance,” PIOJ said, adding that stronger domestic production, export development, and greater diversification would be important to improving Jamaica’s economic resilience.

It calculated Jamaica’s import concentration index at 0.303 in 2025 and pointed out that China was already supplying 19.9 per cent of the country’s capital imports in 2023, compared with 42.3 per cent from the United States.

“Supply shocks, such as shipping disruptions, geopolitical tensions [and] tariff changes, could significantly affect transport, construction and energy sectors, where Chinese inputs dominate,” PIOJ said.

For Jamaica to capture more of that spending locally, however, Seaga believes some longstanding problems have to be addressed.

He named poor productivity, bureaucracy, and labour arrangements among his biggest concerns, putting electricity costs lower down the list than is often heard in discussions about manufacturing.

“Our lack of productivity is a huge one. Bureaucracy is a huge one. The cost of electricity to me is less important,” he said. “People can do solar, there are opportunities to deal with electricity in many industries, not all. There are some that are very electricity intensive, and we can’t do those here.”

Seaga also wants it made easier for overseas workers with specialised skills to work alongside Jamaicans and pass on technical knowledge, while arguing that delays within the public sector continue to frustrate businesses trying to invest and expand.

“Productivity is key. Our labour laws are key. Relaxing the importation of labour is key; and bureaucracy, I don’t want to diminish that in any way. Bureaucracy in the Government, it is too difficult to get anything done,” he said.

“To move a document from one civil servant desk to another, the same office can take months. It is not right.”

The special economic zone programme, in his view, should be doing more to marry overseas investment with businesses already operating locally.

Seaga, who previously chaired the Jamaica Special Economic Zone Authority (JSEZA), said the structure built for the SEZ regime is sound, but its development has been too slow.

“We do have a very good system with a good structure around it that international companies can live by and live in and operate in. Now, we need to move faster,” he said.

SEAGA… we have the ability to use our location as an asset… and we have to develop our economy as a logistics-centred economy where people can come in, add value to products here, and then distribute them throughout the Americas

That includes deliberately seeking investors whose operations could create more business for companies already producing in Jamaica.

“We need SEZ to be a vibrant organisation that’s looking to bring companies here to twin with manufacturers here and to bring industries that are relevant to the manufacturers here,” Seaga said.

“So if you have a box manufacturer here, you want to bring people who will use the box manufacturer here and increase their business tenfold. So those are the types of businesses you need to look for. Look for what is in your ecosystem now that’s efficient and effective, and then bring companies that come to Jamaica,” he argued.

While Jamaica’s purchases from China have been racing towards US$1 billion, the flow in the opposite direction remains small.

Exports to China were valued at US$25.9 million in 2025, up sharply from US$5.2 million a year earlier but still equal to only 1.6 per cent of Jamaica’s total exports. Jamaica bought almost US$34 worth of Chinese goods for every US$1 of goods it sold to China last year.

The detailed Statin tables show US$16 million of those exports falling under crude materials, inedible, except fuels; another US$5.9 million under mineral fuels, lubricants, and related materials; and US$3.9 million under food and live animals.

Statin describes the crude-materials category as raw, unprocessed commodities used as manufacturing inputs, while its food category covers products for human and animal consumption. The mineral-fuels category covers organic energy sources and petroleum-based products.

PIOJ sees room for Jamaica to tackle the imbalance from several directions, including more agro-processing and light manufacturing at home and some production of renewable-energy components. It also pointed to opportunities to grow sales to China.

“Target niche areas such as rum, coffee, seafood, cultural products, and services [tourism, education]. The World Trade Organisation data show China’s applied Most-Favoured-Nation tariff average is 7.5 per cent, but for many agricultural and cultural goods there is duty-free access,” the institution told the Business Observer.

Seaga, though, does not believe Jamaican manufacturers need to look halfway around the world first.

When asked how Jamaica could sell more to China, he quickly turned the conversation towards the United States.

“We don’t need to go so far as China. As I said, our location in the Americas allows us access to the richest market in the whole world, which is the United States of America,” he said.

“If most companies in Jamaica — which every company is a small company, even the greatest that Wisynco that we think of is a small company — if they get into one city in America with their products, it changes the shape of their business.”

“Whilst we want to sell to everywhere in the world — China, Africa, Europe, Asia, the rest of Asia — we don’t want to concentrate on far away yet. Let’s concentrate on who is beside us, America,” Seaga argued.

His idea of production is broad enough to include some of the relatively simple work that takes place between importing a product and selling it.

“Bring rice, package it here, label it here, use the packaging and the labelling from here. Use the labour that’s here to store it, to do the value-added,” Seaga said.

“Our economy is too small; and we need to grow that outside of Jamaica.

“It may not be that we’re manufacturing — complete manufacturing — but you may be doing semi-manufacturing or screwdriver industry or some form of value add.

“I don’t care what it is, just add some value here,” Seaga said.

The Business Observer also asked JSEZA about efforts to attract more manufacturing and assembly operations, including Chinese investment, and whether the SEZ framework is already helping Jamaica capture more value from imports through local production. See the companion story in this edition for JSEZA’s response

(Pages 10 & 11).

World.title: ‘WHISPER’ GOAL
World.content:
Jamaica Reggae Boyz winger Dujuan “Whisper” Richards sits in the stands of AFC Wimbledon’s stadium on Tuesday.

After a difficult start to senior club football, Reggae Boyz winger Dujuan “Whisper” Richards says he’s looking to finally make his mark after joining English Football League (EFL) League One club AFC Wimbledon on a season—long loan from Chelsea FC.

Richards sealed the move to England’s third division outfit just before the summer transfer window closed, making it his second loan spell away from Premier League giants Chelsea. The young Jamaican reportedly had several options but made the decision after seeing the South London club’s win against Wigan Athletic on Sunday.

“[It’s a] great feeling. [I] can’t wait to get started and hit the ground running. Just trying to get back… and score some goals,” he said.

The 20-year-old was not part of Chelsea’s preseason under new manager Xabi Alonso and was not involved with the Under-21s for their Premier League 2 and EFL Trophy fixtures last month.

Richards joined former Premier League champions Leicester City in the EFL Championship on deadline day in January. However, he struggled for playing time, making just three substitute appearances in his first 10 games, totalling 26 minutes. He was then left out of matchday squad altogether for the remaining five games of the season as Leicester suffered relegation.

Richards’ lack of minutes ultimately played a role in not being part of the Reggae Boyz squad for the FIFA World Cup Play-offs in March against New Caledonia and DR Congo. He had previously played the final four games in the final round of Concacaf World Cup qualifying.

Despite the challenges during the Leicester loan spell, Richards believes it was a teachable moment.

“I think it was the right thing, it went the right way in my opinion to see where I’m at and to just start focusing on the things that are right,” he said.

He now joins Wimbledon, who finished 19th in League One last season, avoiding relegation by four points. The club are currently have four points from their first three games of the league season.

“I’ve been watching [the team] for the last couple of days. I think after the game against Wigan I was like, they’ve really got a good team that could be successful this season. I’m ready [and] ready to do what it takes to be the fans’ favourite,” Richards said.

He joins former Reggae Boyz Jason Euell and Marcus Gayle as well as 2023 debutant Delano Splatt as Jamaica internationals to play for AFC Wimbledon.

Richards could be involved in today’s contest against Burton Albion at 1:45 pm Jamaica time.

During the announcement by the club, Richards credited his “idol”, fellow Reggae Boy Leon Bailey, for inspiring him.

“When I was growing up it was only him to watch on YouTube back then so he was basically our Messi in Jamaica at the time [and] still is. I’m grateful, he’s basically the person that brought me to the Phoenix Academy so I’m grateful,” he said.

Bailey, meanwhile, was unable to secure a deadline day move from Aston Villa, after being linked with Premier League club Hull City and La Liga side Sevilla.

The 29-year-old was seemingly on the verge of joining newly promoted Hull in July but talks broke down with agent and Phoenix Academy owner Craig Butler telling the Jamaica Observer that he had several options on the table.

Bailey returned to Villa in January after an unsuccessful loan spell at Serie A club AS Roma. Despite making 21 appearances and winning the Europa League, he was told he would not be part of manager Unai Emery’s plans for the season, despite being involved in preseason.

“We were expecting him to leave,” Emery said last Friday “When we left for Asia, he was close to leaving, but he is still with us now. Hopefully, he can get a good opportunity to leave and join another club and continue his career, and this is our objective.”

Reports from England say Bailey, currently training alone at Villa’s facilities, could move to Saudi Arabia with their transfer window open until Sunday. Al-Diriyah are reportedly front-runners who have former Liverpool star Darwin Nunez and former PSG and Everton midfielder Idrissa Gueye in their ranks. Al-Ittihad, former club of French stars Karim Benzema and N’Golo Kante, are also interested.

Bailey joined Villa from Bayer Leverkusen in 2021 and scored 23 goals in 163 appearances in all competitions.

World.title: Amber eyes Jamaica IoT roll-out as Africa device count tops one million
World.content:
Engineers work on electronic components at Amber IoT’s South Africa operation, which designs and develops hardware used in areas including utilities, security, vehicle tracking, and other connected-device applications.

AMBER Group is eyeing an early 2027 start to the roll-out of a network for Internet of Things (IoT) devices in Jamaica, as its South Africa-based Amber IoT business surpasses one million devices manufactured, sold, and deployed across Africa.

Founder and CEO Dushyant Savadia said the Jamaica-headquartered technology group expects the local roll-out to require an investment of about US$750,000.

“Hopefully, from the starting of next year we’ll start putting our own base stations designed by us internally across Jamaica,” Savadia told the Jamaica Observer in an interview from India on Tuesday.

The timetable is not firm. Amber plans to deploy an 0G network, a low-power, low-cost system designed for machines that need to transmit small amounts of information rather than make calls or stream data.

Savadia said Amber IoT has grown from two product lines in 2023 to about 20 today, including vehicle trackers, electricity and water-meter technology, security equipment, and panic buttons.

“What has happened since then, because there’s a diverse amount of products now inside Amber IoT, it also allowed us to scale very, very fast,” he said.

South Africa remains its main market, accounting for an estimated 70 per cent of the devices, with the remaining 30 per cent spread across countries including Ghana, Morocco, Nigeria, and Kenya.

The business now accounts for a sizeable share of Amber Group’s revenue.

“In terms of revenue share, Amber IoT, I would say, is at least eight to 10 per cent of our global revenue now,” Savadia said.

He did not disclose the dollar value, but said most of Amber Group’s income is earned outside Jamaica.

“The majority of our revenue comes from overseas markets, not from Jamaica. Jamaica is perhaps one of the smallest markets for us in the world,” he told the Business Observer.

Amber’s African IoT operation grew out of its 2022 acquisition of South African hardware manufacturer Intelli-Business Solutions, which it bought outright and renamed Amber IoT.

The company had already spent about 13 years developing IoT products, including equipment for the banking, insurance, and security industries, before Amber acquired it.

“We acquired a company with all of these specialisations and then built up even further to add a lot more devices than what they had produced prior to the purchase of 100 per cent of the shares by Amber Group Jamaica,” Savadia said.

He said South Africa was targeted first because businesses there were already more familiar with IoT technology and how it could be used to cut costs and gather information remotely.

The Jamaican roll-out has taken longer than previously envisaged. In September 2024, Savadia told the Financial Gleaner that Amber would “start deploying next year”, pointing at the time to a 2025 start.

Savadia said Amber has since developed its own transponders and radios for the Jamaican network. Potential uses include remote utility-meter readings, vehicle and asset tracking, and security systems that can send alerts when equipment or containers are breached.

“We will have similar impact like in Africa, in the Caribbean too, where we will roll out our own 0G network on which our devices will speak,” he said.

World.title: China threat bolsters support for EU industrial policy
World.content:
The next wave could be even more destructive, industry officials warned.

Unlike the first shock, the industries now under pressure include sectors that Europe considers central to its economic and technological future, such as electric vehicles and batteries, as well as steel, chemicals, and wind turbines.

The IAA is designed partly to blunt that pressure, limiting Chinese investments in strategic sectors like EVs, raw materials or solar panels. It would also set Made-in-EU requirements for public procurement, potentially excluding Chinese suppliers.

“The level of ambition is justified. If it’s Europe’s main tool to respond to the second China shock, it’s essential to make it count,” Sander Tordoir, chief economist at the Centre for European Reform think tank, told MEPs. “Do it right or don’t do it at all.”

Beijing has strongly objected to the IAA, but — despite some initial misgivings — it is gaining more support among EU countries and there is broad backing in the Parliament.

“The urgency has increased,” Green MEP Anna Cavazzini, co-lead on the file, said. She called the IAA a “cornerstone” of the EU’s response to China’s aggressive trade policies. “There’s a lot of alignment that we need to strengthen the Commission proposal.”

World.title: Kallas pushes back on Franco-German reform plans for EU diplomatic service
World.content:
Kaja Kallas take part in a joint press conference following an informal meeting of EU Foreign Affairs ministers, at Druids Glen in Wicklow, south of Dublin, Ireland, on September 2, 2026. | Paul Faith/ AFP via Getty Images

EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas on Wednesday poured cold water on plans to overhaul the bloc’s diplomatic branch, arguing that better enforcement of the current rules would make its foreign policy more effective.

France and Germany have floated plans for root-and-branch reforms of Kallas’s European External Action Service, or EEAS, according to a discussion paper seen by POLITICO. The plans include giving her oversight of policy units in the European Commission that deal with external relations.

But after a debate on the proposed reforms among EU foreign ministers in Wicklow, Ireland, Kallas said that a “majority” of envoys had supported “the current institutional setup” of the EEAS. She added that there was “broad support” from member countries to make it work without big institutional changes.

World.title: No budget deal without new EU taxes, Costa warns
World.content:
Finding an agreement on new EU taxes — so-called own resources — is key to facilitating an overall budget deal in December before national elections in France, Spain and Italy in 2027 threaten the negotiations.

Costa is touring the EU’s 27 capitals to sound out their concerns and assess where there is room for compromise. The Portuguese politician plays a key role in the negotiations as he chairs leaders’ meetings and brokers compromises among different camps.

The issue of EU-wide taxes is among the thorniest in the discussions because national capitals are reluctant to hand more taxing powers to the European Commission and agree to new levies that would hit some countries harder than others.

Last year, the Commission proposed five new levies — targeting carbon imports, emissions, non-collected electronic waste, corporate profits and tobacco products — worth €66 billion per year to finance the budget. But most of the ideas have been met with resistance from governments, who must unanimously approve each new levy.

Tensions were on full display when Luxembourgish Prime Minister Luc Frieden rejected the proposed EU tobacco tax after a meeting with Costa earlier on Wednesday.

"We won’t accept proposals that impact [Luxembourg] in a disproportionate manner," he told reporters.

World.title: Von der Leyen, Rutte say Russian ‘intimidation will not work’ to stop Ukraine aid
World.content:
EU and NATO chiefs pledge continued support for Ukraine after a thwarted attack on a German airport sending aid to Kyiv was attributed to Russia.

BRUSSELS — The EU and NATO will not back down from supporting Ukraine despite attacks against European countries blamed on Russia, the leaders of the two institutions said Wednesday.

The rare joint statement came after Germany said Russia was behind a foiled attack on an airport used as a key logistics hub for military aid to Ukraine.

“This was an attack using military-grade material carried out by Russian operatives on European Union soil — we will not tolerate it,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen told reporters in Brussels. “If the intention was to make us think twice about supporting Ukraine, I can tell you it has only strengthened my resolve; intimidation will not work.”

World.title: Britain’s new finance minister sets date for first big speech on growth
World.content:
Burnham revealed in mid-August that Healey was working on a speech on the government’s economic agenda. The date of next Monday was first reported by Politics at Sam and Anne’s, the morning briefing podcast by POLITICO and Sky News.

The speech will focus heavily on growth, said two of the people quoted above — weeks after Burnham moved responsibility for local economic growth strategy from the Treasury to his new prime ministerial office in Manchester, No. 10 North.

One of the four people cited at the start of this story said the speech is likely to focus less on individual spending policies ahead of the Oct. 28 budget and more on a broader vision and initiatives, including Burnham’s promises to hand more economic levers to regional leaders.

“This isn’t a rushed job — it’s a serious bit of thinking,” they added. Another of the four people said: “It’s the government’s version of their theory of growth.”

A government official, who is not one of the four individuals cited above, said the speech has involved work by multiple government departments contributing potential ideas. “It’s crossed a lot of people’s radar,” they added.

Some in Westminster may see the speech as Healey seeking to emphasize his own role.

World.title: Bardella’s international blitz hints at new role for French far-right leader
World.content:
“Bardella has always been attached to the international credibility of the National Rally,” said the aide, who was granted anonymity to share details of Bardella’s plans. “He will give great attention to the international press during the campaign.”

Since shooting up the National Rally’s ranks in his twenties, Bardella has brought a polished professionalism to a party that long struggled to run a tight ship. He led the party to impressive victories in the 2019 and 2024 European elections and is now the head of the Patriots group in the European Parliament. The party is now more popular than ever, and Le Pen is the front-runner to win next year’s presidential election.

But when it looked like an embezzlement conviction would doom Le Pen’s chances at running for the presidency, Bardella, as the National Rally’s presumptive candidate, tried to woo more fiscally conservative voters — including France’s business elite — by flirting with a more market-friendly platform than his mentor.

But Bardella has been adjusting to a secondary role since an appeals court cleared a path for Le Pen to run as the party’s presidential nominee — and she has made clear that fiscal discipline won’t come at the expense of the promises she has made to her core voters. That includes her pledge to lower the retirement age for most workers to 62 at a cost of €9 billion per year.

Bardella is now eyeing a role similar to the one Giorgia Meloni held before she became Italian prime minister in 2022.

Bardella “watched with great interest the campaign of Giorgia Meloni, who flooded the international press to reassure institutions and the financial markets,” the aide said.

World.title: Ulrich Siegmunds Erfolgsrezept
World.content:
Share on LinkedIn

Kurz vor der Landtagswahl in Sachsen-Anhalt analysieren Pauline von Pezold und Frederik Schindler, wie es AfD-Spitzenkandidat Ulrich Siegmund gelungen ist, einen regelrechten Gute-Laune-Wahlkampf zu inszenieren und dabei auch viele Nichtwähler zu mobilisieren. Trotz Umfragewerten um die 40 Prozent bleibt fraglich, ob es für seine einzige Option, eine absolute Mehrheit, tatsächlich reicht.

Außerdem sprechen die beiden darüber, wie gleich vier Mitarbeiter der AfD-Landtagsfraktion um Siegmund früher in der inzwischen verbotenen Neonazi-Organisation „Heimattreue Deutsche Jugend“ aktiv waren, darunter auch Fraktionsgeschäftsführer Patrick Harr und Fraktionsjustiziar Laurens Nothdurft. Eine Distanzierung von dieser Vergangenheit gibt es weder von den Betroffenen noch von Siegmund selbst.

Zum Schluss schauen von Pezold und Schindler auf den zurückliegenden Bundeskongress der AfD-Jugendorganisation „Generation Deutschland“ in Magdeburg. Dort haben sich deutliche inhaltliche Differenzen zur Mutterpartei gezeigt: Der Vorsitzende Jean-Pascal Hohm widerspricht Parteichefin Alice Weidel offen in der Europapolitik. Bei gleichzeitig radikalen Forderungen nach millionenfachen Abschiebungen.

Die ZDF-Sendung „Lanz“, in der Frederik Schindler diese Woche zu Gast war, gibt es hier online zu sehen.

„Inside AfD“ ist der POLITICO-Podcast über die umstrittenste Partei des Landes. Trotz Radikalisierung und Beobachtung durch den Verfassungsschutz wächst die AfD weiter. Wie ist das möglich? Was treibt ihre Anhänger, Strategen und Gegner an? Wie funktioniert das Innenleben der Partei? Und was bedeutet ihr Aufstieg für das politische System Deutschlands?

Antworten liefern immer mittwochs Pauline von Pezold von POLITICO und Frederik Schindler von WELT — unaufgeregt, aber kritisch.
