See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Alex van Halen, one of two Dutch brothers who founded the US rock band Van Halen, has been given one of the Netherlands’ highest civil honours.

The 73-year-old drummer was made a knight in the Order of the Netherlands Lion after being nominated by his home city of Nijmegen.

The city said it had recognised Van Halen for his distinctive drumming style, calling it “powerful, dynamic and precise.”

Van Halen, who flew from the United States to receive the honour at a ceremony in from the mayor of Nijmegen, Hubert Bruls, said he was “very grateful”. He also signed the book of the city.

“I think institutions like this are important in people’s lives because it adds a dignity and a gravity to what we do,” he said.

“Whether it’s actually deserved or not, that’s another question. But we can live up to it.”

Nijmegen to Pasadena

Alex and his younger brother Eddie started the band in 1970, eight years after the family moved from Nijmegen to Pasadena in the United States.

Their best-known hits were Jump and Runnin with the Devil, distinguished by Eddie van Halen’s virtuoso performances on guitar.

Originally Eddie wanted to be a drummer while Alex played guitar, but the brothers swapped roles by the time they formed their first band in school, The Broken Combs. They were also classically trained pianists.

In 2019 part of the Hunnerpark was temporarily renamed Van Halenplein and a mural was painted in honour of Eddie van Halen.

The band Van Halen stayed together until Eddie’s death in 2020 at the age of 65.

World.title: Dutch woman living in Nepal found alive after surviving floods
World.content:
The Dutch foreign office has made contact with a woman living in Nepal who had been reported missing in the wake of last week’s devastating floods, which have killed more than 1,100 people.

Foreign affairs minister Tom Berendsen said there had been “good news” as he spoke to reporters during a meeting of EU foreign ministers in Ireland.

The woman is one of three Dutch nationals who were known to be in Nepal when a glacier in the Himalaya region collapsed last Wednesday, causing water and mud to surge down the Bhote Koshi river and wipe out villages in the Rawusa border region with Tibet.

She was in the Himalaya region when the disaster struck, but has reached the Nepalese capital Kathmandu, where she contacted the foreign ministry.

A spokesman said the government was still “very concerned about the fate of the two other Dutch nationals”, 29-year-old Christiaan Berghuis from Nijkerk and 51-year-old Maaike Moolhuijsen from Haarlem.

They were on a pilgrimage to Mount Kailash, a sacred Tibetan mountain, when the floods hit. The group of 80 pilgrims were believed to be in an immigration office that was in the path of the floodwaters.

World.title: Cheap Chinese parcels to the Netherlands fall 46% after EU levy
World.content:
The number of small parcels arriving in the Netherlands from outside the EU fell by 46% in July and August compared with the previous six months, according to customs figures presented to parliament. It is the first clear sign that a new €3 import charge is changing the flow of cheap goods from China.

The drop was revealed by Eelco Eerenberg, the junior finance minister responsible for customs, during a debate in parliament on Tuesday.

Around one million such parcels were arriving in the Netherlands each day before the change, 80% to 90% of them from Chinese platforms such as Shein, Temu and AliExpress.

Since July 1, a new EU-wide charge of €3 has applied to parcels worth up to €150 sent from outside the bloc, which were previously exempt from import duties. The fee is levied per type of product rather than per parcel, so an order containing several different items can be charged more than once.

Customs officials say online retailers are already changing how they operate, moving away from sending millions of individual packages and instead importing goods in bulk to store in warehouses inside the EU before shipping them on to shoppers. The same shift has been seen in France and Belgium.

“The figures give a first indication that fewer loose parcels are going straight to the consumer,” Nanette van Schelven, director-general of the Dutch customs service, told broadcaster NOS, “which makes it easier for us to check whether products are safe.”

A single large shipment is easier to screen for unsafe or banned goods, she said, than a constant stream of separate parcels.

The Dutch share

The charge raised about €134 million in import duties in July alone, of which roughly a quarter went to the Dutch treasury. Customs duties are collected as an EU revenue source: member states keep a share to cover the cost of collection and pass the rest to Brussels.

The Netherlands had drawn up plans for a national surcharge of its own on cheap parcels but dropped them in January, choosing to rely on the EU charge after France and Belgium shelved similar schemes and Brussels brought its levy forward.

World.title: Polish drone plant fire “undoubtedly” arson and likely ordered by Russia, says Tusk
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. There is now “no doubt” that a fire this week at a drone factory in Poland was caused deliberately, says Prime Minister Donald Tusk, who also suggested it was carried out on behalf of Russia. World.title: Polish court orders Catholic diocese to compensate child sex abuse victim and priest to apologise
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. A court has ordered a Catholic diocese in Poland to pay 550,000 zloty (€128,250) in compensation to a woman who suffered sexual abuse as a child at the hands of a priest over four decades ago. It has also ruled that the priest himself must publish an apology to his victim and admit his guilt. The ruling, which can still be appealed, represents one of the largest compensation orders ever issued against Poland’s Catholic church, which has in recent years been hit by a series of revelations of clerical child sex abuse, as well as of negligence by bishops in dealing with such cases. Iwona Dudzik-Osińska, who has allowed her name to be published, was first raped in 1981 at the age of 12 by a priest, who has only been named so far as Father Jan and is now 76 years old, in the city of Kielce. The abuse continued for a period of three years, she revealed to the Gazeta Wyborcza daily. In 2007, Dudzik-Osińska decided to report the crimes to prosecutors, but was told that the statute of limitations had expired. In 2019, after the release of a major documentary on sex abuse in Poland’s Catholic church, she also informed Jan Piotrowski, the bishop of Kielce, of what she had suffered. Dudzik-Osińska said that the bishop was sympathetic but told her he could not meet her request to provide church funds to pay for therapy. However, she later received a bank transfer (for an amount that has not been revealed) from Piotrowski’s personal account. Meanwhile, Father Jan was suspended by the diocese of Sosnowiec, where he had been working since the 1990s, banned from contact with children, and brought before an internal church court. A spokeswoman for the Sosnowiec diocese confirmed to Gazeta Wyborcza that, in 2023, the church court removed Father Jan from public exercise of priestly ministry (though he remains in the priesthood) and ordered that he must reside at a location designated by the bishop (which has not been publicly revealed). In the meantime, Dudzik-Osińska launched a civil case against the church, demanding 900,000 zloty in compensation and an annual lifetime payment. The case lasted over four years, but in July the district court in Kielce issued a ruling, which is only now being reported. It ordered the Kielce diocese to pay the victim 550,000 zloty. Moreover, Father Jan must send a personal apology to Dudzik-Osińska in which he admits to sexually abusing her, and also publish such an apology and admission of guilt, under his real name, in a local newspaper, reports Catholic magazine Więź. The ruling can still be appealed by any of the parties involved. A spokesman for the diocese, Paweł Ścisłowicz, told Gazeta Wyborcza that they would only decide on further steps once the court had sent the justification for its decision. Dudzik-Osińska’s attorney, Michał Sochański, celebrated the ruling as “one of the first of its kind in Poland” and said that it “reflects an extremely important trend in case law that can offer hope to those sexually abused by clergy many years ago”. “Institutional mechanisms for resolving cases of sexual abuse in the church have proven insufficient for victims, but fortunately the court system remains an option,” he added. “Justice may come very late, but this verdict demonstrates that it is not unattainable.” A Catholic diocese has been ordered to pay compensation to a man sexually abused as a child by a priest. The victim was treated as an “accomplice in the sin of adultery” at a church trial that acquitted the priest, who was later convicted by a state court https://t.co/IHay5h56SG — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 10, 2022 Poland’s Catholic church has in recent years faced a growing number of claims of sexual abuse by clergy and of negligence in dealing with the issue by bishops. The Vatican has taken action against a number of Polish bishops over the issue. Most recently, in 2024, the Holy See announced the resignation of the bishop of Łowicz, Andrzej Dziuba, due to his “negligence in handling cases of sexual abuse against minors”. Meanwhile, the Polish church has introduced new rules intended to protect children and other vulnerable people from abuse,held meetings with victims, and apologised for its neglect in dealing with such cases in the past. A church commission set up to investigate child sex abuse in a Catholic diocese in Poland has identified at least 50 victims and 29 abusers. It also found that bishops repeatedly failed to take action when credible reports of abuse were submitted to them https://t.co/MRNl5vWp4E — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 13, 2026 In 2018, a court in the city of Poznań ordered the Society of Christ, a Polish Catholic congregation, to pay 1 million zloty in compensation as well as lifelong monthly payments of 800 zloty to a woman who had been abused by one of its priests as a child. In 2022, the Catholic diocese of Toruń was ordered by a court to pay 600,000 zloty in compensation to a man who was sexually abused for almost a decade while serving as an altar boy. Last year, Bielsko-Żywiec diocese was ordered to pay 400,000 zloty to another victim, who is also seeking a further 20 million zloty in compensation from the archdiocese of Kraków A court has begun hearing the largest-ever compensation claim against Poland’s Catholic church by a victim of clerical sexual abuse. World.title: Poland grants Ukraine permission to search for remains of Ukrainians massacred by Polish partisans
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland has granted permission for Ukraine to conduct a search for the remains of Ukrainian civilians killed by Polish resistance fighters during World War Two. The decision marks the latest step towards reconciliation between the two countries over their difficult shared history. Following a diplomatic breakthrough last year, Kyiv has also granted Poland permission to search for and exhume the remains of Poles massacred by Ukrainian nationalists. On Tuesday, Ukrainian deputy culture minister Ivan Verbytskyi announced that the Polish authorities had granted a permit for a Ukrainian group to conduct exploratory work in the village of Łasków in southeastern Poland, around 10km from the border with Ukraine. The search aims to uncover the remains of Ukrainian civilians killed by the Peasant Battalions (Bataliony Chłopskie), a major underground resistance movement that emerged in Poland during the German occupation of World War Two. Łasków, which had a predominantly ethnic Ukrainian population, was attacked by a Peasant Battalion unit on 10 March 1944, with some estimates suggesting around 300 civilians were killed. Among those who died was a local Orthodox priest, Lev Korobchuk. On the same day, members of the Home Army (Armia Krajowa), Poland’s largest armed resistance movement, also attacked the nearby village of Sahryń. According to estimates, they killed hundreds more Ukrainians. Ukraine has also submitted an application to carry out exploratory work there. Dariusz Kopciowski, the conservator of monuments in the Lublin province where Łasków is located, confirmed to the Polish Press Agency (PAP) that a permit for exploration work in Łasków had been granted. The issue had recently begun to cause tension, with Ukrainian media reporting last week that Ukraine has been waiting over a year for permission to carry out searches in Łasków. By contrast, Kyiv has granted permission for Poland to conduct such searches on its territory. Those Polish efforts are focused in particular on finding and exhuming the remains of victims of the so-called Volhynia massacres, in which Ukrainian nationalists killed around 100,000 Poles, mostly women and children, as part of an ethnic cleansing operation. Poland regards those massacres as a genocide. However, Ukraine strongly rejects that label and also points to the fact that Polish partisan units killed Ukrainian civilians during the war. Poland, in turn, argues that many such incidents were acts of reprisal for the massacres carried out by Ukrainians. Long-simmering tensions between Poland and Ukraine over WWII massacres have finally boiled over, prompting a diplomatic crisis.@danieltilles1 looks at how we got here and what it may mean for the two countries and Europe more broadly https://t.co/a8tiYJJHRr — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 22, 2026 In 2017, Ukraine introduced a moratorium on search and exhumation work on its territory in response to the dismantling of a monument in Poland dedicated to the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA). The UPA led the Volhynia massacres but is still celebrated by many in Ukraine for its role in fighting for independence from Moscow-backed Soviet rule. Last year, following negotiations with Poland, Ukraine lifted that moratorium and again began issuing permits for searches and exhumations of Polish victims on its territory, a number of which have already taken place. Last Sunday, Verbytskyi attended a funeral ceremony for 55 Polish massacre victims, around half of them children, whose remains were recently found and exhumed in a former Polish village located in what is now Ukraine. The remains of 55 Poles massacred by Ukrainian nationalists in WWII have been reburied at a ceremony in Ukraine attended by political and religious figures from both countries. The victims, around half of them children, were exhumed this summer https://t.co/4q3giZhBAL — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 31, 2026 However, as well as those moves towards reconciliation, there have also been regular clashes between Warsaw and Kyiv over World War Two history, in particular following President Volodymyr Zelensky’s decision in May this year to name a military unit after the UPA. That triggered strong protests from Poland, whose president, Karol Nawrocki, stripped Zelensky of Poland’s highest honour, the Order of the White Eagle. Poland has also expressed concern over a new national pantheon being established by Ukraine. It has warned that, if figures associated with the massacre of Poles are included, that could have consequences for Ukraine’s ambitions to join the European Union. President Zelensky has signed a law establishing a national pantheon to commemorate Ukrainian heroes, prompting Poland to again warn that Ukraine "will have a huge problem" integrating into the EU if it honours figures associated with massacres of Poles https://t.co/fN7Zgbovvu — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 24, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Poles eating more meat but drinking less alcohol
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poles are eating more meat but drinking less alcohol, continuing a long-term trend, the latest data from Statistics Poland (GUS), a state agency, show. The average person in Poland ate 82 kilograms of meat in 2025, which was 7.5% more than a year earlier. It also marks an increase of 15.7% since 2015 and 22.7% since 2005. Likewise, consumption of eggs rose 8.5% in 2025 to an average of 218 per person. The increases have come amid rapidly rising incomes, which make such products more affordable. A separate GUS study earlier this year showed that the proportion of Poles who cannot afford to eat meat at least every other day fell from 8.2% in 2015 to 3% in 2025. By contrast, vegetable consumption has changed little, with the average Pole eating 108 kg in 2025, compared with 107 kg a year earlier and 110 kg in 2005. However, consumption of potatoes, a starchy staple of the Polish diet presented by GUS separately from other vegetables, has fallen sharply over the longer term, despite a slight increase last year. The average Pole ate 96.5 kg of potatoes in 2025, down 23.4% since 2005. Meanwhile, alcohol consumption last year continued its recent decline. In 2025, the average Pole drank 81.7 litres of beer, down 4.9% from the previous year and 18.7% from the peak of 100.5 litres per person in 2018. Likewise, consumption of spirits and liqueurs fell 5.9% year-on-year in 2025 to 3.2 litres per person. That was 13.5% down from a peak of 3.7 litres in 2019. In 2025, the amount of wine drunk per person, at 4.9 litres, fell even more, by 9.3% year-on-year. However, alcohol consumption is still higher than it was two decades ago, with the average Pole drinking 28% more spirits and 1.2% more beer in 2025 than in 2005. A 2023 study by ProVeg, an NGO, conducted in partnership with the University of Copenhagen and Ghent University, found that Poles were the most carnivorous among ten European countries surveyed. Three quarters of Poles (74%) said they ate meat frequently, compared to an average of 62% across all countries. Italians and Spaniards (both 69%) were the next biggest meat eaters, while Germans (45%), Austrians (48%) and the Dutch (53%) were the least likely to eat meat frequently. Meanwhile, 7% of people in Poland said they were either vegan (2%), meaning consuming no animal products at all, or vegetarian (5%), meaning they do not eat meat or fish. That was just below the European average of 8%. In terms of what kinds of meat are favoured by Poles, GUS’s most recent such breakdown, from 2017, showed that pork was most popular, with the average Pole consuming 39.8 kg that year, followed by poultry (26.kg) and beef (2.3 kg). Poland's first company to produce cultured meat – which is grown in a lab from animal cells without the need to raise and kill livestock – has received a state grant to support its work. From the start of the new school year, which began today, school canteens are expected to serve meat no more than twice a week, offer fish at least once per week, and offer a plant-based option at every meal. They should also limit fried food to no more than twice a week, use seasonal and locally sourced products, and include fruit and vegetables with meals. However, an attempt by the government to further raise taxes on alcoholic, sugary and sweet drinks was vetoed by opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki last December. A fundraiser for an eight-month-old baby who survived an accident in the Polish city of Kraków in which his parents were killed by a speeding driver has reached more than 1 million zloty (€231,000). The tragedy has prompted widespread anger, with calls from residents and local politicians for the authorities to take action to deal with dangerous driving in the city. To będzie jedna z najtrudniejszych zbiórek, jakie wspólnie przeprowadzimy.💔Proszę o RT🙏 Kilka dni temu rozpędzony kierowca w Krakowie wjechał w młode małżeństwo. Mateusz i Klaudia zginęli. Ich kilkumiesięczny synek, Oliwier, trafił do szpitala. Mam dla Was dobrą wiadomość.… pic.twitter.com/R8L1xgEBPn — Damian Żurawski (@damian_zurawski) August 26, 2026 On 22 August, a married couple, Mateusz and Klaudia, both 32, were walking with their baby on Solna Street, close to the southern bank of the Vistula river, when a car driven by 26-year-old Hubert B., whose surname is masked under Polish privacy law, mounted the pavement, killing both parents. The child, eight-month-old Oliwier, survived the accident but was hospitalised. His condition is continuing to improve, reports broadcaster TVP Kraków. According to prosecutors, the car was travelling around 40 km/h (25mph) faster than the speed limit in the area. Hubert B. has been charged with unintentionally causing a fatal accident, for which he could face up to eight years in prison. “The suspect pleaded not guilty to the offence he was charged with, explaining, among other things, that the car skidded due to the uneven road surface,” prosecutors said, adding that the suspect has been placed in pretrial detention. An online fundraiser set up last week to provide Oliwier “with financial security for years to come” shared the news that the baby’s condition is now stable, although “his arm and leg are in plaster”. “We can’t give Oliwier back his mum and dad,” reads the fundraiser’s description. “However, we can do everything we can to ensure he has the resources for his education and a peaceful start to adult life.” At the time of writing, the fundraiser has reached more than 1.05 million zloty, over double its initial target. There have been more than 23,300 donations so far. Meanwhile, Oliwier’s grandfather, Andrzej, told newspaper Fakt that the family had given its consent for the fundraiser and was very grateful for those who had donated. A court in Kraków has granted Mateusz’s brother custody of the child. As well as sympathy for the victims, the accident aroused anger from residents. Several hundred people attended a protest at the site, holding signs reading “How many more people must die for something to change?” and “Stop road killers”. They installed their own mock-up pedestrian crossing and speed bumps. “Such tragedies are not isolated incidents,” said the organisers, quoted by news website Interia. They cited police figures showing that Kraków had the most road accidents of all Poland’s provincial capitals in 2025. Its figure of 941 was over 100 more than in Łódź and over 250 more than in Warsaw. Local councillor Rafał Zawiślak told news website Onet that he was filing a complaint with the prosecutor’s office, saying the city authorities had been negligent, failing to respond to warnings from 2024 that the site of the accident was dangerous. Godzina ciszy w Krakowie. Mieszkańcy upamiętniają parę, która zginęła w sobotniej tragedii przy ulicy Solnej. Na miejsce przybyły tłumy. „Nie chcemy bać się chodzić po chodnikach” – apelują.@RadioKrakow pic.twitter.com/DlOn5GvyL5 — Elżbieta Raczyńska (@_eraczynska) August 25, 2026 Acting mayor Stanisław Kracik said that an inspection of the street carried out after the accident had not shown any problems with the existing signage or need for traffic-calming measures. He added, however, that the city would be installing a speed bump. “I believe that this is simply what we should do…as a kind of expression of solidarity with the victims of this tragedy,” he said, quoted by broadcaster TVN. City police said they had been monitoring and taking action about road safety issues in the district for years, but that the street in question had not previously been reported as a particularly dangerous place, with just one incident causing one injury in the five years before the fatal accident. MPs from The Left have called for tougher rules on illegal street racing, saying police currently do not have sufficient legal tools. It comes after a crash on Saturday in which four men died after their car was filmed driving at dangerously high speeds https://t.co/OSRvyPAtVA — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 18, 2023 The police also claimed that Kraków is “one of the safest cities” in Poland, with 768 road accidents per 100,000 residents this year, compared to over 1,000 in some other cities. However, TVN points out that the same statistics show that, this year, Kraków has had 71 accidents per 100,000 inhabitants in which someone was injured or killed, compared to 28 in Katowice and 27 in Warsaw. Road safety in Poland has improved dramatically, with the country recording the EU’s largest decline in road deaths between 2019 and 2024. However, its overall number of road deaths in relation to population is still above the EU average. Road deaths have fallen by 35% in Poland since 2019, which is the largest decline in the EU. World.title: Polish student accused of planning Islamist terrorist attack on Christmas market to stand trial
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. A Polish student is to stand trial accused of planning a terrorist attack on a Christmas market in Poland as an act of support for Islamic State. On Monday, prosecutors announced that they have filed an indictment against the 20-year-old suspect, a student at the Catholic University of Lublin (KUL) who can be named only as Mateusz W. under Polish privacy law. Jacek Dobrzyński, spokesman for Poland’s security services, confirmed that Mateusz W. had been “preparing a mass attack at a Christmas market, which he planned to carry out using explosive materials”. Wracamy do sprawy 20-letniego Mateusza W. – studenta Katolickiego Uniwersytetu Lubelskiego podejrzewanego o przygotowywanie masowego zamachu na jednym z jarmarków świątecznych, którego planował dokonać z wykorzystaniem materiałów wybuchowych. Do Sądu Okręgowego w Koszalinie… https://t.co/6vGPcjiDnc pic.twitter.com/seFGV8nHMz — Jacek Dobrzyński (@JacekDobrzynski) August 31, 2026 The suspect was detained late last year, when details of his alleged plot and plans to establish contact with Islamic State were first revealed. He has remained in custody since then. Though the authorities have confirmed that Mateusz W. was a first-year student at KUL, a leading Catholic university that counts the late Pope John Paul II among its former students and lecturers, and that they have also searched premises in the province of Łódź, they have not revealed where his alleged attack was planned. However, prosecutors reported today that the suspect had established contacts through which he could gain access to explosive materials and devices, had looked for bomb-making instructions, and had tried to recruit others to his terrorist cause. “Mateusz W.’s actions were intended to further the policies of the terrorist organisation known as Islamic State and to seriously intimidate people with views contrary to the ideology espoused by the suspect,” wrote Katarzyna Calów-Jaszewska, a spokeswoman for the National Prosecutor’s Office. In a separate statement, the Internal Security Agency (ABW) revealed that the suspect had “intended to join a terrorist organisation affiliated with the so-called Islamic State and sought people who could help him carry out this plan”. Neither the security services nor prosecutors have indicated whether Mateusz W. denied or admitted to his alleged crimes or has offered any explanation for his actions. If convicted of preparing a mass attack, he could face up to ten years in prison. Last year, after Mateusz W. was detained, Dobrzyński said that he came from a devoutly Catholic family but had become “deeply infatuated with Islam” and had “fallen in love with terrorism”. In an appeal to parents, Dobrzyński said that, “if you see your children interested in Islam, communism, or fascism, and collecting all sorts of information and items on the subject, that’s the first sign. Take care of your own children, because things can only get worse from there”. Poland has detained a man who was allegedly planning a terrorist attack on a Christmas market as an act of support for Islamic State. The suspect, a 19-year-old Pole, had become "infatuated with Islam", say the security services https://t.co/N4WDVZdlai — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 16, 2025 After news of Mateusz W.’s detention emerged, KUL suspended his student status. The university’s spokesman, Wojciech Andrusiewicz, said that neither fellow students nor lecturers had noticed any unusual behaviour by the suspect. World.title: Polish WWII massacre victims reburied in Ukraine at ceremony attended by officials from both countries
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The remains of 55 Poles – around half of them children – massacred by Ukrainian nationalists in World War Two have been reburied at a ceremony in Ukraine attended by political and religious figures from both countries. The victims, many of whose bones show signs of brutal deaths, were exhumed this summer after Ukraine recently ended a moratorium on searches for tens of thousands of victims of the so-called Volhynia massacres who are believed to remain buried in unmarked mass graves. “This is an important moment for [the victims’] families, but also the Polish state, because this funeral follows decades of waiting,” said Polish culture minister Marta Cienkowska at the ceremony in Ostrówki (Ostrovky in Ukrainian), a depopulated former village that, before the war, was part of Poland and now lies in Ukraine. “Poland has the right and obligation to speak about the crimes committed against its citizens. It has the obligation to commemorate the victims, search for their remains, and provide them with a dignified burial…We will continue this work…everywhere that the graves of the victims of the Volhynian crimes still remain.” Pogrzeb ofiar Zbrodni Wołyńskiej w Ostrówkach i Woli Ostrowieckiej Na cmentarzu w Ostrówkach na terytorium Ukrainy odbyła się uroczystość pogrzebowa 55 ofiar zbrodni dokonanej 30 sierpnia 1943 roku. W uroczystości, zorganizowanej w 83. rocznicę tragicznych wydarzeń,… pic.twitter.com/4dXPOj4m7y — Ministerstwo Kultury i Dziedzictwa Narodowego (@kultura_gov_pl) August 30, 2026 Others to attend the reburial included deputy Ukrainian culture minister Ivan Verbytskyi; Vitaly Skomarovsky, the bishop of Lutsk and president of Ukraine’s Roman Catholic episcopate; Piotr Zgorzelski, the deputy speaker of the Sejm, Poland’s lower house of parliament; and former Polish Prime Minister Mateusz Morawiecki. Karol Polejowski, the deputy head of Poland’s state Institute of National Remembrance (IPN), which led the exhumation work, said that the presence of Ukrainian representatives “fills me with optimism for the future”. While Polish President Karol Nawrocki did not attend, one of his advisors, Jakub Banaszek, read a letter on his behalf, quoted by the Polish Press Agency (PAP). “We will never forget those who died in agony simply because they were Poles,” wrote Nawrocki. “We will not cease our efforts to ensure that all our compatriots murdered by members of the OUN-UPA are properly buried and commemorated.” ✝️ W 8⃣3⃣. rocznicę zbrodni dokonanej przez ukraińskich szowinistów, na cmentarzu w Ostrówkach pochowaliśmy ofiary ludobójstwa na Wołyniu. 🔻🔻🔻 pic.twitter.com/5oh3uiCKX4 — Instytut Pamięci Narodowej (@ipngovpl) August 30, 2026 The Volhynia massacres, in which around 100,000 Poles were killed, were led by the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), which was a partisan group founded by a faction of the Organisation of Ukrainian Nationalists (OUN) faithful to nationalist leader Stepan Bandera. They sought to ethnically cleanse areas that they saw as Ukrainian territory by wiping out other ethnic groups, in particular the large Polish population. Massacres took place in dozens of villages, including Ostrówki and the neighbouring Wola Ostrowiecka (Volya Ostrovetska in Ukrainian), where on 30 August 1943 the UPA killed over 1,000 Poles and razed the villages to the ground. Exhumations previously took place on the site of the two villages in the 1990s, and again in 2011 and 2015, uncovering the remains of hundreds of victims. However, hundreds more are believed to remain buried. In 2017, Ukraine imposed a ban on searches for victims on its territory in response to the dismantling of a monument to the UPA in Poland. However, in a diplomatic breakthrough last year, it allowed them to resume, including granting permission in December for work in Ostrówki and Wola Ostrowiecka. In April this year, mass graves were discovered there, with exhumations then beginning in July. Earlier this month, the IPN announced the results of that work. They uncovered the remains of 55 victims, 26 of them children (mostly under 12 years of age, with the youngest a few months old) and 20 women. In the Volhynia massacres as a whole, the majority of victims were women and children. The remains of a further 55 victims of massacres by Ukrainian nationalists during WWII have been exhumed in Ukraine. Around half were children, and most show signs of brutal deaths, including skulls pierced with farming tools https://t.co/LbLPzJcG1b — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 8, 2026 The locations and conditions of the remains reveal much about the manner of their death. Most were buried “at random” without coffins, which is consistent with contemporary accounts that they were killed in a barn and then thrown into a mass burial pit. Most of the remains, in particular skulls, show signs of injuries that are also consistent with contemporary accounts, which said that victims were ordered to lie on the ground before being killed with farm tools, including hammers for slaughtering cattle. Material from the bones has been secured for genetic testing, which was recently used for the first time to identify massacre victims exhumed at another location in Ukraine last year. Poland has for the first time used DNA testing to identify the remains of Poles massacred by Ukrainian nationalists in WWII. “After more than 80 years, families are receiving the answer they have awaited for generations,” says the culture minister https://t.co/c1gM3kQ83s — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 14, 2026 The Volhynia massacres have long been a point of tension between Poland, which recognises them as a genocide, and Ukraine, which rejects that label. The decision by Kyiv to allow exhumations to resume last year was regarded as a major step towards reconciliation. However, that process was undermined in May this year, when Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky decided to name a military unit after the “heroes of the UPA”. That prompted an angry response from Warsaw, where Zelensky’s counterpart Karol Nawrocki stripped him of Poland’s highest honour. In his letter read at Sunday’s ceremony, Nawrocki warned those who “continue the tradition of Banderite ideology” that they “place themselves outside the community of citizens of the free, civilised world” and are sending “a clear sign of hostility towards Poland and Poles”. President Zelensky has signed a law establishing a national pantheon to commemorate Ukrainian heroes, prompting Poland to again warn that Ukraine "will have a huge problem" integrating into the EU if it honours figures associated with massacres of Poles https://t.co/fN7Zgbovvu — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 24, 2026 Since the crisis broke out in May, there have been efforts to reach a diplomatic solution. Last month, Zelensky pointed specifically to the exhumation work in Ostrówki and Wola Ostrowiecka as evidence that “Ukraine is doing its part to fairly establish the facts about those who were killed in those years”. Subsequently, he announced a five-point plan to alleviate the crisis, including allowing more exhumations and opening up historical archives. Poland welcomed the move but said that it would wait to see how it was implemented in practice. Earlier this month, Zelensky signed a law establishing a new national pantheon of Ukrainian heroes. Poland has warned that the inclusion of figures associated with the massacres could have consequences for Ukraine’s ambitions to join the European Union. A survey conducted this month by Rating Group, a Ukrainian research agency, which asked Ukrainians to name their country’s greatest hero found that Bandera was the fourth most popular choice, having been chosen by 11% of respondents. World.title: Ambiente to Open Its 35th Prague Establishment This September
World.content:
Restaurant group Ambiente is preparing to open its 35th establishment, with a second location of its Pult beer concept set to launch in Prague’s Holešovice district in mid-September.

The new venue will be located on Tusarova Street and will follow the concept of Pult in Prague 1, which opened in the Celnice building in 2021.



While both locations will focus on Czech lager, the new Holešovice branch will introduce a different food concept and its own selection of beers.

The original venue serves beers from six breweries, with an emphasis on precise storage, serving and temperature control.

A different approach to food

Food will be one of the main differences between the two Pult locations.

The original Pult in Celnice focuses largely on smaller dishes and snacks. The Holešovice restaurant will instead offer a more substantial menu designed specifically to accompany beer.

The menu is expected to focus heavily on Czech beef, including several versions of steak tartare and steaks. Unlike many restaurants where the kitchen closes earlier than the bar, the new Pult plans to serve food until closing at 1 a.m.

The restaurant will have space for around 130 guests.

Another new destination for Holešovice

The opening comes as Holešovice continues to attract new restaurants, cafés and cultural venues. The area has become home to places including Vnitroblock, Mexická, Slice Slice Baby, Eatery, Ema, Typika, Osada and Polepšovna.

Ambiente itself has expanded its presence in Holešovice this year. At the Holešovice Market, the group has opened a second location of its Myšák confectionery and Naše maso butcher shop, as well as Skô, a Slovak-focused restaurant concept.

World.title: 7 Autumn Bike Trips to Take Around Czechia
World.content:
With cooler temperatures and autumn colours arriving, September and October are among the best months for cycling in Czechia.

The country’s extensive network of marked trails makes it easy to plan anything from a relaxed day trip to a multi-day adventure.

Here are seven routes worth considering this autumn.



1. Prague–Mělník–Litoměřice

One of the easiest options for Prague residents is to head north along the Elbe. The route passes through Mělník, known for its vineyards and historic centre, before continuing towards Litoměřice.

Along the way, cyclists can see Roudnice Chateau, Mount Říp and the historic fortress town of Terezín. Mělník is particularly appealing in September, when its wine season is in full swing.

2. Znojmo Wine Route

For a combination of cycling and wine, South Moravia is hard to beat in autumn. The 63-kilometre Znojmo Wine Route connects vineyards and villages around Znojmo and is suitable for cyclists of different abilities.

September and October are also the region’s main wine-harvest season, with numerous wine and burčák events taking place.

3. Mikulov and Pálava

The Mikulov Wine Trail offers another relaxed way to explore South Moravia. The route takes cyclists through vineyards and the countryside around Mikulov, with the Pálava hills providing one of the region’s most distinctive landscapes.

It is particularly attractive in September, when the annual Pálava Wine Festival takes place.

4. Singltrek pod Smrkem

If road cycling isn’t your thing, head towards Liberec. Singltrek pod Smrkem has more than 60 kilometres of purpose-built mountain-bike trails, ranging from easier sections for beginners to more challenging routes.

The surrounding Jizera Mountains also make it a good destination for a weekend trip.

5. Bečva Cycling Trail

The almost 160-kilometre Bečva Cycling Trail follows the Bečva River across Moravia. The route can be completed over several days and is largely downhill when ridden from the river’s source towards its confluence with the Morava.

Highlights along the way include Helfštýn Castle, the Zbrašovské Aragonite Caves and the open-air museum in Rožnov pod Radhoštěm.

6. Ploučnice Cycle Path

The nearly 100-kilometre Ploučnice Cycle Path runs from the river’s source near Ještěd to Děčín. It passes through Česká Lípa, the Ralsko area and the Kokořínsko-Máchův kraj landscape before reaching the Elbe.

7. Prague–Vienna Greenway

For a more ambitious trip, the Prague–Vienna Greenway stretches 368 kilometres between the two capitals. The route passes through historic towns, castles and monasteries, including Tábor, Znojmo and Mikulov.

It takes roughly a week to complete with stops, making it better suited to a longer autumn holiday than a weekend ride.

World.title: How to Buy TikTok Followers Without Risking Your Account
World.content:
Building a TikTok audience from zero can be frustrating. Even well-produced videos may struggle to attract attention when an account has only a handful of followers.

This slow beginning encourages some creators and businesses to purchase followers in the hope of making their profiles appear more established. Follower count can influence first impressions. When visitors discover a profile with an existing audience, they may be more willing to watch its videos, explore older content, or follow the account themselves. However, purchased followers cannot replace engaging videos or genuine interaction. Low-quality services may also deliver inactive accounts that disappear quickly or create an unnatural gap between follower numbers and actual engagement. Anyone considering this approach should understand how follower services operate, what they can realistically provide, and which warning signs suggest that a seller should be avoided.

Why Creators Purchase TikTok Followers

New accounts frequently face a credibility problem. Viewers have little information to judge whether the creator is worth following, so the visible follower count becomes one of several signals they use to make that decision. A larger audience can make a profile appear more established. This is particularly relevant for businesses, influencers, musicians, and other new TikTok creators trying to build authority in a competitive category. Some creators also purchase TikTok followers to reach eligibility thresholds for particular TikTok features. TikTok commonly applies age, location, and follower requirements to features such as LIVE, although the exact conditions may differ between markets and can change over time. The important distinction is that purchased followers mainly affect appearance. They may strengthen the profile’s initial social proof, but they do not guarantee greater reach, more sales, or stronger engagement.

What Purchased Followers Can and Cannot Do

Follower count is visible to anyone who visits a TikTok profile, which means it can shape the visitor’s first impression. A profile with several thousand followers may look more credible than an otherwise similar account with fewer than 100. TikTok’s recommendation system, however, evaluates much more than audience size. Signals such as watch time, completion rate, rewatches, shares, comments, saves, and viewer satisfaction are generally more important when determining whether a video should reach a wider audience. This creates a potential problem. If an account displays 30,000 followers but its videos consistently receive only a few dozen views, the imbalance may look unnatural to both TikTok and real visitors. Brands evaluating the creator for a partnership may notice the same discrepancy. Purchased followers should therefore be understood as a limited form of social proof. They cannot:

Make weak videos more entertaining

Guarantee placement on the For You feed

Produce meaningful comments or conversations

Create loyal customers

Replace a consistent publishing strategy

Automatically generate revenue

The greatest risk comes from purchasing followers that are obviously automated, inactive, or created only to inflate account statistics. These profiles add little value and may be removed during platform cleanups.

How to Evaluate a TikTok Follower Provider

The market contains everything from established social media marketing platforms to temporary websites selling automated accounts. A professional design alone does not prove that a service is dependable, so each provider should be evaluated carefully. Platforms such as SocialWick offer clearly defined TikTok packages and a conventional ordering process. Regardless of which company is being considered, several basic checks should be completed before placing an order.

Check the Website’s Security

A provider should use HTTPS encryption to protect information submitted through its website. This can usually be confirmed by checking for the padlock symbol beside the address in the browser. Secure payment methods are equally important. Credit cards and reputable payment processors normally offer better consumer protection than cryptocurrency transfers, gift cards, or other payment methods that are difficult to reverse.

Never Provide a TikTok Password

A follower delivery service generally needs only the public username or a link to the TikTok profile. It should not require the account password, email login, recovery code, or two-factor authentication details. Requests for private credentials are a serious warning sign. Sharing this information could allow an unknown company to access the account, change its settings, publish content, or lock out the owner.

Review the Delivery Time

Instant delivery may sound convenient, but an enormous follower increase within minutes can look unnatural. A newer account is unlikely to gain tens of thousands of followers suddenly without a viral video or another clear reason. More credible providers commonly offer gradual delivery. This spreads the order across several hours or days and makes it easier to monitor the quality of the accounts being added.

Understand the Package Quality

Follower packages are often divided into labels such as standard, high quality, active, real, or premium. These terms are not standardized, so they can mean different things on different websites. A higher-priced package may include accounts with profile photos, usernames, existing posts, or more complete activity histories. Cheaper options frequently consist of empty or inactive profiles. Before paying extra for a so-called premium tier, buyers should read the description carefully and determine what the seller is actually promising. Independent comparisons of TikTok follower providers and package quality may provide additional context, but customer reviews and seller claims should still be treated cautiously.

Look for Accessible Customer Support

A legitimate business should provide a clear way to request assistance. Live chat, email support, or a functioning contact form gives customers somewhere to report missing followers, delayed orders, or payment problems. Support availability does not automatically prove that a provider is trustworthy. However, a website with no contact information, unanswered messages, and no stated resolution process presents a much greater risk.

Warning Signs That Should Not Be Ignored

Very low pricing is one of the most common signs of poor-quality delivery. Maintaining accounts that look authentic requires more resources than operating a large collection of disposable bots. Consequently, offers promising thousands of “real and active” followers for a few cents are unlikely to match their description. Other warning signs include:

Requests for passwords or security codes

Guaranteed viral results

Promises of automatic monetization

No terms of service or privacy policy

Prices far below comparable providers

Only irreversible payment methods

Broken pages or copied website content

No delivery estimate

No refund or replacement policy

Large numbers of identical customer reviews

Claims of guaranteed engagement also deserve scrutiny. No external provider can honestly promise that purchased followers will watch every video or become paying customers.

Why a Refill Policy Matters

Follower losses can occur after an order is completed. TikTok may remove suspicious accounts, users may deactivate their profiles, or low-quality followers may simply disappear. A refill policy allows customers to request replacements when the follower count drops within a specified period. Depending on the provider, this protection may last for several days or a month. The conditions should be reviewed before checkout. Some companies refill only when the loss exceeds a minimum amount, while others exclude certain packages. Buyers should also check whether the replacement is automatic or must be requested manually. A refill guarantee cannot eliminate every risk, but it shows that the provider has at least acknowledged the possibility of follower loss and established a process for addressing it.

Avoid Unnatural Growth Patterns

Sudden, unexplained growth can draw unwanted attention. An account that gains 10,000 followers overnight without publishing anything new may appear suspicious, particularly if its views and interactions remain unchanged. Gradual delivery is generally less disruptive than receiving an entire order immediately. However, spreading out a purchase should not be treated as a method for bypassing TikTok’s enforcement systems. Buying followers may still conflict with platform rules, and no delivery method can guarantee that an account will avoid restrictions or removals.

Creators who choose to purchase followers should keep the order proportionate to the profile’s existing size. Adding a modest number to an active account is less conspicuous than transforming a nearly empty profile into a large one overnight. Content should also continue to be published consistently. A larger number beneath the profile image will have little effect if visitors arrive and find outdated, irrelevant, or poorly produced videos.

Keep Engagement and Follower Numbers Balanced

Follower count is only one part of a TikTok profile. Views, likes, comments, shares, and posting frequency provide a broader picture of its actual performance. If follower growth significantly outpaces every other metric, the account may lose credibility. A profile with 20,000 followers and almost no interaction may look less trustworthy than one with 2,000 followers and an active community. Maintaining a reasonable balance requires genuine content work. Creators should continue to:

Publish videos on a consistent schedule

Capture attention within the opening seconds

Respond to real comments

Participate in relevant trends

Use searchable captions and keywords

Test different formats and video lengths

Review analytics to identify strong topics

Collaborate with creators in the same niche

These activities provide TikTok with behavioral signals that purchased followers cannot produce.

Turning Social Proof Into Organic Growth

The most practical reason to purchase followers is to improve the profile’s initial presentation. If that stronger appearance encourages more people to explore the content, it may indirectly support organic growth. This effect depends entirely on what visitors find after opening the profile. A clear bio, recognizable niche, strong video covers, and a useful collection of content can convert curiosity into a genuine follow. An inflated number without quality content is unlikely to accomplish the same result. Creators should prepare their profiles before purchasing anything. A complete profile should include:

A memorable username

A clear profile image

A concise description of the account

Several high-quality published videos

Pinned content that represents the creator’s best work

A consistent subject or visual identity

An appropriate call to action

Purchased followers may bring the profile closer to the starting line, but the content determines whether real viewers remain interested.

Final Considerations Before Buying TikTok Followers

Buying TikTok followers can improve the visible size of an account, but it should never be confused with building a real community. The number may influence first impressions, yet it cannot reproduce the value of genuine viewers who regularly interact with the content. Anyone considering a purchase should choose a provider carefully, avoid sharing login information, use protected payment methods, read the refill conditions, and remain skeptical of unrealistic guarantees. It is also important to recognize that follower purchases may violate TikTok’s rules and could lead to removals or other account consequences. The strongest TikTok profiles combine credibility with content that earns attention. Purchased followers may change how a profile looks, but sustainable growth still depends on originality, consistency, audience understanding, and videos that people genuinely want to watch.

World.title: Vinohrady’s Americká Street Block Party Returns on September 12
World.content:
Americká and Záhřebská streets in Prague’s Vinohrady will turn into a pedestrian festival zone on Saturday, September 12, for the 15th edition of Zažít Americkou jinak.

From 10:30 AM to 9:30 PM, the streets will host a full-day programme of live music, dance, workshops, design, food and activities for children. The festival is free to attend.

A major part of this year’s programme will focus on Mexico and Latin American culture, including a celebration of Mexican Independence Day.



The main programme will take place on the La Calle Mexicana Stage, hosted by DJs Roxana Velasco and José. Visitors can look forward to performances by Studio Anyo, traditional Mexican music, a piñata, a dance workshop and appearances by Mexican musicians Razcarmelo and Andrea Viruega.

One of the highlights will be El Grito, the traditional ceremony marking Mexico’s Independence Day. The event has become an annual gathering point for the Mexican community in Czechia and festival visitors.

The programme will also feature Mariachi Azteca de Praga, described as the first authentic mariachi band based in the Czech Republic.

The evening will continue with international acts including Faustina Calavera, a ten-member band from Wrocław combining Latin American cumbia, Balkan brass and ska, followed by ONIXIA, an Argentine singer, dancer and songwriter based in Berlin who blends electronic music with Latin American rhythms.

More Space to Relax

This year’s festival will also feature an expanded chill-out zone at the intersection of Americká and Jana Masaryka streets, with seating, workshops and space to meet friends and neighbours.

Music will also be played at two additional locations. The Burza #4 Stage will return by the fountain at the corner of Americká and Záhřebská streets, while another stage on Záhřebská Street will focus on world and house music.

MINT Market, Food and Local Businesses

The festival will once again include MINT Market, bringing together dozens of Czech designers, independent makers and creators from Latin America. Visitors can browse fashion, jewellery, illustrations, ceramics, natural cosmetics and other handmade products.

Food will be another major part of the day, with Mexican, Latin American and international cuisine, street food and special offers from cafés, restaurants and other local businesses.

During the festival, Americká and Záhřebská streets will be closed to traffic and parking.

World.title: New Pharmacy Partnership Makes Prescription Drugs Easier for Foreigners in Czechia
World.content:
Foreigners from outside the EU insured with Maxima pojišťovna can now collect prescription medicines at selected pharmacies without paying upfront.

The Czech insurer has expanded its network of partner pharmacies through a new agreement with LÉKÁRNA U MUZEA in Prague 1.

Under the arrangement, the pharmacy and insurer handle the reimbursement directly, bringing the process closer to the system used by patients covered by Czech public health insurance.



The change is aimed at simplifying access to medicines for foreigners, who can face difficulties navigating the Czech healthcare system and understanding the costs associated with medical treatment.

According to figures cited by the insurer, nearly 900,000 people from non-EU countries have been living in the Czech Republic on a long-term basis. They account for about 8.2 percent of the country’s population.

How the new system works

Previously, foreign clients with commercial health insurance could be required to pay for prescribed medicines at the pharmacy and then submit the receipts to their insurer for reimbursement.

Under the new arrangement, this step is eliminated. Eligible Maxima clients can collect their prescribed medicines through the partner pharmacy, while the financial settlement takes place directly between the pharmacy and the insurance company.

The model has already been operating for more than a year at the pharmacy operated by Maxima’s healthcare partner Innova Healthcare at the Hůrka Polyclinic in Prague.

The data also highlights some of the most common medical needs among patients visiting the participating clinics. More than 63 percent of patients seen by general practitioners, pediatricians and gynecologists were prescribed antibiotics.

More than 37 percent required treatment for sideropenic anemia, or iron deficiency, while 20 percent received prescriptions for blood-thinning medication following injuries.

The pharmacy in Prague 1 will also stock medical equipment and rehabilitation aids. Its range includes orthoses, crutches, wheelchairs and products for convalescence, rehabilitation and everyday healthcare.

Maxima says it intends to expand the direct-settlement model to additional partner pharmacies in the future.

World.title: Dozens of Hot Air Balloons to Fill Czech Skies During September Festival
World.content:
Dozens of hot air balloons are expected to take to the skies over eastern Bohemia this week as the Balonové Nebe festival returns to Hradec Králové, Jaroměř and nearby areas.

The five-day event will run from Wednesday, September 2, through Sunday, September 6, with a program combining competitive balloon flights, mass launches and evening shows. All public events are free to attend.

Weather will play a major role in the festival schedule. Balloon flights can only take place under suitable conditions, meaning launch sites and departure times may change at short notice.



Organizers say the exact location of each flight will depend mainly on wind direction and other weather conditions. Planned flights may also be postponed or cancelled if conditions are unsuitable.

The festival has established itself as one of the country’s major hot air balloon gatherings. Last year’s event set a Czech record when 81 balloons flew into the sky at the same time.

The 2026 edition will once again feature morning competitions, during which pilots will complete a series of tasks while large groups of balloons rise over the region.

Evening programs will offer a different spectacle, with balloon shows planned for spectators. The precise locations of these events will be announced according to the weather forecast and flying conditions.

Visitors planning to attend are advised to check the festival’s official website before setting out. The organizers will publish the latest information about launch locations, times and any changes to the schedule there.

World.title: VIDEO: Golden STARLUX Lands in Prague for the First Time
World.content:
A golden Airbus A350-1000 operated by Taiwan’s STARLUX Airlines landed at Václav Havel Airport Prague for the first time on Tuesday, September 1.

The aircraft, registered as B-58554, carries the special AIRSORAYAMA Gold livery created in collaboration with Japanese artist Hajime Sorayama.

Prague is one of only three destinations where STARLUX plans to operate the specially designed aircraft on a regular basis, alongside Tokyo and Phoenix.



The arrival marks another step in the expansion of STARLUX’s new direct connection between Prague and Taipei.

The airline launched the route on August 1, initially using the smaller Airbus A350-900. From September, the carrier has switched to the larger A350-1000, which can carry up to 350 passengers in four travel classes.

STARLUX, Airbus and paint manufacturer Mankiewicz developed a multilayer coating using mica particles to create the metallic effect while meeting aviation safety requirements.

Increasing capacity on Prague route

STARLUX launched Prague as its first European destination on August 1, connecting the Czech capital directly with Taipei three times a week. The service currently operates on Tuesdays, Thursdays and Saturdays.

Flight JX101 leaves Taipei at 12:10 a.m. and arrives in Prague at 8:35 a.m. The return flight, JX102, departs Prague at 10:35 a.m. and arrives in Taipei at 7:55 a.m. the following day.

The switch to the A350-1000 increases the available capacity on the route. The aircraft has four travel classes, including First Class, Business Class, Premium Economy and Economy.

An additional Monday flight is scheduled to operate from October through November, bringing the route to four flights per week during that period.

World.title: September 19: Celebrate South Africa’s Heritage Braai Day in Prague
World.content:
On Saturday, 19 September, Prague’s Rohan Beer Garden will host Heritage Braai Day, bringing the flavors and traditions of South Africa to the city.

The event is organized by Saffa Maso.



From noon, visitors can enjoy a relaxed day of grilling, music and socializing outdoors.

Heritage Day in South Africa is a public holiday celebrating the country’s cultural diversity. It has also become closely associated with the tradition of braai, or South African-style barbecuing, with friends and family gathering around the grill to share food.

In Prague, the event is open to everyone and will feature multiple grills, allowing visitors to prepare their own food. Those who prefer to leave the cooking to someone else can use the on-site grill master service, available for an additional fee.

Standard tickets include grills, coals and all braai equipment. Visitors can also choose a braai package, which includes 500g of traditional boerewors sausage and 150g of biltong.

On-site, guests will also be able to purchase Nando’s sauces, chutney, braai spices and other South African products.

Visitors should not bring their own drinks, as a selection of alcoholic and non-alcoholic beverages will be available at the venue. Guests should bring their own plates and cutlery, although disposable options are also allowed.

Tickets are available via SMSTicket at this link. Children under 12 enter free.

World.title: Hungary could publish up to 80,000 names in Communist-era secret service files
World.content:
Hungary could soon see tens of thousands of names revealed from the country’s Communist-era secret service files, with government estimates suggesting that as many as 60,000–80,000 people could be identified.

Bálint Ruff, head of the Prime Minister’s Office, told Telex that the figure was based on professional estimates concerning the potential disclosure of names contained in the files.

“I have an idea of the number,” Ruff said, while stressing that he did not know whether the documents would include people who later became important political or economic figures after the fall of Communism in 1990.

“The agent files are a very important part of our shared past, and there will be many things in them that will cause sadness for many families,” he said.

Who could appear in the files?

The possible publication of tens of thousands of names could make the Communist-era secret service files one of the most politically and socially sensitive historical disclosures in modern Hungary.

Ruff did not say that all of the people whose names could appear were necessarily secret agents or informants. The files may contain the names of people who had various connections to the state security apparatus, meaning that the precise nature of an individual’s involvement would need to be established from the documents.

He also said he did not know whether people who went on to become prominent political or economic figures after 1990 would be among those named.

If you missed it: Hungary submits landmark bill to open Communist-era secret service files

Around 100 documents could be declassified this week

Ruff said he hoped that approximately 100 documents known as “No. 3,000 resolutions” would be declassified and published later this week. He said questions of potential criminal responsibility would have to be decided by investigating authorities.

According to Ruff, the documents concern decisions and contracts that were signed by identifiable officials. He noted that the relevant “3,000” documents were signed by the prime minister in office at the time.

The government has also indicated that it intends to make public information concerning the travels of János Lázár, who served in senior government positions under Viktor Orbán. Ruff claimed that he knew where Lázár had travelled, what he had done and why the information had previously been kept secret. He said these details would also be made public.

Government says complaints involve HUF 2 trillion

The disclosure of the historical documents comes alongside a broader government investigation into the use of public money under previous administrations.

Ruff said the government had so far filed complaints in cases involving a total value of HUF 2 trillion (EUR 5.4 billion).

One of the ongoing investigations concerns Századvég, a Hungarian think tank that Ruff said had received between HUF 20 billion and HUF 30 billion in public money over the past decade for research and studies. He said a criminal complaint would also be filed in connection with that case.

The government has already filed a complaint concerning Observer, a media-monitoring company, over what Ruff described as “exorbitant” sums paid for its services.

He also referred to the Kommentár Foundation, claiming that properties worth “twenty billion” forints had been purchased for the organisation. Ruff added that colleagues were currently calculating the sums paid to the Nézőpont Institute.

The allegations and complaints mentioned by Ruff do not in themselves establish criminal wrongdoing; any potential criminal liability will ultimately be determined by the competent authorities.

Stay up-to-date with our Hungary Weekly Briefing: subscribe on Substack!

A long-running question in Hungary

The fate of Hungary’s Communist-era secret service files has been a contentious issue for decades. Successive governments have faced pressure to make the records more accessible and clarify the activities of the former state security services. The issue is particularly sensitive because some people who were connected to the Communist-era system later became influential figures in post-1990 Hungary.

If the government proceeds with the planned disclosures, the publication of tens of thousands of names could reignite long-running debates about political responsibility, collaboration with the former regime and the extent to which the past has been fully confronted. For many Hungarian families, however, the revelations could have consequences far beyond politics, potentially exposing secrets that have remained hidden for generations.

World.title: Orbán government secretly allocated more than EUR 1.35 billion public funds just before April’s election
World.content:
The Orbán government secretly allocated at least HUF 500 billion (EUR 1.36 billion) in public funds in the months before the April election, according to an investigation by Hungarian news outlet 24.hu based on previously non-public government decisions obtained through a public-interest data request.

The money was allocated to companies, foundations, associations, cultural organisations, dioceses and various areas of the state budget. Funding was also provided for sporting events, other programmes and property purchases.

55 secret Orbán government decisions released

According to 24.hu, the documents consist of 55 so-called “2000” government decisions obtained from the Prime Minister’s Office. They had not previously been publicly available. The Prime Minister’s Office reportedly determined that these 55 documents could be disclosed because their publication did not conflict with national security, defence or law-enforcement interests.

Based on their numbering, however, 24.hu estimates that another 28 decisions could remain confidential. The disclosed documents reveal hundreds of billions of forints in government allocations and commitments.

Billions allocated to companies

Sixteen companies received a combined HUF 47 billion (more than EUR 127.67 million), with individual allocations ranging from HUF 190 million to HUF 14 billion (from around EUR 516,000 to more than EUR 38 million). One of the largest packages, worth around HUF 14 billion, was conditionally offered to Rosenberger Magyarország Elektronikai Kft. and Rosenberger Automotive Cabling Kft. for manufacturing capacity expansions at three sites outside Budapest.

Vajda-Papír Kft. was awarded more than HUF 11.5 billion (more than EUR 31.2 million) for an investment in Dunaföldvár, with a substantial part of the funding reportedly due to be paid in 2027.

HUF 6.2 billion for heritage foundation

The Orbán government also awarded HUF 6.2 billion (more than EUR 16.8 million) to the Central European Foundation for the Preservation of Built Heritage, which has been associated with Foreign Minister Péter Szijjártó.

Companies established by the foundation have acquired properties in neighbouring countries, including derelict historic buildings, with plans to convert some into hotels. The reason for the HUF 6.2 billion allocation was reportedly not clear from the Orbán government’ decision.

Other spending included HUF 706 million (around EUR 1.9 million) for the state company responsible for managing state-owned castles and HUF 76 billion (almost EUR 206.5) for the construction of the Danube bridge at Mohács.

Stay up-to-date with our Hungary Weekly Briefing: subscribe on Substack!

HUF 8.6 billion for motorcycle racing

The Orbán government also allocated HUF 8.6 billion (more than EUR 23.35 million) to support the year’s MotoGP and Superbike motorcycle racing events. Meanwhile, HUF 1.043 billion (around EUR 2.83 million) was set aside for the establishment of two infant homes in Esztergom and Zalaegerszeg.

One of the final confidential decisions reportedly came after the government’s election defeat. Signed by Prime Minister Viktor Orbán, it instructed ministers to take steps to ensure previously undertaken financial commitments were fulfilled before the government handover, where their lawful fulfilment could be established.

In case you missed it: Internal documents show Orbán-linked politician and businessman had unlimited power over Hungary’s public media

Legal questions over secret decisions

Miklós Ligeti, legal director of Transparency International Hungary, told 24.hu that using “2000” decisions to allocate budgetary funds was unlawful in formal terms. According to Ligeti, Hungarian law requires budget reallocations and financial allocations to be published in the Official Gazette, meaning they cannot be made through unpublished decisions of the Orbán government.

This is a legal assessment rather than a court ruling, and the legality of individual decisions remains a matter for the relevant authorities or courts. The disclosures have nevertheless raised fresh questions over the transparency and timing of the Orbán government’s use of public funds in the period surrounding the election.

World.title: Hungary condemns Russia’s ‘serious threat’ after alleged drone plot in Germany
World.content:
Hungary has condemned what it describes as an increasingly dangerous pattern of Russian hybrid activity in Europe, offering its “full solidarity” to Germany after Berlin accused Moscow of involvement in an attempted drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport.

Hungarian Foreign Minister Anita Orbán said Hungary was “deeply concerned” by the growing number and intensity of Russian hybrid operations on European soil.

“Recent incidents in Germany demonstrate an increasingly dangerous and reckless pattern of behaviour that poses a serious threat to European security and resilience,” she wrote on X.

The foreign minister added that Hungary was ready to support Germany in tackling hybrid threats.

Hungary is deeply concerned by the growing number and intensity of Russian hybrid activities on European soil. Recent incidents in Germany demonstrate an increasingly dangerous and reckless pattern of behaviour that poses a serious threat to European security and resilience.… — Anita Orban (@_OrbanAnita) September 1, 2026

Germany blames Russia for attempted airport attack

The statement came after Germany formally accused Russia on 1 September of being behind an attempted explosive drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport.

German authorities reportedly discovered a drone carrying explosives at the airport in August, close to several Ukrainian cargo aircraft. Evidence gathered at the scene was said to point towards Russian involvement.

Berlin responded by summoning Russia’s ambassador and ordering the closure of Russia’s Consulate General in Bonn, among other measures. Moscow has denied any involvement in the incident.

The alleged attack is being investigated as part of a larger pattern of suspected Russian hybrid operations in Europe, which have included alleged sabotage, cyberattacks, disinformation campaigns and other forms of covert activity.

Budapest calls for stronger EU and NATO cooperation

Orbán said these developments demonstrated the need for Europe to strengthen its ability to withstand hybrid threats.

“In the face of these challenges, strengthening the resilience, unity and collective preparedness of the European Union and NATO is more important than ever,” she said.

Hungary also expressed its willingness to help Germany respond to the threats, saying it stood in “full solidarity” with its European partner. The position is notable given Hungary’s traditionally more accommodating relationship with Moscow compared with many other EU and NATO members.

Under former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán, Budapest frequently criticised EU sanctions against Russia and maintained diplomatic and economic links with Moscow even as relations between Russia and the West deteriorated following the invasion of Ukraine.
