World.title: Initiated by First VP Mehriban Aliyeva, wage reforms contribute to healthcare dev't - MP
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 2. The increase in salaries for doctors of various specialties, introduced on September 1 at the initiative of First Vice President Mehriban Aliyeva and upon the instruction of President Ilham Aliyev, is another important step toward improving the compulsory health insurance system, which has been developing steadily for years, and enhancing the social welfare of healthcare workers, member of the Azerbaijani Parliament’s Health Committee, MP Soltan Mammadov told Trend.

According to Mammadov, the increases will contribute to the development of the compulsory health insurance system and help address a number of existing challenges in the sector by strengthening outpatient and primary healthcare services and emergency medical care, as well as introducing incentives to tackle the shortage of medical professionals in the regions.

The MP welcomed the comprehensive nature of the wage reform, which will cover 72,212 healthcare workers.

“The reforms cover a range of areas, including selected medical specialties, the quality of work performed, improvements to certain healthcare services and working conditions for doctors in the regions, as well as measures to attract qualified doctors to the regions. In line with the reforms, the annual payroll budget across the TABIB system has been increased by 189 million manat (around $111 million),” Mammadov said.

“Salary increases of 60, 70 and even up to 100% for certain doctors, particularly pediatric anesthesiologists and intensivists, neonatologists and hemodialysis specialists working in the regions, will help improve the quality of these services and provide additional incentives for doctors. At the same time, in regions facing shortages of doctors, excluding Baku, Absheron, Sumgayit and Ganja, a 1.3 coefficient will be applied to additional performance-based payments for surgical care, inpatient therapeutic care, physiotherapy and rehabilitation, anesthesia and interventional radiology services. This will help improve access to healthcare services,” the MP said.

Furthermore, Mammadov noted that the reforms will include corresponding salary increases for doctors working in emergency medical services. For example, doctors at the Republican Center for Emergency and Urgent Medical Care and emergency departments of medical centers are expected to receive a 61% salary increase.

The MP emphasized that the reforms also cover primary care physicians working in outpatient services, as well as head nurses and other mid-level and junior medical staff at several healthcare facilities. Monthly salaries for 36,041 mid-level healthcare workers will increase by 17%, while salaries for 20,367 junior healthcare workers will rise by 18%.

Mammadov added that the initiatives and decisions of President Ilham Aliyev and First Vice President Mehriban Aliyeva provide significant support for the development of the healthcare sector and complement the healthcare policies pursued by TABIB and the Ministry of Health, as well as the targeted reforms being implemented in the sector.

World.title: Dutch Embassy thanks Azerbaijan for rescuing injured national in Sheki
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 2. The Embassy of the Netherlands in Azerbaijan has thanked the Azerbaijani authorities for rescuing a Dutch national who was injured in Sheki.

This was reflected in a post published by the embassy on its X account.

“We express our gratitude to the relevant Azerbaijani authorities for the rescue and provision of emergency medical assistance to the Dutch national who was injured on August 29 while hiking in the mountainous area of Sheki.

In particular, we thank the State Border Service of the Republic of Azerbaijan for the emergency rescue operation carried out in challenging mountainous terrain and in darkness, the prompt evacuation by helicopter, and the provision of initial medical assistance at the scene,” the post said.

The embassy also expressed its appreciation for the medical assistance, professional approach and prompt intervention provided by Sheki District Central Hospital and Yeni Klinika in Baku.

“The swift and coordinated response of the relevant authorities during this incident made an important contribution to ensuring the safety of the Dutch national,” the embassy said.

On August 29, a Dutch national who sustained serious injuries after being attacked by dogs in a mountainous area near Bash Zayzid village in Azerbaijan’s Sheki district was rescued by State Border Service personnel. The injured person received initial medical assistance at the scene and was evacuated by helicopter to Sheki District Central Hospital, where they underwent emergency surgery.

The rescue operation was carried out at an altitude of 2,000 meters above sea level, in darkness and difficult mountainous terrain.

World.title: 'I'm numb': What it looks like to 'quietly quit' a marriage
World.content:
From the outside, Elodie's marriage looks pretty ordinary.

She and her husband are busy working parents of two young kids, going through the motions.

But Elodie, not her real name, has been quietly quitting the relationship.

"I don't know anymore the person I loved and spent decades with," she says.

Having children led to a shift in their relationship, Elodie says. And after a death in the family, her husband withdrew emotionally and romantically.

Elodie hasn't been able to reconnect with him since. And has given up trying.

Cassandra Shields is a clinical psychologist who has helped people with being, what she calls, "The Burnt-Out Pursuer".

Dr Shields says when one half of a couple is constantly trying to change the circumstances of the relationship, but getting nowhere, they don't always leave, but instead check out.

"The result looks like quiet quitting. It looks like 'I'm here, but I'm not really here … I'm almost numb because that's actually how I've got to function in order to make this relationship tick along.'"

"Quiet quitting" began as a social media trend in 2022, where workers were encouraged to avoid burnout in their jobs by doing only the bare minimum — just enough to avoid getting the flick.

Yumi Stynes, host of ABC podcast Ladies, We Need to Talk, explores what it's like when you apply that concept to your romantic relationship.

How big life changes can lead to quiet quitting

Quiet quitting usually happens after someone has poured a lot of energy or fight into making a relationship work, but their bids for connection have been ignored, explains Dr Shields.

Women on taking a marriage break Do you ever feel like taking a break from your marriage? Three women share how a marriage sabbatical changed their relationship.

It can often happen around big life transitions, such as becoming parents, going through perimenopause or moving into retirement.

"There is a transition in the nature of the relationship, requiring someone to step in more, step up more," Dr Shields says.

"We're requiring more of them, and if they aren't able to, then that can be profoundly disheartening."

Elodie says doing the bulk of the caregiving and domestic duties at home, while also being the higher income earner in the relationship, has taken its toll.

"I'm the one bringing most of what we need to live … I have this pressure of maintaining this, and at the same time, I'm the one doing most of what needs to be done at home.

"When it comes to school, medical appointments … it feels like things have changed a lot for me, but things haven't changed so much for him in terms of responsibilities," she says of becoming parents.

Things "really started crumbling", Elodie says, when her husband's grief was thrown into the mix.

"He would refuse to have any kind of difficult emotions ... [instead] having a meltdown or yelling.

"He would basically either shut down or become very angry."

Elodie says she finds herself walking on eggshells to manage her husband's mood.

The ways Elodie is quietly quitting her marriage

Quiet quitting relationships can often happen around big life transitions. (Pexels: Ozkan Keklik)

Elodie stopped trying to be intimate with her husband after bids for connection — even hugs or kisses — were repeatedly shut down.

"After we had our second kid, he completely refused to be intimate at all.

"I completely stopped when I realised that I felt like I was kind of almost forcing him."

Elodie says she has tried to talk to her husband about their drifting apart, but he would make excuses like being tired or busy.

So she began quietly quitting the marriage. While she continues to do everything in the house, Elodie says she is focusing on herself, kids and other relationships.

"I stopped sleeping in our bed … I see friends a little bit more … I don't organise anything for us.

"I'm basically living my life as a single mum."

Listen to the episode Yumi Stynes talks to women who have taken a step back from their marriages but aren't ready to officially split. They're staying for the sake of the kids, to save money or are biding their time, waiting for the right moment to leave.

'Empty inside'

Like Elodie, Vera has struggled in her relationship since becoming a mum.

After a traumatic birth with her daughter, she says her partner, while "very loving", didn't provide the support she needed.

"From housework, cooking to anything that I needed support with, I had to ask for it," says Vera, not her real name.

"And he would willingly do it, but there was no initiative. I don't think he has insight into how little he was actually doing."

Sign up to the ABC Lifestyle newsletter Get a mid-week boost and receive easy recipes, wellbeing ideas, and home and garden tips in your inbox every Wednesday. You’ll also receive a monthly newsletter of our best recipes.

Resentment grew further when Vera's dad died.

At the time, she had a toddler and was the sole income earner for the family, after her partner had become unemployed.

"I was unable to travel to be with my family, and I just had to go back to work after a few days and carry on.

"I was going through grief and being very isolated.

"That also hampered my attempts at trying to connect and revive the relationship. I just ran out of energy to try and do it."

Vera says she feels "empty inside" and worries about the kind of relationship they are modelling for their daughter.

"I feel I'm doing my child a great disservice that this is what she's seeing.

"She sees my frustration, and she also even says, 'Mama, why does Daddy sit on the couch on his phone and you're doing all the chores?'

"I'm like, 'Yes, why indeed?'"

The consequences of quiet quitting

So how can you tell if someone has quietly quit a relationship? Dr Shields says it's helpful to look at the three pillars of secure attachment that healthy relationships have.

Someone who has quietly quit a relationship is not accessible, responsive or emotionally engaged.

"If you're quiet quitting your relationship, then you're missing out on a whole part of connection and love and attachment and intimacy that I think we all need as humans.

"And it also means that our partners aren't getting an opportunity to really be loved, as well.

"We're not getting fully loved, and they're not getting fully loved, and that's kind of shit."

But ending a relationship to find love elsewhere isn't simple for everyone, says Dr Shields, with things like culture, faith and finances playing a role.

For some women, it's about waiting until the "right time" to leave.

That's true for Elodie, who isn't planning to separate from her husband — yet.

"He made it very clear that he would make things difficult if I left.

"I don't have the mental space at the moment to deal with things going really ugly.

"I'm staying until I have enough a bit of money on the side to do what I need to do."

Vera, who also feels financially trapped, says she's given up on what the relationship once was, instead focusing on making the best of what it is now.

"It seems to be a friendship."

While she does worry about the implications of leaving, she hopes in several years' time, things will look different.

"I'm hoping to be happily co-parenting from separate homes

"There's a lot of love there. I just wish I could reciprocate that.

"I feel like I just can't do it anymore. And I think we're years past that now."

World.title: 'She could leave him': What fame really meant for Darren Hayes
World.content:
Darren Hayes learned to sing by listening to his mother.

"She had the most beautiful, melodic voice and I would mimic her," the musician and former frontman of Savage Garden says.

"A lot of my singing education came from mimicking people — but she was the first person I ripped off."

Hayes's mother, Judy, would never have admitted her influence.

"She wouldn't think that she taught me how to sing because she had such a low self-esteem," he says on Take 5 With Zan Rowe.

Hayes grew up in a home wracked by domestic violence, saying his father was "an extremely violent man".

" But my mother was an angel, and she was the very inception, the seed, the beginning of music for me. "

And he says it was music that saved his life.

"I know that's a cliché and everyone says this, but I was a very, very lost kid."

'I'm not a freak … I'm famous'

Growing up in Logan, Queensland, Hayes never fit in.

"It was a very hyper masculine community, I remember being afraid of that. Everyone smoked, everyone played football," he says.

"And I was just this delicate kid that was recreating scenes from Star Wars by making the toys kiss."

"I can't believe that I survived my childhood," Darren Hayes tells Zan Rowe on Take 5. (Supplied: Facebook)

He was bullied from a young age for being gay, years before he even knew what that was.

"My father was the first person to call me the F word, and it's not the one that rhymes with truck."

His way of coping with that was deep denial.

"I just decided, 'Oh no, I'm not a freak, I'm not all these terms they call me'. From a very early age, I decided that I was just famous."

Throughout it all, he also felt a strong duty to protect his mum from violence, particularly if his father had been drinking. That could look like driving the car to get her out of the house in the middle of the night, or using his sister's hockey sticks to fight back.

Pretending he was a star, years before he actually was, helped him see a way out.

"I knew [I'd be famous], but not for the arrogant reasons you might think," he says. "I knew because it was either be famous and magical and special, or die.

" I lived in a family where my job was to keep my mum alive. But I thought if I could just be famous, I could save her, us, me, everything. "

Success and secrets

While Hayes never doubted his fame, it wasn't until high school that he realised he could sing.

His music teacher made him join the school choir, and it was a revelation.

"I felt the molecules in the room change, as they always do when people sing. That's what music does," he says.

"But I could feel it and that was it."

Daniel Jones and Darren Hayes played together in a pub rock band called Red Edge before forming Savage Garden. (Supplied: Tim Roney/Getty Images)

Hayes was in his early 20s in 1996 when Savage Garden, the pop duo he formed with friend Daniel Jones, released its first hit single 'I Want You'.

From there, Savage Garden's ascent was dizzying. Their debut, self-titled album won a record 10 ARIA Awards in 1997.

Being so firmly in the public eye also brought extreme vulnerability for the young man.

Watch Take 5 with Zan Rowe on ABC iview Take 5 with Zan Rowe returns for its fifth season, bringing together an exceptional line-up of global music, cultural and political icons.

"I was so grateful to have it…in the beginning," he says.

"But there were secrets. Gay: secret. Depression: secret. Don't tell anyone."

Hayes says the American record companies did everything they could to ensure the audience didn't "find out" he was gay, including changing his hair, telling him not to move much in music videos and doing audience surveys about which pictures were the "most masculine".

"So it became hell, but I learned how to keep it in," says Hayes.

"I mean, you never know, it could end tomorrow."

Savage Garden performs in Melbourne in 2000. (Supplied: Martin Philbey/Redferns)

But it didn't end, even when Savage Garden called it quits in 2001. Hayes has gone on to have a successful solo career, releasing five studio albums. In 2019, he received an Order of Australia for services to the music industry.

And when he came out publicly, he could be the artist he'd always wanted to be.

"Oh my god, to be able to use the pronoun that I want to use," he says with a relieved laugh.

"My biggest success to me is my least commercially successful record. It's called Homosexual — how fun was that, to make an album basically called 'Super Gay'?"

Released in 2022, Homosexual is Darren Hayes's fifth studio album. (Supplied: Powdered Sugar)

Hayes says the biggest personal impact was when he started to see queer people turn up in the audience of his shows.

"I felt so seen and understood," he says.

"It was like having lived in solitary confinement without a window all your life and suddenly the first dapple of sunlight hits your face."

'Fly on, ride through'

Getting out of Logan and being able to perform as a proud gay man "is the equivalent of winning the Lotto" for Hayes.

"I'm really happy that I think maybe I got to break the cycle of toxic abuse."

As for his mum, he says she "couldn't have given a shit" if he was famous or not, she just wanted him to be happy — and that came through music.

"I remember laying in Mum's lap and her just letting me cry and letting me know that I'm going to be OK," Darren Hayes says of his mum Judy. (Supplied: Darren Hayes)

"Do you know what music was for me? It was that I was able to pay cash for a house for my mum so she could finally leave him."

Hayes still struggles to speak in the past tense about his mum, who died in early 2025 from complications with COPD.

While he'd known she was terminally ill, Hayes had thought they'd get "a decade or more with her". But she died suddenly when he was away.

Hear extended episodes of Take 5 right here Dive even deeper into the music that has inspired your favourite artists on the Take 5 podcast.

"The thing that makes me sad about Mum is she was so afraid to die because she loved being alive," he says.

"She used to say, 'oh, I don't want to die because I'm going to miss you all so much'."

The grief still sits raw and heavy on Hayes, but music helps him cope. When it came to choosing a song for her memorial, he decided on 'O' by Coldplay.

"There's this line where he says: 'Fly on, ride through/Maybe one day I'll fly next to you', and that's how I feel about my mum.

"I remember trying to hold onto her, because all of our lives there was an invisible string connecting us, there was a tether," he says.

But at her wake he realised he had to cut the string, "like a beautiful balloon".

"I had to let her go," says Hayes, with tears in his eyes.

"I think that's a theme of my entire life."

World.title: Woman charged with juror intimidation at Lindsay Clancy trial
World.content:
Jurors deliberating the verdict in the Lindsay Clancy murder trial have been questioned by the judge after a woman was accused of filming them as they left the courthouse a day earlier.

Dawn Light, 56, of Sutton, Massachusetts, was arraigned on Wednesday, local time, at the same courthouse in Plymouth, south of Boston, where she was yesterday seen filming jurors outside a day prior.

Warning: This story contains details that may be distressing for some readers.

She was charged with intimidation of a witness, jurors or person furnishing information in connection with criminal proceedings. A not-guilty plea was entered on her behalf and she was released without having to post bail, but was ordered to stay away from the court, the jurors and any witnesses.

Ms Light was attending the courthouse where Ms Clancy has been on trial for five weeks.

Jurors are still deliberating Ms Clancy's verdict after five days. She is charged with murdering her three children in 2023.

The former labour and delivery nurse does not deny strangling her three young children at the family's Massachusetts home, but has said postpartum psychosis led to her actions.

Prosecutors argued she knew what she was doing.

Dawn Light was charged with intimidation in connection with the Lindsay Clancy's murder trial. (Greg Derr/The Patriot Ledger via AP)

Ms Clancy, 36, has pleaded not guilty by reason of lack of criminal responsibility.

Ms Clancy's live-streamed trial has generated intense interest, with reporters and spectators packing the courtroom.

The case has also sparked deep public divisions over her culpability and the issues around maternal mental health after childbirth.

The jurors had told Judge William Sullivan on Tuesday that they were unable to reach a unanimous decision, but he instructed them to keep trying — a common instruction in criminal trials when juries say they're having trouble reaching a verdict.

Judge William Sullivan has asked jurors to continue deliberating after they earlier said they could not reach a unanimous verdict. (AP: Greg Derr/The Patriot Ledger/Pool)

'Crime junkie' claims juror ordeal a 'misunderstanding'

Surrounded by reporters while going to her car, Ms Light was asked why she filmed outside the courthouse on Tuesday, local time.

"To see Lindsay. And I did see her. She was getting picked up by the van," she said.

Ms Light's attorney, Jennifer White, called it a "misunderstanding" and said the retired nurse was only trying to take a photo of Ms Clancy and "not interact with the jurors."

Dawn Light faces her own media frenzy after being arraigned with intimidation in connection to the Lindsay Clancy murder trial. (AP: Leah Willingham)

Light described herself as a "crime junkie" and Ms Clancy supporter, in an interview with Hearst Connecticut Media Group before her arraignment.

Assistant District Attorney Nicole Piacentini said Ms Light was parked in a restricted area behind the courthouse and is accused of filming the jurors as they left court.

Ms Light told state police that she was waiting to film Ms Clancy and denied recording jurors, however, troopers found video of jurors in her phone's deleted-files folder, Ms Piacentini said.

"The sanctity of the judicial system is at risk because of her actions," Ms Piacentini told a judge during the arraignment.

AP

World.title: Rupert Murdoch 'very happy' to be played by Guy Pearce in new film
World.content:
Australian-born media mogul Rupert Murdoch is "very happy" to see compatriot Guy Pearce play him in a new, largely sympathetic movie about his early business life, the actor has told the Venice Film Festival.

Pearce, known for his role as a dashing detective in LA Confidential and lately in The Brutalist, was cast by Oscar-winning British director Danny Boyle to play Murdoch in his upcoming film, "Ink".

Rift laid bare in Murdoch court documents Newly unsealed court documents reveal how the world's biggest family succession drama played out in court.

"I had some messaging with Elisabeth, [Murdoch's] daughter, and she did say to me, 'Dad's very happy that you're playing him,'" Pearce told reporters at the Venice Film Festival, where Ink is the opening film.

"But he hadn't seen the film at that point, so we'll see," Pearce added.

Hit HBO series Succession was inspired by the Murdoch family, with the ruthless and cruel patriarch Logan Roy providing a hugely unflattering portrait of the real-life billionaire.

Boyle, despite his own left-wing politics, said he had not set out to make a negative film about Murdoch, now aged 95.

The tycoon's right-wing media empire is still a major political force in Britain, the United States and his native Australia, backing a string of conservative nationalist politicians and their agendas.

In Ink, Boyle focuses on Murdoch's move into Britain in the late 1960s, when he bought the struggling tabloid The Sun and transformed it into a runaway success with a daily diet of sex, sport and scandal.

Rupert Murdoch's media outlets have long wielded significant political influence in the US, UK and Australia. (Reuters: Carlo Allegri)

It is an adaptation of a play by British playwright James Graham, which ran in the West End and Broadway between 2017 and 2019.

"The stage play doesn't … monsterise Rupert Murdoch, which, of course, a lot of people do now," Boyle said.

"I think it's because he represented at the time … a breath of fresh air in what was a very rigid British society. And he's dealing with a lot of prejudice against him as an Australian, which I can understand," the Trainspotting and Slumdog Millionaire director added.

" He particularly had a loathing for the British establishment, which I personally share as well. "

Ink follows the relationship between Murdoch and his first editor of The Sun, Larry Lamb, with the latter the main character in the film, Boyle told reporters.

Media magnate

Murdoch, his business empire and his feuds with his six children have become rich pickings for authors, screenwriters and directors.

As well as Succession, the five-times married tycoon has been the subject of a spate of biographies, as well as a new Netflix documentary, Dynasty: The Murdochs which was released in March this year.

The latter focused on Murdoch's fight with his children over efforts to install his eldest son Lachlan as his chosen successor to run an empire comprising Fox News, The Wall Street Journal, The Sun and publisher HarperCollins.

The Murdoch family's internal dynamics have been the inspiration of multiple movies and TV shows. (Reuters: Peter Nicholls)

That ended with a multi-billion-dollar settlement and court case that spilled some of the family's secrets into the public domain.

Murdoch has transformed tabloid newspapers, cable TV and satellite broadcasting over the last few decades while facing accusations of stoking nationalist populism across the English-speaking world.

Britain's exit from the European Union and the rise of Donald Trump are credited at least partly to Murdoch, while his media have long carried a pro-business agenda and have been sceptical about climate change.

AFP

World.title: Tiger Woods loses driving licence for five years after plea deal
World.content:
Golfing champion Tiger Woods has pleaded no contest to a reckless driving charge following a rollover crash in March near his home in Florida where he initially was accused of driving under the influence.

Woods appeared in a courtroom in Martin County where he agreed to the reduced charge.

A judge ordered that his driver’s licence be suspended for five years.

Woods, 50, said little during the hearing and beforehand sat at the defence table, looking back at the courtroom gallery.

He arrived at the courthouse with his girlfriend, Vanessa Trump, President Donald Trump’s former daughter-in-law.

She sat behind him during the hearing. Woods left the courthouse without addressing reporters.

Tiger Woods stands by his overturned vehicle following a crash in Florida. (AP: Jason Oteri)

He also pleaded no contest to refusing to submit to testing and was fined court costs, according to court documents.

A no-contest plea is not an admission of guilt, but means the accused will offer no defence.

The plea is treated as a conviction in the criminal justice system.

Woods was arrested after his SUV clipped a truck and rolled over on its side on a beachside residential road on Jupiter Island.

A sheriff’s report said deputies found two pain pills in his pocket and he showed signs of impairment. He did a Breathalyzer test, which came out negative, but refused to take a urine test.

He had pleaded not guilty to the original DUI charge.

Neither Woods nor the person in the other vehicle were injured in the crash, according to officials.

But his Land Rover caused $US5,000 ($7,000) in damage to the truck, according to a police report. Woods had told a deputy that he was looking down at his phone and changing the radio station when he hit the truck.

Woods is among the most influential figures in golf, but his career has been derailed by multiple back and knee surgeries, car crashes and dependence on pain medication.

Woods has been involved in four crashes over the years.

He took a leave from the golf tour after the 2009 crash and again after the latest crash and has yet to return to tournament play.

He left the United States to seek treatment at an inpatient treatment facility, according to court records.

Woods made his first public appearance since returning from treatment on June 23 when he introduced the PGA Tour’s plans to revamp its schedule for 2028.

Woods remained as chairman of the tour’s Future Competition Committee after his arrest. He did not take questions during that appearance.

AP

World.title: Iran accuses US of a 'war crime' after strikes kill people at wedding party
World.content:
Iranian authorities are accusing the United States of committing a "war crime" after people at a wedding party were killed by missile strikes.

Footage of ruined decorations, abandoned shoes and debris strewn on the ground circulated widely in Iran on Wednesday, local time, following a celebration that was turned "into a funeral" by strikes in the coastal town of Kuhestak along the Strait of Hormuz in southern Iran.

Iranian officials have since compared the incident to a strike on a girls' school that killed 160 people on the war's first night.

The strike hit on Tuesday night, local time, according to the Iranian Red Crescent, after the United States announced attacks against targets belonging to Iran's Revolutionary Guards.

Authorities say this piece of a projectile was found at the site of the strike in Kuhestak, southern Iran. (Masoud Mohammadi/Tasnim News Agency via AP)

Iranian authorities said the strike killed at least four people, including a child, and wounded 68 others at the wedding.

Iranian Foreign Minister Esmaeil Baquaei described the attack on X as a "war crime" and vowed that: "Iran will respond to these savage crimes with firmness."

"Make no mistake: these crimes will not go unpunished," Ebrahim Azizi, chairperson of the Iranian parliament's National Security and Foreign Policy Committee, added on X.

Shortly after the strike, footage began circulating online showing debris and rubble at the wedding site, with people heard screaming as rescuers rushed to provide assistance.

US launches fresh strikes on Iran The US has launched a barrage of air strikes on Iranian targets, prompting Iranian retaliation and a warning it would "tighten the lock" on the Strait of Hormuz.

Another video showed colourful decorations on the ground and shoes apparently left behind in the chaos, with the man holding the camera picking up a white sandal with glittering straps and remarking sarcastically: "Another pair of military boots in this military base."

"You wicked people have attacked people's homes and turned their wedding ceremony into a funeral," said the man in the video carried by Fars news agency.

In other footage, a state television reporter holds up a charred piece of metal he said was a fragment from "the American missile... that turned a wedding celebration into a tragedy".

The United States did not specify what it targeted in Kuhestak.

In a post on X, US Central Command said it was carrying out strikes against targets of Iran's Revolutionary Guards following their "recent attempted attacks … against commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and against American service members deployed to the region".

A CENTCOM spokesman, when asked about reports of civilian casualties, insisted "the US military never targets civilians".

Iran has been at war since February 28, when the United States and Israel launched a surprise bombing campaign that killed its supreme leader.

An April ceasefire brought an end to the initial phase of intense bombardment, but sporadic exchanges of fire have continued, particularly in and around the Strait of Hormuz, which Tehran has virtually blocked since the start of the war.

The renewed exchanges have punctured a pause in hostilities between the US and Iran. (Razieh Poudat/ISNA via AP)

'Still shaking'

Authorities in the southern province of Hormozgan said several "telecommunications and internet towers and sites were also seriously damaged" in the latest strikes, causing disruptions to communication networks in the area.

In Kuhestak, state television showed footage of a collapsed communications tower, with twisted metal debris spread across a street.

Some Iranian media outlets estimated the tower to be around 140 metres from the wedding site.

On Wednesday morning, the Red Crescent shared a video apparently filmed from above after daybreak, showing a hole in the roof of a house at the wedding site, with wreckage and rubble strewn across nearby alleyways.

In a separate video carried by state media, the father of the bride, Ali Mallahi, called it "a very saddening incident".

"I really don't know what to say. Thank God the casualties were not higher."

Loading...

Other footage carried by Iranian media showed wounded children lying in hospital beds.

One man, apparently suffering from a head injury and lying in a hospital bed, said he had been on his way to the wedding when he heard fighter jets overhead.

"As we arrived there, an explosion happened. It was really powerful, so powerful that even before I arrived there, pieces and debris from the building smashed into my head and face and I passed out," the unnamed man said in a video carried by local media.

"Lots of children and women were horribly injured. All the people were ordinary people," he added.

On Instagram, a woman with her hands covered in henna and wearing purple posted a video following the strike, saying: "My hands and feet are still shaking."

"May god have mercy," she said, adding in another post that the bride, the groom and all their immediate family were "safe".

AFP/Reuters

World.title: Armed gang raids security cars of gold in one of PNG's biggest robberies
World.content:
Police in Papua New Guinea are investigating what could be one of the biggest robberies in the country's history, after armed men held up a security convoy in Port Moresby and made off with 25 gold bars and $315,000 in cash.

Police Commissioner David Manning confirmed a major investigation was underway into the early morning hold-up on Wednesday, in which two private security vehicles were intercepted while transporting the bullion and cash through a city street.

"It is reported that at around 4:30 this morning two private security vehicles were intercepted by unknown vehicles in Port Moresby," Commissioner Manning said.

" Ten armed assailants held the security crews at gunpoint and proceeded to steal a quantity of gold and cash, as well as firearms. "

It is understood the stolen haul included 20 gold bars from the Porgera Gold Mine in Enga province, operated by mining company New Porgera Limited, along with five gold bars from Lae-based gold buying and exporting firm Golden Valley Enterprise Limited.

Also taken was a million kina ($315,000) in cash, along with a pump-action shotgun and a carbine belonging to the security crew.

A major investigation is underway into the hold-up in Port Moresby. (Supplied)

It is unclear how heavy the gold bars were, or how pure the gold was, but a standard retail gold bar weighing 1 kilogram usually sells for about $200,000.

A larger brick, like the gold held in central bank reserves, weighs about 12.4kg and is worth more than $2 million.

While the estimated value and weight of the 25 stolen gold bars are yet to be confirmed, a senior police source has described this week's theft as one of the biggest robberies in the country's history in terms of the value of gold stolen and is likely worth millions.

Convoy ambushed in staged road block

According to a timeline of events provided to police, the two cash-in-transit vehicles pulled out from their security base shortly after 4:30am and headed for Papua New Guinea's International Airport via the Poreporena Freeway.

As the vehicles approached a roundabout, they encountered what appeared to be a staged roadblock.

The driver of the lead vehicle opened the door to ask to pass, but was held at gunpoint before three more vehicles pulled up behind the convoy, blocking their exit.

Close to 10 armed men, some allegedly carrying military-style rifles, are reported to have forced the security crews from both vehicles at gunpoint before making off with the gold, cash and firearms.

No shots were fired and no injuries were reported.

Police Commissioner David Manning says a major investigation is underway. (Facebook: Royal Papua New Guinea Constabulary)

Commissioner Manning said early indications suggested shortcomings in how the transport had been handled.

"Police had not been alerted to the movement prior to it taking place," he said.

"There are a number of witnesses that are being interviewed, including the private security crews, as well as management and workers from the firm.

" This is a very serious incident. Early indications are that the movement of these valuables by the security company leave a lot to be desired in terms of how the private operation was conducted. "

Police sources said there were further concerns about the security arrangements around the transport, including how alarm and response procedures were handled.

It is understood at least four people are currently being questioned by an investigative team, as police work to identify those involved and recover the stolen gold and cash.

Echoes of the Kapris era

Kapris killed PNG's most notorious criminal, William Kapris, killed in a shoot-out with PNG police.

Police Deputy Commissioner of Specialist Operations Donald Yamasombi, who is overseeing the investigation, said the robbery was one of the biggest since the days of notorious criminal figure William Kapris.

Kapris was linked to a 2007 armed robbery in which thieves stole K78,000 ($25,000) in cash and gold bars worth more than K2 million ($630,00) from a Port Moresby refining operation.

He was later shot and killed by police in 2013, after spending months on the run following his escape from Bomana maximum-security prison.

World.title: AUKUS makes Australia a nuclear target, top experts warn
World.content:
PoliticsFederalAUKUS AUKUS makes Australia a nuclear target, top experts warn Rob Harris September 3, 2026 — 4:37am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Australia is significantly more likely to be dragged into a destructive conflict with China — and potentially targeted with nuclear weapons — under the AUKUS security pact, two former senior national security figures have warned. Michael Keating, a former Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet secretary, and former public servant Jon Stanford argue that the federal government’s current defence posture has “sacrificed considerable sovereignty” to the United States while leaving the country uniquely vulnerable without a guaranteed security safety net. A Virginia class submarine off the coast of Western Australia. The pair will front a crowd-funded public inquiry into the AUKUS submarine pact on Thursday, urging the federal government to immediately redesign its national strategy, cancel plans to acquire American Virginia-class and British-designed SSN AUKUS nuclear-powered attack submarines, and pivot to low-enriched uranium vessels sourced from France or South Korea. Keating, the most senior public servant during the Hawke-Keating era, spent 11 years on the Secretaries Committee on National Security – including five years as chairman – while Stanford has extensive background in submarine research and defence policy.



“Under AUKUS, Australia’s security is under greater threat while it has become increasingly clear that we cannot rely on the US for our defence,” they write in their submission. “We are now in a situation where, because of the AUKUS strategy of integrated deterrence in defence of US regional primacy, Australia is more likely to be attacked, potentially with nuclear weapons”. Jean-Yves Le Drian, France’s former foreign minister. AP They cite prescient warnings from former French foreign minister Jean-Yves Le Drian, who noted in 2021 that Australia had made a choice “to the detriment of sovereignty” and predicted it would discover later it had sacrificed both security and self-determination. According to the submission, the policy of “integrated deterrence” and “pooled sovereignty” effectively converts Australian military facilities into forward operating locations for US forces without giving Canberra oversight or veto power. They point out that unlike allies such as Japan, South Korea, and the Philippines, Australia lacks a formal US security guarantee, such as NATO’s Article V.



Yet, by developing command and basing infrastructure – such as the US submarine squadron facilities at HMAS Stirling in Western Australia – Australia becomes a prime military target. “If there is a war between the US and China, Australia will inevitably be involved ... even if we do not provide military support,” the submission states, adding that escalating hostilities could leave Australia open to nuclear strikes. Former secretary of the Department of Home Affairs Mike Pezzullo. Alex Ellinghausen Fronting the first day of the hearings in Canberra on Wednesday, former home affairs secretary Mike Pezzullo called for a deeper military integration with the US, agreeing that Australia could surrender sovereignty under the current AUKUS without gaining a meaningful say in decisions that could draw it into a war with China. Pezzullo, a national security hawk and former senior public servant under the Abbott, Turnbull and Morrison governments, was sacked by Labor in 2023 after confidential messages between him and Liberal Party powerbroker Scott Briggs were leaked to this masthead. The Australian Public Service Commission subsequently found he had breached the public service code of conduct on 14 occasions.



“If I was a Chinese war planner,” Pezzullo said, “I would flatten every single potential facility that might be used overnight by Americans flying in.” He said facilities including Tindal, Stirling, North West Cape and Pine Gap could be targeted in such a conflict. But Pezzullo said AUKUS’s nuclear-powered submarine program would transform Australia’s military options, giving the navy greater speed, endurance and reach while opening the way for a new generation of autonomous underwater systems. Undersea warfare would be critical in any future conflict, from anti-submarine operations to intelligence gathering, he said. At the same time, Pezzullo said Australia should not commit to fighting alongside the US in every future conflict.



“Alliances are political documents first and foremost,” he said, arguing that countries must retain the ability to make sovereign decisions when a conflict actually occurs. Related Article Analysis

UK Britain just shelved a key defence goal. That’s not good for Australia But he said those political alliances needed military planning and preparation underneath them. Australia, he said, could either try to remain outside a future US-China conflict and accept the consequences if Washington lost, or strengthen its alliance with the US in the hope that the combined deterrent would prevent war. “The only choice would be whether we want to sit it out and hope for the best,” Pezzullo said. “I think that’s not plausible.”



The choice was whether to remain on the sidelines and accept the consequences if Washington lost, or deepen the alliance in the hope that Australian involvement would strengthen deterrence. “I prefer that latter approach,” Pezzullo said. “The war machine is the thing that prevents the war.” Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. World.title: Primary school friends the perfect study pairing
World.content:
NationalVictoriaVCE Primary school friends the perfect study pairing September 3, 2026 — 4:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Expert tips to help you do your best in this year’s exams, plus meet the students doing Year 12 differently. See all stories .

These VCE stars are proof that when it comes to acing year 12, two heads really can be better than one. Clarence Antonmeryl and Dinith Premaratne turned their friendship into an academic advantage, studying side-by-side, challenging each other and finishing with identical scores: perfect ATARs of 99.95. Clarence Antonmeryl (left) and Dinith Premaratne were students at Haileybury. They even landed in the same bachelor of science degree at the University of Melbourne with Chancellor’s scholarships, knocking back offers from US campuses. But while their paths are remarkably similar, they say it’s their differences – comparing approaches, filling each other’s knowledge gaps – that has helped them shine.



“We really supported each other through the VCE – we’ve known each other since year 4,” says Clarence, now 18. “We would constantly build upon each other’s work and understanding and I think that really helped make us better learners.” Sometimes they disagreed, and that was the point. “We argued a lot about approaches, such as the best way to solve a problem in maths methods, but it optimised our learning,” says Dinith, also 18. “We didn’t focus on comparing marks with each other either, and rather just on trying to build each other up.” The duo were among a record 65,586 students to complete their VCE in 2025, a 3500 rise from the year before. As a new crop of students prepare to sit their exams, VCAA boss Andrew Smith is encouraging students to support each other. “It is a stressful time because you want to do your best; you want to make sure you put your best foot forward,” he says. “Talk to people about how you’re feeling, about how they are feeling. There are others who’ve been through this who can give you good advice. Those are all things that, to be honest, I wish I had thought about when I was doing my HSC.”



VCAA chief executive Andrew Smith. For Dinith and Clarence, it was part of a wider school culture at Haileybury. “We always saw each other as one cohort, so whenever one of us did well, we’d say it was a win for all of us,” Clarence says. Their collaboration continued outside school, with Zoom calls before SACs (school-assessed coursework) to brainstorm possible questions and “push each other’s understanding to the limit”. An iMessage group with nine of their peers provided both light relief and extra study support. When VCE results began arriving in December last year, the chat was buzzing. “We were congratulating each other on results, and were genuinely happy for each other,” Dinith says.



Study right, not all night Surviving year 12 doesn’t have to involve spending every waking hour with your head in the books. The study buddies embarked on their final year armed with a strategy that included taking four subjects instead of five to ease the load. Clarence studied specialist maths, physics, English and French, after ticking off algorithmics and maths methods in year 11. “We gave ourselves more downtime by doing four subjects, so in our spare periods we would go on walks with a group, or play chess or some sport,” he says. Dinith adds: “It’s important to not see downtime as your enemy because as they say, quality over quantity. It helped keep our minds sharp, and stopped us from burning out.”



They regularly reviewed each other’s work and taught each other new material in their shared subjects, such as more advanced grammatical structures in French. Dinith studied English, French, specialist maths and chemistry in year 12, and maths methods and accounting the year before. He says injecting a sense of fun into their studies was also helpful. They would discover idioms in English that translated into French, turn content into games, listen to French music and devise their own maths quizzes with classmates. “There’s that phrase that if you enjoy what you do, you don’t work a day in your life, and that’s true too of studying,” Clarence says.



Top exam tips When asked for their best exam advice by other students, there’s one thing that tops the list: start early. Frankston High School graduate Blake Alford-Ryan juggled many things during his final year of school. Clarence and Dinith took a systematic approach to their exam preparation, including using the study design as a checklist to consolidate their learning, doing practice exams under timed conditions, reading examiner’s reports and putting on examiner’s hats where they could. “By starting the practice exams early, you really cement your understanding,” Dinith says.



“The key is to plan ahead to avoid stress and panic.” Before an exam, he would spend about a week reviewing his mistakes, keeping a running list so he didn’t make the same errors twice. The pair did practice exams until the second-last day, particularly in subjects like maths, so the content remained fresh. Then came the clincher: they stopped. ″⁣On the last day before the exam, it’s all about getting into that exam mode, sleeping for nine to 10 hours and just being hydrated, eating well, and being relaxed,” Clarence says. Dinith agrees being mentally prepared is just as important as knowing the content, after sacrificing sleep to study during year 11.



“In a content-heavy subject like accounting, I tended to go to sleep at 1am and then get up at 4am or 5am on the day of the SAC,” he recalls. “But I found that not only was I less focused and jittery, but I also tended to get more sick during year 11.” By year 12, he had changed tack, prioritising sleep, downtime, planning and consistency. Juggling study and a start-up Frankston High School graduate Blake Alford-Ryan had more on his plate than the average student in year 12. On top of his studies, the school captain was leading uniform reform, campaigning for solar panels, collecting leadership awards, hitting the gym ... and building a media agency.



But surprisingly, the VCE top performer believes his packed schedule didn’t hurt his studies – they enhanced them. “It’s a little bit different but for me, I managed stress in the VCE by working on my business,” he says. “It allowed my brain to switch off study mode.” The VCE Leadership Award 2025 recipient was recognised for his “strong commitment to student voice, leadership and meaningful change”. He was accepted into his dream course, a bachelor of law at Swinburne University but has recently deferred to run the brand agency Habits of the Few. The 19-year-old says he is also a big believer in the value of teamwork, whether it’s during the VCE or in the world of business. He intentionally sought students who were more advanced in subjects such as English so he could learn from them, and benefited from lunchtime group study sessions. “If you can collaborate with other people, you get perspectives that you would not have [otherwise],” he says.

World.content:
NationalVictoriaVCE Goals and determination driving Steph to succeed September 3, 2026 — 4:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Steph Woods has a clear goal for her future: to become a lawyer and advocate for other people with disabilities. And she’s not letting her own health needs stand in the way. Steph Woods is battling mitochondrial disease and studying through Virtual Schools Victoria. The 18-year-old lives with a degenerative disorder called mitochondrial disease and is completing her VCE from home through Virtual Schools Victoria (formerly Distance Education Centre Victoria). “I want to become a human rights lawyer so people with disabilities know what they are entitled to,” she says. By all accounts, she’s got what it takes.



Woods won a VCE Study Award in 2025 after earning a perfect score in legal studies in year 11, reflecting both her academic ability and determination to succeed. She says that moving from a bricks-and-mortar school to VSV was a game-changer, particularly the flexibility to watch recorded classes and support setting up a tailored learning environment. With symptoms ranging from chronic migraines, nerve damage and vision and hearing impairments to ataxia and scoliosis, she’s not always well enough to log on: “You pick an organ and it doesn’t work.” Woods is one of about 5500 students who study through VSV each year, from professional sportspeople or performing artists to students living in rural and remote communities or experiencing health difficulties. Her mum, Kylie Poppins is as proud as punch. On the day of Steph’s award ceremony, Poppins and her son looked over as they prepared to leave to find Steph studying.



“She works so hard,” she says. “I teach year 12 and there’s not many kids who wake up and can’t sit up because of this massive migraine, and are throwing up from nausea, but then crawl out of bed an hour later to study for a SAC.″⁣ For Steph, one of her biggest motivators is simple. “I probably shouldn’t be quoted on this, but I want to beat the able-bodied kids,” she says, laughing.

World.content:
NationalVictoriaVCE The simple question that set Isabella on a new path September 3, 2026 — 4:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Expert tips to help you do your best in this year’s exams, plus meet the students doing Year 12 differently. See all stories .

It was during a woodworking class in year 9 that Isabella Mavrogiannis discovered she might be better suited to a construction site than the classroom. Her teacher noticed her budding skills with a saw and sander and asked whether she’d considered pursuing a future in carpentry. Carpenter Isabella Mavrogiannis says she did not like being stuck in a classroom. Jeff Hoogenboom “I said, ‘What’s carpentry?‘” laughs Mavrogiannis, now 18. But that simple question set Mavrogiannis on an entirely different path from year 10, moving to the Northern College of the Arts and Technology (NCAT) in Preston and kickstarting her career in the trades at just 15.



She remembers being captivated by the facilities and opportunities on offer at the school, gaining hands-on experience in automotive, electrical, plumbing, engineering, furniture making, painting, decorating and building and construction. “I did not like being stuck in a classroom,” she says. “I was very stressed. My dad is a tradie and he was a bit iffy at first about me going into a male-dominated industry, but it was the right thing for me.” During year 11 and 12, she’d drag herself out of bed at 3.30am every Wednesday for work placement with a domestic builder, as part of her VCE Vocational Major (VCE VM). Isabella is passionate about encouraging women to work in trades. Chris Riordan “I did everything from learning how to read all the plans, to standing the wall frames and installing windows once the slab was poured,” she says.



“My boss taught me about everything, from wall frames on the first and second levels, to ... demolition at some big homes around Malvern.” Even Mavrogiannis’ core VCE VCM subjects were connected to the world she wanted to work in. In numeracy, for example, she could apply maths to real-life situations such as estimating a concrete pour or calculating the weekly cost of running a car. The aspiring carpenter was passionate about using her skills to support those around her, whether it was mentoring other female students in trades through the Young Women in Trades and Technology (YWTT) group, attending industry expos or even helping with school building upgrades. The impact she made on her school and wider community was among the reasons she received a VCE Premier’s Award for Outstanding VCE Vocational Major Students. She was also recognised for displaying a high quality of work, strong leadership skills and a dedication to her learning and future.



While she did not receive an ATAR, Mavrogiannis finished her VCE with a Certificate II in Building Construction and a carpentry apprenticeship with Hutchinson Builders, giving her a head start. The biggest question she gets asked about entering a trade as a woman is: “Is it scary?” “I tell people, no it’s not scary whatsoever,” she says. “I’ve found everyone on site so helpful and supportive. And the number of females studying trades and technology at my old school has grown so much; we really wanted to get the word out.”

World.title: Flexible futures shift focus off ATAR
World.content:
NationalVictoriaVCE Flexible futures shift focus off ATAR September 3, 2026 — 4:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Expert tips to help you do your best in this year’s exams, plus meet the students doing Year 12 differently. See all stories .

Victorian senior students are increasingly looking beyond a single career and recognising that the ATAR isn’t the only measure of success, the state’s curriculum body says. Victorian Curriculum Assessment Authority chief executive Andrew Smith says today’s students have a growing awareness of the need to be flexible, particularly as artificial intelligence reshapes the workplace. VCAA chief executive Andrew Smith says there are ‘many right ways’ to handling year 12. “They’re looking more at that understanding that they will have multiple career pathways as they progress through their lives,” he says. “The other thing that we’re hearing in speaking with young people is that they have a greater appreciation of ... how they best learn, so that they can unlearn, learn, unlearn and relearn over time.”



The shift comes as interest in vocational and applied learning continues to grow alongside traditional VCE studies. The number of students earning the VCE Vocational Major (VM) increased by 13 per cent in 2025, with 9777 students opting for the skill-based pathway. The VCE VM, introduced in 2023, provides hands-on training and work-related skills in fields such as early childhood education and IT. Smith says the VCE is designed to be flexible, with major reforms in recent years aimed at broadening the pathways available to students. “I think what we’re seeing is there’s a greater understanding that there’s no single definition of success when it comes to senior secondary schooling,” he says.



“Students are defining success more personally ... versus what was, for many students previously, a singular focus on the ATARs.” He says there is also continued growth in the Victorian Pathways Certificate (VPC), as well as uptake of Vocational Education Training (VET) subjects in the VCE. While there is no evidence young people are choosing subjects specifically to ″⁣AI-proof″⁣ their careers, Smith says there are signs they are responding to the world around them. He points to a growing interest in economics, with VCAA figures showing enrolments rose from 3158 in 2021 to 4464 in 2026, or 41 per cent. “I wonder how much that [comes from] living in a world where there’s uncertainty, interest rates are high, people are feeling the [rising] cost of living ... whether that’s developed an interest in understanding the mechanics underneath,” Smith says.



His advice to year 10 students choosing their senior secondary pathway is to understand the options, choose subjects matching their interests and strengths, and avoid feeling pressured to have their entire futures mapped out at 16. “My message is that there are many right ways, so choose the one that best suits you,” Smith says. For those about to start exams, he says it is not too late to “put your best foot forward”. “Some students feel at this point in time of the year that maybe it’s too late,″⁣ Smith says. ″⁣But there are plenty of opportunities to prepare yourself well, take the advice of your teachers, and keep up with the work and the preparation.” The VCAA also introduced a new Recognition of Learning statement this year for students unable to complete the VCE, VCE VM or VPC for personal reasons such as trauma, incarceration, or cognitive disabilities. ″⁣Now the system will be able to say to them: ‘We see you, we recognise your effort, and we want to acknowledge that formally’,” Smith says.

Ananya Hariharan’s first singing lesson as a six-year-old was sparked by being told off in class. The little girl with a big voice would belt out her favourite song from Disney’s Frozen as she did her times tables and learned to write. Ananya Hariharan says song choice should be guided by personal preference. “My teachers would get really annoyed at me, so they asked my mum to put me into singing lessons,” recalls Hariharan, now 18. “They thought that I could be really good.” They weren’t wrong.



Fast-forward 12 years and Hariharan has graced stages from Hamer Hall to John Cain Arena, landed lead vocalist roles in multiple Victorian State School Spectaculars, and added a Premier’s VCE Study Award for Music Performance (VCE VET) to her impressive CV. She even made the final audition rounds for a popular TV talent show during her final year of school. The classically trained singer was the first in her family to pursue music, and last year studied both VCE and VET music in year 12 at Mount Waverley Secondary College. “The two music subjects were incredibly different,” Hariharan says. “VET music taught me how to play in a band, work with other people and more industry-based skills, whereas VCE music taught me more of the technical side, such as theory and learning how to perform in a more professional environment.”



She admits that the music exams were her most nerve-filled performances to date. Ananya’s biggest goal is to open a singing school. “I think it’s even more daunting than auditioning for TV, just because you know someone’s examining you, marking you,” Hariharan says. “With a TV show, they’re just watching you to see if you’re fit for a show. The exams were terrifying, but also a lot of fun actually. I just let myself feel the music.” The VCE Music Repertoire Performance exam required a 20-minute set of songs from multiple genres, while for the VET subject, she performed a 35-minute set with a band. Her advice on song choice is to be guided by personal preference. “You need to pick pieces that you actually like because you’re going to have to sing them or play them for a very long time,” Hariharan says. “When you get in the exam room, you want music that makes you feel comfortable, not stressed.”



She adds that it’s important to focus on “making yourself proud”, rather than doing “what you think the examiners want to hear”. Hariharan’s advice comes from experience, having changed her VCE set list just one month before the exams as they weren’t the right fit. She also credits a support system of teachers, family and friends for her success in the VCE. She was accepted into a bachelor of music at Monash University, specialising in popular music, and is performing R&B, soul and jazz songs around Melbourne. “I want to put my music out there and make people happy through my music, but I think my biggest goal is to open a singing school,” she says. “I’ve been put through some really rough coaching experiences in the past. I want to nurture younger kids in a way where they can embrace their uniqueness.”



The 2026 VCE music examinations start on Monday, October 5. VCAA tips for performers Bring ID with clear photo and your name

Don’t wear a school uniform

Rehearse regularly in a range of environments and to different audiences to help boost confidence

Seek regular feedback from teachers, and balance study time between all exams.

World.title: Minister intervenes as open day Perth film studio actors paid with lunch and ‘opportunity’
World.content:
Exclusive NationalWAFilm & TV production Minister intervenes as open day Perth film studio actors paid with lunch and ‘opportunity’ Hamish Hastie September 3, 2026 — 3:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Cook Government has intervened to ensure actors appearing at the $233.5 million Perth Film Studios’ first-ever open days are paid for their time after they were initially only offered meals and the “opportunity” to work with experienced directors and crew. The open days, set for September 11 and 12, will feature a real music video recording for a Perth band, organised by contractor West Coast Crew. Perth Film Studios is hosting open days on September 11 and 12. Hamish Hastie Last month West Coast Crew put out a callout for more than 30 volunteer actors to be part of the event across four sets in roles including Kung Fu fighters, cops, and zombies. The email stated the directors and crew would also be donating their time. “Although this is an unpaid opportunity, all participants will be provided with meals while working; given access to the completed music video for possible show reel use; [and] given the opportunity to work with experienced Perth directors and crew inside the new studio,” the email read.



The Cook government embarked on the film studios project in Perth’s north-eastern suburbs to turbocharge the state’s small screen industry in 2021, and the callout for unpaid actors incensed the opposition and Chamber of Arts and Culture WA. Creative Industries shadow minister Julie Freeman raised the issue with Creative Industries Minister Simone McGurk and said it was “a pretty ordinary way” to start what was supposed to be a major investment in WA’s creative industries. “So much for diversifying the economy and creating jobs,” Freeman said. “Perth Film Studios was sold as an investment in Western Australia’s screen industry, designed to attract productions, create jobs and build a sustainable local industry. “Instead, the studio’s opening weekend is relying on local actors and crew to work for free.



“To ask Western Australian talent to volunteer their time to showcase a facility that is supposed to create jobs for them is insulting.” A spokeswoman for McGurk said the government had intervened to ensure the actors would be paid. She said the state was not aware actors were being asked to volunteer for the open day. Creative Industries Minister Simone McGurk. Hamish Hastie “West Coast Crew have been contracted and paid to deliver the behind-the-scenes experience by Arts and Culture Trust who manage the Perth Film Studios, on behalf of the state government,” she said.



“It was a decision of West Coast Crew to call for extras to appear in a music video on a voluntary basis and the state government was not aware the call-out was being made. “It is the state government’s expectation that actors are paid for their time and expertise and has intervened to ensure that happens.” West Coast Crew was approached for comment but did not respond by deadline. Chamber of Arts and Culture WA executive director Rick Heath said he was grateful for the state’s intervention. “When first hearing about it, I would say it’s a request that’s actually deeply offensive to professional actors and performers,” he said.



“The notion of professional people volunteering their time for ‘exposure’ is something that we absolutely need to address and move on from, which is about the sustainability of the industry and the careers for West Australian talent.” The open days include a careers open day for school students on September 11 and a public open day on September 12. The tickets have all been snapped up.

World.title: Judge issues jail warning to Tiger Woods after plea deal in DUI case
World.content:
Updated WorldNorth AmericaTiger Woods Judge issues jail warning to Tiger Woods after plea deal in DUI case Daniel Kozin Updated September 3, 2026 — 1:00am ,first published 11:13pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Tiger Woods pleaded no contest to a reckless driving charge and his driver’s licence was suspended for five years on Wednesday following a rollover crash in March in Florida, where he initially was accused of driving under the influence (DUI). Before the hearing in Marin County began, Woods, 50, sat at the defence table looking back at the mostly empty courtroom gallery. He said little as he agreed to the reduced charge. Tiger Woods arrives at court in Florida with girlfriend Vanessa Trump. AP Photo/Lynne Sladky He arrived at the courthouse with his girlfriend, Vanessa Trump, US President Donald Trump’s former daughter-in-law, and she sat behind him during the proceedings. Woods, still one of golf’s most influential figures and as recognisable as any athlete in the world, has had a remarkable fall since winning the 2019 Masters for his 15th major. His career has been derailed by multiple back and knee surgeries, car crashes and dependence on pain medication.



Woods in court on Wednesday. Crystal Vander Weit/Treasure Coast Newspapers via AP He was arrested in March after his SUV clipped a truck and rolled over on its side on a beachside residential road near his home on Jupiter Island. A sheriff’s report said deputies found two pain pills in his pocket and he showed signs of impairment. He did a Breathalyser test, which came out negative, but refused to take a urine test. He had pleaded not guilty to the original DUI charge. Tiger Woods strapped into a patrol car after his arrest. AP The prosecutor in the case said two toxicologists found there was insufficient proof of his impairment and determined Woods had built up a “pharmacological” tolerance.



Thomas Bakkedahl, a state attorney, defended his decision to accept the plea, saying, “I did what I think is right.” Woods left the courthouse without addressing reporters. He also pleaded no contest to refusing to submit to testing after the crash and was fined $US1500 ($2092), according to court documents. “If you were to drive for any reason at all, you would immediately go back to jail,” Judge Darren Steele told Woods. Woods’ overturned vehicle on Jupiter Island, Florida. AP Woods’ attorney did not immediately respond to a message seeking comment.



A no-contest plea is not an admission of guilt, but means the accused will offer no defence. The plea is treated as a conviction in the criminal justice system. Related Article Updated

Tiger Woods Tiger Woods arrested on suspicion of DUI after crash Neither Woods nor the person in the other vehicle were injured in the crash, according to officials. But his Land Rover caused $US5000 ($7000) in damage to the truck, according to a police report. Woods had told a deputy that he was looking down at his phone and changing the radio station when he hit the truck. Woods has been involved in four crashes over the years. He took a leave from the golf tour after the 2009 crash and again after the latest crash and has yet to return to tournament play. He left the United States to seek treatment at an inpatient treatment facility, according to court records.



Woods made his first public appearance since returning from treatment on June 23 when he introduced the PGA Tour’s plans to revamp its schedule for 2028. Woods remained as chairman of the tour’s Future Competition Committee after his arrest. He did not take questions during that appearance. World.title: AUKUS makes Australia a nuclear target, top experts warn
World.content:
PoliticsFederalAUKUS AUKUS makes Australia a nuclear target, top experts warn Rob Harris September 3, 2026 — 4:37am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Australia is significantly more likely to be dragged into a destructive conflict with China — and potentially targeted with nuclear weapons — under the AUKUS security pact, two former senior national security figures have warned. Michael Keating, a former Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet secretary, and former public servant Jon Stanford argue that the federal government’s current defence posture has “sacrificed considerable sovereignty” to the United States while leaving the country uniquely vulnerable without a guaranteed security safety net. A Virginia class submarine off the coast of Western Australia. The pair will front a crowd-funded public inquiry into the AUKUS submarine pact on Thursday, urging the federal government to immediately redesign its national strategy, cancel plans to acquire American Virginia-class and British-designed SSN AUKUS nuclear-powered attack submarines, and pivot to low-enriched uranium vessels sourced from France or South Korea. Keating, the most senior public servant during the Hawke-Keating era, spent 11 years on the Secretaries Committee on National Security – including five years as chairman – while Stanford has extensive background in submarine research and defence policy.



“Under AUKUS, Australia’s security is under greater threat while it has become increasingly clear that we cannot rely on the US for our defence,” they write in their submission. “We are now in a situation where, because of the AUKUS strategy of integrated deterrence in defence of US regional primacy, Australia is more likely to be attacked, potentially with nuclear weapons”. Jean-Yves Le Drian, France’s former foreign minister. AP They cite prescient warnings from former French foreign minister Jean-Yves Le Drian, who noted in 2021 that Australia had made a choice “to the detriment of sovereignty” and predicted it would discover later it had sacrificed both security and self-determination. According to the submission, the policy of “integrated deterrence” and “pooled sovereignty” effectively converts Australian military facilities into forward operating locations for US forces without giving Canberra oversight or veto power. They point out that unlike allies such as Japan, South Korea, and the Philippines, Australia lacks a formal US security guarantee, such as NATO’s Article V.



Yet, by developing command and basing infrastructure – such as the US submarine squadron facilities at HMAS Stirling in Western Australia – Australia becomes a prime military target. “If there is a war between the US and China, Australia will inevitably be involved ... even if we do not provide military support,” the submission states, adding that escalating hostilities could leave Australia open to nuclear strikes. Former secretary of the Department of Home Affairs Mike Pezzullo. Alex Ellinghausen Fronting the first day of the hearings in Canberra on Wednesday, former home affairs secretary Mike Pezzullo called for a deeper military integration with the US, agreeing that Australia could surrender sovereignty under the current AUKUS without gaining a meaningful say in decisions that could draw it into a war with China. Pezzullo, a national security hawk and former senior public servant under the Abbott, Turnbull and Morrison governments, was sacked by Labor in 2023 after confidential messages between him and Liberal Party powerbroker Scott Briggs were leaked to this masthead. The Australian Public Service Commission subsequently found he had breached the public service code of conduct on 14 occasions.



“If I was a Chinese war planner,” Pezzullo said, “I would flatten every single potential facility that might be used overnight by Americans flying in.” He said facilities including Tindal, Stirling, North West Cape and Pine Gap could be targeted in such a conflict. But Pezzullo said AUKUS’s nuclear-powered submarine program would transform Australia’s military options, giving the navy greater speed, endurance and reach while opening the way for a new generation of autonomous underwater systems. Undersea warfare would be critical in any future conflict, from anti-submarine operations to intelligence gathering, he said. At the same time, Pezzullo said Australia should not commit to fighting alongside the US in every future conflict.



“Alliances are political documents first and foremost,” he said, arguing that countries must retain the ability to make sovereign decisions when a conflict actually occurs. Related Article Analysis

UK Britain just shelved a key defence goal. That’s not good for Australia But he said those political alliances needed military planning and preparation underneath them. Australia, he said, could either try to remain outside a future US-China conflict and accept the consequences if Washington lost, or strengthen its alliance with the US in the hope that the combined deterrent would prevent war. “The only choice would be whether we want to sit it out and hope for the best,” Pezzullo said. “I think that’s not plausible.”



The choice was whether to remain on the sidelines and accept the consequences if Washington lost, or deepen the alliance in the hope that Australian involvement would strengthen deterrence. “I prefer that latter approach,” Pezzullo said. “The war machine is the thing that prevents the war.” Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis.
