World.title: Primary school friends the perfect study pairing
World.content:
NationalVictoriaVCE Primary school friends the perfect study pairing September 3, 2026 — 4:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Expert tips to help you do your best in this year’s exams, plus meet the students doing Year 12 differently. See all stories .

These VCE stars are proof that when it comes to acing year 12, two heads really can be better than one. Clarence Antonmeryl and Dinith Premaratne turned their friendship into an academic advantage, studying side-by-side, challenging each other and finishing with identical scores: perfect ATARs of 99.95. Clarence Antonmeryl (left) and Dinith Premaratne were students at Haileybury. They even landed in the same bachelor of science degree at the University of Melbourne with Chancellor’s scholarships, knocking back offers from US campuses. But while their paths are remarkably similar, they say it’s their differences – comparing approaches, filling each other’s knowledge gaps – that has helped them shine.



“We really supported each other through the VCE – we’ve known each other since year 4,” says Clarence, now 18. “We would constantly build upon each other’s work and understanding and I think that really helped make us better learners.” Sometimes they disagreed, and that was the point. “We argued a lot about approaches, such as the best way to solve a problem in maths methods, but it optimised our learning,” says Dinith, also 18. “We didn’t focus on comparing marks with each other either, and rather just on trying to build each other up.” The duo were among a record 65,586 students to complete their VCE in 2025, a 3500 rise from the year before. As a new crop of students prepare to sit their exams, VCAA boss Andrew Smith is encouraging students to support each other. “It is a stressful time because you want to do your best; you want to make sure you put your best foot forward,” he says. “Talk to people about how you’re feeling, about how they are feeling. There are others who’ve been through this who can give you good advice. Those are all things that, to be honest, I wish I had thought about when I was doing my HSC.”



VCAA chief executive Andrew Smith. For Dinith and Clarence, it was part of a wider school culture at Haileybury. “We always saw each other as one cohort, so whenever one of us did well, we’d say it was a win for all of us,” Clarence says. Their collaboration continued outside school, with Zoom calls before SACs (school-assessed coursework) to brainstorm possible questions and “push each other’s understanding to the limit”. An iMessage group with nine of their peers provided both light relief and extra study support. When VCE results began arriving in December last year, the chat was buzzing. “We were congratulating each other on results, and were genuinely happy for each other,” Dinith says.



Study right, not all night Surviving year 12 doesn’t have to involve spending every waking hour with your head in the books. The study buddies embarked on their final year armed with a strategy that included taking four subjects instead of five to ease the load. Clarence studied specialist maths, physics, English and French, after ticking off algorithmics and maths methods in year 11. “We gave ourselves more downtime by doing four subjects, so in our spare periods we would go on walks with a group, or play chess or some sport,” he says. Dinith adds: “It’s important to not see downtime as your enemy because as they say, quality over quantity. It helped keep our minds sharp, and stopped us from burning out.”



They regularly reviewed each other’s work and taught each other new material in their shared subjects, such as more advanced grammatical structures in French. Dinith studied English, French, specialist maths and chemistry in year 12, and maths methods and accounting the year before. He says injecting a sense of fun into their studies was also helpful. They would discover idioms in English that translated into French, turn content into games, listen to French music and devise their own maths quizzes with classmates. “There’s that phrase that if you enjoy what you do, you don’t work a day in your life, and that’s true too of studying,” Clarence says.



Top exam tips When asked for their best exam advice by other students, there’s one thing that tops the list: start early. Frankston High School graduate Blake Alford-Ryan juggled many things during his final year of school. Clarence and Dinith took a systematic approach to their exam preparation, including using the study design as a checklist to consolidate their learning, doing practice exams under timed conditions, reading examiner’s reports and putting on examiner’s hats where they could. “By starting the practice exams early, you really cement your understanding,” Dinith says.



“The key is to plan ahead to avoid stress and panic.” Before an exam, he would spend about a week reviewing his mistakes, keeping a running list so he didn’t make the same errors twice. The pair did practice exams until the second-last day, particularly in subjects like maths, so the content remained fresh. Then came the clincher: they stopped. ″⁣On the last day before the exam, it’s all about getting into that exam mode, sleeping for nine to 10 hours and just being hydrated, eating well, and being relaxed,” Clarence says. Dinith agrees being mentally prepared is just as important as knowing the content, after sacrificing sleep to study during year 11.



“In a content-heavy subject like accounting, I tended to go to sleep at 1am and then get up at 4am or 5am on the day of the SAC,” he recalls. “But I found that not only was I less focused and jittery, but I also tended to get more sick during year 11.” By year 12, he had changed tack, prioritising sleep, downtime, planning and consistency. Juggling study and a start-up Frankston High School graduate Blake Alford-Ryan had more on his plate than the average student in year 12. On top of his studies, the school captain was leading uniform reform, campaigning for solar panels, collecting leadership awards, hitting the gym ... and building a media agency.



But surprisingly, the VCE top performer believes his packed schedule didn’t hurt his studies – they enhanced them. “It’s a little bit different but for me, I managed stress in the VCE by working on my business,” he says. “It allowed my brain to switch off study mode.” The VCE Leadership Award 2025 recipient was recognised for his “strong commitment to student voice, leadership and meaningful change”. He was accepted into his dream course, a bachelor of law at Swinburne University but has recently deferred to run the brand agency Habits of the Few. The 19-year-old says he is also a big believer in the value of teamwork, whether it’s during the VCE or in the world of business. He intentionally sought students who were more advanced in subjects such as English so he could learn from them, and benefited from lunchtime group study sessions. “If you can collaborate with other people, you get perspectives that you would not have [otherwise],” he says.

World.content:
NationalVictoriaVCE Goals and determination driving Steph to succeed September 3, 2026 — 4:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Expert tips to help you do your best in this year’s exams, plus meet the students doing Year 12 differently. See all stories .

Steph Woods has a clear goal for her future: to become a lawyer and advocate for other people with disabilities. And she’s not letting her own health needs stand in the way. Steph Woods is battling mitochondrial disease and studying through Virtual Schools Victoria. The 18-year-old lives with a degenerative disorder called mitochondrial disease and is completing her VCE from home through Virtual Schools Victoria (formerly Distance Education Centre Victoria). “I want to become a human rights lawyer so people with disabilities know what they are entitled to,” she says. By all accounts, she’s got what it takes.



Woods won a VCE Study Award in 2025 after earning a perfect score in legal studies in year 11, reflecting both her academic ability and determination to succeed. She says that moving from a bricks-and-mortar school to VSV was a game-changer, particularly the flexibility to watch recorded classes and support setting up a tailored learning environment. With symptoms ranging from chronic migraines, nerve damage and vision and hearing impairments to ataxia and scoliosis, she’s not always well enough to log on: “You pick an organ and it doesn’t work.” Woods is one of about 5500 students who study through VSV each year, from professional sportspeople or performing artists to students living in rural and remote communities or experiencing health difficulties. Her mum, Kylie Poppins is as proud as punch. On the day of Steph’s award ceremony, Poppins and her son looked over as they prepared to leave to find Steph studying.



“She works so hard,” she says. “I teach year 12 and there’s not many kids who wake up and can’t sit up because of this massive migraine, and are throwing up from nausea, but then crawl out of bed an hour later to study for a SAC.″⁣ For Steph, one of her biggest motivators is simple. “I probably shouldn’t be quoted on this, but I want to beat the able-bodied kids,” she says, laughing.

World.content:
NationalVictoriaVCE The simple question that set Isabella on a new path September 3, 2026 — 4:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Expert tips to help you do your best in this year’s exams, plus meet the students doing Year 12 differently. See all stories .

It was during a woodworking class in year 9 that Isabella Mavrogiannis discovered she might be better suited to a construction site than the classroom. Her teacher noticed her budding skills with a saw and sander and asked whether she’d considered pursuing a future in carpentry. Carpenter Isabella Mavrogiannis says she did not like being stuck in a classroom. Jeff Hoogenboom “I said, ‘What’s carpentry?‘” laughs Mavrogiannis, now 18. But that simple question set Mavrogiannis on an entirely different path from year 10, moving to the Northern College of the Arts and Technology (NCAT) in Preston and kickstarting her career in the trades at just 15.



She remembers being captivated by the facilities and opportunities on offer at the school, gaining hands-on experience in automotive, electrical, plumbing, engineering, furniture making, painting, decorating and building and construction. “I did not like being stuck in a classroom,” she says. “I was very stressed. My dad is a tradie and he was a bit iffy at first about me going into a male-dominated industry, but it was the right thing for me.” During year 11 and 12, she’d drag herself out of bed at 3.30am every Wednesday for work placement with a domestic builder, as part of her VCE Vocational Major (VCE VM). Isabella is passionate about encouraging women to work in trades. Chris Riordan “I did everything from learning how to read all the plans, to standing the wall frames and installing windows once the slab was poured,” she says.



“My boss taught me about everything, from wall frames on the first and second levels, to ... demolition at some big homes around Malvern.” Even Mavrogiannis’ core VCE VCM subjects were connected to the world she wanted to work in. In numeracy, for example, she could apply maths to real-life situations such as estimating a concrete pour or calculating the weekly cost of running a car. The aspiring carpenter was passionate about using her skills to support those around her, whether it was mentoring other female students in trades through the Young Women in Trades and Technology (YWTT) group, attending industry expos or even helping with school building upgrades. The impact she made on her school and wider community was among the reasons she received a VCE Premier’s Award for Outstanding VCE Vocational Major Students. She was also recognised for displaying a high quality of work, strong leadership skills and a dedication to her learning and future.



While she did not receive an ATAR, Mavrogiannis finished her VCE with a Certificate II in Building Construction and a carpentry apprenticeship with Hutchinson Builders, giving her a head start. The biggest question she gets asked about entering a trade as a woman is: “Is it scary?” “I tell people, no it’s not scary whatsoever,” she says. “I’ve found everyone on site so helpful and supportive. And the number of females studying trades and technology at my old school has grown so much; we really wanted to get the word out.”

World.title: Flexible futures shift focus off ATAR
World.content:
NationalVictoriaVCE Flexible futures shift focus off ATAR September 3, 2026 — 4:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Expert tips to help you do your best in this year’s exams, plus meet the students doing Year 12 differently. See all stories .

Victorian senior students are increasingly looking beyond a single career and recognising that the ATAR isn’t the only measure of success, the state’s curriculum body says. Victorian Curriculum Assessment Authority chief executive Andrew Smith says today’s students have a growing awareness of the need to be flexible, particularly as artificial intelligence reshapes the workplace. VCAA chief executive Andrew Smith says there are ‘many right ways’ to handling year 12. “They’re looking more at that understanding that they will have multiple career pathways as they progress through their lives,” he says. “The other thing that we’re hearing in speaking with young people is that they have a greater appreciation of ... how they best learn, so that they can unlearn, learn, unlearn and relearn over time.”



The shift comes as interest in vocational and applied learning continues to grow alongside traditional VCE studies. The number of students earning the VCE Vocational Major (VM) increased by 13 per cent in 2025, with 9777 students opting for the skill-based pathway. The VCE VM, introduced in 2023, provides hands-on training and work-related skills in fields such as early childhood education and IT. Smith says the VCE is designed to be flexible, with major reforms in recent years aimed at broadening the pathways available to students. “I think what we’re seeing is there’s a greater understanding that there’s no single definition of success when it comes to senior secondary schooling,” he says.



“Students are defining success more personally ... versus what was, for many students previously, a singular focus on the ATARs.” He says there is also continued growth in the Victorian Pathways Certificate (VPC), as well as uptake of Vocational Education Training (VET) subjects in the VCE. While there is no evidence young people are choosing subjects specifically to ″⁣AI-proof″⁣ their careers, Smith says there are signs they are responding to the world around them. He points to a growing interest in economics, with VCAA figures showing enrolments rose from 3158 in 2021 to 4464 in 2026, or 41 per cent. “I wonder how much that [comes from] living in a world where there’s uncertainty, interest rates are high, people are feeling the [rising] cost of living ... whether that’s developed an interest in understanding the mechanics underneath,” Smith says.



His advice to year 10 students choosing their senior secondary pathway is to understand the options, choose subjects matching their interests and strengths, and avoid feeling pressured to have their entire futures mapped out at 16. “My message is that there are many right ways, so choose the one that best suits you,” Smith says. For those about to start exams, he says it is not too late to “put your best foot forward”. “Some students feel at this point in time of the year that maybe it’s too late,″⁣ Smith says. ″⁣But there are plenty of opportunities to prepare yourself well, take the advice of your teachers, and keep up with the work and the preparation.” The VCAA also introduced a new Recognition of Learning statement this year for students unable to complete the VCE, VCE VM or VPC for personal reasons such as trauma, incarceration, or cognitive disabilities. ″⁣Now the system will be able to say to them: ‘We see you, we recognise your effort, and we want to acknowledge that formally’,” Smith says.

Fast-forward 12 years and Hariharan has graced stages from Hamer Hall to John Cain Arena, landed lead vocalist roles in multiple Victorian State School Spectaculars, and added a Premier’s VCE Study Award for Music Performance (VCE VET) to her impressive CV. She even made the final audition rounds for a popular TV talent show during her final year of school. The classically trained singer was the first in her family to pursue music, and last year studied both VCE and VET music in year 12 at Mount Waverley Secondary College. “The two music subjects were incredibly different,” Hariharan says. “VET music taught me how to play in a band, work with other people and more industry-based skills, whereas VCE music taught me more of the technical side, such as theory and learning how to perform in a more professional environment.”



She admits that the music exams were her most nerve-filled performances to date. Ananya’s biggest goal is to open a singing school. “I think it’s even more daunting than auditioning for TV, just because you know someone’s examining you, marking you,” Hariharan says. “With a TV show, they’re just watching you to see if you’re fit for a show. The exams were terrifying, but also a lot of fun actually. I just let myself feel the music.” The VCE Music Repertoire Performance exam required a 20-minute set of songs from multiple genres, while for the VET subject, she performed a 35-minute set with a band. Her advice on song choice is to be guided by personal preference. “You need to pick pieces that you actually like because you’re going to have to sing them or play them for a very long time,” Hariharan says. “When you get in the exam room, you want music that makes you feel comfortable, not stressed.”



She adds that it’s important to focus on “making yourself proud”, rather than doing “what you think the examiners want to hear”. Hariharan’s advice comes from experience, having changed her VCE set list just one month before the exams as they weren’t the right fit. She also credits a support system of teachers, family and friends for her success in the VCE. She was accepted into a bachelor of music at Monash University, specialising in popular music, and is performing R&B, soul and jazz songs around Melbourne. “I want to put my music out there and make people happy through my music, but I think my biggest goal is to open a singing school,” she says. “I’ve been put through some really rough coaching experiences in the past. I want to nurture younger kids in a way where they can embrace their uniqueness.”



The 2026 VCE music examinations start on Monday, October 5. VCAA tips for performers Bring ID with clear photo and your name

Don’t wear a school uniform

Rehearse regularly in a range of environments and to different audiences to help boost confidence

Seek regular feedback from teachers, and balance study time between all exams.

World.title: Minister intervenes as open day Perth film studio actors paid with lunch and ‘opportunity’
World.content:
Exclusive NationalWAFilm & TV production Minister intervenes as open day Perth film studio actors paid with lunch and ‘opportunity’ Hamish Hastie September 3, 2026 — 3:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Cook Government has intervened to ensure actors appearing at the $233.5 million Perth Film Studios’ first-ever open days are paid for their time after they were initially only offered meals and the “opportunity” to work with experienced directors and crew. The open days, set for September 11 and 12, will feature a real music video recording for a Perth band, organised by contractor West Coast Crew. Perth Film Studios is hosting open days on September 11 and 12. Hamish Hastie Last month West Coast Crew put out a callout for more than 30 volunteer actors to be part of the event across four sets in roles including Kung Fu fighters, cops, and zombies. The email stated the directors and crew would also be donating their time. “Although this is an unpaid opportunity, all participants will be provided with meals while working; given access to the completed music video for possible show reel use; [and] given the opportunity to work with experienced Perth directors and crew inside the new studio,” the email read.



The Cook government embarked on the film studios project in Perth’s north-eastern suburbs to turbocharge the state’s small screen industry in 2021, and the callout for unpaid actors incensed the opposition and Chamber of Arts and Culture WA. Creative Industries shadow minister Julie Freeman raised the issue with Creative Industries Minister Simone McGurk and said it was “a pretty ordinary way” to start what was supposed to be a major investment in WA’s creative industries. “So much for diversifying the economy and creating jobs,” Freeman said. “Perth Film Studios was sold as an investment in Western Australia’s screen industry, designed to attract productions, create jobs and build a sustainable local industry. “Instead, the studio’s opening weekend is relying on local actors and crew to work for free.



“To ask Western Australian talent to volunteer their time to showcase a facility that is supposed to create jobs for them is insulting.” A spokeswoman for McGurk said the government had intervened to ensure the actors would be paid. She said the state was not aware actors were being asked to volunteer for the open day. Creative Industries Minister Simone McGurk. Hamish Hastie “West Coast Crew have been contracted and paid to deliver the behind-the-scenes experience by Arts and Culture Trust who manage the Perth Film Studios, on behalf of the state government,” she said.



“It was a decision of West Coast Crew to call for extras to appear in a music video on a voluntary basis and the state government was not aware the call-out was being made. “It is the state government’s expectation that actors are paid for their time and expertise and has intervened to ensure that happens.” West Coast Crew was approached for comment but did not respond by deadline. Chamber of Arts and Culture WA executive director Rick Heath said he was grateful for the state’s intervention. “When first hearing about it, I would say it’s a request that’s actually deeply offensive to professional actors and performers,” he said.



“The notion of professional people volunteering their time for ‘exposure’ is something that we absolutely need to address and move on from, which is about the sustainability of the industry and the careers for West Australian talent.” The open days include a careers open day for school students on September 11 and a public open day on September 12. The tickets have all been snapped up.

World.title: Judge issues jail warning to Tiger Woods after plea deal in DUI case
World.content:
Updated WorldNorth AmericaTiger Woods Judge issues jail warning to Tiger Woods after plea deal in DUI case Daniel Kozin Updated September 3, 2026 — 1:00am ,first published 11:13pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Tiger Woods pleaded no contest to a reckless driving charge and his driver’s licence was suspended for five years on Wednesday following a rollover crash in March in Florida, where he initially was accused of driving under the influence (DUI). Before the hearing in Marin County began, Woods, 50, sat at the defence table looking back at the mostly empty courtroom gallery. He said little as he agreed to the reduced charge. Tiger Woods arrives at court in Florida with girlfriend Vanessa Trump. AP Photo/Lynne Sladky He arrived at the courthouse with his girlfriend, Vanessa Trump, US President Donald Trump’s former daughter-in-law, and she sat behind him during the proceedings. Woods, still one of golf’s most influential figures and as recognisable as any athlete in the world, has had a remarkable fall since winning the 2019 Masters for his 15th major. His career has been derailed by multiple back and knee surgeries, car crashes and dependence on pain medication.



Woods in court on Wednesday. Crystal Vander Weit/Treasure Coast Newspapers via AP He was arrested in March after his SUV clipped a truck and rolled over on its side on a beachside residential road near his home on Jupiter Island. A sheriff’s report said deputies found two pain pills in his pocket and he showed signs of impairment. He did a Breathalyser test, which came out negative, but refused to take a urine test. He had pleaded not guilty to the original DUI charge. Tiger Woods strapped into a patrol car after his arrest. AP The prosecutor in the case said two toxicologists found there was insufficient proof of his impairment and determined Woods had built up a “pharmacological” tolerance.



Thomas Bakkedahl, a state attorney, defended his decision to accept the plea, saying, “I did what I think is right.” Woods left the courthouse without addressing reporters. He also pleaded no contest to refusing to submit to testing after the crash and was fined $US1500 ($2092), according to court documents. “If you were to drive for any reason at all, you would immediately go back to jail,” Judge Darren Steele told Woods. Woods’ overturned vehicle on Jupiter Island, Florida. AP Woods’ attorney did not immediately respond to a message seeking comment.



A no-contest plea is not an admission of guilt, but means the accused will offer no defence. The plea is treated as a conviction in the criminal justice system. Related Article Updated

Tiger Woods Tiger Woods arrested on suspicion of DUI after crash Neither Woods nor the person in the other vehicle were injured in the crash, according to officials. But his Land Rover caused $US5000 ($7000) in damage to the truck, according to a police report. Woods had told a deputy that he was looking down at his phone and changing the radio station when he hit the truck. Woods has been involved in four crashes over the years. He took a leave from the golf tour after the 2009 crash and again after the latest crash and has yet to return to tournament play. He left the United States to seek treatment at an inpatient treatment facility, according to court records.



Woods made his first public appearance since returning from treatment on June 23 when he introduced the PGA Tour’s plans to revamp its schedule for 2028. Woods remained as chairman of the tour’s Future Competition Committee after his arrest. He did not take questions during that appearance.
