World.title: Apprenticeship numbers hit 15-year low
World.content:
The number of people in apprenticeships and workplace training hit a 15-year low last year and continued falling in the first quarter of the year.

Education Ministry figures showed there were 108,315 people in workplace-based learning last year, fewer than in any year since 2011 and down 32 percent from a 15-year high of 158,570 reached in 2022.

A briefing to Tertiary Education Minister Penny Simmonds in July showed enrolments had fallen further in the first three months of the year - 11 percent lower than in the same period of 2025.

Industry insiders said the drop was caused by factors including a struggling economy, the expiry of various government subsidies for apprentices, and several years of change in vocational education and training policy.

The annual figures showed workplace learning in Agriculture and Environmental Studies was worst hit, halving since 2022 to 9390 learners.

Engineering and related technologies dropped by a third to 29,870 enrolments and Architecture and Building by 29 percent to 28,650.

Energy and Infrastructure Industry Skills Board chief executive, Philip Aldridge, said the drop in numbers was a worry.

"We have certainly noticed it and we are concerned," he said.

Energy and Infrastucture Industry Skills Board chief executive Philip Aldridge RNZ/John Gerritsen

He said business was likely to improve, but the current downturn would have a lasting effect.

"We're going to struggle for labour and that means we're going to have difficulty resourcing up for key initiatives, whether its roading, water, extractive projects and we'll be over-reliant on immigration to fill those gaps," he said.

"Water for example, there's a $48 billion investment plan over the next 10 years with the new water entities and that requires 6000 new people and so we're worried about where we're going to find those people because the training pipeline is nowhere near 6000 people."

Primary Industry Training Organisation (ITO) chief executive Ginny Vincent said the primary sector's big drop in trainees and apprentices was partly a comedown from abnormally high enrolments post-Covid and partly a response to the economy.

Primary Industry Training Organisation chief executive Ginny Vincent. Supplied / Primary ITO

"If I talk about primary sector businesses they're probably operating cautiously because of cost pressures and some uncertainty, probably not recruiting as much as they would so employers are deferring starting any new apprenticeships or trainees," she said.

Vincent said there was also confusion after six years of constant change in vocational training.

"From an industry perspective, six years-plus of structural change has meant considerable disruption and a little bit of uncertainty around how the workplace training is funded ... and how things are being arranged and delivered."

Vincent said another factor was that many farm employees were immigrants on work visas and they were not eligible for government-subsidised training.

Vincent said the Primary ITO's numbers were still down but she was confident they would pick up.

Building and Construction ITO (BCITO) chief executive Jason Hungerford said there was no shortage of people wanting an apprenticeship but the industry was in tough times.

"At BCITO for the trades we cover we've got around 600 people ready and willing to start an apprenticeship right now. What we don't have is perhaps the confidence of some of those employers that are willing to take that next step and take them on," he said.

Building and Construction ITO chief executive Jason Hungerford. Supplied / Building and Construction ITO

Hungerford said 75,000 people had left the sector in the past year or two and while many had been replaced, that churn was itself a problem in terms of the industry's skill base.

"I think a bigger issue than growing our apprentices is how do we retain them. How do we retain them in the sector, both from an industry point of view but also from a completing-a-qualification [point of view]," he said.

Hungerford said the boom-bust cycle in industry training was a problem and the government could help by investing in infrastructure projects when the economy was lagging.

He said in the meantime there were signs that building and construction were starting to recover, and that should result in more apprenticeships and workplace training.

The Manufacturing and Engineering Industry Skills Board said manufacturing companies were intending to increase apprentice numbers.

"Apprenticeship numbers have generally been subdued for a few years now, as we've come down off a post-Covid high, and business confidence has been hit by the extended war in the Gulf," it said.

"However, our manufacturing and engineering industries have seen continuing signs of recovery and growth over the past year, and many companies now face skills shortages and are consequently looking to take on more apprentices."

World.title: 'Young people aren't drinking anything like we used to': Alcohol intake at record lows
World.content:
Hospitality businesses in Christchurch have pointed to changing habits among young people as a factor amid record low levels of alcohol consumption.

Stats NZ reported total alcohol consumption per capita fell to below 7 litres of pure alcohol for the first time for the year ending June.

New Zealand's per capita consumption now sat among the lowest of all OECD countries.

It comes at a time when hospitality businesses were struggling although there was confidence further south that the Garden City was potentially bucking national trends.

Over 420 hospitality companies entered liquidation in the past year, a 42 percent jump on the previous 12 months.

There were 2900 hospitality businesses that ceased trading altogether, an increase of almost 40 percent.

Hospitality businesses in Christchurch have pointed to changing habits among young people. 123RF

In central Christchurch, the picture was a bit more rosy.

Dux Central operations manager Ross Herrick said the bar and restaurant had been steady.

The nearby One New Zealand Stadium which opened earlier this year had made a huge difference.

"On game day, it's a game changer," Herrick said. "It's fantastic. Stadium's doing a lot of good for the city in general, I think."

The sale of low and non-alcohol options had been exponential. But Herrick also pointed to the popularity of alcohol, or lack thereof, among younger people.

"I noticed from my own daughter, the young people aren't drinking anything like we used to. Young people are drinking less and less often, I think. I know my daughter's the worst customer you could ever want," he said.

He estimated young people contributed to about 8 percent of the bar's turnover.

Within a stone's throw on High Street was bar and burger joint Smash Palace.

Smash Palace owner Greg May. RNZ/LouisDunham

Owner Greg May felt Christchurch was bucking the trend seen in other centres.

"I am surprised looking at it from a Christchurch-centric point of view. I think nationally there's some hard times up north."

There had been generational shifts among young people which had contributed to a decline in alcohol consumption, May said.

"A lot of young people are more worried about their health. Alcohol isn't one of the healthiest choices they can make," he said.

There were also economic factors that were keeping things in check, May said.

"Times are tighter at the moment. Energy costs have gone up, housing costs have gone up so people have to cut their cloth where they can."

Smash Palace. SUPPLIED

Several people RNZ spoke to had also seen changes among the habits of younger age groups, and felt there was waning enthusiasm for going out.

"I think in general younger generations are far more emotionally intelligent and see things in slightly different ways than my generation and above," one woman said.

Others also pointed to the cost-of-living, health and greater awareness of the negative effects for a dip in alcohol consumption.

Based on the Stats NZ numbers, beer remained the most popular alcohol beverage of choice, accounting for 59.7 percent of all alcohol available for consumption in 2026. Wine's share had fallen in recent years to 19.9 percent with spirits picking up the difference.

The government has been reviewing the hospitality sector.

World.title: Businesses still paying the price eight months on from catastrophic Moa Point failure
World.content:
Businesses on Wellington's south coast say they're still paying the price eight months on from the catastrophic failure at Moa Point treatment plant.

In the early hours of 4 February, a trapped air bubble in the plant's sewage bypass pipe caused wastewater to back up, flooding critical electrical equipment.

It has since spewed about 14 billion litres of untreated sewage into Cook Strait.

On Wednesday, a damning Crown review found no single decision or isolated failure caused it, instead, it identified a litany - the cumulative effect of weaknesses in management, stewardship, and accountability, as well as longstanding systemic failures of leadership across Wellington City Council, Wellington Water and the plant's operator Veolia.

It found communication was poor between the organisations and that crucial warning signs were missed.

Roger Titcombe, owner of Real Surf. RNZ / Mary Argue

Speaking to RNZ after it was made public, owner of Real Surf in Lyall Bay, Roger Titcombe, had a few choice words.

"It's just a clusterf***. Like, nobody's taking responsibility or acting on information that they've got."

He said business had been brutal since the disaster - worse than the 2008 global financial crisis - and said he hadn't paid himself in months.

Two staff had been laid off and were unlikely to be replaced any time soon, he said.

A few doors down, owner of Ocean Hunter dive shop, Hugh Collins said the report was frustrating to read and felt the disaster was avoidable.

"[That's] sort of the worst part for us - y'know the fact that we've struggled through this period and we are continuing to struggle - it's the most frustrating thing."

Maranui Cafe in Lyall Bay. RNZ / Mary Argue

Heads should roll according to Bronwyn Kelly, co-owner of Maranui and Queen Sally's Diamond Deli cafes near the beach.

"Pretty disgusted, really. It was such an oversight.

"You think it shouldn't be too hard to hold people accountable, particularly having no staff on site when this was happening, no warnings, no alarms, no one's holding anyone accountable - that's really shameful."

The report found Wellington City Council was ultimately accountable at the time of the incident as the owner of the plant and consent holder.

It had accepted the report's findings and Wellington Mayor Andrew Little had apologised again, but business advocacy group, Destination KRL, wanted the council to go further.

General manager Steve Walters told RNZ well-managed infrastructure was the bare minimum expectation from ratepayers.

"When people are paying the highest commercial rates in the country, you want that infrastructure to work, so it's really disappointing to see the level of oversight, and management, clearly isn't where it should have been."

He said businesses were still suffering and called on the council to review, and expand, its business relief package.

"The way that the compensation was managed was based on an unforeseeable event. Now, we can see that it was foreseeable, so that deserves a reconsideration of the support that we can expect for these few businesses [affected]."

Dive Wellington owner Dave Drane said the criteria for relief was "ridiculous", with businesses having to prove a more than 50 percent drop in revenue year-on-year between February and March.

By that time, "your doors are closed, you're bankrupt, and you've let all your staff go", he said.

Dave Drane, owner of Dive Wellington. RNZ / Mary Argue

A council report tabled at a meeting on 27 August said its $200,000 relief scheme for Moa Point-affected businesses received 15 applications.

It said three were approved and a total of $84,540 paid out. It noted two businesses reported drops in revenue of between 34 and 38 percent, while five businesses saw a reduction of less than 20 percent. The remaining were down less than 10 percent, with one business up about 7 percent, it said.

Council acting chief executive Anna Calver said the council had to be sure the loss in business was because of the plant's failure - not just a general downturn.

She said it wasn't planning to revisit the scheme.

"We don't have the ability to just ... set up a compensation scheme, as much as we might want to, but we have to be really careful about the investments we make on behalf of ratepayers."

Calver said the council was recruiting for a new role for a dedicated official to oversee Tiaki Wai, the region's new water services entity.

Hugh Collins, owner of Ocean Hunter. RNZ / Mary Argue

Tiaki Wai said it accepted the report's six recommendations - including restoring compliance with consents, public communication, and improving risk management - and that the moment was an opportunity to do better.

Operator Veolia said it was still working through the report and was focused on fixing the plant, which it expected to be treating sewage from November and be fully operational in February next year.

World.title: 'I don't need to carry her anymore': Family relieved by newly installed lift
World.content:
A dad who has been lifting his teenage daughter from her wheelchair up the stairs to their front door is relieved a lift has been installed with the help of a generous benefactor.

The Thomas family live on a steep section in Wellington and work to put in a lift was on hold for more than a year because the funding would not cover the cost.

After hearing the story on Morning Report in April, a farmer got in contact with RNZ to offer help and the lift is now complete.

Dinson Thomas said his 13-year-old daughter Ann was already using the lift herself.

"She's very happy because before when I carried her, she was scared. Now she's very happy because she's operating the lift and she's happy with it."

He said he is relieved to have a lift and thanks the farmer, who wishes to remain anonymous.

"Now it's really easy I don't need to carry her anymore," Thomas said.

"She's very safe now and I am also safe I don't need to carry her, it's also [good for] my health."

The Thomas family have seven steps to their front door in Newlands, which became a hazard as Ann grew older.

They bought the house when Ann was three and carrying her was much easier.

She weighs close to 40 kilograms and has cerebral palsy and complex needs.

Thomas said they received the maximum funding to have a platform lift installed, just over $15,000. The work started last February but a month later he was advised the quote came in $4000 over the funding - so he put the project on hold because he could not afford it.

The farmer earlier said that sounded like a hard situation to be in, and he wanted to help.

World.title: Explainer: Why you need to enrol to vote by 25 October
World.content:
Explainer - If you plan on casting a vote in November's general election, the clock is ticking - unlike past elections, you have to enrol well before Election Day this year to get your say at the ballot box.

You must enrol by no later than 25 October to vote in the 7 November election.

The decision has been promoted by the government as boosting efficiency and quicker results, but the opposition and some other groups have criticised it as making it harder to vote.

The nonpartisan Electoral Commission has launched a campaign to make sure all eligible voters know about the changes.

"We are working hard to make sure voters are aware of the changes to this year's enrolment deadline," said Anusha Guler, the commission's deputy chief executive of operations.

The goal now is to get the message out to as many as possible before the window closes.

"We have seen a lot of enrolment activity in the past few months and our engagement teams report high interest in enrolling for the election when they are at community events," Guler said.

But there's still concern the new changes won't get across to everyone.

"The majority of New Zealanders - young and old - don't fully understand the changes to election rules," said Kassie Hartendorp, director of the progressive campaign organisation ActionStation Aotearoa.

"Even long-term voters we are talking to are unaware of the changes."

As of 31 August, the commission reports that 89.75 percent of eligible voters are now enrolled, and the rate for youth aged 18 to 24 - which has been falling fast - has risen some to 57.45 percent at the end of August, from 53.89 percent at the end of July.

"There are now 3,636,524 people enrolled to vote, up from 3,609,435 on 31 July," Guler said.

Of course, there could be even more.

Here's what you need to know about getting sorted to vote this year.

VNP / Daniela Maoate-Cox

You must enrol to vote by midnight Sunday, 25 October

In the past few elections, you could enrol at any time during early voting right up to Election Day.

Not any more. Enrolment ends before the early voting period begins 26 October.

How to enrol to vote:

Online: Visit the Electoral Commission website and put in your details.

Phone: Call 0800 36 76 56 to get an enrolment form sent to you in the mail.

Text: Text your name and address to 3676 to get a form sent to you in the mail. Calls and texts are free.

If you need additional help to enrol, the Electoral Commission has details on that too.

But actually, enrolling by 4 October is even better

If you enrol by 4 October, which is Writ Day, you can get your EasyVote card - which isn't mandatory, but helps staff find your name and details on the electoral roll on Election Day.

Many people this year may get their EasyVote card by email instead of the post - read here for more details on why that is.

You'll also be on the printed roll, which closes 4 October - if you enrol after that date and before 25 October, your vote will be a "special vote."

Special votes are by anyone who isn't on the electoral roll or unpublished roll, lives overseas or votes away from a polling place because they can't get to one.

I think I'm already enrolled - how do I check?

More than 3.6 million enrolment packs were sent out to enrolled voters between 17 to 22 August so they could confirm their details were up to date.

If you didn't receive an enrolment pack in the mail, you definitely want to check your status.

Once again, you'll go online to check that. You'll need to have a New Zealand driver licence, passport or RealMe verified identity.

"We're getting a lot of packs returned to us because people have moved. If you didn't receive a pack, it means you are not enrolled or need to update your address," said the Electoral Commission's director of strategic engagement and partnerships Shane Whitfield.

The commission will also send 2 million followup email reminders to voters, and eight community hubs will be set up at shopping malls and other locations in major cities to sign up voters.

Some electorate boundaries and names have also changed since the last general election, so make sure you know where you vote from.

If you need additional help, contact the commission at the freephone number 0800 36 76 56.

Voter enrolment packs returned to the Electoral Commission this year because the intended recipient has moved. Supplied

Will earlier enrolment deadlines actually affect many people?

Going by the last election, it sure could. The Electoral Commission said that in 2023 there were about 450,000 new enrolments or updates during the early voting period, including 110,000 on Election Day.

Guler said the commission is using a "multi-channel approach to reach people on the channels they use every day and in person, so that we reach all voters, including younger voters and new New Zealanders".

"We are using a wide range of advertising channels including TV, radio, print, digital advertising and social media."

That work may be paying off.

"We are seeing higher enrolment numbers than in the previous two elections," Guler said.

The number of main roll electors signed up as of 31 August is up 5.9 percent from the same time in 2023 and 10.4 percent from 2020, the commission said.

The Electoral Commission has previously estimated about 55,000 party votes and 73,000 electorate votes could be disallowed this year due to a lack of enrolment.

The Electoral Commission has said it won't be keeping track of how many voters are turned away on Election Day if they're not enrolled, Newsroom reported.

Groups such as the Citizens Advice Bureau, ActionStation and local ratepayers associations are among many leading the drive to enrol voters.

"ActionStation is working alongside thousands of community leaders, local groups, and organisations in the biggest community-led 'get out the vote' effort Aotearoa has ever seen," Hartendorp said.

"In 12 years, we've never seen such passion and energy from local people to get involved in an election. We're seeing communities in every single electorate work hard to make sure their friends and whānau are enrolled before October 25."

Christopher Luxon casts his vote in 2023. RNZ / Tim Collins

What's the reason for these changes, anyway?

The coalition government eliminated same-day enrolment as part of a suite of changes in the Electoral Amendment Bill which was passed last December.

In announcing the changes last year, Justice Minister Paul Goldsmith said that "allowing late enrolments, however well intentioned, has placed too much strain on the system".

Special votes have to undergo checks before they're finalised, and the number of special votes has been growing in recent elections - in 2023, nearly 21 percent, or 603,257 of all votes cast, were special votes. Only 78,030 of those were from overseas voters.

In 2023 it took three weeks for special votes to be counted to confirm the election results.

This year the Electoral Commission is expecting to process about 700,000 special votes.

"I just think three weeks is way too long to count special votes, I think that needs to be sped up," Prime Minister Christopher Luxon said in 2023.

Special votes have tended to tilt election results to the left in past elections - in 2023 they gave Te Pāti Māori two more electorates and the Greens an extra list seat. National lost two MPs and needed New Zealand First to form a government.

RNZ / Russell Palmer

Labour Party leader Chris Hipkins has promised if elected his government would reverse the changes to electoral enrolments.

Senior Labour MP Damien O'Connor said the coalition was trying to "cut out and eliminate" the votes of poorer, more transient people, while Labour's campaign chair Kieran McAnulty has said the electoral law changes could have a "massive" impact on the election.

National's campaign chair Simeon Brown has said there is "plenty of time" for people to sort their enrolment.

"People know that they need to enrol to vote," he said. "There'll be an advertising campaign run by the Electoral Commission. There's plenty of opportunity for people to enrol. Plenty of time."

But ActionStation's director said the change will make it harder for people to vote.

"These changes are dangerous to democracy. Any expert in how voter turnout works will tell you these changes will likely disenfranchise voters," Hartendorp said.

"For the last 100 years, we've had a history of making it easier to access our right to vote. The current government has quietly flipped that proud tradition, knowing this change would make it harder for people to have their say."

Goldsmith said there was enough time before the next election for people to enrol in time: "I absolutely reject any idea that people will not be able to vote, they just need to be enrolled."

Despite a delay in results being one of the main reason the government pushed to change enrolment dates, the Electoral Commission has said it won't dramatically speed up the official results.

World.title: Move-on orders age change a good start, but still 'morally reprehensible' - city missioner
World.content:
Youth homeless collective Manaaki Rangatahi says it's "outraged" by the proposed move on orders, saying they will impact many in urban areas across Aotearoa. Manaaki Rangatahi

Organisations supporting homeless people still want move on orders scrapped completely, but say the likely exclusion of 14- to 18-year-olds is a good first step.

The Summary Offences (Move-on Orders) Amendment Bill would give police the power to move people on elsewhere if they were being disorderly, begging, or rough sleeping.

The justice minister is not commenting until the committee's report is officially released, but in the meantime the bill's opponents including youth workers, the Police Association and Retail NZ have urged the government to adopt the committee's recommendation.

Auckland City Missioner Helen Robinson added her voice to theirs, telling RNZ that retaining the age at 14 would be "morally reprehensible".

"If there is a 14- or 15-year-old who is rough sleeping or just more broadly on the street, our first response needs to be to look after them, not to move them on," Robinson said.

"So honestly when I first read the news, like I was so excited - I couldn't be more delighted - and I think it adds a sense of hope that actually the select committee will continue to listen to that good evidence."

Auckland City Missioner Helen Robinson. Supplied

But Robinson said the mission still had concerns about the legislation's references to begging and rough sleeping, and could not support the law change if those aspects remained.

"It still remains morally reprehensible in my view," Robinson said.

"If the legislation goes through with rough sleeping and begging, it is going to be both ineffectual and harmful. And no, I will not be in support of it.

"People who are rough sleeping have no choice. It is a survival behaviour. So if you have nowhere to stay tonight ... the only option you have is to sleep outside. Very very similarly, people who are begging, it's a survival behaviour. So why is someone begging? Because they literally do not have any money, so what we are saying is let's recognise these behaviours as survival behaviours, and let's address those behaviours."

She hoped politicians would listen.

"Perhaps I'm naive to say you've listened to evidence once, can you please keep listening to us?

"It's been reported that there are four deaths of homeless people who have been rough sleeping this winter ... move on orders does not stop that."

She said the way to do that would be to provide immediate shelter, then access to a permanent home, and the support to sustain that tenancy and figure out why those people were begging.

However, those supports simply were not available to many.

"If you can't get access to emergency housing - and thousands of people in our country cannot get access to emergency housing - what is the other option? There are no other nationally accessible options for shelter tonight.

"There are night shelters in some areas up and down the country, and in Auckland we have 65 what we call immediate-access beds and the mission runs 20 of those 65. We believe we need 200 for Central Auckland and 1000 for Auckland more broadly.

"To have 65 is so incredibly welcome, but there are hundreds of people who need access to shelter tonight, and where will they go?"

Manaaki Rangatahi Waikato regional co-ordinator Danielle Marks. Supplied / Danielle Marks

Youth housing and homelessness collective Manaaki Rangatahi aims to prevent and end youth homelessness.

Its Waikato regional co-ordinator Danielle Marks said New Zealand had no providers that were able to house homeless children under the age of 16, and lifting the age to 18 would ensure young people were not being housed with "35-year-olds who have a different life experience".

"Youth housing providers only cater between basically 16 - is the lowest we've seen go into youth housing providers - up to 18.

"We know that there are young people that are homeless - they're either on the streets or they're couch surfing with friends and whānau.

"Fourteen is way too young to be put into the justice system ... move-on orders would have rangatahi moving into the justice system pipeline and so we're trying to avoid that by at least raising it to the age of 18."

Manaaki Rangatahi had focused its advocacy on changing the age, but like the mission would prefer the bill be scrapped entirely.

"It's not our favourite legislation. We'd love to have it scrapped completely.

"Where are they being moved to? A lot of these rangatahi, even here in Hamilton, some of them want to be living in their ancestral whenua, they want to be living in the regions whether it's Tokoroa, Putāruru, but there are no housing opportunities there for them," Marks said.

"They have to move to a city and then separate themselves from the support systems that they have in these other places."

Robinson said the international evidence showed move-on orders were ineffective, would not work, and would cause great harm to the vulnerable.

Even if the references to begging and rough sleeping were removed, it was unclear what its purpose would be, she said.

World.title: 'We've lost half our deposit': About 4000 first-home buyers owe more than their homes worth
World.content:
Rising interest rates are not welcome news for most borrowers, but they hit especially hard for those who are paying off a home loan on a house that is now worth less than they paid for it.

Cotality chief economist Kelvin Davidson said, assuming all first-home buyers had a 20 percent deposit at the time they purchased, there were still about 3600 households nationwide who now owed more than the value of their homes.

Most would be people who had bought during the peak of the market, in late 2021 and early 2022. Prices are still down about 17 percent since that point, and more than 20 percent in Auckland and Wellington. Some parts of the country, such as Canterbury and Otago, have since returned to the prior peaks.

The true number in negative equity is likely to be higher than 3600 because many bought with a deposit much smaller than 20 percent. Cotality said about 29,000 first-home buyers bought properties during the 18-month peak of the market and a large proportion of them would now still be worth less than they paid.

Some recent buyers have posted anonymously on social media in recent weeks, sharing the human implications of the downturn.

Is there any point in KiwiSaver if I'm on a total remuneration package? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 10m

One said they were separating from a partner and worried that their townhouse would not sell because next door was vacant and had not sold. "Our CV is down by $100,000 from our purchase price. Either way we will be in debt with mortgage repayments even if the house sells."

Another who said they had bought a house in 2023 had seen their house value drop $80,000, even though they missed the peak.

"When you add the $35,000 agent fee to sell, we've lost half our deposit."

Another said they had been left jealous of renters. "I bought at the peak in 2021 and the house has dropped at least $200,000 easily. It's taken years to accept this is one financial mistake I've made which won't kill me but still hurts."

Some buyers talked about being stuck in townhouses and apartments longer than they intended to, because they had listened to advice that they did not need to buy a "forever home" first up.

Cotality chief economist Kelvin Davidson. SUPPLIED

Davidson his data assumed that they had not paid off much of the mortgage yet, which would be normal for a new borrower with a table loan. A large part of early repayments is interest and only a small amount goes to principal.

"It can't be great for the mindset to be in negative equity, but it's not necessarily a huge problem if people keep servicing the debt, which the majority are, there are hardly any non-performing loans at present. The bank won't come knocking solely because of negative equity."

Kiwibank chief economist Jarrod Kerr said it could be tough going for some people. He said he bought his first house in 2007, which then lost value and did not recover for years. There was a mental element to falling prices, he said.

"With interest rates going up on top of what is being labelled a cost of living crisis, it's unhelpful, it really is. It's not what we should be doing right now, in my opinion."

Bruce Patten, chief executive at New Zealand Financial Services Group, said negative equity was primarily a problem when people needed or wanted to move.

New Zealand Financial Services Group chief executive Bruce Patten. Supplied / NZFSG

"Our recommendation to them is, sit tight for a few more years, until the market starts moving again. So far, touch wood, we haven't had a situation similar to that during the GFC, when there were lots of mortgagee sales with negative equity, leaving people with personal loans after their properties sold and nothing to show for it.

"The main advice is to speak to your adviser if you are struggling. We can help negotiate interest-only payments or repayment holidays in some cases but do your best to ride this point in time out."

Campbell Hastie, of Hastie Mortgages, said he advised people to keep paying their mortgages and try not to think about it. He said he would look at borrowers' equity positions when they came to refix mortgages because people who had bought with less than a 20 percent deposit were usually also paying a low equity premium on top of their interest rates, too.

"The fact of whether your equity position is improving or not in a sense sort of doesn't matter so long as your loan is going down.

"That's what a principal and interest loan is… so long as you're making your minimum commitment there as long as the bank is concerned, they are not going to squawk at you."

While Kerr said falling house prices could make people more reluctant to invest, such as business people seeking borrowing secured against their home, Otago University economist Murat Ungor said the number was likely too small to make a large difference.

"For those 3600 households, this is real and it is painful. Negative equity is a balance-sheet problem, not a cash-flow one, as long as they keep servicing the mortgage. The bank is not calling the loan provided they keep paying. But it does trap people: they cannot easily sell to move for a better job, and they cannot use their home as collateral to start a business. So there will be individual stories of lost opportunity. But as a drag on national investment or the wider economy? No. This is a personal finance story, not an economic one."

World.title: Aftershocks from earthquakes near Milford Sound could last for days - seismologist
World.content:
A seismologist says small aftershocks following Wednesday night's earthquakes near Milford sound could potentially last for days.

A 5.5 magnitude earthquake struck at 6.16pm, followed by a 5.6 quake at 6.57pm.

Those two were followed by weaker quakes - 4.8 at 7.12pm, 4.6 at 7.39pm and 3.8 at 8.05pm.

The first quake hit 40km northeast of Milford Sound. The first two were listed on Geonet as moderate in intensity, while the third and fourth were light and the fifth, weak.

Sam Taylor Offord from Earth Sciences NZ said there were after frequent aftershocks on Wednesday evening, and people could expect the smaller shocks to continue for days - he added there was always potential for a larger earthquake and the agency was monitoring the situation.

He said Wednesday night's earthquakes were not big enough to cause landslides going into the fiord, to cause a tsunami.

However, Offord said people should still take precautions and move away from steep or unstable slopes when the ground is shaking.

Offord said the earthquakes struck about 15 to 20 kilometres from the plate boundary.

World.title: Ciraldo calls out NRL over delayed rule-change communication
World.content:
Cameron Ciraldo wants rule changes for 2027 to be communicated to clubs well in advance of the season's start date as Canterbury prepares to become the latest crash-test dummies in trials for the NRL's kick-off experiment.

With the Bulldogs and Thursday's opponents Brisbane both out of finals contention, the NRL has again opted to stress-test changes to the kick-off rules, where teams conceding a try can opt to kick or receive from the restart.

The concept was widely panned by players in Melbourne's win over Brisbane, and Ciraldo claimed on Wednesday he only learned his team would be guinea pigs in their regular-season game via email.

Beach sprinting was just the start of Damien Cook's NRL story It's been a long time since Damien Cook was known merely as a beach sprint champion, but ahead of the champion hooker's final NRL game, all the old stories are being told one last time.

Ciraldo would have a right to feel aggrieved by the NRL's constant tinkering, given his side were firmly entrenched in the top four last year.

The Dogs slipped back in the pack when the NRL changed the six-again threshold from the 40-metre line to the 20-metre mark weeks out from the season starting.

Canterbury has righted the ship since officials have eased off on calling six-agains.

And while Ciraldo won't solely attribute his club's early-season form slump to the changes, he would prefer clearer communication so clubs can plan their conditioning and roster management accordingly.

"If you look at our form at the start of the year you can blame that, but I think there's a lot of factors that went into our results at the start of the year," Ciraldo said.

"We'll look to address those over the next few weeks.

The Bulldogs have corrected their form of late after referees eased off on the six-again calls. (Getty Images: Brendon Thorne )

"As the rules came back to what they were last year, we sort of found our rhythm a little bit more, and were able to get back to our style of footy.

"I think it coincides with a number of other things as well.

"I think everyone would like to know what the rule changes are to start the pre-season and not find out about them during the trial period."

Ciraldo said Canterbury had little time to put the trialled kick-off interpretations into practice this week.

"I don't check my emails that often, so someone had to tell me," Ciraldo said.

Canterbury's clash with Brisbane will be the last for Bronson Xerri (Melbourne) and Josh Curran (Perth) before they move on to new clubs in 2027.

Ciraldo paid tribute to the pair for being key parts of the Dogs' revival, and confirmed Sean O'Sullivan had agreed to a contract at Belmore for 2027, despite interest from the Super League.

AAP

World.title: AFL boss backflips by scrapping controversial 'Opening Round' experiment
World.content:
The AFL has scrapped the Opening Round experiment after three seasons and will return to a traditional nine-game first week.

League boss Andrew Dillon today confirmed the demise of the much-criticised concept that featured four games played exclusively in Queensland and New South Wales between only a selection of eight clubs.

Designed to build a foothold in rugby league heartland, it instead drew criticism given the fixturing created a staggered start and early-season byes.

Defending it in March, Dillon said Opening Round was "key" to growing the sport north of Victoria, citing record attendances and membership rises.

Australia and England will play a one-off Test next year at the MCG to celebrate 150 years of Test cricket, pushing the AFL season back. (Getty Images: Robbie Stephenson/PA Images)

"What we've found in the last couple of years is that focus on NSW and Queensland is helping to grow awareness in NSW and Queensland and at the same time it hasn't taken away from our round one," Dillon said at the time.

But, with the season to begin a week later next year due to the MCG hosting the 150th anniversary cricket Test between Australia and England, it has been taken out with the trash.

"We have been working through alternative options to deliver the start of the AFL season," Dillon said in a statement.

"After important feedback from fans and stakeholders, and consultation with clubs and broadcasters, round one will see the return of a traditional nine-game round played across the country."

The first round will be played from Wednesday or Thursday, March 17 or 18, just days after the final day of the historic Ashes Test.

The 24-round home-and-away season will conclude on Sunday, August 30, with the five-week finals series beginning with two wildcard finals in the first week of September.

The grand final will be held on Saturday, October 2 and Gather Round in South Australia is locked in for April 8-11.

AAP

World.title: Police speak with four men over Sydney Swans scandal
World.content:
Victoria Police detectives have spoken with four Sydney men as part of their sexual assault investigation linked to the Sydney Swans.

In a statement, police confirmed they travelled to NSW this week.

Sexual Crimes Squad detectives spoke with a 26-year-old Randwick man, a 30-year-old Maroubra man, a 25-year-old Randwick man and a 25-year-old Paddington man.

Investigators say the interview process with the four men has now concluded.

The allegations relate to events at East Melbourne's Pullman Hotel where it is understood players were joined by several adult entertainers in the early hours of August 17.

Three women subsequently made a report to police.

No-one has been arrested and no charges have been laid.

Authorities say they also spoke to, or will speak with, three men also believed to be in the hotel room, who are being treated solely as witnesses at this time.

The club stood down five players — vice captain Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, James Jordan, Riley Bice and Nick Blakey — for breaching club standards for drinking and bringing women to the hotel in the hours after the team's round 23 clash against Essendon.

Police now believe they have identified all parties who were in the room at the time of the alleged incident.

The investigation into the alleged incident remains ongoing, and Victoria Police said it does not expect to provide any further updates for about eight weeks.

Detectives believe they have identified everyone who was in the hotel room at the time of the alleged incident. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

The club released a statement acknowledging the update on Wednesday afternoon.

"The wellbeing of those impacted remains of paramount importance," the Swans said.

"The club again extends its sincere apologies to our members and fans, sponsors and the wider community, along with all of our staff and players across both the women's and men's programs, for the distress and disappointment this matter has caused."

Two separate law firms have been engaged to represent three women considering civil action over the alleged incident.

Their lawyers have previously alleged the women are suffering severe stress and anxiety and may pursue damages.

World.title: Clarkson sacked as Kangaroos hunt 'coach for the modern game'
World.content:
North Melbourne says "gaping holes" within Alastair Clarkson's game plan led to the club parting ways with the veteran senior coach.

Clarkson was contracted with the club until 2027, but the Kangaroos opted to end his tenure early.

Kangaroos president Sonja Hood and head of football Todd Viney both pointed to key game plan issues when questioned on the reasons behind the decision to not proceed with Clarkson into the final year of his deal.

"I think if there was one thing that Clarko did was he tried too hard in trying to fix that, and then therefore what happens is we get into more meetings, more information, and the players at the end of the day become a little bit confused, and we don't get the cohesion that we need to win more games," Viney said.

"There's still parts of our game plan that we haven't been able to improve in the four years, and that's some stuff that we need to get right when we talk to the next coach to bring us in line with where the modern game is right at the moment."

Viney also conceded that Clarkson had been run down by the investigation into racism at Hawthorn under his tenure.

"I'm not sure the scars have fully healed, to this point. He's gone through enormous trauma," he said.

"I'm not sure of the exact impact, but I know it's had an affect. He's been through a lot and he's managed it well and coached us well, but it's definitely had an affect.

" He's not the same bubbly person that I knew early days. "

Despite former Kangaroos stars-turned-coaches Adam Simpson and John Longmire both being on the market, Hood said North Melbourne will run a full process to find its next coach.

Hood added that assistants already at the club who worked under Clarkson are also welcome to throw their hats in the ring for the full-time role.

When questioned over what type of coach the Kangaroos are after, Hood said: "a coach who can coach for the modern game".

Clarkson was blindsided by the club's decision to not proceed with him into 2027, with Hood saying he was "upset" by the call.

Despite Clarkson being Hood's star hire four years ago, she envisages continuing in her role as president, while Viney also said he was prepared to remain at North Melbourne.

Former Swans premiership coach John Longmire (pictured) has been linked with the Kangaroos vacancy, but will need to go through a process if he wants the job. (Getty Images: Morgan Hancock)

Clarkson released a statement in response to his exit via his manager James Henderson.

"My time as coach of the North Melbourne Football Club has come to an end," he said.

"We set out to stabilise the club and lay the foundations for a return to playing deep in September.

"The challenge was a difficult one that I embraced with my whole being.

"My family and I have been privileged to be involved in AFL football for over 40 years, but it is now time for a new chapter."

The Kangaroos will begin their coach search next week, and Hood said there is no timeline on when an appointment should be made official, despite the trade period taking place next month.

Hood said the Kangaroos were in a better position now than when Clarkson took over, but the club wanted more success over the next four years.

"We asked Alastair to give our club stability and strength and help return us to the top of the AFL ladder," she said.

"Four years later, we have created an environment where our staff and players want to be at our club. This is a testament to the culture Alastair has helped create and the belief that he has built in this group.

"Although we have clearly made progress and won more games, we won't shy away from our desire to want more from this talented group.

"We are incredibly grateful to Alastair for the work he's done over the last four years and we wish him all the very best for his next chapter."

Live Moment Look back at North Melbourne president Sonja Hood and football boss Todd Viney's press conference after Alastair Clarkson was relieved of his duties as Kangaroos coach. What was going to happen next year? Did the North Board refuse a contract extension prior to the 2027 season? Did the want Clarkson to coach for his future? - Roos Member From what Hood said, they determined that they weren't going to extend Clarkson beyond 2027, therefore believed that it would be unfair to expect him to coach next season. Is it time for Simpson or Longmire? I think it's the right thing to do. He has laid a foundation but it needs a new voice to get that bit more. I prefer Simmo to Horse and think he could really push this group forward. - Nathan Hood wasn't prepared to say they're the preferred candidate, but both of their reactions will be interesting. The stuff about a modern coach makes me think they'll go for a highly-credentialled assistant. Should the players be blamed? Why get rid of a 4 time premiership coach with 1 more year left. Makes no sense. Maybe players should be held more accountable. - Davo It is interesting, Davo, that the players often seem to skirt responsibility with this kind of stuff. I guess it's easier to remove one employee than multiple. At the end of the day, this is a players' league. Show more

Under Clarkson, North won 20 of its 82 AFL matches, including nine this season. Clarkson took over the Kangaroos after the club had collected back-to-back wooden spoons in 2022 and 2021, while also finishing second-last in 2020.

North has not made the finals in a decade, when the club made consecutive preliminary finals in 2014 and 2015 and an elimination final in 2016 under Brad Scott.

The 2026 season was North's best under Clarkson, and most successful since 2019, with the Kangaroos finishing 14th on the ladder with nine wins.

World.title: Ferrari's Schumacher-inspired livery, F1 leader to cop penalty in Italy
World.content:
Ferrari will be celebrating the legacy of Michael Schumacher this weekend at its home race, with a special livery dedicated to the seven-time Formula 1 world champion.

This year marks 30 years since Schumacher joined the Scuderia, and 20 years since his final F1 victory in the 2006 Chinese Grand Prix.

Piastri searching for answers as teammate re-enters F1 title picture Oscar Piastri's "disappointing" end to the Dutch Grand Prix leaves the Australian and his McLaren team searching for answers, while his teammate has roared back into the Formula 1 title picture.

With Schumacher at the wheel, Ferrari rose to the top of F1 after years spent without championships.

Ferrari's constructors' championship win in 1999 ended a 16-year wait in the teams' competition, while Schumacher's drivers' championship triumph in 2000 made him the first Ferrari race to become world champion since Jody Scheckter in 1979.

Schumacher won five of his seven drivers' championships with Ferrari, from 2000-2004.

This weekend at the Italian Grand Prix in Monza, a race Schumacher won five times with Ferrari, the Scuderia has a one-off livery which pays tribute to the F1 champion.

Among the features are seven stars on the nose of the car, representing Schumacher's world titles, and drivers Lewis Hamilton — the sport's other seven-time world champion — and Charles Leclerc will wear racing suits that also feature the seven stars and Schumacher's logo.

F1 championship leader to take grid penalty at Monza

Kimi Antonelli has celebrated his 20th birthday as the Formula 1 drivers' championship leader, and heads into his home grand prix with a significant 59-point advantage over his two nearest rivals.

F1 drivers' championship leader Kimi Antonelli is set to start the Italian Grand Prix from the back of the grid. (Reiters: Benoit Tessier)

But the youngest-ever leader of the F1 championship heads into this weekend's race at Monza knowing he has work to do to be near the front of the grid.

Mercedes announced during the previous race weekend in the Netherlands that Antonelli will take an engine penalty this weekend.

F1 teams have an allocation of power unit components they can use in a season. When a driver is fitted with a power unit component that exceeds the allocation, they are handed a penalty at the first event that new part is used.

Mercedes has had multiple power unit issues this year, with Antonelli failing to finish in Barcelona and teammate George Russell suffering issues in Canada and Belgium.

Despite the Italian Grand Prix being Antonelli's home race, Mercedes boss Toto Wolff said now was the right time to do it for the championship leader.

"Our calculations say that that's the best track to take it," Wolff said.

"Obviously, algorithms don't take their nationality into consideration. We're here to fight for a championship and not get the most PR. So yeah, that's what we're going to do."

Monza, known as the Temple of Speed, is expected to be a strong track for Mercedes, which is likely why it is taking the penalty now.

With long straights, there should be plenty of opportunities for Antonelli to pass with his impressive Mercedes power unit.

Monza has been the scene of impressive drives through the field in recent years.

Pierre Gasly won from 10th on the grid driving for AlphaTauri (now Racing Bulls). Max Verstappen won in 2022 after taking a five-place grid penalty, while Lewis Hamilton charged from the last row on the grid to place fifth.

Last year, Isack Hadjar started in the pit lane for Racing Bulls and was able to finish 10th.

ABC Sport will have a live blog of the Formula 1 Italian Grand Prix from 9pm AEST on Sunday, September 6.

World.title: Bledisloe Cup quadruple-header announced as sevens added to ticket
World.content:
Australia's sevens teams will share the stage in a scheduling first, with the Wallabies and Wallaroos creating a Bledisloe Cup quadruple-header in Sydney.

The Stadium Australia Test against the All Blacks on October 17 already had a support act secured, with the Wallaroos due to host Scotland for the first time in their WXV Global Series clash.

Kick-off times for Bledisloe Cup in Sydney Wallaroos v Scotland, 12pm

Australian sevens men v Fiji, 2:05pm

Australian sevens women v New Zealand, 2.25pm

Wallabies v New Zealand, 3:45pm All times in AEDT

Now two more fixtures will be added to the ticket, with Australia's world champion sevens women to face rivals New Zealand and the men up against two-time Olympic gold medallists Fiji.

"This is an historic moment for Australian rugby, with all four of our Teams In Gold competing on the same pitch, on the same day, on an unmissable occasion," Rugby Australia chief executive Phil Waugh told AAP.

"The day will showcase the very best of rugby with our elite male and female players across the XVs and Sevens formats taking on famous rivals from around the world in an unprecedented line-up of international rugby.

"We look forward to celebrating this extraordinary occasion with our great Australian rugby community and we thank our friends from New Zealand Rugby, Fiji Rugby Union and Scottish Rugby for helping make this day a reality."

The Wallaroos will begin the action before the men's and women's sevens outfits take the field, followed by the Wallabies, who will complete the four-course menu with a late afternoon kick-off at the venue set to host next year's World Cup final.

AAP

World.title: Thea Frodin, Serena Williams's body double in movie, makes US Open debut
World.content:
Making a US Open debut as a teenager is a daunting task, but American Thea Frodin is no stranger to the bright lights.

The 17-year-old played at her home slam for the first time, going down in straight sets to world number two Elena Rybakina 6-3, 6-2.

There were plenty of fans at Grandstand who were there to see Rybakina, this year's Australian Open champion, but Frodin was a mini-celebrity in her own right.

Frodin, from California, was a body double at the age of 12 in the 2021 film King Richard, a movie starring Will Smith about the rise of Serena and Venus Williams with the help of their father, Richard Williams.

Fordin was the body double for actor Demi Singleton, who played Serena in the film, and is now forging her own path at Flushing Meadows.

There was no Hollywood screenwriting for Fordin's debut, with Rybakina never troubled in the win that came after a near three-hour rain delay.

Fordin was not disgraced in the straight-sets defeat. Down 1-5 in the second set, the teenager fired four aces, saving three match points, to extend the match just one extra game.

"She played really well today, and she has great shots," Rybakina said of her teenage opponent.

Fifth seed comes from behind to avoid another US Open boilover

Italian fifth seed Flavio Cobolli has rallied from two sets down to win his first-round match at the US Open, avoiding another early upset on the men's side.

Flavio Cobolli needed more than four hours, and five sets, to make it to the US Open second round. (Getty Images: Julian Finney)

The French Open runner-up beat Francisco Comesana 3-6, 2-6, 6-3, 6-4, 6-4, finishing his match that lasted 4 hours, 12 minutes, not long after some sun had broken through the clouds and allowed play to start on all the outside courts after a morning of rain.

Cobolli made his first career two-set comeback to avoid joining Novak Djokovic (fourth seed) and Arthur Fils (10th seed) among early losers in a men's draw that was already missing top-ranked Jannik Sinner due to injury.

Cobolli said he took a bathroom break after the second set and decided to change everything.

"So I changed all the dress that I started with today and it works," Cobolli said.

"In grand slams it's never done. You have to fight until the last point."

Ninth seed Taylor Fritz, the 2024 runner-up, rolled to a 6-3, 6-2, 6-4 victory over 18-year-old fellow American Darwin Blanch.

Kokkinakis withdraws from US Open before hitting a ball Thanasi Kokkinakis concedes he may have contested his last US Open without even hitting a ball after the cursed star's body failed him once again.

Madison Keys was the only other player to move into the second round early in a tournament where rain threatened to hamper the schedule for a couple of days.

Showers that began Monday night, local time, and could be on and off through the middle of the week delayed play on all the outer courts, allowing action only in Arthur Ashe Stadium and Louis Armstrong Stadium, which have retractable roofs.

Keys, the 22nd seed, beat 19-year-old Alina Korneeva 7-5, 6-4 in the leadoff match in Ashe. The 2017 US Open runner-up was knocked off in the first round last year in Flushing Meadows.

"It's always tough playing someone young and up-and-coming, and they're going after their shots," Keys said.

"And it's so hard to play a first round of a Grand Slam, so nervous and just wanting to do so well. So, really happy I was able to kind of fight through that and win today."

Coco Gauff, the 2023 US Open champion, 17th seed Alex Eala, and men's first seed Alexander Zverev are scheduled to play later on the final night of round one matches.

ABC/AP

World.title: Aussies march on at US Open, De Minaur washed out, Kokkinakis withdraws
World.content:
Diminutive Dane Sweeny and qualifier Tristan Schoolkate have stormed into the US Open second round to continue Australia's excellent start to the season's final grand slam.

Sweeny was leading the crafty Corentin Moutet 7-6(4), 6-4, 3-0 when the Frenchman retired injured on Tuesday, local time.

Schoolkate then celebrated like Lleyton Hewitt when he finished off American qualifier Nishesh Basavareddy 7-6 (4), 3-6, 6-3, 6-4 in a tick over three hours.

The 25-year-old Sweeny marked his maiden appearance in the US Open main draw with a first-ever victory at an overseas grand slam.

The wildcard next faces either Italian 13th seed Lorenzo Musetti or rising Brit Arthur Fery for an improbable place in the last 32.

Schoolkate is into round two for a second time and will next play Italian fifth seed Fabio Cobolli, the 2026 French Open runner-up.

Sweeny, who only stands 170 centimetres high, and Schoolkate give Australia at least seven players in round two, joining Taylah Preston, Kim Birrell, Maya Joint, Alexei Popyrin and James Duckworth.

Men's sixth seed Alex de Minaur will have to wait another day to try to follow suit after more rain in New York wiped out the day-three night session.

De Minaur did not even make it onto The Grandstand for his first-round clash with Italian qualifier Andrea Guerrieri.

Injured Kokkinakis withdraws from US Open before hitting a ball

Thanasi Kokkinakis concedes he may have contested his last US Open without even hitting a ball after the cursed star's body failed him once again.

Kokkinakis formally withdrew from the season's last grand slam after being unable to take the court for his scheduled first-round clash with Spanish wonder boy Rafael Jodar because of an ankle sprain.

Thanasi Kokkinakis has pulled out of the year's final grand slam. (Getty Images: NurPhoto/Robert Szaniszlo)

The Australian suffered his latest injury in Cincinnati two weeks ago and has been racing the clock to be fit for the Open ever since.

He ran out of time and, after a decade battling endless back, shoulder, abdominal, knee and arm injuries, Kokkinakis admits he is losing patience.

"It is a possibility for sure," the 30-year-old told AAP when asked if his US Open career might be over.

"I'm not going to say never. The thing is, I feel like the tennis part, I've still got a lot of good tennis left in me.

"On the limited matches that I've played, I've shown that I'm more than good enough to still compete and then beat some good players.

"But, to be honest, I'm sick of going into tournaments not feeling like I can do it physically and everyone asks me how my body is."

The 30-year-old used — or "wasted" — the fifth of nine injury-protected ranking entries available to him to make the US Open draw.

The one-time Roger Federer slayer now plans on continuing his recovery and trying to be fully fit for the Australian summer.

"I want to go into it being confident in myself and, if I do win, give myself a chance to back up and try and play again," Kokkinakis said.

"That's always the thing. So it's about feeling strong in myself.

"I'll definitely obviously give the next Aussie a crack and see where I'm at after that."

AAP

Tech.title: Amazon’s AI assistant can now spot fake emails from the company
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Amazon is trying to combat impersonation scams with a new feature that allows you to use its AI assistant to determine whether an email, text message, or phone call actually came from the company. With the update, you can ask Alexa for Shopping about a message you received, and it will use AI to compare it “against a record of every message Amazon has sent,” while also analyzing its contents, formatting, and the sender.

As noted by Amazon, the assistant will only confirm that a message is real if it’s “completely certain.” An example shared by Amazon shows a customer asking, “Did Amazon just text me an OTP from 98626? Message came around 4:50pm.” Alexa for Shopping responds by confirming that Amazon actually did send the message, saying, “This was a genuine One Time Password from Amazon.”

If Alexa for Shopping determines a message isn’t from Amazon, it will instruct customers to check their orders in the app and contact Amazon’s support team directly. The company launched a similar feature earlier this year that lets you forward suspicious messages to “verify@amazon.com” to check if they’re real.

This isn’t the only recent update Amazon has launched for Alexa for Shopping, as it added an “Update Me When” feature that can now help you track new product releases as well.

Tech.title: Range Rover’s new EV looks just like a regular Range Rover — that’s refreshing
Tech.content:
is transportation editor with 10+ years of experience who covers EVs, public transportation, and aviation. His work has appeared in The New York Daily News and City & State.

I think automakers are finally getting the memo. Rather than try to reinvent the wheel with its new electric vehicle, Range Rover just made one that looks nearly identical to its lineup of gas-powered SUVs. They didn’t try to pass off some sleek, spaceship-looking pod as a Range Rover. Sometimes familiar designs are the way to go.

Of course, under the surface the Range Rover Electric is nothing like its internal combustion engine sporting brethren. Twin permanent magnet 260kW electric motors are powered by a double-stacked 118.5 kWh lithium-ion battery, with an estimated range of 330 real-world miles.

The all-wheel drive system puts out 542 horsepower and 627 lb.-ft. of torque, which Range Rover describes as “V8 levels of power.” An 800-volt architecture enables DC fast charging from 10–80 percent in just 22 minutes, or about 137 miles in 10 minutes, when plugged into a 350 kW charger. A zero to 60 mph time of 4.3 seconds won’t win it any awards, especially compared to EV rivals like Lucid and Rivian. But this Range Rover probably doesn’t need to blow up any records to make its mark. With a familiar design and decent enough specs, it should be more than sufficient for anyone who has been pining for a touch of British sophistication in their EV shopping.

Previous Next



















1 / 11

The wait has certainly stretched on longer than it should have. Range Rover first announced it was working on an electric model over five years ago. It first opened preorders in 2023, promising that customer deliveries would begin a year later. The Jaguar Land Rover–owned brand took its sweet time fulfilling these promises, but now that the cover has been lifted, the automaker is taking orders at a starting price of £154,070 in the UK (or about $140,450 in the US).

JLR says it will produce the Range Rover Electric at its Solihull factory, alongside gas and hybrid models. It’s also touting the number of patents submitted for this EV — 300 — making it the most technologically custom-built Range Rover ever.

How technologically advanced? Try lightning-fast grip control. Instead of waiting for mechanical gears to adjust when tires slip, the electric motors adjust power in 50 milliseconds — 100 times faster than a gas car. This gives instant control on ice, mud, or loose gravel. The one-pedal drive system is tuned for super steep slopes of up to 45 degrees, so you can climb mountains or crawl over obstacles using just the accelerator. And the battery and motors are fully sealed, allowing you to drive through nearly 3 feet of water (900mm) without damaging the vehicle. Lastly, a built-in heat pump reuses waste heat to warm the cabin and keep the battery at the right temperature, preserving up to 25 extra miles of driving range in freezing weather.

All of this sounds great on paper. Stacked up against rivals like the Porsche Macan EV or the Lotus Eletre, the SUV may look even better — especially for those car buyers who still prefer a familiar face on their electric vehicle.

Images by Range Rover

Tech.title: The best tech and gadgets announced at IFA so far
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid.

The doors to Europe’s largest consumer tech show haven’t opened to the public yet, but there’s already plenty of news coming out of IFA 2026 in Berlin, Germany. If you’re already struggling to keep up with what has been announced, here are some of the best new gadgets and upgrades from the show — including more competition for Apple’s MacBook Neo, an excellent portable controller for gaming-on-the-go, and a concept handheld designed to balance work and play.

To catch up on everything announced at IFA 2026 you can follow The Verge’s complete coverage right here.

Image: Acer

Flipping the gaming laptop script, Acer’s latest concept is a Windows-based gaming handheld, similar to its Predator Atlas 8, that can transform into a tiny portable PC thanks to a swiveling design that repositions its screen atop a mini keyboard. The DualPlay Mini’s display is just 8-inches in size, which could make productivity a challenge if work involves sprawling spreadsheets, but the concept could be used for answering emails during a daily commute and then connected to a larger display at work for more demanding tasks.

Image: Dell

The Dell 14S isn’t as thin or light as its recently launched XPS 13, but the company is looking to make this model even more accessible for students or others on a tighter budget. The laptop starts with 8GB of RAM and 256GB of storage, and those specs can be bumped to 16GB/1TB. It features a 1080P webcam with face unlock support, two USB-C ports, a headphone jack, and like Apple’s MacBook Neo, will be available in four bright color options: linen, dusty rose, washed denim, and velvet green.

Image: iRobot

The $1,199 Roomba Max 875 Combo is iRobot’s latest flagship floor cleaner and introduces a new feature the company calls “SealForce.” When it detects it’s cleaning carpeting, the robovac lowers a skirt around the cleaning head to create a better seal that increases suction for a deeper clean. The Max 875 also offers up to 35,000 Pa of suction power, mopping capabilities, lidar and camera-based autonomous navigation, and the ability to climb over obstacles and thresholds up to 3.5cm tall.

Image: Jsaux

Released under Jsaux’s new Voidjoy brand, the $49.99 SkyLark S1 Pro is a compact portable controller that appears to do a lot of things right. It’s got drift-resistant TMR thumbsticks that are recessed so they won’t get snagged on other devices in your bag, a pair of analog triggers ideal for racing games, and three different ways to connect to devices and consoles: Bluetooth, USB-C, and 2.4GHz. If you opt for a 2.4GHz connection, you can also pair two S1 Pros to a single transmitter and swap back-and-forth between what character you’re controlling in a multiplayer game, making it useful for parents playing with a kid who may struggle with some challenges.

Image: Acer

Is Framework’s approach to easily repairable and upgradeable laptops finally rubbing off on other companies? Acer’s 16-inch Vero 16 offers tool-free access to several internal components including its user-replaceable SSD and battery. The company says the laptop’s processor can also be upgraded down the line, but that will require it to be sent in to an Acer service center. Pricing is still unknown, but the Vero 16 is expected to launch early next year outside North America.

Image: Jsaux

If you’re lucky enough to have an original Nintendo Switch Pro controller that hasn’t succumbed to joystick drift and want to expand its capabilities, Jsaux’s new Elite Extender is an easy aftermarket upgrade. For $39.99 it attaches to the back of the controller and adds four mappable buttons that can be programmed to reproduce multiple button presses. It’s got its own rechargeable battery, but does hinder Amiibo functionality while it’s piggybacking.

Tech.title: Researchers fear safety disaster ahead of OpenAI’s Astra release
Tech.content:
is a London-based reporter at The Verge covering all things AI and a Senior Tarbell Fellow. Previously, he wrote about health, science and tech for Forbes.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

OpenAI is on the cusp of releasing its most powerful AI model yet, Astra, following weeks of delays to shore up safety protocols after its agents attacked real targets during testing. As details about the model trickle out, researchers are warning it “may be the single worst development for AI security/safety to date.”

Shortly after OpenAI said on Tuesday that it had delayed Astra’s release to work on safety issues, The Information reported that Astra shows far less of its “thinking” than other frontier AI models, sparking concern it could be dangerously hard to monitor.

Most top AI systems today are built using a technology known as a transformer, which processes some types of information linearly through layers before producing an answer. Models can be made to show their reasoning as they go, essentially “thinking out loud.” This “chain of thought” allows researchers and automated safety systems to monitor what AI models are doing and potentially spot undesirable behavior, such as lying or plans to circumvent safety guardrails, before they act.

According to The Information, citing an unnamed person familiar with the unreleased model’s development, Astra uses a more opaque technique known as a recurrent depth or looped transformer, which cycles information through internal layers before producing an output. This would mean much more of the model’s “thinking” happens inside the system, and in a form that looks a lot less like natural human language, rather than being expressed in a way that researchers can easily monitor. This can boost model performance, but makes potential threats and unwanted behavior harder to detect.

OpenAI has limited its use of the looped transformer / recurrent depth technique with Astra so researchers can continue to monitor the model’s reasoning, according to The Information’s unnamed source.

In a blog post published Tuesday, OpenAI said it is “deploying Astra with additional chain-of-thought monitoring to rapidly detect and contain potentially misaligned actions.” It did not mention if the model has a different technical foundation.

The Information’s report sparked widespread concern among AI safety researchers on social media. It was Redwood Research’s chief scientist Ryan Greenblatt, one of three outsiders OpenAI permitted to research the Hugging Face hack, who said a decision to use a more opaque architecture for Astra “may be the single worst development for AI security/safety to date.”

Greenblatt said the investigation into the Hugging Face incident relied heavily on the models’ chain-of-thought, warning that less visible reasoning could allow AI systems to devise and execute strategies that would be far harder for researchers to detect.

Greenblatt’s primary concern, echoed by other safety experts, is that competition to develop more advanced AI systems could lead to “a race to the bottom on architectures that could be catastrophic for our ability to oversee/monitor AIs” — with developers adopting increasingly opaque systems to gain an edge until models become difficult, or even impossible, to monitor. He added that OpenAI’s communications left him concerned that the company “plans on being extremely reliant on chain-of-thought monitoring for safety.”

OpenAI bigwigs responded to the criticism in a series of social media posts that do not explicitly deny the company’s use of the technique. Several expressed concerns about the possibility of unmonitorable AI or a race to the bottom in terms of transparency, including OpenAI safety researchers Micah Carroll and Tomek Korbak, head of strategic futures Dean Ball, and chief scientist Jakub Pachocki, who voiced fears of “a race into unmonitorability kicked off by confused reporting.” He said the depth of Astra’s computation — a measure of how many steps it can perform internally — “is within a factor of two of GPT-4,” indicating that if the technique was used, the increased opacity is less dramatic than some reactions imply. OpenAI did not respond to The Verge’s request to confirm or deny whether looped transformers were used for Astra and directed us to Pachocki’s X post.

“OpenAI has worked to preserve and utilize chain-of-thought monitoring since our very first reasoning models,” Pachocki wrote, adding that such monitoring “is fragile and unfortunately trending in a negative direction, for reasons not contingent on architecture changes that I will write about soon.”

Tech.title: The Trump administration is supporting OpenAI in the NYT copyright lawsuit
Tech.content:
is The Verge’s senior AI reporter. An AI beat reporter for more than five years, her work has also appeared in CNBC, MIT Technology Review, Wired UK, and other outlets.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

The Trump administration has intervened in The New York Times’ copyright lawsuit against OpenAI, making an argument in favor of the AI lab.

The landmark lawsuit, filed in December 2023, alleging that OpenAI unlawfully trained its AI systems on articles from The New York Times and seeks to recoup “billions of dollars” in damages from both Microsoft and OpenAI. This week, the Trump administration filed a statement of interest in the case, supporting OpenAI’s argument that it’s fair use to train an AI model on copyrighted text.

“The New York Times seeks to narrow fair-use doctrine to exclude the training of OpenAl’s large language models (LLMs),” US attorneys wrote in the statement. “That result would be inconsistent with basic copyright law principles and severely hamper ‘the Progress of Science and useful Arts.’” The attorneys went on to write that “LLMs are already helping researchers across fields achieve major breakthroughs” and that “constraining LLM development under a misunderstanding of fair use doctrine would thwart such creative and scientific progress while hindering American prosperity and economic mobility.”

The Trump administration has leaned heavily on statements of interest in private litigation, which one official has called “incredibly” successful at advancing its policy aims. It’s argued previously that AI training should count as fair use, making the case in its National AI Legislative Framework. Trump also holds a personal animus toward the Times, against which he is currently pursuing a defamation suit.

The Times case could set precedent for other media outlets frustrated over AI systems training on their work. Copyright disagreements between media outlets and AI labs have intensified in recent years, including lawsuits from the Center for Investigative Reporting, Chicago Tribune, and New York Daily News. In a milestone 2025 decision, a judge found Anthropic could legally train its models on lawfully purchased books, but that it could still be held liable for piracy, resulting in a $1.5 billion settlement with authors.

At the same time, dozens of media outlets have inked licensing deals with OpenAI, including The Associated Press, Axel Springer and Vox Media. In 2025, The New York Times entered into a licensing deal with Amazon allowing its editorial content, including news articles and recipes, to appear in Amazon’s generative AI tools.

“The fair-use inquiry hinges on the specific facts and uses at issue in each case,” the US attorneys wrote in the statement. “But it would be problematic — and legally incorrect — to impose broad copyright liability that would generally render training of Al models impermissible without licensing. LLM training is ‘consistent with that creative ‘progress’ that is the basic constitutional objective of copyright itself.’”
