Apple’s iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max are expected to be unveiled at the company’s Sept. 9 launch event, and a new rumor appears to be firming up the three-color lineup for these phones.

According to leaker Fixed Focus Digital on Weibo (h/t MacRumors), the iPhone 18 Pro is now in full production and is set to come in sky blue, pure black and burgundy models. Prior iPhone 18 rumors have pointed to these colors, although the names have varied (dark cherry instead of burgundy, for instance).

For anyone hoping for a silver or gray shade, this report suggests Apple may skip that color this year, instead bringing back black after abandoning it on the iPhone 17 Pro series. Last year, black was available on other iPhone models, such as the iPhone Air, the base iPhone 17 and the iPhone 17E.

With just about a week to go until Apple’s official event, it’s likely that reports on the iPhone 17 Pro’s looks will continue to leak.

Even more prescient than the color of the iPhone 18 Pro will be its cost. The tech giant has hiked prices across other Apple products amid the ongoing memory shortage that’s making consumer electronics more expensive.

The new Mac Mini with an M6 processor, for instance, starts at $899, which is quite a bit higher than the $599 Mac Mini with an M4 processor it replaced. It’s entirely possible that the iPhone 18 Pro line could have a higher starting price than the $1,099 iPhone 17 Pro, should Apple follow this trend. We’ll find out more on Sept. 9.

Tech.title: Is The Calorie Counter on Your Smartwatch Accurate? Not Really, Study Finds
Tech.content:
If you use your smartwatch for activity and sleep tracking, that’s great, but if your main goal is to track calories burned during those activities, you may want to find a new method. According to a new Florida International University study, smartwatches overestimate how many calories people are actually burning, with some watches making more mistakes than others.

The study focused on four smartwatches: the Apple Watch Series 8, Fitbit Sense 2, Samsung Galaxy Watch 5 and Garmin Forerunner 955, and had a total of 58 participants.

Each participant in the study wore the smartwatches along with a Cosmed K5, a device that measures energy burn, and an electrocardiogram chest strap to track heart rate. Participants’ age, sex, height and weight were entered into all of the devices. They then completed a workout on a stationary exercise machine in a controlled setting and the results from each device were compared.

The study found that the watches averaged a 15 to 25% margin of error and overestimated calories burned across the board. That means that if you take a brisk evening walk and your watch says you burned 200 calories, your actual burn would likely be somewhere between 160 and 174 calories.

However, accuracy also varies by brand. The study found that the Apple Watch had the smallest margin of error, while Samsung and Garmin struggled more with overestimation. It was also noted that Fitbit had numerous glitches during testing, so researchers excluded some data due to its tracking issues.

From left, FIU student Gabriel Cabeda Ramirez, Ph.D student Daimien Campos and FIU researcher Jason Kostrna participate in a demonstration of the study protocol Friday, Aug. 21, 2026, at Florida International University in Miami. Taimy Alvarez/Florida International University

The researchers also found that accuracy worsened when body fat increased, but have not discovered why that is.

In a press release about the study, Jason Kostrna, the study’s lead author and associate professor of kinesiology and exercise science in FIU’s College of Arts, Sciences & Education, cautioned against relying too heavily on your smartwatch’s calorie readings day in and day out.

“You could be hundreds of calories off each week and easily end up in a calorie surplus when you think you’re in a calorie deficit,” he said.

Instead, smartwatch wearers should take those calorie numbers with a grain of salt and pay close attention to how their bodies and energy levels feel.

Tech.title: Circular’s New Smart Ring Brings Mobile Payments to Your Finger
Tech.content:
Circular is putting mobile payments at your fingertips with its new Circular Ring 3 series. Announced at IFA, the consumer tech show in Berlin, the Circular Ring 3 Pro and Circular Ring 3 Slim are bringing more smartwatch-like capability to the ring category.

Both models add contactless payments to Circular’s existing health tracking and bring back the haptic vibration feature from the original Circular Ring. That means the rings can buzz your finger for app notifications, medication reminders and health alerts without a screen or phone as the middle man.

The screen-free wearable category is having its moment in the spotlight with an explosion of new rings and wrist-based trackers from Oura, Ultrahuman, Google and Garmin promising to track long-term health trends round the clock without the battery limitations and distractions that come along with tiny smartwatch screens. But that same lack of a screen has limited how much these devices can do beyond collecting health data.

Circular, based in Paris, is carving out its own lane by pushing more functionality onto the finger. Its FDA-cleared ECG feature and AFib detection, and NFC payments and haptic alerts push the Ring 3 series closer to smartwatch territory, without giving up the low-profile design that draws people to rings in the first place.

The trade-off is that Circular’s platform still isn’t as established as competitors such as Oura, Whoop and Google, which have had more time to build out their health insights, coaching and ecosystems.

The Ring 3 lineup also expands Circular’s health tracking with blood pressure trends, glucose trend estimates and advanced sleep metrics. But without FDA clearance, these remain wellness features designed for spotting trends and more conversation starters with a doctor rather than diagnostic tools.

Circular/CNET

Circular Ring 3 Slim vs. Circular Ring 3 Pro

Both rings share Circular’s core health tracking, NFC payments and the returning haptic vibration motor, but there are some important hardware differences.

Dimensions: As the name suggests, the Ring 3 Slim is a lot smaller, in both height and width, than the Pro and the previous generation, putting it closer to the ultra-slim Oura Ring 5, which was the smallest ring I’d tested at the time. The Ring 3 Pro, by contrast, is also slightly shorter than its predecessor, but it’s gained thickness and weighs exactly the same as the Gen 2 ring.

Circular Ring 3 Slim Circular Ring 3 Pro Oura Ring 5 Width 5.9mm 6.8mm 6.09mm Thickness 2.35mm 2.78mm 2.28mm Weight 1.9–3g, depending on size 3–4g, depending on size From 2g, depending on size

Materials: The Pro uses titanium, while the Slim is made from a biocompatible resin with a titanium coating.

Battery: The Pro will outlast the Slim by about two days. Circular claims up to 12 days for the Ring 3 Pro, versus 10 days for the Slim.

Health tracking: Only the Pro has the ECG feature and blood pressure tracking.

Circular

Circular Ring platform and AI coach

Circular has built its following on a subscription-free model, giving ring owners full access to core health tracking metrics along with its Kira AI health companion, a feature most competitors charge for even when they offer a free tier.

However, the company isn’t fully closing the door on charging for advanced medical features, with some of these showing as “limited time” in the app.

Price and availability

Circular hasn’t announced pricing or a firm release date for either Ring 3 model yet. The company says those details, along with preorder timing, will arrive in the coming months. We’ll update this article when the company announces more details.

Tech.title: Miele Put a Camera in Its New Dishwasher. Here’s Why
Tech.content:
AI-powered cameras have made their way into most major kitchen appliances. Ovens now watch food as it cooks and tell you when it’s done. Smart refrigerators will ping you when you’re running low on milk or suggest recipes based on what they see lingering in the crisper drawer.

The dishwasher seemed like the final frontier for cameras in kitchen appliances. When I heard that Miele had snuck one into its latest model, unveiled this week at IFA Berlin, I was suspicious. But after a rep walked me through the shiny new Diamond G8 and its camera-focused features, I started to see the appeal.

A camera in Miele’s new dishwasher helps it pick the perfect cycle.

The small camera, mounted on the back of the dishwasher door, provides a clear view of the dishwasher’s interior. It uses that view to take inventory of what’s inside, recognizing dozens of common kitchen items and tailoring the wash cycle and detergent amount accordingly.

The Diamond G8 is one of the smartest dishwashers we’ve encountered, and it’s easy on the eyes.

Got portable bottles or reusable straws in the dedicated slots? The dishwasher’s brain will recognize them and make sure those areas get the spritz they need. Load it up with pots and pans, and the camera identifies them, triggering a more intensive cycle so everything comes out clean. A smaller load prompts a light cycle, so you’re not wasting more hot water or soap than you need.

The G8 recognizes straws, flatware, silverware and cookware and adjusts its cycle for optimized cleaning.

The camera also determines how full the dishwasher is. Command the G8 to start when it reaches, say, 80% capacity, and it’ll monitor the load and automatically begin a cycle once it hits that threshold.

One of my favorite features has nothing to do with the camera

The dishwasher can be programmed to run when energy costs are cheapest in your area.

The G8 Diamond takes advantage of fluctuations in electricity prices throughout the day. Tell it to run when electricity is cheapest, and the dishwasher waits for those lower-cost hours before starting its cycle. It’s a small detail, but it points to where Miele – and kitchen appliances more broadly – seem to be headed: machines that don’t just perform a task, but figure out the best and most efficient way to do it.

The camera paired with a smart detergent dispenser doles out just the right amount of soap.

Miele’s newly unveiled machine has other AI-powered features that encourage efficiency and performance. The G8 features careful water and energy monitoring, trackable through Miele’s app. There’s also a smart detergent-dispensing system, first introduced by the brand in 2018, and a beefed-up hot-air drying system, which Miele says gets dishes bone-dry every time.

The Diamond G8 is scheduled to roll out later this year, according to a spokesperson. A retail price is still under wraps, but I expect it to land in the super-premium zone. For a top-performing dishwasher you can buy today, see our list of the best models in 2026.

Editors’ note: David Watsky’s travel costs for the IFA conference were covered by IFA. The judgments and opinions of CNET are our own

Tech.title: People’s Picks ISP Winners: Is Your Internet Service Provider a Flop or Favorite?
Tech.content:
Your internet service provider choice will depend on what’s available in your area, but CNET readers’ survey responses can help narrow down your choice if you have several options. Jeffrey Hazelwood/CNET

The internet service provider you choose hinges on a lot. We rely on the internet for many daily tasks, streaming, shopping, work and social media. Several factors that go into choosing the right one, like cost effectiveness, satisfaction, speed and customer support are important. But Joe Supan, CNET’s broadband principal writer, says a reliable connection is paramount.

We asked CNET readers what they like (and don’t) about their ISP for People’s Picks, CNET’s community awards program. Did your provider make the cut? Here’s what they said and what we didn’t expect to find out.

CNET’s People’s Picks ISP Winners

J. Hazelwood/CNET GFiber GFiber, previously known as Google Fiber, is a household name among internet service providers and a popular fiber internet option. CNET readers give it high scores, making it the overall top pick among ISPs. GFiber has an overall satisfaction score of 4.72 out of 5, and scores highly for reliability (4.70) and plan speed (4.82). GFiber also scores 4.28 out of 5 for price, Verizon Fios and AT&T Fiber are close runners-up to GFiber. Both score highly for reliability (4.39 and 4.48, respectively) and plan speed (4.41 and 4.49, respectively). But GFiber wins by a landslide for its customer support. Most CNET readers who have contacted customer support within the past year rate their experience as “Excellent,” while other GFiber customers say customer service was “Good” and don’t have any negative ratings for the fiber-optic ISP. Winner for: Fiber internet, customer service, price, reliability and speed See at GFiber

J. Hazelwood/CNET T-Mobile Home Internet (5G) T-Mobile is often known as a popular cellphone provider, but it wins CNET’s People’s picks for 5G internet. T-Mobile scores 4.20 out of 5 for customer satisfaction, the highest among 5G internet providers. CNET readers say their T-Mobile internet connection rarely drops, noting only a few times a year. And there’s no noticeable difference in speed during peak hours. T-Mobile readers haven’t experienced unexpected price hikes within the past year and many wouldn’t change providers if a new one moved into their neighborhood. T-Mobile’s 5G internet is a close runner-up to GFiber in terms of price. Verizon’s 5G internet is just behind T-Mobile, with a price score of 4.10 out of 5. T-Mobile won 5G internet by narrowly beating Verizon in speed and reliability. Wins for: 5G internet See at T-mobile

J. Hazelwood/CNET Starlink Starlink wins among major internet companies with a high overall satisfaction rating of 4.47 out of 5, compared to Verizon Fios and T-Mobile, which score 4.16 and 4.20, respectively. And it has the second-highest reliability score among major winners. Starlink scores 4.59 in reliability while GFiber scores 4.70. “A few years ago, it would have been unfathomable that a satellite company would be considered this reliable. This really speaks to how massive Starlink’s technical improvements have been,” said Supan. Satellite internet also scores fairly highly for plan speed (4.41 out of 5), with no noticeable changes during peak hours. However, Starlink falls short on price satisfaction compared to other major internet providers because it has traditionally required an upfront $349 charge for a satellite dish. However, it recently switched to a $10 monthly charge. “Starlink isn’t particularly fast or affordable, but it serves customers who essentially had no modern internet options before it came along,” said Supan. Wins for: Rural satellite internet, overall satisfaction for satellite, reliability for satellite and speed for satellite See at Starlink

CNET’s People’s Picks regional ISP winners

We pored through our readers’ responses to find the best ISP in each region based on the internet service features you rely on every day. Here’s how each regional winner compares to other ISPs in your area and what to know before choosing one.

West: Sonic

Wins for: Customer service, overall satisfaction, price, reliability and speed

J. Hazelwood/CNET

Sonic is a California-based fiber optic ISP that wins in several of CNET’s categories compared to other Western providers. It earns high marks for price (4.65 out of 5), speed (4.80 out of 5) and overall satisfaction (4.85 out of 5) — the highest among other Western providers. It even beats out national ISPs GFiber and Verizon FiOS for its reliability.

Sonic received nearly flawless feedback from CNET readers. Many readers never experience internet drops or need to reset their router. They also report no noticeable speed differences during peak hours. And when it comes to customer service, no readers report poor or fair customer service.

South: EPB (Electric Power Board)

Wins for: Customer service, overall satisfaction, price, reliability and speed

J. Hazelwood/CNET

Electric Power Board is a fiber optic ISP based in Chattanooga, Tennessee that scores highly compared to other southern ISPs. It scores 5 out of 5 for overall satisfaction, speed and reliability, and 4.5 out of 5 for price satisfaction, beating out national ISPs AT&T Fiber, GFiber, Comcast Xfinity and Spectrum.

CNET readers also give EPB an “Excellent” customer satisfaction rating with no lower ratings. They don’t experience connection drops or speed lags, and wouldn’t change providers if another ISP came to their area.

J. Hazelwood/CNET

Northeast: T-Mobile Home Internet 5G

Wins for: Overall satisfaction and price

T-Mobile Home Internet 5G scores the highest overall satisfaction score in the northeast — earning a 4.40 out of 5. Verizon Fios comes as a close contender with a 4.19. CNET readers also give T-Mobile’s 5G home internet 4.60 out of 5. T-Mobile still has solid customer satisfaction scores (4.20), with many readers noting no noticeable difference in speed during peak hours and no unexpected price hikes.

Midwest: Quantum

Wins for: Overall satisfaction, reliability and speed

J. Hazelwood/CNET

Quantum Fiber wins among Midwest ISPs with a satisfaction score of 4.67 out of 5. Quantum has a flawless 5 out of 5 for reliability. CNET readers say the connection rarely drops — only a few times a year and they don’t experience speed lags during peak hours, which earns Quantum another 5 out of 5 score for speed.

Quantum Fiber was acquired by AT&T earlier this year. Even though customers still see Quantum on their bills, they now have some AT&T perks and benefits like bundling wireless discounts.

GFiber is a close second to Quantum with an overall satisfaction score of 4.64. It falls short on reliability, plan speed and price.

These top 4 ISP features matter most

Speed of plan

J. Hazelwood/CNET

Speed and price are the two most important factors when shopping for internet. “The more people and connected devices in your home, the more speed you’ll need,” Supan says.

Supan adds that even though ISPs generally highlight their download speeds, upload speeds are arguably just as important, especially if you work from home or play games online. CNET has an internet speed guide to help you determine whether you’re getting the right amount of speed for your home.

GFiber scores a 4.82 out of 5 for speed, and most users don’t have any speed issues during peak hours. Regionally, Ting scores the highest 5 out of 5 score for speed compared to other regional providers. Your home internet speed will vary depending on your needs and usage.

Price of plan

J. Hazelwood/CNET

Choosing an internet service provider at a reasonable price can be tough, as prices continue to rise due to improvements in internet technology and equipment. How much you can expect to pay depends on your plan’s speed, connection type and which providers are available in your area.

Supan says that pricing isn’t always straightforward because many ISPs, especially cable providers, will hike your price after a year or two. However, providers are required to list increases in a broadband label so you can see exactly how much your bill will increase and when, he says. It’s also worth noting that some providers charge a fee if you exceed your plan’s data cap. And your price may change if an introductory promotional period ends.

T-Mobile Home Internet scores highly with a 4.24 out of 5. It doesn’t have equipment fees, data caps or contracts, which makes its home internet service a more flexible and cost-effective option. Pricing starts at $50 per month, or $35 per month if you bundle with any T-Mobile voice line and 

Reliability

J. Hazelwood/CNET

Earlier this year, CNET found that 86% of US adults experience wonky Wi-Fi connections or drops. And 1 in 5 (19%) regularly have Wi-Fi problems. Internet reliability can depend on a number of factors that may or may not be your ISP’s fault.

Supan says some internet connection types can be more susceptible to drops or disconnections, but your ISP may still be able to help. You may be able to get your router replaced or switch your internet channel from 2.4 to 5GHz. Your connection reliability may also depend on where your router is placed in your home or on the type of router you’re using. Bigger homes can usually benefit from a mesh router system to extend your connection and reduce dead zones.

CNET readers highly recommend GFiber for reliability and give it a 4.70 out of 5. It offers mesh networking and Wi-Fi 7, the newest and fastest router generation, without data caps or throttling. Sonic scores even higher as a regional provider with 4.90 out of 5. Most don’t experience random connection drops, while others say only a few times a year. Sonic also offers a free Wi-Fi check when installing your internet to double-check your connection and Wi-Fi, which could speak to its high reliability score.

Customer service

J. Hazelwood

Trying to troubleshoot your internet troubles on your own can be tough. The right customer support can help — whether it’s extended live assistance hours, online assistance or text message notifications of outages. Some providers even let you schedule in-person appointments online and provide up-to-date articles.

When choosing a provider, review the support options to ensure you’re comfortable with the availability and resources in case you need them. CNET readers give GFiber high marks for its fast, helpful customer support.

GFiber scores a 4.72 out of 5 for CNET readers. It offers a customer support page and several ways to get help, including scheduling a call or an online chat. There’s also a list of FAQs covering topics such as billing, internet support and self-installation. EPB scores a flawless 5 out of 5 for excellent customer service ratings. It offers a comprehensive FAQ page with troubleshooting assistance, live online chat, short videos and phone assistance.

Did you agree with these findings? CNET’s People’s Picks is community-driven and helps us spread the word about the tech and services you love. Take our ongoing TV survey to tell us what you love about yours.

Correction, July 10: An earlier version of this story gave an incorrect starting price for T-Mobile Home Internet.

Tech.title: Hurry! You Only Have a Few Days Left to Play These Great Games on Xbox Game Pass
Tech.content:
September is off to a rough start for Xbox Game Pass. Microsoft announced on Tuesday, Sept. 1, that it’s removing Cyberpunk 2077, as well as other awesome games, from the service on Sept. 15. Microsoft also announced that Game Pass was getting a few games, like Call of Duty: Cold War, but an uninspiring CoD and a few roguelike deck builders don’t make up for the games the company is removing.

Microsoft pulling awesome games, like Cyberpunk 2077, definitely hurts the quality of the library. Years after its initial, rocky release, Cyberpunk in particular has evolved into a rich, complex game full of impressive environments, wild storylines and unforgettable allies. The level of customization also ensures that nearly every playstyle is accessible and fun. The Phantom Liberty expansion seals this as one of my favorite games of all time. I mean, Idris Elba’s performance alone made the expansion worth checking out.

Don’t take just my word for it. Former CNET Editor Daniel Van Boom wrote in 2020 that the game tells “a surprisingly focused and compelling story, and is set in a giant city that you’re constantly rewarded for exploring.” Tom Marks wrote for CNET’s sister site IGN in 2024 that Cyberpunk “kicks you into its beautiful and dazzlingly dense cityscape with few restrictions.”

Cyberpunk 2077 isn’t the only game getting yanked from the service on Sept. 15. Here are all the other games Microsoft is pulling soon, so you better hurry if you want to finish your campaigns.

“Yikes, that’s a lot of quality games leaving,” one Reddit user wrote. I couldn’t agree more. Even if you already played Cyberpunk, Dead Cells and Frostpunk 2 are great, while Mullet Madjack and Superliminal are chaotic good times. It makes me sad to see all these games get pulled from Xbox Game Pass.

Although Microsoft is adding a handful of games to the service in the coming weeks, Call of Duty: Black Ops Cold War, arguably the biggest title coming to the service, is boring compared to games being removed — let alone other CoD games. The end result is a lopsided equation where the quality of the games leaving the service is greater than the games being added to the service.

Still, maybe you’ll enjoy one of the new titles as much as I enjoyed any of the games getting pulled from Game Pass in September. Here are the games Microsoft is adding to the service and when you can play them.

The high-octane racing game Speedrunners 2: King of Speed comes to Game Pass Ultimate and PC Game Pass on Sept. 3.

Roguelike deck builder Dice a Million lands on Game Pass Premium on Sept. 4, joining Game Pass Ultimate and PC Game Pass.

Fight in East Berlin, Vietnam, Turkey, the Soviet Union and other locations in Call of Duty: Black Ops Cold War. Coming to Game Pass Ultimate, PC Game Pass and Game Pass Premium on Sept. 8.

Medieval roguelike deck builder The Royal Writ comes to Game Pass Ultimate, PC Game Pass and Game Pass Premium on Sept. 10.

The fighting series Virtua Fighter continues to evolve with Virtua Fighter 5 R.E.V.O. World Stage. That game comes to Game Pass Ultimate, PC Game Pass and Game Pass Premium on Sept. 10.

Gather supplies, build items and survive in RuneScape: Dragonwilds. That game arrives on Game Pass Ultimate, PC Game Pass and Game Pass Premium on Sept. 15.

Even if you’re not looking forward to these games, there’s hope on the horizon. Gears of War: E-Day is coming to Game Pass on Oct. 6, and that game will be here in all its chunky, gory bits before you know it.

For more on Xbox, here’s our Xbox Game Pass review and discover which Game Pass plan is right for you.

Tech.title: Oura’s Menopause Impact Scale Expands Out of the App and Into Women’s Health Care
Tech.content:
Despite 1.3 million women entering menopause each year, this stage in a woman’s life remains stigmatized and understudied. But a rise in femtech centered on menopause could help change that.

In June, Apple announced that its Health app now supports cycle tracking for both menopause — when a woman’s menstrual period permanently stops, and she can no longer get pregnant — and perimenopause, the transition to menopause. One month earlier, Oura released its Menopause Impact Scale, a self-reported questionnaire in its app that establishes how menopause symptoms impact a woman’s quality of life.

On Wednesday, Oura, maker of the Oura Ring, announced in a press release that its MIS is expanding beyond the app and into women’s health care and tech. The first 10 partners include menopause-focused clinical care companies Alloy Health, Gennev, Wisp and Pomelo; women’s health care companies Maven, Tia and Xella; and hormone and biomarker tracking companies Oova, Mira and Hertility.

“By integrating the MIS into how our partners work with patients, we’re giving women a measurement that travels with them and gives every provider they see the same starting point,” said Dorothy Kilroy, Oura’s chief commercial officer, in the press release.

How the MIS works

Developed by Oura’s own science and clinical teams, the company explains on its website that the MIS differs from current menopause assessment tools, which were created decades ago and measure only symptom frequency and severity. Instead, the MIS has Oura app users reflect on 22 symptoms associated with perimenopause and postmenopause across seven domains: sleep maintenance, cognitive functions, body image, hot flashes, sexual function and vaginal symptoms, musculoskeletal pain and urinary tract symptoms.

Both the total and domain scores can be exported as a PDF, so users can share this information with a doctor. Oura

For each symptom, a user is asked about how much it has affected their quality of life over the past two weeks. They can select: none, a little, moderately, quite a bit or extremely.

A mean score is calculated for each of the seven domains, ranging from 0 to 4, and the sum of these scores yields a total impact score from 0 to 28: 0 to 7 means minimal impact, 7 to 14 means mild impact, 14 to 20 means moderate impact and 21 to 28 means high impact.

Once the first assessment is complete, a reminder is sent 30 days later for reassessment and to monitor symptom trends over time.

According to the press release, over 600,000 Oura members have taken the MIS, and 35% of the members who have completed it once complete it at least one additional time.

Note that just like the Oura Ring and the Oura app’s other features, this questionnaire is not for diagnosis or treatment of medical conditions. A doctor is still required for that.

When will the MIS partner integrations occur?

Starting Wednesday, Oura members can integrate their MIS results with Alloy Health, Oova, Xella, Pomelo and Wisp.

Although there’s no specific release date, Maven, Mira, Hertility, Gennev and Tia integrations will be available later this year.

How much does Oura cost?

To access the MIS, you need both an Oura Ring and an Oura subscription. The Oura Ring 5 starts at $399, and the membership is $6 per month, totaling $72 per year.

The transition to menopause typically lasts between seven and 14 years, adding up to an additional $504 to $1,008 if someone wants to use the MIS repeatedly and, most importantly, as intended to keep track of their symptom trends.

Oura and privacy

In its privacy policy, Oura states that it doesn’t sell or rent members’ personal information. Members control third-party integrations and can disconnect them at any time.

Following an Electronic Frontier Foundation report in July about how most smart fitness devices lack essential data protection, Oura committed to issuing transparency reports in the future.

However, you should always exercise caution before sharing your information — especially health data — with any company.

What this means for women’s health

As femtech expands and more companies create technology that brings women’s health to the forefront, the stigma surrounding topics such as menopause could decrease, expanding into doctors’ offices as medical professionals start to take women’s symptoms seriously.

At the same time, this also means more companies will attempt to capitalize on the trend or, as a 2022 New York Times article called it, the “menopause gold rush.” We’ve already seen devices costing hundreds of dollars that are marketed toward women experiencing menopause in the name of hot flash relief.

With the rise of menopause-focused femtech, there are both benefits and drawbacks. Hopefully, the former will outweigh the latter, making it easier for women to have conversations about what they’re experiencing in their bodies — especially where it may matter most: in doctors’ offices.

Tech.title: The Cheap Kitchen Tool I Bring to Every Rental House or Airbnb
Tech.content:
You don’t need chef training to be picky about the tools you use in the kitchen. That goes doubly for when you might be called to someone else’s kitchen, whether that’s a family holiday situation or a rental property. If you’re cooking for the group — by coercion or self-nomination — you have every right to want to use whatever tools and gadgets make you most confident about the outcome. Especially when feeding a crowd.

I’m known to travel with cooking supplies and have even taken my cake pans across the Atlantic. In my defense, I was A) making a multi-tiered birthday cake and B) making it for my future siblings-in-law, whom I was meeting for the first time. My then-boyfriend, now-husband, is a great cook, it must be said, but cake wasn’t a regular part of his repertoire, and I didn’t want to take my chances with whatever might have been lurking in the darkest corners of his kitchen cabinets.

I used to travel to summer beach rentals with all manner of basic tools: tongs, a whisk, a rubber spatula, you name it, plus a fleet of knives, a good bottle of olive oil and bagged-up samples of my entire spice rack.

After a couple of years, I realized that most beach rentals, at least on the East Coast, were pretty well-equipped, and I was happier not having to schlep my entire kitchen to feel empowered to make dinner. I might stash a chef’s knife, just in case, but more often than not, even that would stay tucked in my bag.

Kitchen gear at a rental house is always hit-or-miss. Connect Images/Getty

There is only one tool, however, whose utility is so singular that it can’t be substituted, that, in my experience, is the key between a good dinner and a great dinner (and dessert) and that, surprisingly, you can’t always reliably find in other people’s kitchens.

My Microplane, myself

The Microplane is an essential tool I can’t count on finding in the drawers of an Airbnb. Pamela Vachon/CNET

Yes, it’s a Microplane. If you’re now puzzling over how a handheld zester of all things is that important a tool, well, some of you have never enjoyed scraped-together key lime pie for breakfast at the beach, and it shows.

But seriously. There is no other tool that does what a Microplane does to the same degree. Using a paring knife to gingerly cut the rind off citrus fruits without taking the pith with you and then mincing that up? I’ve done it. Hard pass.

A box grater is not likely to do the trick. Pamela Vachon/CNET

Don’t start with me about some cheap grocery store zester that manages to be both ergonomically overcomplicated and entirely ineffective. A box grater that you would typically use for cheese or carrots that has that one plane dedicated for zesting? Have you tried it lately? (Actually, has anyone ever? It just looks like a recipe for pulpy zest and bloody knuckles.)

Microplane Zester $18 on Amazon

Why the zester is an essential kitchen tool

Maybe your dubiousness isn’t so much the quality of the tool itself, but why any kind of zester is that critical? To which I challenge you: the next time you make salad dressing or pasta, enchiladas or pad thai, or anything at all that calls for citrus juice, add a hit of zest and see what that does to the outcome. Citrus zest adds several times the flavor, minus the sharp acidity. In a word, it adds vibrancy to whatever you’re doing, without the pucker. It’s a wow factor with the simplest execution. Not to mention: key lime pie for breakfast.

A hit of zest is like fairy dust for food. Pamela Vachon/CNET

And the economics are inarguable. Even in today’s economy, a lemon or lime can only set you back so far, but it contributes so much. And the Microplane itself? Is all of about $18.

Here I am waxing all poetic about citrus, but let’s also talk about two other cooking champions whose processing is made infinitely easier by a Microplane. Garlic and ginger — also cheap yet dynamic ingredients. A garlic press is a fine thing, but if yours is as difficult to clean after use as most I’ve owned have been, ditch it. The microplane can do that work for you, and basically rinses clean afterward.

A zester will inspire you to grate cheese over, well, everything. Pamela Vachon/CNET

Or if you’ve been buying pre-shredded Parm or another hard cheese, here’s another taste test challenge for you. It’s so quick to just grab a hunk and shave directly into or onto whatever you’re making or eating, with the added bonus of leaving out the additional starches that act as anti-clumping agents in the pre-shredded stuff. I could also make a point here about freshly grated nutmeg, but that would be extra. Suffice to say, I never make béchamel without it.

Microplanes of a different color

My go-to zester comes in more than a dozen colors.

If you’re convinced, I am partial to the Microplane brand here, whose handles are especially comfortable and which includes a protective sleeve for storage. Incidentally, you can also get a Microplane in over a dozen colors, and they are made in the US, if buying locally is a compelling argument.

If you’re already a Microplane evangelist and have made it this far, here’s an invitation to maybe upgrade yours. They don’t last forever, as the blades will dull over time. I recently switched out my 15-year-old model, and it has brought new life to my kitchen.

Pamela Vachon/CNET

For argument’s sake, I also checked out one of Amazon’s best-selling and least expensive models, the MasterChef version, which retails for only $10. It’s a little more generous in width, and its protective cover is admittedly a little easier to maneuver. Functionally, it works just like the Microplane, but is made in China for those keeping score.
